Stage 3 shifts the designer's frame from what they want to accomplish to who the learners are and what they need, individually and collectively, to reach the Stage 1 results and perform the Stage 2 tasks.
A design must be user-friendly as well as intellectually defensible: like software design, it must keep the actual users maximally engaged and productive.

The Stage 3 designer must resist falling back on comfortable familiar techniques and instead ask which instructional approaches, resources, and experiences the desired results and targeted performances actually require.

Stage 3 plans learning activities, of which direct instruction is only one; every proposed activity, teaching included, must be tested against the particulars of Stages 1 and 2 regardless of the teacher's strengths or preferred style.

Because learners will predictably misunderstand key ideas and make performance errors — not necessarily signs of poor teaching or learning — the design must ensure both teachers and learners get the feedback needed to rethink, revise, and refine.
Building in feedback and the opportunity to use it is a vital part of a good learning plan, as it is on the field, on stage, or in the studio.

A good learning plan must be both engaging and effective: engaging means learners find it thought-provoking and are pulled into worthy intellectual effort centred on big ideas, not merely that they enjoy it.

Effective means the design pays off in substantive, value-added learning: learners become more competent at worthy work, surpass usual expectations, and know they have achieved something of intellectual substance.

Teachers report that learners are most engaged when the work is hands-on, involves mysteries or problems, provides variety, allows personalization, balances cooperation and competition, is built on a real-world challenge, uses simulated challenges such as case studies and mock trials, and involves real audiences or authentic accountability.

Teachers report that learning is most effective when work is focused on clear worthy goals, students understand its purpose and rationale, models and exemplars are provided, clear public criteria let students monitor their own progress, fear is limited and risk-taking is rewarded, ideas are made concrete through links beyond the classroom, and there are many opportunities to self-assess and self-adjust on feedback.

Engagement and effectiveness overlap substantially: genuine application to meaningful real-world problems, hands-on opportunities to do the subject, and helpful feedback along the way each enhance both.

The WHERETO elements are the Stage 3 design filter: Where is it going, Hook the students, Explore and equip, Rethink and revise, Exhibit and evaluate, Tailor to student needs and interests, Organize for maximum engagement and effectiveness.
The Stage 2 design filters are that evidence be focused on big ideas and core challenges, valid, reliable, and sufficient.

Working from a desired understanding through the apply and explain facets produces paired evidence: a performance that applies the idea, plus an explanation, letter, or brochure in which the student justifies why the analysis holds.

Educators across levels and subjects consistently name the same features of the best learning designs: clear performance goals from a genuine challenge, a hands-on approach with far less front-loaded teaching than typical, focus on important questions and problems, obvious real-world application, a powerful feedback system with room to learn from trial and error, personalization, clear models and modeling, time for focused reflection, variety, a safe environment for risk, a coaching teacher role, and a big picture kept visible throughout.
Design criteria generated by the participants themselves are more credible and acceptable as a basis for making the traditionally private work of design public and subject to scrutiny.

WHERETO names the Stage 3 design elements: ensure students understand WHERE the unit is headed and why; HOOK and hold attention; EQUIP students with the experiences, tools, and know-how to meet the performance goals; provide opportunities to RETHINK, reflect, and revise; build in chances to EVALUATE progress and self-assess; TAILOR to individual talents, interests, styles, and needs; and ORGANIZE for deep understanding rather than superficial coverage.

WHERETO is an analytic tool for checking the elements of a design, not a recipe or prescribed sequence for constructing it — just as Bloom's Taxonomy judges cognitive difficulty rather than dictating teaching order.
Design work can emerge along many different paths and sequences, as when a teacher introduces a unit with the final task done in preliminary form such as a written draft.

Clear goals is the single most frequently cited characteristic of good design, and it requires making the goals clear to students — demystifying the big ideas, essential questions, desired performances, and evaluative criteria — not merely clarifying the teacher's own targets.
Instructors must supply a rationale for the desired learnings — identifying what is most important, what is not, and why it is worth learning.

Students do not need to know much about what the teaching will be, but they must understand what the learning eventually requires them to do; knowing the topic, the readings, activity directions, and that a test is coming does not suffice to focus attention and guide effort.

As early as possible in a unit, students should know the key questions and the performance specifics — tasks, tests, assignments, evaluative criteria, and performance standards — that they must meet by the end.

A design meets the W standard only if students can answer, with specificity, what they must understand and what that understanding looks like, what their final obligations are, what resources support them, how today's task serves the overarching obligation, how to allot their time and set priorities, and how their work will be judged and improved.

However abstract the key ideas, the design must transform them into intelligible practical tasks and criteria the student can grasp as soon as possible, so the work is purposeful from the student's point of view.

Opening a literature unit with the culminating performance challenge, its rubric, and a framing question gives students a purpose and context for their reading from day one, in contrast to distributing the book with a reading syllabus and grading requirements.

A recurring reading-response journal asking what was most important and what remains the most important unanswered question both supplies the teacher with comprehension evidence and trains students in the strategies of effective readers.

Closing a unit by asking students what changed in their view over time, what their own misunderstandings were, and how they would teach the material for understanding turns the unit's end into self-knowledge evidence.
Telling students the essential questions from day one, and that those questions frame the key assessments, lets them study, research, take notes, and ask questions with far greater clarity and focus.

The W element also asks where the learners are coming from — their prior knowledge, interests, learning styles, talents, and possible misconceptions — which makes diagnostic assessment early in the learning plan essential.

K-W-L gives an immediate read on a group's prior knowledge and surfaces potential misconceptions, while the Want-to-learn column reveals interest areas and can yield student-generated essential questions.
A nongraded pretest paired with a matched post-assessment yields invaluable evidence about growth in understanding, particularly when the items target key misconceptions.
condition: particularly when the questions target key misconceptions

statement: Achieving complex performance goals requires planned adjustment in light of goals, feedback, and predictable problems; a plan that is impervious to feedback is not a virtue.
Teachers can never achieve excellent results without improving their diagnostic skill and adaptive planning; responsiveness to learner data is not a nicety practised by caring teachers.
Teachers must leave room in the syllabus for adjustments based on gathered feedback; such built-in flexibility is a key aspect of effective instructional design.
The design goal is neither to pander to students' likes nor to make them fear bad results, but to tap intrinsic motivation more effectively.
The best way to create interest in a subject is to render it worth knowing — making the knowledge gained usable in one's thinking beyond the situation in which it was learned.

Schoolwork is often needlessly dull — mind-numbing skill worksheets and excessive passive listening divorced from interesting problems and worthy performance challenges — and reaching higher intellectual standards requires improving teachers' ability to provoke thought, curiosity, and drive.
Stage 1 questions should be framed as the field would frame them for the designer, then edited and adapted into learner-facing versions when the student materials are built.
Simply posting an essential question at the start of a unit may generate no interest, because students may not yet know or care enough about the issues to see its value.
An essential question that fails to resonate should be rewritten in the students' own idiom, and student suggestions are a legitimate source for that revision.

Working with a topic can reveal that the standard's real big ideas differ from the teacher's original question, in which case the questions and unit design are revised and the original question is retained as a hook.
The essential question can be introduced immediately or engineered to arise later and inductively, after focused problem solving, instruction, or other learning activity.

Effective hooks include puzzles, real-world problems, role-plays exploring an issue from different perspectives, far-out theories, paradoxes, incongruities, anomalies, and mysteries whose answers raise essential questions.
A multiyear examination of Harvard undergraduate education found that the most engaging and effective courses were organized around controversies or opposing arguments.
An element of mystery is central to awakening students' powers of inquiry and to teaching them that their job is to inquire into what is learned.

Lecturers commonly err by front-loading too much information before an application task or essential question has created the need for it in students' minds; technology now allows lectures to be delivered just in time so class hours go to facilitated inquiry and coaching.
Seeding a research collection with a few false and disreputable sources forces students to be skeptical and cross-check their references.
A course can be structured so that direct instruction is supplied only on demand — a lecture provided only when a student team asks for it — with the performance challenge driving the sequence.
The hook should be intrinsic rather than extrinsic: motivation increases when the work is of obvious value, has intrinsic interest, and provides transfer.

Asked what they learned, students most commonly list a fact or topic, with responses implying acquired intellectual power noticeably absent — except in the arts, physical education, vocational education, and courses outside the mainstream, where students shift toward naming an acquired ability.

A large multi-institution survey of college engagement found that courses emphasizing application, judgments about the value of information and arguments, and synthesis into complex interpretations are highly related to educational and personal gains, as are perceived quality of faculty relationships and the frequency of prompt feedback.

Foreign-language courses draw strong student ratings because instructors require every student to contribute regularly, encourage small-group work outside class, demand regular written assignments, and give constant feedback that enables repeated midcourse corrections.

Students are enthusiastic when classes are structured to maximize personal engagement and collegial interaction, and the most effective and engaging designs involve challenging, meaningful applications of learning.
The design challenge for a hook is to point toward what is essential, not merely to provide work that is entertaining.
A well-chosen puzzling artifact lets important questions and researchable issues emerge naturally and lets misconceptions be elicited and addressed through deliberate design.
Instant immersion in a question, problem, or story that requires the student's wits rather than school knowledge piques intellectual interest, as in problem-based learning and the case method.

Five conditions pique intellectual interest: instant immersion in a wits-demanding challenge, thought provocations such as anomalies and counterintuitive ideas, experiential shocks, personal connection to the topic, and a deliberate shift to differing points of view.
Thought provocations work by making the strange familiar and the familiar strange, appealing at gut level rather than through argument.
Students become more engaged when given opportunities to make a personal connection to the topic, and a personal-history inquiry can open onto the universal themes the unit is about.
A deliberate shift of perspective nudges students out of their comfort zone and stimulates wonderment and deeper thinking.
Teachers, especially at high school and college level, often fail to consider deficiencies in students' prior experience and then wrongly conclude that what students need is more knowledge.
Understanding requires an iterative mix of well-designed experiences, reflection on those experiences, and targeted instruction in light of the experiences and goals.

A big idea is a useless abstraction without a rich experience base in which the idea clarifies the experience — the common core of language immersion, hands-on materials, the practicum, and the case method.

A sustained simulation in which students live the conditions they are studying — building their own furniture, forming a cooperative, growing and processing their own materials — brings curricular abstractions to life through the empathy facet.
Equipping means enabling the learner to eventually perform with understanding and increasing autonomy, which is very different from preparing them for a chapter or state test of discrete items.

In the equipping phase designers must ask which knowledge, skill, and habits of mind are prerequisites for the final performance, and which instructional activities will deepen understanding of the key ideas.

Instructors routinely complain that students cannot transfer, yet on examination they have planned no coaching in how to transfer knowledge to varied situations — defining as a learner deficit what is actually a teaching need.

Complaints that students read too literally usually trace to two design flaws: assignments rarely involve genuinely ambiguous readings, and no instruction was designed to help students judge, absent obvious clues, what kind of reading requires what kind of response.
A unit's learning events can be explicitly tagged with the WHERETO elements they serve, which makes visible whether each element is actually covered by the plan.

An explicit inference organizer that asks students to add up given facts and state the big idea helps learners construct meaning inductively and hands them a cognitive tool transferable across subjects.
Using the same organizer for teacher planning and for student work produces the transparency all designers should seek.
Good organizers scaffold by providing tools for mental processes the learner must internalize, so that when no scaffolding is supplied the learner has a repertoire of moves to employ.

Scaffolded instruction follows a fading sequence: the teacher shows her own completed example, provides partial examples, models use with a think-aloud, guides practice with feedback, and then shifts students to independent application in more sophisticated uses.
The goal of a routine is that repeated use makes the process internal, so that the learner no longer needs the physical organizer as a prompt.
Performing autonomously with the scaffolds and cues removed is the essence of transfer, and learners are rarely adequately equipped for it.
Students must be equipped and assessed for exactly the situations where the conclusion is not obvious, the issues are murky, and it is ambiguous which knowledge and skill are required.
A linear march through content is a mistake when overarching questions and recurring tasks anchor the curriculum, because students cannot master complex ideas encountered only once.

A unit should run iteratively rather than linearly, with learners explicitly told that current lessons oblige them to revisit and amend earlier conclusions, and with the work looping back to the ideas it started from.

Rethinking can be engineered by having students state an initial theory, then confronting them with a case that the theory cannot accommodate, then with conflicting maxims that force a third revision.

Separating observations into facts, near-facts, knowledge claims, and a final interpretation — colour-coded and physically arranged — makes the inductive method itself visible and criticizable by classmates.
Withholding an artifact's established name while students interpret it prevents that label from influencing their interpretation.

Having students write a definition at the unit's start and a more sophisticated one at its end, plus a journal entry on the strengths and weaknesses of the method used, makes the growth in understanding and the method's limits both explicit.
Comparing one's own interpretation against the published expert interpretation of the same artifact is a rethinking move that keeps the expert account contestable rather than authoritative.

Built-in rethinking is a critical deliberate design element: students must be made to reconsider earlier understandings if they are to get beyond simplistic thinking and grasp the care and circumspection at the heart of understanding.

The most effective designs for in-depth understanding highlight the facets of perspective, empathy, and self-understanding, because constant shifts of perspective or required empathy demand rethinking and reflection.

In upper-level science, rethinking is commonly engineered by having students adopt one theoretical approach, then confronting them with new data and analysis suggesting a different approach is more fruitful.
Self-understanding is arguably the most important facet for lifelong learning, and it rests on honest self-assessment about what one does and does not understand and what remains to be done.
The most successful people self-monitor and self-adjust proactively while working, considering what is working and what might be done better as they do it.

Teaching of metacognitive skills should be integrated into the curriculum across subject areas, because metacognition often takes the form of an internal dialogue and many students remain unaware of its importance unless teachers make the processes explicit.

Metacognitive moments can be designed in cheaply: a mid-lesson and end-of-lesson pause on what has been concluded and what remains unresolved, a self-assessment attached to every formal product, a one-minute closing essay, and a postscript in which students state honestly what they do and do not understand.
Students must know they will not be penalized for admitting what they do not understand, or the honest postscript cannot work.
Training students to evaluate work the way exam readers are trained makes them more accurate as peer reviewers and self-assessors and more inclined to think like assessors in their own work.

Deliberately leaving the second part of a unit open, so students frame and pursue the inquiry from the questions and clues remaining at the end of part one, is a standard device of case-method and problem-based courses.
Knowing in advance that a reflective one-minute paper is coming focuses students' thinking throughout the class on what the big idea is and on what remains unclear to them.

Self-assessment can be treated as a graded enabling ability in its own right: early attempts at complex performance can be graded on the student's self-assessment and improvement plan rather than on the product itself.

Constant reflection must be designed in and expected of all learners, not just the naturally reflective ones, and it requires a transparent system of performance goals plus robust feedback against them or the reflection will not be focused or helpful.
The T element requires differentiating instruction to accommodate students' developmental needs, learning styles, prior knowledge, and interests while remaining true to the desired results.
condition: while remaining true to the desired results

statement: The Stage 1 desired results should remain consistent for all students, because the content standards and the understandings are learning targets for everyone.
Essential questions naturally accommodate diverse learners because of their open-ended nature: students with differing prior knowledge can all engage them, though some will answer in greater depth.
Diagnostic assessment identifies students with gaps in prior knowledge and skill, and those gaps are addressed by targeted small-group instruction rather than by lowering the goal.

Process can be differentiated by using resources at different reading levels, presenting information orally, visually, and in writing, and allowing options in how students work and how they communicate their learning.

When students are allowed a choice of product for an assessment, all the differing results must be evaluated against common criteria, which permits diversity without sacrificing valid assessment or scoring reliability.
condition: when students are given a choice of products as part of a Stage 2 assessment

statement: High-level content can be tailored for students with limited reading ability by supplying audio and video of key scenes, assistance with reading and writing tasks, and access to abridged and simplified versions of the text, without changing the essential questions.
Dictionary definitions of key terms are best introduced at the teachable moment the conversation creates rather than before the discussion that gives them meaning.
The O element requires putting the design elements into the sequence that actually produces the most engaging and effective experience, which is a decision many teachers do not think through.
The typical sequence of marching through content is rarely the best choice for engagement or understanding, especially when the sequence is dictated by the organization of the textbook.
A good sequence moves constantly back and forth between whole-part-whole and learning-doing-reflecting, returning to earlier provisional facts and techniques rather than only moving forward.

Better sequences immerse learners early in intriguing issues, problems, or experiences and postpone the teaching of definitions, rules, and theories until they are needed to make sense of that experience.

Opening a textbook with dozens of pages of definitions, rules, and drills — including technical hair-splitting presented out of context — is unacceptable pedagogy, because it confuses getting going with precision the learner has no use for yet.
When teaching for understanding, the Why? and So What? questions must be addressed early and often.
The belief that all basic facts and skills must be presented up front is not how effective and long-lasting learning works.
A whole-to-part practice flow — discrete skill, game-like, game conditions, game, then back to the discrete skill at higher demand — is a transferable sequencing model for developing any major skill.
Every drill, not only every practice session, should maximize the full set of target elements — in the soccer case fitness, set plays, technical skill, teamwork, and strategic thinking.

Analysing familiar time-tested drills against explicit design elements can reveal that some of them are badly ineffective, and giving participants that analytic frame supports transfer to designs never explicitly demonstrated.
Applying the WHERETO elements can lose sight of the whole, so the designer must ensure that big ideas frame the work and that transfer based on those ideas is accomplished.
Without care, a design can produce successful short-term learning of many discrete facts and skills while bypassing understandings and transfer tasks entirely.

The six facets, originally conceived as assessment indicators, also work as a Stage 3 generator: listing them and brainstorming activities against each surfaces the understanding-related work the unit needs.

Some facets seem more natural to certain content areas than others, yet teachers report that forcing an unnatural facet produces energizing and effective activities by pushing them outside habitual designs.
To design for explanation, ask what artifacts, data, behaviours, and events students must try to explain in order to practise generalizing and drawing sound inferences.
To design for perspective, arrange the materials, assignments, and discussions so students can both generate multiple points of view and critically evaluate them.

To design for empathy, ask what direct or simulated experiences would make students viscerally connect with others and find possible value in texts or ideas that initially strike them as unappealing or alien.
To design for self-knowledge, ask which experiences will help students self-assess what they do and do not understand and will evoke the habits of mind and biases they bring to the work.
Introducing the assessment tasks, evaluation criteria, and rubrics early in a unit makes the goals clearer and lets students see the purpose of the particulars they are learning.
Peer review in cooperative groups followed by time for revision before the final product is due builds the feedback loop into the culminating task rather than leaving it to the grade.

Differentiation can extend as well as support: the same task can be made more demanding for advanced students by shifting its audience or adding constraints, while non-writers demonstrate the same understanding orally.

Backward design deliberately delays the selection of teaching strategies to the last phase, because until the desired results, implied assessments, and required learning activities are specified, a discussion of teaching strategy is premature.
The right moves in teaching are made in light of what learning requires, so backward design forces the designer out of comfortable teaching habits.

Teaching should be judged by its results: the methods to use in teaching for understanding are any that work to cause understanding, with no ideological commitment to old-fashioned or modern, conventional or progressive.
Teaching on its own never causes learning: only successful attempts by the learner to make sense of the teaching cause learning.

To have taught well is to have caused understanding through words, activities, tools, guided reflection, the learner's efforts, and feedback — a complex interactive achievement, not a one-way set of skills.

Direct instruction — talking, professing, informing, telling — is only one aspect of causing learning, and the design of work for learning is as important as, and perhaps more important than, any articulate sharing of the teacher's knowledge.

Only experts or highly gifted thinkers can hear a teacher's words and do all the constructivist work in their heads without experiences, process guidance and tools, response-eliciting tasks, and feedback.
Uncoverage is not a type of teaching or a philosophy of education but the way to make any idea accessible and real, regardless of the instructional methods used.

Covering material focuses unwittingly on surface details, so from the learner's perspective everything appears of equal value — a bunch of facts with no hierarchy, memorable priority, or connected meaning.
A breathless march through sketchy isolated facts, activities, and skills cannot deliver in-depth understanding or even lasting recall, however good the intentions.

Justifying coverage by external standards, textbook obligations, or standardized testing does not survive scrutiny: teaching by mentioning cannot yield effective learning culminating in competent performance.

The hurried tour is the Expert Blind Spot at work: the false logic that if teachers discuss it learners get it, and the more discussed the more they get, confuses teaching with resultant learning — planting with yield, marketing with sales.
An understanding can never be covered if it is to be understood: it sets an end goal and demands the right experiences, discussion, and reflection.
An idea told to someone arrives as another given fact rather than as an idea; ideas are tested by acting upon them and serve to guide further observation and experiment.
To uncover is to reveal what would otherwise remain hidden, so the challenge of working with textbooks is to understand what they conceal, not only what they reveal.

Textbooks by design survey and summarize what is known and simplify expert knowledge to suit student levels and competing constituencies, which can hide from students and teachers the true nature of the subject and of scholarship.
Few textbooks help students understand the inquiries, arguments, and judgments behind the summaries they present.
The paradox of educating for understanding is that extensively researched texts can themselves become an impediment to more engaging and thought-provoking learning.

A national review of secondary education found that most textbooks present a highly simplified view of reality with practically no insight into the methods by which the information was gathered and the facts distilled.

A rigorous evaluation of popular middle-school science books rated all of them unsatisfactory as full of disconnected facts that neither educate nor motivate, and found no widely used high-school biology text worthy of a high rating.

That same study found most textbooks cover too many topics and develop none of them well, and include many classroom activities either irrelevant to the key ideas or unconnected to them for the student.

Research shows essentially all students, including the best, have predictable difficulties with many ideas covered in textbooks, yet most books fail to take those obstacles into account in their activities and questions.
Textbooks often obscure the most important ideas by focusing on technical terms and superfluous detail — exactly the material that translates easily into multiple-choice items.

Lavish textbook illustrations are rarely helpful because they are too abstract, needlessly complicated, or inadequately explained, and students receive little guidance in interpreting activity results in terms of the concepts to be learned.

The major problem in unit design is not the textbook itself but the assumption that the textbook is the course of study from which all design must flow; the text is a resource supporting the Stage 1 desired results.

Even the best textbook serves only some of the desired results, so teacher-designers must proactively supply the essential questions, assessments, and experiences the rest require, reading the text selectively and supplementing it.
The textbook is neither a map nor an itinerary but a guidebook in support of a purposeful journey.

Under uncoverage the text is one resource among many including primary sources, read in a sequence that serves the learning goals; under coverage the text is the syllabus, read in page order, with its summaries taken as givens to be learned rather than accounts to be analysed and critiqued.

Textbooks at their best organize information and supply exercises reinforcing key knowledge and skill; they typically do a poor job of framing work around ongoing questions and complex assessments based on big ideas and of offering different perspectives.
The designer's responsibility is to use the textbook for what it does well and compensate for what it does poorly.
Textbook simplification hides the questions, issues, history of ideas, and inquiries that led to what is now known — precisely the process the learner needs in order to come to an understanding.
Textbooks distort how understanding develops in both expert and novice by presenting only the cleaned-up residue; one cannot learn to do a subject by studying a simplified summation of findings.

Because big ideas are unobvious, counterintuitive, and abstract, understandings must be earned through carefully designed experiences that uncover the possible meanings of core content — and well-designed experience is the only way to make ideas real.
Teaching is best defined as the organization of learning for authentic results, which resolves the futile argument over whether the teacher should guide or direct — the truth is both.

A key antidote to the Expert Blind Spot is the recognition that adults lend children their own ideas rather than entering into the children's, which heaps up follies and errors even when the truths supplied are correct.

The teacher's enthusiasm cannot be transmitted by making the learner attentive to what moves the teacher, because the learner perceives the objects but not the relations linking them, lacking the necessary experience.

Ideas are not genuine ideas unless they are tools for searching out material to solve a problem; a concept becomes real rather than abstract only when it makes sense of experience or opens new intellectual powers.

A learner can repeat a statement until it is welded into memory without acquiring the idea; the idea is acquired only when the learner has first met confusing observed facts that the concept is then used to interpret.

The student needs experience not only with the key idea but with the phenomena that created the need for the idea, so as to see big ideas for what they are — mental models that solve problems, not facts.

Depth means getting below the surface of a topic — knowing how something works and how to diagnose and fix it, not merely how to operate it — whereas breadth expands a narrow topic to its connections, extensions, and larger implications.

Excessive and exclusive depth is no better than excessive coverage: digging the same hole deeper on a single idea is ineffective, and a good course of study needs helpful detail plus bridges to related topics and issues of meaning.

Uncoverage is vital rather than optional because all big ideas are counterintuitive and abstract, and no effective transfer via big ideas is possible unless the student is helped to uncover their meaning and interconnection.

Coverage actually makes learning harder: levelling content into verbal material for recall is more difficult for the learner than a telling experience plus a conceptual framework for making sense of it.
Teaching for understanding always requires something before teaching: designed and artfully facilitated experiences that raise the right questions and make the ideas seem real and worthwhile.
Teaching after a revealing experience is often more effective than teaching a good amount before any experience.

Teaching only from textbooks without active inquiry into their claims misleads students into believing knowledge is just there for the plucking rather than the result of trial and error, inquiry, and argument.
The text may be accepted where it usefully simplifies, but when it oversimplifies a big idea it must be questioned.
condition: when the text oversimplifies a big idea rather than usefully simplifying it

statement: The best teacher-designers know exactly what their students will gloss over and misunderstand in the text, and design lessons that deliberately require students to find the issues, gaps, and inconsistencies hidden in those accounts.
A textbook writing style suggesting that inquiry is over and the student's job is to apprehend what is known needlessly closes off thought.
A fruitful uncovering strategy is to scour the text for passing statements that can be reframed as essential questions for investigation across units and courses.

When a text asserts what a historical figure believed and felt with finality, the facets supply the interrogation: where is the evidence for this theory, what primary sources justify it, and how do the authors know.
A textbook can simplify an argument for younger readers without making a simplistic claim, leaving a genuinely debatable question open for students to research and argue.
Even a text that opens a question cannot do the job alone: the teacher must supply the research materials and direction the inquiry requires.
Treat the textbook as a platform to jump off from and return to in the course of inquiry, which naturally prompts consultation of other sources including other textbooks.
A foundational distinction can be buried as an unexplained aside hundreds of pages after the concept was introduced, leaving neither students nor most teachers able to appreciate its significance.

Students will never understand an axiomatic system until they see the assumptions as the needed underpinnings of the theorems one wanted to prove, and discover that other assumptions yield other systems of practical value.

Key assumptions in any field are not brilliantly intuited nor found whole; they come from inquiry over time, from a careful search for the logical grounds of the insights one holds and the proofs one wants to make.
Teaching for understanding means identifying the big ideas and revisiting them via problems of increasing sophistication as the work unfolds, whether or not the textbook is organized to do so.

The lesson that good assumptions have limits and that every simple starting point hides deeper issues transfers to all walks of life, and revisiting assumptions that first seemed adequate is what rethinking is for.
Presenting big ideas as obvious things to be apprehended rather than comprehended abets student misunderstandings and encourages students to keep them hidden.

A key teacher role is uncoverer of student misunderstandings and persistent performance errors through artful experiences and discussions, teaching students that such mistakes are unavoidable and not shameful but key episodes in gaining understanding.
At the heart of uncoverage is the designed learning of how to question the material: important claims must be tested, not just mentioned, if they are to be understood.

The danger of a textbook-based syllabus is that a single simplistic representation goes unchallenged, so students learn there is one official viewpoint to be taken in for recall with no need for proactive questioning.

Students ask whether they are on the right track because textbooks have presented the subject as a march of facts to a single settled outcome; after learning to keep their facts straight they must learn that experts disagree widely on how those facts are to be interpreted.

All teaching must simplify, but there is a fundamental difference between an appropriately simplified account and an overly simplistic, inquiry-ending one that hides the uncertainties, arguments, and subtleties central to understanding a subject.
An education for understanding treats the lurking and emergent questions as essential, not as a pleasant tangent to be dropped when time is short or reserved as work for gifted students.
Teaching comprises three distinct roles — didactic or direct instruction, constructivist facilitation, and coaching of performance — so teaching is not to be equated with direct instruction alone.
The person called teacher also plays three noncontact roles key to backward design: designer, evaluator of student work, and researcher into one's own effectiveness.
No blanket ratio among the three teaching roles can be prescribed without knowing the desired results and assessments; the mix depends on goals, learners, and situation.

Some goals call unambiguously for direct instruction — asking directions when lost — while others cannot be met by instruction at all, as thirty lectures on cooking without entering a kitchen would fail.

Discrete factual and procedural content is most efficiently learned through explicit teaching and reading followed by checks for understanding, while the unit's essential questions call for guided inquiry and facilitated discussion.
The ratio among the three roles changes across units and among teachers teaching the same unit, and some units may involve only two of the three.
Choose instructional approaches by what is needed for learning, not by what is comfortable for teaching; the right proportions are likely to be a ratio the teacher is not in the habit of using.

Each teaching preference has a characteristic failure mode: lecture-lovers overlecture, lecture-avoiders underinstruct, ambiguity-lovers leave discussion needlessly confusing, task-oriented teachers cut off fruitful inquiry, coaching-lovers overdrill and neglect transfer, and big-picture teachers underdevelop core skills.

Pedagogical self-understanding — the self-knowledge facet applied to the teacher — is required when planning, because teaching for understanding demands routine use of all three teaching types in ways that may challenge comfortable habits.

It is a misconception that teaching for understanding condemns lecturing and prescribes discovery learning; all coaches lecture, and even devotees of the Socratic seminar provide explicit instruction and feedback.
When lecturing is properly criticized it is usually because the goals call for more learner attempts to play with, test, and apply ideas than the lectures allow for.
If a unit's goal is primarily skill development then coaching is key, though facilitating understanding of the strategic big ideas remains necessary for using the skill wisely.
condition: when the unit goal is primarily skill development

statement: If the goal is understanding a counterintuitive idea, much facilitated inquiry of well-designed experiences is needed even though it feels like a loss of time, and lectures are then most useful after the experiences to solidify learning.
condition: when the goal is understanding a counterintuitive idea

statement: Excess teacher talk correlates with unclear goals: without an explicit performance goal to focus the learning, teachers tend to become excessively didactic and to overinstruct.
Good coaches teach in smaller and more timely doses than many classroom teachers because they stay focused on the bottom-line goal of enabling the learner to perform.

Distinguish just-in-time from just-in-case instruction: memory cannot hold much when key information is presented in large amounts before opportunities for meaningful use, so save extended telling for after learners have applied the learning.
We do not learn by doing unless we reflect on what we have done: it is the guided reflection on the meaning of the activity, not the activity itself, that causes the learning.

The teacher's job is not to explain the textbook but to use resources so learners can understand important ideas and use knowledge and skill in performance; making the textbook the course makes overlecturing more likely.
Letting models do the teaching works because comparing strong and weak models develops increasingly refined conceptual and procedural distinctions in the learner.

Use direct instruction and focused coaching for knowledge and skill that is discrete, unproblematic, and enabling, and reserve constructivist facilitation for ideas that are subtle, prone to misunderstanding, and in need of personal inquiry and verification.

The content dichotomy runs facts against concepts and principles, discrete knowledge against systemic connections, definitions against connotations, the literal against symbolism, the self-evident against the counterintuitive, discrete skills against strategy, and algorithms against heuristics.

It does not follow that learners should work only on discrete content for a long time before moving to the conceptual: deriving understandings inductively requires the grist of particular facts, and understanding facts requires seeing the problems that make them relevant.

Students need enough knowledge and skill to get going without being bored or overwhelmed, while simultaneously confronting the big-picture ideas that give the learning meaning — the two columns work as a double helix requiring cycles of each teaching type.

The discrete-content column represents old understandings so well internalized they have become facts, so advanced students can apprehend through direct instruction what costs the less experienced student great constructive labour to comprehend.

Teachers are long past being novices, so unless they are vigilant they lose empathy for the likelihood of misunderstanding; the profound danger is that we are most prone to covering content inappropriately when we lose empathy for the objective difficulty of new ideas.
A major mistake in teaching for understanding is not overreliance on a single approach but failure to consider the timing of each approach — when to instruct and when to let learn.

The lecturing question is not whether to lecture but when: when to answer versus question, when to advocate versus purvey equally plausible alternatives, when to state the purpose versus let it be inferred, and when to do the research versus have students do it.

Facilitating a discussion likewise poses timing decisions: when to frame the talk versus let students launch it, when to challenge an inappropriate answer versus let a student challenge it, when to correct a wrong statement of fact versus let it stand, and when to observe versus coparticipate.

An international comparative study found that U.S. teachers tend merely to present terms, rules, and tactics, whereas teachers in better-performing nations develop key ideas through problems and discussions, with the problems typically presented first and the direct instruction following.
Less telling can yield more and better learning when the assignments and assessments are well designed and the teaching approaches are judicious, well timed, and goal directed.
condition: when assignments and assessments are well designed and the teaching is judicious and well timed

statement: In many secondary and collegiate classrooms there is too much front-loaded direct instruction, not too little.

The case method, in which students derive meaning from specific cases with Socratic facilitation, has spread from business schools to medical schools, engineering programmes, and secondary problem-based learning courses.

Teaching for understanding requires aggressively assessing while teaching, uncovering learners' understandings and misunderstandings along the way rather than restricting assessment to culminating tasks and final exams.
Vigilance is needed because teachers are prone to believe correct answers indicate understanding while students want to seem as if they get it even when they do not.

That eight students get it and no further questions are asked does not mean the rest understand, and answering a simple question on cue does not mean a student can use that knowledge unprompted or recognize when it applies.

Informal checks for understanding are assessment techniques that are not used for grading: their purpose is timely feedback on current conceptions and misconceptions and the instructional adjustments those imply.
A two-sided index card asking students to state a big idea they understand and something they do not yet understand is a fast recurring check for understanding.
An anonymous question box, board, or e-mail address helps students who are uncomfortable admitting publicly that they do not understand.
Asking students to build a visual representation such as a web, concept map, flow chart, or timeline effectively reveals whether they understand the relationships among a topic's elements.

A misconception check presents students with a common predictable misconception and asks them to agree or disagree and explain, which surfaces the misconception directly rather than inferring it from errors.
Follow-up probes — why, how do you know, give your reasons, what do you mean by that, what data support your position, could you give an example — convert an answer into evidence of understanding.

Anonymous or semi-anonymous response systems work better than asking for a show of hands, because students do not want to answer against the person sitting next to them; low-tech coloured index cards serve the same purpose.
Even in large lecture courses, interspersed response questions let the instructor see the distribution of right and wrong answers in real time and slow down or backtrack accordingly.
Checks for understanding are as essential to teaching as any reading, lecture, or discussion, because they let both learner and teacher know what is not being understood in time to adjust.

Teaching is much more than informing: understanding occurs through the learner's repeated and increasingly successful attempts to learn, coupled with the teacher's feedback and guidance in addition to the initial instruction.

The doctrine that students should first learn passively and only afterwards apply knowledge is a psychological error: applications are part of the knowledge, and unapplied knowledge is knowledge shorn of its meaning.
Because understanding is wise performance rather than recall, teaching for understanding must be closer to coaching than to professing.

An education for application aims early at the desired performance even in simplified or scaffolded form, builds performance progressively, revisits the fundamentals repeatedly, and eventually removes the cues, prompts, and tools to see whether students can perform on their own.

The objection that students must learn all the basics before they can perform goes against common sense: no complex performance in music, drama, athletics, or the professions is mastered by front-loading knowledge out of context in a linear scope and sequence.
Part to whole and whole to part is how learners come to understand and use their knowledge, so the design moves back and forth between content and performance and between discrete skill and strategy.

Feedback from whole-performance results sends the performer back to targeted drill work to overcome misunderstandings, bad habits, or forgotten lessons, in a constant recycling among elements, chunks, and the whole.

In case-method professional education, instructors no longer cover all the laws of the field first; working authentic cases lets students see the importance of the basics in the context of meaningful application.
Case-method work is structured as repeating loops of challenge, model, practice, feedback, practice, performance, and feedback, with complexity increasing across loops.

Coaches revisit the basics with every new group no matter how expert a student is, and do not treat that reinforcement as time lost, because embedding review of the basics in work toward excellent performance yields better results.
Two kinds of learning by doing must both keep occurring: practising new ideas in simplified drill or exercise form, and applying those discrete moves in a more complex and fluid performance.
Direct instruction occurs while learners perform and after they perform, as a way of deriving understanding from the attempts to perform.
The logic of learning how to do things with content differs from the logic of transmitting the content, which has consequences for the kinds of teaching used and the sequence in which they are used.
Would-be performers profit little from lengthy up-front lectures; they need explicit instruction on a need-to-know basis so they see knowledge and skill as tools for accomplishing a specific task.

International comparative research shows that mathematics teachers in top-performing nations begin with challenging problems in order to develop mathematical understandings inductively, whole-part-whole.

Beginning a history course in a remote past unmoored from contemporary events, learner interests, overarching questions, and specific tasks makes students far less likely to engage in doing history or to grasp the big ideas that transfer to the present.

A course can be restructured to open and close on the same essential question with an authentic role for the student, moving backward and forward in time as needed — a sequence that is logical though not chronological — without sacrificing content.

Understanding aimed at performance requires an iterative curriculum focused on overarching questions and explicit tasks, with teaching approaches varied as the learners' need to master those questions and tasks dictates.

A characteristic teaching failure is over-teaching by restating the textbook in different words while under-coaching by withholding feedback against models and rubrics until after the student has presented.

Asking what the best use of the limited class time together is, for the teacher and for each student, is the governing question that reallocates time from giving information toward assessing and coaching.
Improvisation is not a substitute for planning: the purpose of planning is to achieve predictable results, and intelligent improvisation occurs on the foundation of a good blueprint.

The belief that good teaching comes through artful spontaneous interaction minimizes the importance of planning increasingly effective lessons and supports the folk belief that good teachers are born rather than made.
The template reflects a completed aligned design, but it does not follow that the best way to design is to fill in the boxes in the order they appear.
All design is a nonlinear process: the final product must obey the three-stage logic, but the design process unfolds unpredictably and differently for each designer and challenge.
The template is a format for self-assessing and sharing the final design, not a history of how the design work unfolded or a prescription for how work should proceed.

A designer may enter the process at any stage, including Stage 3, since it is often natural to begin with an existing unit, a key resource, or a planned assessment; what matters is ending with a coherent product.

Even when starting from a text that seems worthwhile on its face, the designer must self-consciously justify the choice by linking it to specific purposes and desired results — why it is being read and what big ideas and standards justify it.

It matters more to test ideas against the backward design logic and standards while playing with them than to treat design as a step-by-step process; filling the template box by box is likely to yield a poor design because it skips the revising and aligning a coherent plan requires.

The best educational designers do two tasks: creatively play with unit ideas regardless of where they fit on the template, and test those ideas before and during use with students so the goals are actually accomplished as concrete learning.

Six common entry points into the design process are content standards, desired real-world applications, a key resource or favourite activity, an important skill, a key assessment, and an existing unit.
Whichever entry point is used, the emerging design should be checked routinely against the UbD Design Standards to ensure quality.

Entering from content standards means grouping related standards, mining the key nouns for big ideas and the key verbs as a blueprint for performance assessments, deriving essential questions, then listing enabling activities and refining for alignment.

Entering from real-world application means clarifying what mastery of the content enables one to do, identifying the core challenges and authentic tasks, then determining the understandings, knowledge, and skill needed and the practice and feedback plan that develops them.

Entering from a favourite activity or key resource requires answering the why question first — what big ideas the resource helps students understand and which standards it serves — and then revising the assessments and activities accordingly.

Entering from a skill means asking what complex worthy performance the skill enables, locating the relevant standard and its implied assessments, identifying strategies for using the skill well, and surfacing the big ideas and essential questions that undergird it.

Entering from an external assessment means clarifying the goals the assessment exists to serve and the transferability it seeks, then inferring the big ideas needed to meet the standard and developing parallel performance tasks.

Entering from an existing unit means placing the current lessons and assessments in the template, checking alignment across the three stages, asking whether the lessons relate to the richest aspect of the goals, and revising to do justice to a clarified Stage 1.

A unit framed as topic-activities-assessments puts the activities literally at the centre, with no identified standards or learning goals, no big ideas or essential questions, and no valid evidence of important learning — only a grading scheme.
Student reflections that name only the enjoyable mechanics of activities are diagnostic evidence that an activity-centred unit produced no enduring understanding.
Simply placing an existing design into the template, without adding anything new, already makes the areas needing improvement visible.
Revision by backward design need not discard the popular activities: the culminating event can remain while being honed to better support the unit goals.

Framing a unit in the template can reveal a missing perspective — in one case the viewpoint of the displaced people whose land was settled — prompting a further revision the designers had not seen the need for.

A unit taught and assessed exclusively from the textbook can be greatly improved in coherence and authenticity by planning backward from state standards, adding understandings and essential questions, and supplementing the textbook assessments with performance tasks.
A revised unit uses K-W-L up front to assess prior knowledge and set learning goals, and reviews the scoring rubrics and product examples with students before they begin the performance tasks.
A performance task can be built to elicit the target understanding directly by asking students to correct a common present-day misunderstanding about the period they studied.
Adding nonfiction sources at varied reading levels is how a revised unit accommodates differing readers while keeping the same desired results.

Adding the displaced group's perspective to a settlement unit generates its own understandings, essential questions (whose story is it, who were the winners and losers, what happens when cultures collide), and a role-play performance task.
A textbook-only unit shows up in the template as a Stage 2 and Stage 3 filled with chapter-review problems, self-tests, and homework, with the Stage 1 boxes empty.

Redesign can keep exactly the same knowledge and skill as core content while embedding it in a more meaningful set of real-world issues, with the textbook problems retained but subordinated to the performance tasks.

A performance task in which the mathematically optimal answer is not the best practical solution makes the understanding that models must be adapted with judgment assessable rather than merely stated.
Using the template as a guide for self-assessment clarifies purposes, sharpens priorities, and makes them clear to learners, producing a more powerful and coherent approach with the same content.

No step-by-step recipe for unit design exists: unit design is more like graphic design or sculpture than following a cookbook, and each design must reflect the interests, talents, style, and resources of the designer.

Instructional design contains irreducible uncertainty and multiple interpretations; not every aspect of human thought and behaviour can be identified or articulated, and that is the nature of the design process.
Too much reliance on a recipe closes off the designer's responsiveness by fostering the false belief that a well-thought-out plan must work and that failure is the students' fault.
Eliminating all ambiguity from task analysis would over-proceduralize a complex set of decisions, since the design process depends largely on the reasoning ability of the designer.
Slavish devotion to recipes robs the practitioner of the experiential knowledge that builds trust in one's own judgment — the most valuable thing an expert can teach a novice.
Designers must get accustomed to a back-and-forth rhythm between creative brainstorming and careful critical testing of the emerging design against the design standards.

Seeking early and frequent feedback on the emerging design against the design standards is a key part of the process, and it concretely shows the teacher-designer why ongoing assessment is vital to performance success.
The tensions within instructional designs are inherent and inevitable, so the work is not merely demanding but inherently problematic, and every design requires weighing pros and cons.

Design dilemmas involve competing or conflicting elements — a big idea against limited time, a complex application against the unreliability of a single performance — and they are not solved but carefully negotiated.

The first standing dilemma is big ideas and transfer versus specific knowledge and skills: focusing on big ideas risks leaving students without essential know-how, while focusing on discrete information leaves little meaningful learning or ability to apply it.

Authentic application is difficult and time-consuming to implement and evaluate precisely, while traditional tests are easy to design and grade but often yield invalid results and unhelpful feedback about what learners understand.

Teacher control versus learner control is a standing dilemma: when it is the expert's job to frame the issues and guide the learning, and when it is wiser to let students pursue their own questions and reach their own understandings.

Direct versus constructivist approaches is a standing dilemma: when explicit teaching is more efficient, and when the messy personalized construction of meaning is required for understanding to occur.

The same direct-versus-constructivist dilemma arises in teacher training: when new teachers should be creative as designers, and when it is wiser to have them work from expert designs to avoid reinventing the wheel.

Depth versus breadth is a standing dilemma, including the question of when interdisciplinary work around a few big ideas is wise pedagogy and when it unwittingly produces superficial learning by attempting too much in too little time.

Comfort versus challenge is a standing dilemma: essential questions may provoke student irritation and confusion and complex tasks may frustrate easily defeated learners, yet a low-stress context is needed for students to take risks.

Uniform versus personalized work is a standing dilemma: how to hold appropriately different expectations of understanding without lowering standards or treating some students as second-class, and when differentiation becomes counterproductive.
Interesting and engaging are necessary but not sufficient criteria: the design must also address the goals and standards efficiently and effectively, making the work minds-on and not merely hands-on.

Simplified versus simplistic is a standing dilemma: making big ideas accessible without dumbing them down, and simplifying a complex subject without cutting off future inquiry or rendering the work vapid.

A well-crafted plan versus appropriate flexibility is a standing dilemma: goals are usually achieved only by deviating from the plan in response to feedback and teachable moments, yet the designer must avoid losing sight of the goals in response to every student reaction.
The individual unit versus larger goals is a standing dilemma: each unit must stand on its own as a logical design while honouring all local programme goals and content standards.
The general advice on design dilemmas is to aggressively seek feedback while working: try something, see how it works, and adjust against both the desired results and the design standards.

A major study of college teaching found that faculty and students both named the same two highest-value changes: enhancing students' awareness of the big picture rather than only topic details, and regular helpful student feedback enabling midcourse corrections.
Ongoing design feedback should be frequent, timely, helpful, and nonintrusive, and must not be confused with official course evaluations.

Asking what worked and what did not work — rather than what students liked — yields much more useful feedback, because it signals there is nothing personal in the anonymous response and makes students less fearful and more honest.

A weekly feedback form can ask students to confirm directly whether the work focused on big ideas rather than unconnected facts, whether the goals and quality standards were clear, whether they had enough freedom in how to reach them, and whether the assessment was a fair test of their learning.
Few teachers voluntarily solicit ongoing feedback from students, peers, supervisors, or outside experts, and that fear is counterproductive to becoming more effective.
A healthy and effective learning organization makes collegial collaboration on design, with feedback against design standards, a regular part of the job, with training and time allocated to it.

Design work is not finished until the particular students are factored in: a diagnostic preassessment of their needs, abilities, and interests is crucial, and the Tailor element cannot be honoured without last-minute adjustments based on who the learners are.
The design must also be adjusted mid-course in light of misunderstandings, unanticipated rough spots, and serendipitous opportunities that arise.
Planning does not reduce spontaneity: keeping clear goals and core performances sharply in focus heightens attentiveness to purposeful teachable moments.
Even the best teachers can get so wrapped up in an excellent plan that they dismiss comments threatening its flow, losing sight of the true goal of causing learning rather than teaching.
Rationalizing a propensity to wing it as being student-centred risks making the teacher a passive victim of whatever students happen to raise — understanding by good fortune rather than by design.
The appropriate teachable moment is more visible and comes more frequently to the teacher-designer who has carefully thought through the goals and how to achieve them.

A criterion for any subject taught is whether, fully developed, it is worth an adult's knowing and whether having known it as a child makes a person a better adult; if the answer is negative or ambiguous the material is cluttering the curriculum.
The unit is the right focus for design work: not so small that it produces isolated lessons and discrete learnings, and not so large that it becomes too broad to guide day-to-day teaching.

Course syllabi and programme frameworks should be designed backward with the same elements as the unit — essential questions, enduring understandings, key performance tasks, and rubrics — so that these overarching elements serve as a blueprint for all units and the connections between them.

How big a big idea should be cannot be answered apart from course and programme goals: the most conceptually general ideas should anchor whole courses and programmes, because no single unit could do justice to them.

Agreeing at district, department, or grade-level on the core ideas and assessment tasks significantly lightens the unit designer's load and removes the incoherence that results from units designed in isolation.

Because essential questions are overarching and recursive by nature and can be properly addressed only across many units or years, they are ideally suited to serve as the backbone of courses and programmes into which individual units fit.
A course-level plan pairs a set of course understandings with matched course essential questions and a list of course skills, so that each unit is constructed under that comprehensive umbrella.

Course-level skills can themselves be stated as analytic capabilities — interpreting primary and secondary sources, connecting past to present, distinguishing relevant from irrelevant information, separating fact from opinion, and defending positions in writing and debate — rather than as content coverage.
Scholars' own framing questions about a domain can be adopted directly as the essential questions of a course, with each unit addressing them through its specifics.

A whole course can be framed by as few as three or four questions declared to govern everything done in it, including the meta-question of how practitioners in the field construct and evaluate their accounts.
Typical curriculum frameworks emphasize lists of discrete content knowledge and skills, which subtly encourages teachers to cover things mechanistically and didactically.
Framing a curriculum around essential questions rather than content makes connective, thought-provoking, recurring inquiry central to the learning experience.

Essential questions often jump curricular boundaries even when cross-disciplinary design is not the aim, which is a virtue of framing curriculum around questions because it makes fruitful connections more likely.

A whole school can build its curriculum around a small set of questions cast as habits of mind — whose viewpoint is this, how do we know and how reliable is the evidence, how are things connected causally, what is new and what is old, and so what — asked in every class and subject.
An education can be built on cross-disciplinary core commonalities paired with companion essential questions explored across all the elementary and middle grades.

An international programme can require every unit to address at least one of a fixed set of generic inquiry questions — what is it like, how does it work, why is it the way it is, how is it changing, how is it connected, what are the points of view, what is our responsibility, and how do we know.

Frameworks built around big ideas and essential questions are not restricted to the humanities: an entire physical education curriculum can be framed with big ideas, enduring understandings, essential questions, and standards.

In a physical education framework each big idea pairs an enduring understanding with a probing question — fitness is a process not a product with what a fit person looks like, and technique with when will you get it and what you do until then.

Robust evidence of achievement requires more than a once-a-year state test, so the local assessment plan must include more high-quality application-focused performance tasks constructed around the six facets.
Most curriculum frameworks ignore or give short shrift to assessments, even though specifying a curriculum requires clarity about the performance targets that embody its goals.
A macro curriculum can be framed via the assessments by asking which key performance types or genres a student should have to master.

A district-wide set of quarterly writing assessments by genre, judged by common rubrics with one common prompt per genre per grade, brought greater coherence to the instructional programme and improved student performance.

A genre-by-grade writing matrix operationalizes progression by naming the specific task type at each level, from research report and position paper through critical lens essay and response to literary criticism.

Having faculty serve dual roles — teaching their subject and sitting on committees that design the assessments for cross-cutting competencies — makes each instructor think about their role in relation to the overall mission and keeps the competencies from falling through the cracks of subject-focused course design.
Treating the essential questions as the general specifications for any particular assessment is a practical strategy for drafting the right higher-order performance tasks.

Students of any age can be told up front and throughout that the course's questions will be considered from various points of view and addressed in various projects, so they should keep them constantly in mind.

When essential questions seem too conceptual for a skill-focused course, identify instead the questions or problems tied to key performance challenges that require the intelligent use of those skills.
condition: when the course is focused primarily on skills

statement: Two questions can frame an entire mathematics curriculum provided students are also given a carefully designed set of problems that suit those questions and require the desired skills.
condition: provided a matching set of problems is supplied alongside the questions

statement: The same recurring problem, based on the same messy data set, can be posed each year, or one basic problem can support answers across several levels of sophistication — which differentiates among students far better than items based on discrete facts and skills.

Framing courses through strategy-flexible assessment tasks is especially helpful for content-packed courses such as history, where each task casts the student in a real professional role with a real audience and product.
Developing core performance tasks naturally leads to selecting or designing the companion scoring rubrics.

A shared bank of roughly thirty criterion rubrics used consistently across a district by teachers and students, amended with task-specific indicators while the general framework remains intact, gives students a consistent message about the nature of quality work.
Once UbD thinking is internalized it becomes very difficult to go back to creating disconnected activities or covering facts without a broader context.
A single criterion rubric can carry both formal descriptors for the teacher and learner-facing bullets that translate each score point into the terms of the specific task and age group.

A clarity rubric distinguishes levels by whether mechanical errors interfere with fluency and whether the intended meaning can be discerned, not by error count alone: minor errors that do not impede meaning sit at the top levels.
Low levels of a clarity rubric attribute the failure to an insufficiently thought-through meaning as well as to imprecise language, treating unclear communication as partly a thinking problem.
For any rubric to be useful for self-assessment, self-adjustment, and understanding the teacher's final judgment, students need to see examples of work at each score point.
Longitudinal rubrics that describe increasing levels of attainment across many years are helpful for charting progress over time and are used in national standards-based curricula.

A developmental inquiry rubric marks progression by growing epistemic sophistication: from describing simple observed features, to recognizing why data must be collected, to recognizing that scientific ideas rest on evidence, to explaining how interpretation of evidence leads to new accepted ideas.

Higher levels of a developmental inquiry rubric require judging one's own evidence: identifying observations that do not fit the main pattern, deciding when to repeat measurements for reliability, and considering whether the data collected are sufficient for the conclusions drawn.

The topmost levels of a developmental inquiry rubric require awareness of the degree of uncertainty and of a range of alternative views, and the ability to explain how evidence modified accepted theories.
The six-facet rubric can serve as a framework for building other developmental rubrics, alongside the existing developmental proficiency guidelines in foreign language and literacy.

An overarching framework of big ideas, core tasks, and developmental rubrics is not sufficient to build a powerful curriculum: scope and sequence assume far greater importance in a macro framework than many educators realize.

Cultivating reflectiveness — leading learners to redefine, reshape, and reorder what they have encountered — is one of the great problems in devising curricula, and children are rarely given work that requires it.
Content and instructional methods can both be of the highest quality while the course still fails to yield effective learning, because the sequencing was wrong.

Sequencing the learning mindful of recurring performances and big ideas is as important as the quality of the curricular elements, and perhaps more so when engagement, understanding, and productivity are the criteria.
Learner understanding is at risk in any sequence that gives one tour of each topic in a flow dictated by the separate content elements rather than by learner performance goals.

A curriculum for wise performance must follow four rules: backward design from explicit performance goals with constant adjustment on feedback, frequent movement between an element of performance and the whole task that justifies it, regular alternation between being instructed and applying the learning, and a sequence that permits learning from results without penalty before formal performance.
The goal in every subject is to be able to do the subject with understanding — acquiring knowledge and skill not for their own sake but as the means for handling key tasks in the field.

Whatever the subject, learning proceeds best through many part-whole-part cycles of trying it out, reflecting, and adjusting: learn just enough content to be able to use it, then tackle increasingly complicated ideas.

Most academic courses have historically been organized as a march through content from basics to advanced material with a long or endless delay in application, to the detriment of engagement and effectiveness.
A subject area is ultimately about the doing of the subject — using the content in a disciplined way — which is why the word discipline is used.

However modern their content, typical courses follow a premodern flow: a march through what is known, organized by the logic of the content, is a medieval tradition predating printing presses, public disagreement about truth, and any aim of serving the learner as a user.
Merely improving how content is framed and delivered is insufficient to make learning understanding-focused; the structure of much curriculum is itself inadequate.
The more content is added and pursued logically in the name of rigor, the harder it becomes for learners to grasp the big ideas and core tasks within a traditional sequence.

The curriculum sequence found in modern performance areas is truer to how and why people learn and should be applied to the traditional academic areas if learner understanding and even recall are to improve.

Software documentation illustrates the split: a reference manual explains every feature one by one, while a tutorial's flow is dictated by the logic of learning to use the content in increasingly complicated applications.
When self-sufficient and productive use is the goal, the approach to both content and sequence changes dramatically — which is precisely what academic learning needs.

The point is maximal transferability — the effective use of content, not merely the learning of it — so performance needs dictate the timing and approach of content learning and the sequence is framed by the key performance tasks rather than the table of contents.
