The main ideas introduced into an education should be few and important and thrown into every combination possible, so the learner makes them their own and understands their application here and now.
Education should be useful, and it is useful because understanding is useful.

A textbook is like a software reference manual: it goes through topics in order divorced from meaningful use or overarching questions, and has unhelpfully become a sealed-off syllabus treated as both form and content.
Content-driven curricula reveal no genuine priorities: every topic appears equal to every other and the flow is impervious to performance need or learner misunderstanding.

Genuine priorities are made tangible as recurring questions related to key performance goals, so learning priorities must be set apart from the textbook — as a coach frames performance goals separately from any resource materials.

The brick-by-brick view of learning — do what you are told piece by piece and the house of understanding will follow — is not how learning works; learning is more like solving a difficult crossword or sculpting with an idea in mind.

An encyclopedic organization is useful only when the reader already has specific questions, curiosities, or performance needs; without them, an endless march is confusing, devoid of meaning, and off-putting.

In far too many courses the most basic learner questions about purpose — why this, why now, so what — are unendingly postponed or ignored by the work itself, regardless of any verbal rationale the teacher supplies.

The students who persevere under a meaning-poor curriculum may simply be those most able to delay gratification or trust adults, which suggests the usual judgment of who is best and brightest may be upside down.

In the original meaning of scope and sequence, scope referred to the major functions of social life and sequence to the centres of interest in students' lives, so the syllabus order was meant to derive from what would seem most natural and interesting to the learner.

The temptation to assume that presenting subject matter in its perfected form is a royal road to learning — starting the immature where competent inquirers left off — has a disappointing outcome written large in the history of education.

Organizing a text by the specialist's order — technical concepts and definitions at the outset, laws early with few indications of how they were arrived at — leaves the pupil learning symbols without the key to their meaning and often acquiring simply a vocabulary.
From the learner's point of view the logic of the content is illogical for learning what matters about the content — what it helps you see and do.

Every subject passes through or remains in an anatomical phase in which understanding is thought to consist of multiplying distinctions and naming each element; in normal growth a specific property is individualized only when it clears up a present difficulty.
Almost all textbooks open with a march through definitions, rules, and algorithms or the most distant events in time, totally removed from any problem, question, or performance context.
A first order of business in any course or programme is to establish the questions and issues that make the content seem interesting, meaningful, and valuable.

One reform proposal for introductory science is to leave the so-called basics aside for a while and concentrate attention on what is not known, teaching the still-imponderable puzzles before any of the fundamentals.
Every topic must be motivated, and the student's question of why they have to learn this material is thoroughly justified.

The claim that mathematics must be taught in the textbook's order because it is sequential confuses the logic of the summary with the logic of learning — as would teaching English via the dictionary or baseball by reading the rulebook in order.

That elements are most easily organized into a logical hierarchy does not entail that the textbook summary of each is the best way to learn the key ideas and the meaning and value of their relationships.

A spiral approach develops curriculum around recurring, ever-deepening inquiries into big ideas and important tasks, revisiting the same ideas and materials in more complex ways to arrive at sophisticated judgments and products.
The spiral curriculum has been praised for a century but few curricula have actually been built to embody it.
Confronting unfamiliar or radical forms after more familiar ones deepens a learner's understanding of the earlier lessons about form, mechanics, and impact.
The bold hypothesis behind the spiral curriculum is that any subject can be taught effectively in some intellectually honest form to any child at any stage of development.

The basic ideas at the heart of the sciences and the basic themes of life and literature are as simple as they are powerful, and commanding them requires a continual deepening that comes from learning to use them in progressively more complex forms.

Basic ideas are out of reach of the young child only when put in formalized terms as equations or elaborated verbal concepts before the child has understood them intuitively and had a chance to try them out.
condition: when the learner has not first understood them intuitively and tried them out

statement: Subject matter should be organized to move from problem to problem so knowledge increases in depth and breadth, moving back and forth between the known and the problematic — for without that movement no problems arise, and problems are the stimulus to thinking.
The teacher's task is to design related challenges so that learning produces new ideas, which then become the ground for further experiences presenting new problems — a continual spiral.

The three criteria for effective curriculum organization — continuity, sequence, and integration — apply to the experiences of the learner and not to how the material looks to someone already in command of it.

Continuity means recurring emphasis on particular elements in the learner's experience, sequence means increasing breadth and depth of the learner's development, and integration means the learner's increased unity of behaviour in relating the elements.
Marching through content chronologically in history does not pass the test of intelligent continuity.

Textbook-driven sequencing persists because it is logical and easy to apply: it simplifies and objectifies the task, lets the least capable teacher assign pages and hear recitation, and supplies an alibi for failure by placing blame on the pupils.

Textbook-driven sequencing also persists because from the administrator's point of view it makes it easy to divide the school's work, say precisely where every child should be, and appear to operate smoothly.

The critique of textbook-as-syllabus was already being made in 1935, and the situation has if anything worsened — in most US science courses from kindergarten through college the textbook is still the syllabus.

Science textbooks front-load technical vocabulary that a well-educated scientist in another field would not know or need to know, and their chapter exercises frequently amount to nothing more than regurgitating those words and definitions.
The deeper incoherence in standard texts is that they throw a welter of concepts and terms at students in confusing order, opening with assertions that are incomprehensible to most learners.

Deriving curricular sequence independently from the content and pagination of textbooks is backward design pushed to a new level: scope and sequence itself must be redesigned against standards related to learning goals.

Fields that redefined themselves in terms of performance rather than content abandoned the piece-by-piece approach: writing is now taught by getting students writing from the start before mechanics are mastered, and novice skiers are introduced immediately to the holistic parallel process on short skis and gentle slopes.
Medicine, engineering, design, and other graduate programmes have revamped their entire curriculum design in a short time to make it more transfer-focused.

Applying performance-field lessons to academic areas requires only agreeing on the core performance tasks in each field and designing programmes and syllabi backward from them, letting learners play the real game in a scaffolded way.
Sequence experimentation is rare partly because many teachers have never thought of other possibilities nor experienced other sequences themselves.
Sequence should first be thought through at a manageable level — the course, or the year of work in a subject at a grade level — rather than attempting whole multiyear sequencing at once.
Course syllabi should be required of all K-12 teachers as they are of college professors, and the syllabus should be a public document available to students, parents, and colleagues.

A syllabus must specify the essential questions and core problems, the core performances that frame all work, the rubrics and scoring systems, a justification of assessment and grading policies against goals and standards, a week-by-week calendar of learning goals rather than topics, and built-in flexibility to adapt to feedback.

Until a course of study is organized backward from big ideas and performance goals with content as the means, educational results will continue to be disappointing and understanding will fall through the cracks of instruction.
A curriculum that constantly postpones the meaning of content cannot yield understanding, maximal recall, or a passion for learning except in the few students willing and able to learn on their own.
The Expert Blind Spot leads many educators to falsely believe that what worked for them will likely work for most others.

That we cannot predict each learner's actual future performance needs is beside the point: the sequence is organized around performance mastery because that is how people learn most effectively, not because students will become professionals.

Any reform of curriculum depends on putting textbooks in their proper place as resources and framing syllabi and programmes around the optimal flow of inherently iterative, nonlinear learning to use big ideas in performance.
The work of design reform is difficult and requires constant revision, and it is particularly difficult for teachers who have to unlearn their prior practice.
High-stakes external testing has unwittingly given teachers a rationalization for avoiding or minimizing the need to teach for in-depth understanding.

The implicit assumption behind teaching to the test is that the only way to safeguard scores is to cover what is tested and make local assessment mimic the state test format — a claim for which research is rarely offered.
Being obligated to teach to content standards does not entail mimicking the state test format in all local testing or haphazardly covering all prescribed content through superficial teaching.
Restated plainly, the teach-to-the-test argument asks us to believe that the only way to raise test scores is to teach worse.
A state test is an audit like an annual physical exam: its validity comes from the fact that a few quick indirect indicators suggest the state of health, not because those indicators define health.

Practising for the indicator rather than living the underlying regimen is the error: the more one concentrates on a single indicator to the exclusion of the daily regimen, the less likely long-run health becomes.
A good test need not involve the core performance one should be engaged in daily; it only matters that the indicators yield valid inferences to the standards.

The state's job is to audit, not to provide the daily regimen; local educators are responsible for the underlying rigor, and in the absence of data showing the indicators yield invalid inferences the task is to focus on that rigor rather than test prep.
condition: absent data showing the indicators yield invalid inferences

statement: The authors hold state agencies partly responsible for the confusion, for not making local assessments part of a comprehensive accountability system and for not designing more transparent accountability such as releasing tests and results after administration.

Face validity misleads: tests that appear inauthentic can yield valid inferences if properly designed, while performance-based projects can yield poor results when they end up unrelated to the standards.
Inferring that instructional practice is dictated by test format leads teachers to a random and superficial survey of content, making engaging and effective learning far less likely.

State standards are like building codes and local instructional design is the architecture: the goal is not to meet the codes slavishly but to design something practical, pleasing, and stylish while meeting them.

Most state standards actually stress in-depth understanding and mastery of key complex performances, so a focus on big ideas with robust assessment makes it likely that standards are addressed and met.

A multi-level study of 24 restructured schools, observing 504 lessons and analysing 234 assessment tasks, found that students in classrooms with high levels of authentic pedagogy and performance were substantially helped whether they were high- or low-achieving.

That same study found inequalities between high- and low-performing students were greatly decreased when normally low-performing students used authentic pedagogy and performance strategies and assessments.
Authentic pedagogy in that study was measured by standards including higher-order thinking, deep-knowledge approaches, and connections to the world beyond the classroom.

A large urban study of test scores from more than 100,000 students and surveys of more than 5,000 teachers found clear and consistent evidence that interactive teaching methods were associated with more learning in both reading and mathematics.

Interactive instruction was operationally defined as the teacher acting primarily as guide or coach, students asking questions and developing strategies, students explaining how they arrived at their conclusions, and mastery assessed through discussion, projects, or tests demanding explanation and extended writing.
In interactive classrooms the process of developing the answer is viewed as important in assessing the quality of the work, alongside content mastery.

The findings call into serious question the assumption that low-achieving, economically disadvantaged students are best served by didactic methods and review; to elevate mastery of basic skills, interactive instruction should be increased and didactic instruction and review moderated.

Authentic intellectual work is defined as construction of knowledge through disciplined inquiry to produce discourse, products, or performances that have value beyond school — original application rather than routine use of facts and procedures.
A three-year study of classroom assignments concluded that assignments calling for more authentic intellectual work actually improve student scores on conventional standardized tests.
Contrary to expectations, that study found high-quality assignments in some very disadvantaged classrooms and found that all students in those classes benefited from exposure to such instruction.

Teaching to the test does raise scores in the short run, particularly where there was previously little attention to common standards, because greater attention to an outcome improves performance on any measure.

Once the test particulars are figured out and students have learned the format and test-taking skills, there is rarely long-term progress, and scores typically drop when the test is altered or re-normed.

Across fifteen years of work with hundreds of schools the authors observed more in-depth teaching and demanding assessment in the higher-performing schools, and drill-and-practice orientations in the lower-performing ones.
The bottom line is to teach to the standards and develop the complex assessments reflected in the language of those standards, not to the audit.

Standards committees working in isolation produced overly ambitious lists of essentials, so rather than streamlining the curriculum the plethora of standards contributed to the overload problem they were meant to solve.
It makes no sense to assume that everything in the textbook should be taught in class or learned by all students, since a course has priorities framed as performance goals and understandings.

Textbook publishers try to cover the waterfront to appease many state adoption committees, national subject organizations, and special-interest groups, and the invariable result is superficial treatment of the entire array of expert knowledge.
The perceived need to cover rests on two unfounded assumptions: that whatever is taught will be adequately learned for tests, and that whatever is not addressed didactically will not be learned.
A superficial and disconnected teaching of information cannot yield optimal results on any test, which again confuses the teaching with the learning.

When teachers cite external pressure to march through texts, the authors were never able to trace the claim to an administrative source; teachers were typically interpreting a focus on test scores as an implied request to stick to textbooks and test prep.

A diagnostic exercise is to have teachers map the overlap between their textbook and their standards: the imperfect correlation shows that part of the textbook does not serve the standards and that other resources will be needed.

Independent review found high-school biology textbooks fail to make important ideas comprehensible because a commercial market requires covering the entire range of facts, sacrificing depth on the central concepts.

The job of design, instruction, and assessment is to shape a syllabus in light of content standards, intellectual priorities, and student needs to achieve explicit goals — treating the textbook as the syllabus ensures a lack of purpose and coherence in the overall design.
Treating the textbook as the course of study is akin to marching through an encyclopedia from A to Z: logical and efficient, but not purposeful or effective.
Few school systems have performance-based job descriptions or ask what the job is when hiring and evaluating staff, so without clarification it is easy to fall into thinking the textbook is the job.
The large international comparative study found that although teachers in the highest-performing nation cover fewer mathematics topics, their students achieve better results.

In the highest-performing nation teachers report that their aim is conceptual understanding and that the goal of a lesson is for students to develop mathematical thinking, whereas elsewhere the goal is to acquire a specific procedure.

The understanding-oriented lesson pattern is: teacher poses a complex thought-provoking problem, students struggle with it, various students present ideas or solutions, the teacher summarizes the class's conclusions, and students then practise similar problems.

The skill-acquisition lesson pattern is: teacher instructs students in a concept or skill, teacher solves example problems with the class, then students practise on their own while the teacher assists individuals.
Student presentation of alternative solutions occurred in 42 percent of eighth-grade mathematics classes in the highest-performing nation versus 8 percent in the United States.

Students in the highest-performing nation spend 44 percent of class time inducing the idea to be learned from problems, versus under 1 percent in U.S. classrooms; conversely 95 percent of U.S. class time is spent practising a procedure versus 40 percent there.
96 percent of middle school teachers in the highest-performing nation made links to other lessons, compared with only 40 percent of U.S. teachers.

Coherence can be measured by threats to it — frequent topic switching and outside intrusions — and U.S. lessons contained significantly more topics and significantly more topic switches than comparison nations' lessons.

Even under a generous definition of developed — a concept explained or illustrated with a few sentences or a brief example — only one-fifth of topics in U.S. lessons contained developed concepts while four-fifths contained only stated concepts, a distribution nearly reversed in the comparison nation.

U.S. lessons presented about twice as many definitions as comparison nations' lessons, which is why researchers characterized the pattern as learning terms and practising procedures with less emphasis on underlying rationale.

The hidden assumption under the need to cover is that everything to be learned must be taught and that teaching key facts is what causes learning — false, since much of what students learn comes from well-designed work and their own effort to understand.

Advocating a rich body of shared factual knowledge does not entail teaching those facts didactically: an extensive curriculum can be delivered in a formal or an informal school, and it must be paired with intensive study.
To understand how isolated facts cohere, learners must acquire mental models of that coherence, and such schemata come only from detailed, intensive study and experience.

The authors believe overly didactic teaching is a major cause of the student misunderstanding documented throughout the book, because big ideas are abstract or counterintuitive to the naive learner and need intensive uncoverage.
The job of teaching is to optimize student learning of what is worthy — not to cover a book, nor to teach, test, and hope for the best irrespective of results.

The three research findings underlying modern learning science are that students arrive with preconceptions that must be engaged, that competence requires a deep factual foundation understood within a conceptual framework and organized for retrieval, and that a metacognitive approach helps students take control of their learning.
Evidence from research indicates that when those three learning principles are incorporated into teaching, student achievement improves.
A major goal of schooling is preparing students for flexible adaptation to new problems and settings, and their ability to transfer provides an important index of adaptive learning.

Knowledge of a large set of disconnected facts is not sufficient: deep understanding transforms factual information into usable knowledge, and organizing information into a conceptual framework allows for greater transfer.

Students develop flexible understanding of when, where, why, and how to use knowledge if they learn to extract underlying themes and principles from their learning experiences, and learning in multiple contexts most likely affects this aspect of transfer.
Superficial coverage of all topics must be replaced with in-depth coverage of fewer topics that allows the key concepts of the discipline to be understood.
Coverage that gives equal attention to each little fact or subskill, as opposed to a focus on the ideas and challenges that give them meaning, simply does not work to maximize test scores.

The time objection is partly valid: aligning curriculum, identifying big ideas, designing authentic assessments, analysing student work, and conducting action research is genuinely challenging work that individual teachers do not have all the time for.

Four hidden assumptions inflate the time objection: that each teacher, school, or district must climb the mountain alone; that the time must come from teaching time; that each standard must be addressed separately in units designed from scratch; and that hard and time-consuming is a bad thing.

The teacher's version of the blind spot — I taught it, so they must have learned it; if I teach more stuff they will learn more — means that left to themselves teachers will always find the habit of coverage more defensible than it is.
Teams and faculties must ask each year which approaches to design, teaching, and assessing actually yield the greatest student learning regardless of their own habits and attitudes.
Professional development must practise what it preaches about understanding: uncover rather than cover the big ideas of learning, through ongoing inquiry and discussion.

Local research should be small in scope but deep — one unit a year, designed collaboratively, tried out and adjusted a few times, with intensive analysis of the student work — which is feasible within existing in-service days and team meetings.
Nobody prepares a gourmet meal every evening, and by the same logic one thoroughly developed unit per year — collected, reviewed, and shared — should be a job requirement backed by supervision.

In the highest-performing nation teacher education seeks depth not breadth and learning on the job rather than being taught new techniques: teachers work in small teams to develop, teach, and refine one research lesson per year.
Lesson-study teams share their results not only in staff meetings but at regional lesson fairs so other teachers benefit from their insights.
Because problems that emerge in lesson study are attributed to the lesson as designed by the group rather than to the individual, it becomes possible for teachers to be critical.
Lesson study also provides a benchmarking process teachers can use to gauge their own skills, while balancing self-critique with the idea that improved teaching is a joint process.

The lack-of-time complaint is only partly true: schools already devote roughly twelve hours a year to professional development days and sixteen to staff and departmental meetings, half of which could be redirected to required lesson study.
Action research should become an obligation of all teams and departments, with annual reports on the achievement targets tackled, the research undertaken, results found, and new inquiry proposed.

A workable collaborative cycle is: bring your best existing unit to a summer design workshop, pair with peers teaching the same topic, work with a content expert, review the work against design standards, revise on feedback, field-test the following year, evaluate the resulting student work together, and submit the result for regional expert review.

Standardized tests sample the standards one at a time through decontextualized items, and the look of those tests misleadingly suggests teaching to the standards one bit at a time as if each were of equal importance.

When units involve rich in-depth work culminating in complex performance, dozens of standards are addressed simultaneously in appropriate hierarchical order and with more coherence from the learner's perspective.
The local challenge is not to design a lesson per indicator but to design rich units that ultimately address all the standards while clearly signalling the priorities to students.

Applying design standards to one's own professional work means designs are validated against those standards rather than assumed sound because the designer worked hard or the students enjoyed the activities.

Using a backward design template develops a productive mental model for planning that helps avoid activity-oriented and coverage-oriented curricula, and is particularly valuable for new teachers not yet reliant on a file of favourite activities or on textbooks.

A searchable database of validated units lets teachers work smarter rather than reinventing the same wheels, and concentrating energy on one or two high-quality units raises design standards and skill over time.

Shared design work is itself rich professional development because, unlike one-size-fits-all sessions on generic topics, it concentrates on teaching and assessing specific content and yields tangible products of immediate value.

Design-team conversations focus on the profession's core questions: what big ideas students should understand, how we will know they really learned it, what meeting these standards means, which experiences are most engaging and effective, and what student work reveals about the curriculum's strengths and needs.
Given limited professional development time it is imperative that it be results-oriented rather than coverage of educational trends by outside speakers.
True learning is always difficult: it upends old learning and leads to disequilibrium and resistance, which is why many educators show a paradoxical resistance to learning.

Redesigning schools around ongoing collaborative research may be the only way to overcome teacher resistance to changing habits, timidity about experimentation, and fear of criticism and failure, because a group working together generates courage and helpful peer pressure to learn.

The blind spot hides from teachers the pain of all learning, not just the likelihood of student misconception, so the job should require action research that keeps teachers inside how learning works and reminds them how difficult it really is.

Real learning is always frightening and frustrating and can cause self-doubt regardless of age or talent, so teachers who never occupy the learner's position miss vital opportunities to make education honest and self-correcting.
Educators are causes of and students of learning rather than merely teachers, and the time needed for that work should be treated as essential rather than extra.

The two central levers for improving performance while preserving intellectual engagement are teaching and assessing for understanding of big ideas and core tasks, and applying design standards to review and refine local curriculum as part of ongoing research embedded in the job.
Habits and misunderstandings are rarely overcome by argument alone; claims must be locally uncovered, tested, argued, and explored in one's own setting to be accepted or rejected on rational grounds.
Because teaching is complex, improvements are most successful when developed in the classrooms where teachers teach; ideas from afar must be tested and adapted to the local classroom.

Regardless of what cannot be controlled about students, schools, and society, the things that are in the educator's control — design, instruction, and giving feedback — can still significantly affect achievement.
A reported paradigm shift came from teachers evaluating every assignment and assessment for validity and letting go of time-honoured favourite lessons that were not aligned to the desired results.

Many educators report they did not fully understand the framework until they had applied it to an actual curriculum design and received feedback from colleagues — as with any big idea, its nuances are grasped after application and reflection.
A design self-assessment and peer-review protocol against explicit design standards establishes quality control while promoting continuous improvement of curriculum design.

Practical starting moves for a team include unpacking content standards into understandings and essential questions, prioritizing standards and textbook content with the three-ovals tool, developing core performance tasks and common rubrics, and jointly evaluating student work to select shared anchors.

Analysing external achievement data and student work to identify areas of student misunderstanding, then developing intervention plans and action-research teams around those areas, targets improvement at diagnosed weaknesses.

Designers should walk the talk by using backward design to plan their own adoption of backward design, and administrators can learn it by codesigning a unit with a teacher or by planning professional development with the same template.

A unit cover page should track design status explicitly — template stages complete, task blueprints, rubrics, directions, materials, accommodations, extensions — and review status from initial draft through peer review, content review, field test, validation, and anchoring.

An assessment task blueprint records which understandings the task assesses, the criteria implied by the standards regardless of task specifics, the task overview, the student products, and the criteria by which those products will be evaluated.
Distinguishing the criteria implied by the standards from the criteria specific to the chosen task keeps the standard's demands visible even as the task changes.

A complete Stage 2 plan pairs the performance tasks and other evidence with explicit student self-assessment and reflection items, including reflection on whether the student's own behaviour changed over the unit.
A completed Stage 3 plan lists the key teaching and learning activities in sequence with each entry coded to the WHERETO element it serves, so coverage of the design elements is auditable.

A unit opens with an entry question that connects the topic to something students already care about, then introduces the essential questions and the culminating performance tasks so the destination is known from the start.
Key vocabulary is introduced as needed by the learning activities and performance tasks rather than front-loaded, and textbook reading is used to support those activities.
An ongoing personal record kept across the unit — such as a daily log of one's own behaviour — supplies the raw material for a self-assessment of change at the unit's end.

A rethinking move can be inserted by following the authoritative guidance with a question that unsettles it — asking whether everyone must follow the same prescription to be healthy after reviewing the official brochure.
Group work products are collected and reviewed by the teacher specifically to look for misunderstandings needing instructional attention, not only to be graded.
Peer assessment against a criteria list followed by permitted revision builds the rethink-and-revise element into an ordinary assignment.
The teacher models how to read and interpret a technical artifact before students practise on real examples of it, rather than assuming the skill from a description.
The unit concludes with the learner self-evaluating against their own accumulated record and producing a personal action plan, which turns the self-knowledge facet into a product.
Calling for active inquiry and application around a big idea is not a blanket endorsement of a discovery approach to instruction.
Both topical and overarching understandings require inference from facts, which is why the authors distinguish them from each other rather than treating topical understandings as facts.
Even when the target is stated as understanding how to do something, students are still expected to grasp specific insights in order to enhance their performance.

The authors do not subscribe to recapitulation as a sound educational theory, but the idea that students should experience authentic inquiry and sometimes re-create how knowledge was developed is part of what uncoverage means.

The authors' longstanding opposition to overreliance on indirect tests is separable from the narrower validity point: indirect inauthentic tests can yield valid inferences just as authentic tasks can yield invalid ones.
Recent studies have cast doubt on the extravagant score-gain claims made by test-preparation companies.

An academic prompt is an open-ended written performance test occupying the space between an authentic task and a short-answer quiz; it is not authentic because school constraints are placed on time, resources, and consultation.
Analytic-trait scoring assesses a performance several times through the lens of separate criteria, in contrast to holistic scoring where a judge forms a single overall impression.
Anchors are samples of work attached to each rubric level, and a rubric without them is typically far too ambiguous to set a clear standard for judges and performers alike.
Anchors contribute significantly to scoring reliability, because phrases like sophisticated and persuasive have little meaning without work samples that give them concrete and stable definition.
To assess derives from the Latin for to sit beside: assessment implies thoughtful observation, disinterested judgment, and clear helpful feedback rather than merely testing.
Good assessment requires a balance of techniques because each technique is limited and prone to error, and a teacher can assess strengths and weaknesses without placing a grade on the performance.

An audit test is a brief instrument that assesses something important and complex using simpler indicators, so its questions are proxies for the real goals and it makes little sense to attend solely to the audit.

What makes an assessment authentic is the context — the messiness of the problem, the ability to seek feedback and revise, access to appropriate resources — not merely that the task is performance-based or hands-on.
Authentic assessments should do more than test: they teach students and teachers what doing a subject looks like and which performance challenges the field actually considers most important.
An authentic test directly measures the valued performance, whereas multiple-choice tests are indirect measures — the contrast between a driving road test and the written test.
Backward design is called backward only because many teachers begin with the means — textbooks, favoured lessons, time-honoured activities — rather than deriving those from the targeted results.

Backward design proceeds by starting with the desired results, identifying the evidence necessary to determine they have been achieved, then determining the enabling knowledge and skill, and only then the teaching needed to equip students to perform.
Educational objectives become the criteria by which materials are selected, content outlined, procedures developed, and tests prepared — the logic of backward design stated more than fifty years ago.

A benchmark anchored by the best possible samples of work sets the highest standard rather than an average one, so an assessment anchored that way should not be expected to yield a predictable curve — standards differ from reasonable expectations.
Big ideas are the meaningful patterns that enable one to connect the dots of otherwise fragmented knowledge, and they are the building material of understandings.

A big idea is a linchpin: an idea essential for understanding without which the learner cannot go anywhere, so that without it students are left with easily forgotten fragments even when highly knowledgeable about facts.
Bloom's Taxonomy was written to solve a testing problem: educators needed to know how ill-defined objectives such as really understand or thorough knowledge of should be measured.

In Bloom's scheme application meant using discrete knowledge or skill in an exam setting rather than drawing on a repertoire to solve a complex contextualized problem; the authors' sense of application better matches Bloom's synthesis, which stresses the student's unique production.

Coverage is a teaching approach that superficially teaches and tests content knowledge irrespective of student understanding or engagement, typically justified by curriculum-framework demands or external testing.
Criteria are the qualities work must meet to measure up to a standard: asking what the criteria are is asking what to look for in student work to know whether it succeeded.

Criteria should be settled before the specific performance task is designed, because designing a task that measures critical thinking requires knowing beforehand what the indicators of such thinking are.
An assessment must also determine how much weight each criterion receives relative to the others rather than treating all agreed criteria as equally important.
Criteria themselves can be valid or invalid: grading authentic historical research only on source count and page length is invalid, because excellent research could fail those criteria.
Criteria should correspond to the qualities of masterful performance, and many performance assessments undervalue impact criteria.

To say something happens by design is to say it occurs through thoughtful planning rather than by accident or winging it, and what happens before the teacher enters the classroom may be as or more important than the teaching inside it.

Design standards treat design as more than good intentions and hard work: they let teacher work be assessed the way student work is, serving both to guide self- and peer review and to provide quality control validating designs.
Desired results come in five kinds: declarative knowledge, skills and processes, understandings, habits of mind, and attitudes.
Though they involve complex learnings, desired results must be cast in measurable terms, since any valid assessment is designed to measure the degree to which the learner's work hit the target.
A direct test measures the targeted performance in the context where it is expected to occur, whereas an indirect test measures the same performance out of context in a deliberately simplified way.

Empathy is a learned ability to grasp the world from someone else's point of view — the discipline of using imagination to see and feel as others do and to imagine that something different might be possible or even desirable.

Enduring understandings are the specific inferences based on big ideas that have lasting value beyond the classroom, and the test question for identifying them is what students should understand and be able to use years from now after they have forgotten the details.
An enduring understanding provides a conceptual unifying lens through which learners can recognize the significance of one case and also examine new ones.

Because enduring understandings are abstract and often not obvious, they require uncoverage through sustained inquiry rather than one-shot coverage, and if the teacher treats an understanding like a fact the student is unlikely to get it.
An entry question is a simple thought-provoking opener framed for maximal simplicity in student-friendly language, with provocation value, pointing toward the larger unit and essential questions.
The design challenge is to enable the essential and unit questions to arise naturally from the entry questions, problems, and activities.

An essential question lies at the heart of a subject and produces different plausible responses about which thoughtful and knowledgeable people may disagree, rather than yielding a single straightforward answer.
The authors revised their own usage: in the first edition essential questions were overarching only, whereas now an essential question can be either overarching or topical in scope.
Understanding in the explanatory sense goes beyond giving back right answers to providing warranted opinions — justifying how the student got there and why it is right.
The more a student can explain, apply, and offer multiple points of view on the same idea, the more likely it is that the student understands that idea — the facets are mutually reinforcing.
A facet is more like a criterion in performance assessment than a learning style: it concerns how teachers judge whether understanding is present, not the learner's abilities or preferences.

Not all six facets are always involved in a particular understanding — self-knowledge and empathy are often not at stake in evidence of many mathematical concepts — so the facets present a framework rather than a quota.

Multiple holistic scores are possible for a multifaceted task involving several standards — separate holistic scores for an oral presentation and a written report — without breaking each mode into analytic components.

An ill-structured task lacks a recipe or obvious formula, is often fuzzy and needs further definition before a solution is offered, and therefore demands judgment and imagination rather than knowledge alone.

Ill-structured tasks invariably require constant self-assessment and revision, not a simple application of transferred knowledge, and all good essay questions, science problems, and design challenges are ill structured.

Most real problems in life are ill structured and most test items are not: well-structured items validly assess elements of knowledge but not the ability to judge which knowledge and skill to use when.
An indirect test can be valid despite being less authentic: if its results correlate with results on direct tests then it is valid by definition.
An intelligent tool puts abstract ideas and processes in tangible form and enhances performance on cognitive tasks; routine use of such a tool builds a mental template of its key ideas.

Interpretation is fraught with more inherent subjectivity and tentativeness than the theorizing involved in explanation: even knowing the facts and principles, one must still ask what it all means and what its importance is.

Handing students prepackaged interpretations without letting them work through and see why some accounts are more valid than others leads to sham understanding and superficial, quickly forgotten knowledge.

The curricular design process is always iterative: designers keep revisiting their initial ideas about what they are after, how to assess it, and how to teach it, and rethink earlier units in light of later designs and results.

Leading questions have correct straightforward answers and a useful role in teaching and checking for understanding; calling a question leading is not to condemn it, only to mark its different purpose.
Most school testing is not longitudinal because tests are one-time events with one-time scoring systems; longitudinal assessment requires scoring scales and tasks usable across many grade levels.
Open-ended does not mean all answers are of equal value: many different acceptable answers are possible, and they are judged justified, plausible, or well-defended rather than correct.

An outcome-based approach focuses on desired outputs rather than inputs: the key question is what students will know and be able to do as a result of instruction, not which methods and materials to use.
Determining whether outcomes have been attained requires agreement on the specific measures — the assessment tasks, criteria, and standards.

A performance assessment involves more than a single test of performance and may include surveys, interviews of the performer, observations, and quizzes; performance assessment and performance test are commonly confused.

In a test of performance the student must put it all together in the context of ill-structured, nonroutine, or unpredictable challenges, whereas conventional items ask only to recall, recognize, or plug in isolated bits one at a time.

Because many performances are ephemeral actions, a fair and technically sound assessment typically involves creating products, which ensures documentation and the possibility of review and oversight in scoring.

A portfolio serves both documentation and evaluation, revealing the student's control over the major areas and genres of the course, letting students select and reflect on their best work, and showing how works evolved and were refined.
Prerequisite knowledge and skill is the more discrete know-how required to put everything together in a meaningful final performance, identified by working back from the culminating task.

Evaluating process skills separately from the product requires caution: the emphasis should remain on whether the final product or performance met the standards set, irrespective of how the student got there.

A product is valid evidence of knowledge to the extent that success or failure in producing it reflects the knowledge being assessed and samples appropriately from the whole curriculum's relative importance.

Targeted understandings should be framed as specific propositions describing a relationship among concepts — principles, generalizations, axioms, laws — not as phrases referring to the topic or content standard.
Measurement error is unavoidable: all tests including the best multiple-choice tests lack complete reliability, and the aim is to minimize error to tolerable levels rather than eliminate it.

In performance assessment the reliability problem takes two forms: whether one can generalize from a small number of performances to the student's likely performance in general, and whether different judges will see the same performance the same way.

Adequate reliability is obtained by having multiple tasks for the same outcome rather than one, and scoring reliability is greatly improved when well-trained supervised judges work from clear rubrics and specific anchor papers.
Resultant knowledge and skill is the goal of the unit and belongs in Stage 1, whereas prerequisite knowledge is what is needed to accomplish that goal and is woven into the Stage 3 learning plan.
A rubric answers the question of what understanding or proficiency for an identified result looks like, enabling both reliable judgment by assessors and self-assessment by students.
All unit and test design is sampling from a vast domain, and sampling supports valid inferences only if the sample of work or questions is appropriate and justified.

The designer's sampling question is which feasible and efficient set of tasks or questions will support valid inferences about overall performance, given that the student cannot be tested on everything taught.

Performance assessment uses a small scoring scale — typically four or six points — because each point must correspond to a specific criterion or quality of work, and because a scale of many discrete numbers reduces scoring reliability.
Most multiple-choice tests must be secure or their validity is compromised, because they rely on a small number of uncomplicated questions; many valid performance assessments are not secure at all.
In a non-secure performance assessment the student knows the piece, topic, or question in advance and the teacher appropriately teaches to the test of performance.
Accuracy of self-assessment means the learner understands what they do not understand with clarity and specificity — the capacity Socrates called wisdom.
One does not simply receive understanding: ways of thinking and categorizing are projected onto situations in ways that inevitably shape what is understood.

There are three kinds of standard: content standards answer what students should know and be able to do, performance standards answer how well they must do their work, and design standards answer what worthy work students should encounter.
Most state documents identify only content standards, so design standards — by which sound units are distinguished from unsound ones — must be supplied locally.

The word standard is variously and confusingly used to mean high expectations, a benchmark of best possible performance, a minimal passing score, a general guideline, and the criteria for judging performance.
A rubric alone is not sufficient for evaluation: an articulated performance standard, usually made real by anchors or exemplars, is also necessary.

A standard must not be confused with an expectation: a standard remains worthy whether or not few or any people can meet it, whereas an expectation is something a good number of students can and ought to meet with persistence and good teaching.
School standards are typically set de facto by the choice of peer-based anchors, so the key questions are where the work samples should come from and what would be a valid choice of anchors.
Students should routinely be given anchors drawn from slightly more advanced and experienced students, to serve as a longer-range target and to guide ongoing feedback.

Criteria are more or less fixed regardless of the student's age or ability — every persuasive essay must use appropriate evidence and effective reasoning — while how sophisticated the argument must be is a question of standard.

Fixing a passing score at 60 is arbitrary because few tests are designed so that a significant qualitative difference distinguishes a 59 from a 61, and treating a standard as a cutoff turns a criterion-referenced system into a norm-referenced one.

Improving content standards will not necessarily raise performance standards, because content refers to input and performance to output: poor-quality work can still come from a demanding course of study.
Raising only the difficulty of what is taught will likely produce worse performance in the short term if teaching and time spent on work remain constant.
condition: if all other factors such as teaching and time spent on work remain constant

statement: The key question in setting a valid performance standard is at what level of performance the student would be appropriately qualified or certified.

Equating internal school standards to an equivalent worthy level of achievement in the outside world lends substance, stability, and credibility to the scoring, as is common in vocational, musical, and athletic learning.
Standardized means only that administrative conditions and protocol are uniform for all students, so a uniformly administered performance task such as a driving road test is also a standardized test.

Three misconceptions attach to standardized tests: that multiple-choice and standardized are synonyms, that standardized tests are always machine scored, and that only national norm- or criterion-referenced tests can be standardized.

All formal tests are standardized, but an assessment is not: in an assessment the administrator may vary the questions, tasks, their order, and the time allotted to be satisfied the results are fair, valid, and reliable.
Transferability is the ability to use knowledge appropriately and fruitfully in a context different from the one in which it was initially learned.

Three types of content demand uncoverage: principles and theories that become meaningful only when the learner can verify or justify them; counterintuitive or easily misunderstood ideas; and the conceptual or strategic element of any skill.
Uncovering the strategic element of a skill means clarifying effective and efficient means given the ends of the skill, which leads to greater purposefulness and less mindless use of techniques.
To understand is to make sense of what one knows, to be able to know why it is so, and to have the ability to use it in various situations and contexts.

Validity asks whether the test measures what it purports to measure, whether its results correlate with other results considered valid, whether the sample accurately represents everything taught, and whether the results predict future success.

One task does not license inference to other task types — one genre of writing does not generalize to all others — so the few tasks used in performance assessment often provide an inadequate basis for generalizing.
One solution to the generalization problem is to use a wide variety of student work of a similar type or genre, collected over the year, as part of the summative assessment.

The same test can be valid for one purpose and invalid for another: a multiple-choice reading test may validly monitor grade-level reading ability while being invalid as a measure of a pupil's repertoire of reading strategies.
An inauthentic test can still be technically valid as an efficient proxy that predicts future performance, and conversely an authentic task may not be valid.

The scoring system raises its own validity question: whether the scoring targets the most important aspects of performance or merely what is easiest to count — that is, whether validity has been sacrificed for reliability.
The W element requires that students themselves can answer where the work is headed, why, what their final performance obligations are, and by what criteria their work will be judged.

The Explore-and-equip element has two halves: learning experiences that let students pursue leads and test ideas, and guided instruction and coaching that equips them with the needed skill and knowledge for the final performance.
The Rethink element digs deeper through the facets and guides students in self-assessment and self-adjustment based on feedback from inquiry, results, and discussion.
The Evaluate element involves students in a final self-assessment to identify remaining questions, set future goals, and point toward new units and lessons.
The Tailor element differentiates approaches and provides sufficient options and variety to maximize engagement and achievement without compromising the goals.
condition: without compromising the goals

statement: What students actively do is more consequential for what they learn than the teacher's performance by itself.

statement: Functioning knowledge depends on a sound declarative base, but theory and application need not be learned in a rigid sequence; they can be constructed together around problems.
condition: when a problem-based design supports simultaneous conceptual and practical learning

statement: If graduates are expected to use theory in professional decisions, teach and assess that application rather than leaving transfer to post-graduation experience.
condition: when professional functioning is an intended programme outcome

statement: Assess functioning knowledge through performance in relevant practice or a defensible simulation of it, not solely through declarations about theory.
condition: when the intended outcome is informed action
exception: some declarative assessment remains appropriate for knowledge students genuinely need to explain or know about

statement: Decide explicitly for each course outcome whether it primarily addresses declarative knowledge, functioning knowledge, or a justified combination.
condition: when designing a degree programme and its courses

statement: Increase emphasis on functioning knowledge as students progress toward advanced professional practice, while retaining declarative outcomes where they are intrinsically warranted.
condition: in later stages of professionally oriented programmes
exception: the appropriate balance depends on the discipline and specific outcome

statement: Identify threshold concepts collaboratively at programme level and give them deliberate attention in outcomes, courses, and learning activities.
condition: when certain concepts reorganize how the discipline is understood

statement: Distinguish a threshold concept that transforms perspective and connects previously separate ideas from a core concept that is necessary but not transformative in the same way.
condition: when prioritizing concepts in a programme

statement: Expect threshold concepts to be troublesome when they conflict with intuition or earlier interpretations, and design support for the conceptual transition.
condition: when learners must cross a counter-intuitive conceptual threshold

statement: Do not use the verb understand without defining the observable performance and level of complexity that will count as understanding.
condition: when writing an intended learning outcome

statement: Use explanation to others, adaptation, application, and changed action as evidence of robust understanding when those performances fit the discipline.
condition: when the intended understanding is higher than recall or paraphrase

statement: Students adapt their form of understanding to what examinations appear to require, even when this displaces more integrated and professionally relevant understanding.
condition: when examination demands reward reproduction or strategic answer structures
exception: assessment that directly rewards integrated use need not have this effect

statement: Review assessment for whether it pre-empts the kind of understanding students will need in professional practice.
condition: when programme rhetoric emphasizes professional judgment or transfer

statement: Require performances that reveal changed reasoning or action when the purpose of a concept is to alter how learners interpret and handle the domain.
condition: when teaching a threshold concept or other transformative understanding
exception: verbal declaration is sufficient when acquaintance with the topic is genuinely the intended outcome

statement: Do not infer conceptual change from correct formula use or stock verbal answers if learners retain contradictory everyday conceptions in relevant situations.
condition: when assessing whether a learner can transfer formal knowledge to a simple real-world case

statement: Set acceptable levels of understanding for each stage of a programme in relation to year level, specialization, and degree pattern rather than applying expert-level expectations uniformly.
condition: when sequencing programme and course outcomes

statement: Understanding typically develops first through increased relevant detail and then through qualitative integration of that detail into a coherent structure.
condition: across the academic outcome domains from which SOLO was developed

statement: Use the SOLO taxonomy as a common structural framework for specifying intended levels of understanding and evaluating the complexity students actually demonstrate.
condition: when the outcome can be described through increasing structural complexity
exception: subject experts still need to interpret an appropriate level for the particular content and stage

statement: A response can contain many correct details yet remain structurally inadequate if it does not organize them to answer the task actually posed.
condition: when evaluating multistructural knowledge-telling

statement: Classify a prestructural response as one that misses the relevant point despite possibly sophisticated wording.
condition: when applying SOLO to a student performance

statement: Classify a unistructural response as one that uses a single relevant aspect but does not address the task in sufficient breadth or relationship.
condition: when applying SOLO to a student performance

statement: Classify a multistructural response as one that provides several relevant components without integrating them into the structure the task requires.
condition: when applying SOLO to a student performance

statement: Classify a relational response as one that integrates relevant components through a coherent organizing concept capable of generating explanation or action.
condition: when applying SOLO to a student performance

statement: Classify an extended-abstract response as one that reconceptualizes the coherent whole at a higher level and applies it to new or broader domains.
condition: when applying SOLO to a student performance

statement: Treat SOLO levels as a cumulative hierarchy in which relevant lower-level constructions support later integration and generalization.
condition: when interpreting development in the structural quality of outcomes

statement: Distinguish the quantitative curriculum aim of knowing more relevant elements from the qualitative aim of restructuring them into deeper understanding.
condition: when designing or evaluating learning progression

statement: State qualitative deepening explicitly in outcomes and support it through teaching and assessment; otherwise only self-directed students may perform the necessary restructuring.
condition: when integrated or transferable understanding is intended

statement: Choose outcome verbs that correspond to the intended structural level of student performance rather than using generic cognition words without a level.
condition: when using SOLO to write intended learning outcomes

statement: Assess professional learning with evidence that theory has improved decision making or action, rather than only with written explanation of relevance.
condition: when improved professional practice is the course purpose

statement: Ask learners to select, justify, and reflect on authentic evidence of their own learning when the evidence cannot be supplied or rehearsed by the teacher.
condition: when portfolio assessment can validly demonstrate a personally enacted outcome
exception: students need examples, criteria, or a trial run when the evidentiary expectations are unfamiliar

statement: Bridge abstract university knowledge and functioning professional knowledge before graduation instead of assuming graduates will independently learn the transfer later.
condition: when the programme intends professional competence

statement: Constructive alignment combines learner construction of knowledge with alignment of outcome, learning activity, and assessment.
Write each intended outcome to specify the learner's activity, the content or object of that activity, its context where relevant, and the expected standard.
condition: when designing a constructively aligned course

statement: Create a learning environment that elicits the activity named in the intended outcome, then assess the quality of that same activity in student performance.
condition: when the outcome verb can be enacted in teaching and assessment

statement: Judge students against the intended content and acceptable standards when the purpose is learning, reserving norm-referenced comparison for genuinely selective decisions.
condition: when deciding between criterion- and norm-referenced assessment
exception: ranking can be relevant when allocating a deliberately limited number of positions, places, or awards

statement: Let the way theory should change interpretation, problem solving, or action guide the intended outcomes for abstract as well as professional subjects.
condition: when sound learning should empower use beyond verbal acquaintance

statement: Use open-ended outcome and assessment designs that recognize desirable learning not predicted in advance.
condition: when learners have freedom to construct knowledge in valid but diverse ways
exception: unintended performance must still be relevant and meet defensible quality standards

statement: Align learning activities intrinsically with both outcomes and assessment, rather than limiting outcomes-based design to criterion-referenced assessment alone.
condition: when applying constructive alignment

statement: Use assessment criteria and rubrics as consistent signposts toward the same agenda expressed by the outcomes and practiced in learning activities.
condition: when students need to understand expected quality throughout a course

statement: Misalignment allows students to substitute low-level strategies that satisfy assessment without achieving the intended outcome.
condition: when assessment or teaching does not require the relevant outcome activity

statement: Give students practice in applying grading criteria to work so they can recognize levels above and below an acceptable standard.
condition: when developing self- or peer-assessment capability
exception: teacher moderation may be needed while students learn to apply criteria consistently

statement: Constructive alignment should make students perform the cognitive work; the teacher brokers access to an environment that supports it rather than completing the work for them.
condition: when distinguishing alignment from spoon-feeding
exception: appropriate scaffolding remains necessary until students can perform independently

statement: Design an aligned course by stating outcome activity, content, context, and standard; eliciting that activity; assessing it with criteria; and translating judgments into standard grading rules.
condition: when implementing the four-stage constructive-alignment design

statement: Write intended learning outcomes from the student's perspective and state the expected level of understanding or performance after the learning experience.
condition: when authoring course outcomes

statement: Replace the ambiguous outcome verb understand with a verb that exposes the required cognitive or practical performance.
condition: when the outcome must guide teaching and assessment

statement: Use verbs such as explain for declarative outcomes and verbs such as apply, reflect, and evaluate for functioning outcomes only when they accurately represent the intended level.
condition: when differentiating kinds and levels of knowledge in outcomes
exception: the same verb may imply different complexity depending on its object, context, and standard

statement: Negotiate unfamiliar learning activities with students when their perspective can reveal what support is needed to enact the outcomes.
condition: when students understand the intended outcomes but are unsure how to produce the required performance
exception: the teacher remains responsible for educational coherence and standards

statement: Use direct teaching to clarify issues learners encounter rather than making exposition the default activity regardless of need.
condition: when pre-reading, independent work, or discussion exposes a need for explanation

statement: Embed learning activities in the authentic workplace or practice context when the outcome requires professional application, reflection, or problem solving.
condition: when students have safe and appropriate access to relevant practice
exception: a valid simulation may be needed when direct workplace activity is unavailable or unsafe

statement: Combine independent preparation, self-questioning, peer partnership, small-group comparison, reflective records, and targeted plenary clarification when each contributes to the outcome verb.
condition: when designing a mixed set of activities for reflective professional learning
exception: do not add a format that lacks a clear role in achieving an outcome

statement: Let learners select authentic portfolio evidence for their outcomes and require them to justify how each item and the portfolio as a whole demonstrate achievement.
condition: when portfolio evidence is an appropriate assessment form
exception: provide enough examples and criteria to make the evidentiary standard intelligible without prescribing every item

statement: Encourage original evidence within a stated range of acceptable forms so learners can demonstrate valid unanticipated outcomes or context-specific application.
condition: when the assessment can remain open without losing comparability of standards

statement: A single task may function as both learning activity and assessment evidence when performing it develops the same outcome whose quality it later demonstrates.
condition: in a tightly aligned design
exception: formative use should remain psychologically safe where early errors are expected

statement: Separate the grading decisions of judging each output against criteria and combining evidence across assessment tasks into a final course grade.
condition: when a course uses multiple pieces of evidence

statement: Use qualitative grading when grades represent distinct qualities of integrated thinking and collective evidence is more meaningful than averaging marks.
condition: when the task and context support holistic judgment against explicit grade descriptions
exception: quantitative combination may be appropriate for other assessment designs

statement: Define each grade category by a defensible quality of learning and understanding rather than by an unexplained accumulation of points or percentages.
condition: when developing course grading criteria
exception: numeric scores may be used as a reporting convention if they faithfully represent the qualitative criteria

statement: Set the highest grade at the best quality reasonably expected for that course and raise the expected performance progressively across programme years.
condition: when calibrating grade standards by course level
exception: specific expectations must be decided by relevant teachers or the programme committee

statement: Treat intended outcomes as the central design decisions from which suitable activities, assessment evidence, and grading criteria follow.
condition: when designing a constructively aligned system

statement: Use the outcome verbs as explicit alignment markers across teaching activities and assessment tasks.
condition: when the same performance can validly appear in all components
exception: mere repetition of a word is not alignment if the demanded level or context differs

statement: Reject coverage as a sufficient curriculum specification; pair content with the level and form of understanding or performance students must demonstrate.
condition: when defining a course curriculum

statement: Audit alignment by checking that every intended performance is practiced and assessed, and that every major teaching or assessment demand traces back to an intended outcome.
condition: when reviewing a course design
exception: open designs may also recognize relevant desirable outcomes that emerge during learning

statement: Use a mismatch between high-level outcome verbs and low-level assessment demands as a direct signal that the assessment is inadequate.
condition: when assessment permits paraphrase or recall for outcomes requiring theory, generalization, reflection, or explanation

statement: Do not use norm-referenced grading in a constructively aligned learning system, because it severs grades from whether individuals met the intended outcomes.
condition: when grades are intended to certify outcome attainment
exception: relative ranking may serve a separate selective purpose but should not be confused with learning certification

statement: Treat large classes, mass lectures, or selected-response tests as design constraints that complicate alignment, not as proof that alignment is impossible.
condition: when resources limit instructional formats
exception: a mandatory curve-based grading policy is incompatible with criterion-referenced alignment and requires policy change

statement: Seek evidence for further improvement even when current teaching is not visibly failing.
condition: when practicing reflective teaching

statement: Align outcomes hierarchically so institutional graduate outcomes inform programme outcomes and programme outcomes are addressed through component courses.
condition: when designing outcomes at multiple organizational levels

statement: For each outcome, state the kind of knowledge, an observable performance verb, the relevant context, and the level at which the performance will be displayed for assessment.
condition: when writing institution, programme, or course outcomes

statement: Distinguish genuinely generic graduate capabilities from capabilities whose meaning and performance are embedded in a discipline or profession.
condition: when defining how graduate outcomes will be taught and assessed

statement: Do not assume that a problem-solving, creative, or critical-thinking performance learned in one domain automatically operates with equal depth in another.
condition: when making claims about generic transfer
exception: some enabling strategies can transfer and should be tested in the target context

statement: Use standalone courses for generic enabling skills such as study strategy, communication, numeracy, or information technology where useful, but not as substitutes for applying higher-order capabilities in disciplinary contexts.
condition: when learners need transferable foundations or targeted support

statement: Include far transfer as an explicit higher-level outcome when students are genuinely expected to adapt learning across domains.
condition: when programme aims require transfer beyond the context of initial learning
exception: do not imply far transfer merely from teaching a generic label

statement: Avoid decomposing broad graduate outcomes into so many sub-goals that monitoring consumes effort better spent developing the outcomes in context.
condition: when designing accountability and assessment systems for graduate capabilities
exception: some decomposition is useful when it clarifies teachable components without overwhelming the curriculum

statement: Treat complex outcomes such as ethical practice, creativity, teamwork, and wisdom as slow-developing achievements fostered across an ethos, repeated experiences, and role models rather than delivered by one course.
condition: when the capability has multiple interacting causes and contexts
exception: a capstone or focused course can help learners integrate and reflect on development across the programme

statement: Use self-assessment, peer assessment, and portfolios with substantiated learner claims for complex graduate outcomes that cannot be validly captured by a single highly reliable test.
condition: when the outcome develops across contexts and requires integrated evidence
exception: evidence still needs transparent standards and appropriate moderation

statement: Make institutional policies and procedures enact the ethical, creative, self-directed, or lifelong-learning outcomes the institution claims to value.
condition: when the institutional climate is expected to foster graduate outcomes

statement: Address graduate outcomes through a coordinated combination of institutional climate, programme and course outcomes, and targeted generic enabling courses.
condition: when setting an institution-wide approach to graduate capability
exception: the mix should depend on the nature of each outcome and local student needs

statement: Derive programme outcomes from the programme's purpose, focus, and professional or disciplinary context, then map relevant graduate outcomes into them.
condition: when translating institution-level outcomes into a degree design

statement: Keep programme outcomes to a small set that expresses the principal reasons the programme exists rather than forcing a large generic template onto every programme.
condition: when writing programme-level intended outcomes
exception: the exact number depends on programme complexity, though the source suggests rarely exceeding about six

statement: Ground graduate outcomes in the content and situations of each programme and use the institutional list as a relevance check, not as a promise of context-free capability.
condition: when programme committees map graduate outcomes

statement: Do not force a graduate outcome into every programme when it is not educationally relevant to that field, because this invites resistance and cynicism.
condition: when applying institution-wide outcome requirements
exception: institution-wide ethical or legal requirements may still need an appropriately contextualized expression

statement: Use an intermediate faculty or college outcome layer when it makes institution-to-programme mapping more coherent and manageable.
condition: when many related programmes share a disciplinary context
exception: an added layer should not create redundant bureaucracy

statement: Align concrete teaching and assessment to course outcomes, while using programme and institutional outcomes to guide what those course outcomes collectively address.
condition: when operationalizing a multilevel outcomes hierarchy

statement: A course outcome should tell a student what performance will be possible after learning that was not possible before, while leaving room for desirable additional outcomes.
condition: when writing course-level intended learning outcomes

statement: Judge an outcome statement by whether students can tell what they must do and how well they must do it to meet the outcome.
condition: when reviewing outcome clarity

statement: Avoid verbs and phrases such as understand, comprehend, be aware of, or demonstrate an understanding unless the statement also makes the specific performance and level unambiguous.
condition: when writing assessable outcomes

statement: Prefer roughly five or six integrated course outcomes that communicate the course's main purposes over a long fragmented inventory that cannot be aligned manageably.
condition: for a typical semester-long course
exception: the appropriate number may differ for an unusually scoped course, but every outcome must remain teachable and assessable
