statement: Consider that a prior norm-referenced system may have depressed grades if more learners meet unchanged standards after aligned activities and transparent assessment.

statement: Monitor staff and student workload as an outcome of constructive-alignment redesign because higher-level learning gains can come with increased burden.
condition: when evaluating a redesigned course
exception: temporary first-run workload should be distinguished from recurring workload

statement: Reject the claim that all predetermined outcomes are behaviourist: qualitative open verbs can specify a process while leaving the learner's product or conclusion undetermined.
condition: when outcomes use verbs such as design, create, hypothesize, or reflect

statement: Use larger controlled longitudinal studies with pre-implementation baselines to relate progressive alignment to lower- and higher-order outcomes, metacognition, independence, satisfaction, learning approaches, and graduate outcomes.
condition: when building stronger evidence for constructive alignment

statement: Investigate implementation costs and which strategies work under which circumstances rather than promoting one universal best-practice rollout.
condition: when translating constructive-alignment evidence into institutional strategy

statement: Align organizational policies, modular structures, rewards, and regulations with course-level teaching because a locally aligned course can fail inside a misaligned institutional system.
condition: when classroom redesign depends on programme or institutional structures

statement: Select external examiners who understand and can work within the department's teaching theory, not solely for subject-matter status.
condition: when an external reviewer can alter assessment and standards
exception: independent challenge remains important, but it should engage the educational rationale rather than ignore it

statement: Do not permit late external changes to examination questions that break alignment with what students were taught and prepared to perform.
condition: when external review occurs after course teaching has substantially progressed

statement: Use external experts as broader educational consultants who advise on assessment and teaching, rather than restricting them to summative paper inspection.
condition: when external perspective is intended to improve rather than merely police standards

statement: Use external panels to assure necessary programme standards while guarding against each panel member adding favored content that produces curriculum overload.
condition: when accrediting or validating new provision

statement: Challenge accreditation requirements that privilege syllabus coverage, marking toughness, stable grade distributions, or fixed invigilated percentages over valid outcome-aligned learning.

statement: Provide a proportionate path to revise validated programmes when evidence, student intake, research, or workload shows the approved design needs material change.

statement: Evaluate teaching against multiple context-sensitive standards and evidence sources rather than a single generic student-rating score used to compare teachers.

statement: After aligning outcomes, learning activities, and assessment, establish feedback from affected parties to monitor implementation and guide adjustments.

statement: Most college teachers set course learning goals no higher than understand-and-remember, with only a minority extending into application learning such as problem solving, thinking, and decision making.
Most college teachers have difficulty identifying teaching activities beyond the two traditional standbys of lecturing and leading discussion.
Classroom-observation studies find the number of questions a teacher asks in a one-hour class period is very low, and sustained student-to-student discussion is extremely rare.

Weak college teaching is partly structural, not merely individual fault: doctoral programs direct nearly all attention to research capability, new faculty are rarely given means to learn teaching, and the reward system signals that publication is the first priority.

Changing how teachers teach requires four conditions in sequence: seeing that significantly different ways of teaching exist, being persuaded those ways produce good outcomes for students and for themselves, receiving guidance on how to do it, and having their institution recognize and support the effort.
A taxonomy of significant learning is needed to give teachers vocabulary for formulating course learning goals that reach beyond understand-and-remember and beyond application learning.
condition: when a teacher or institution wants to provide a learning-centered education

statement: The power of instructional-design ideas comes from linking them to one another rather than adopting them singly; an experiential exercise becomes more potent when linked to reflective dialogue, and authentic assessment becomes more meaningful when linked to student self-assessment.
Learning about and implementing new teaching ideas costs time and effort, so teachers need stronger institutional support for changing how they teach than most currently receive.
Higher education will not meet demand for better quality until professors act as designers of learning experiences rather than as teachers in the transmission sense.

A Gallup survey of college seniors reported that roughly 42 percent did not know the Koran is the sacred scripture of Islam, 42 percent could not place the Civil War between 1850 and 1900, and 31 percent placed Reconstruction after World War II.

A multifaceted study of college student performance on reflexive thinking and metacognition found students could identify main points and supporting evidence but showed little growth during college in identifying implications, articulating an author's assumptions, or relating an argument to their own lives and society.

The same study found students weak in problem-solving and reasoning, in recognizing the assumptions needed to solve a problem, in scientific reasoning and the role of controls, and in establishing chronology and causal relations among historical events.
The core cause of poor learning outcomes is a mismatch: faculty say they want higher-order learning but continue to use a form of teaching that is not effective at producing it.
In a study of eighteen hundred faculty across five institution types, 73 to 83 percent named lecture as their primary method of instruction.

A long history of research indicates lecturing, even good lecturing, has limited effectiveness at helping students retain information after the course, transfer knowledge to novel situations, develop thinking or problem-solving skill, and achieve affective outcomes such as motivation or attitude change.

In a controlled test of a deliberately well-designed lecture, students' average recall was 42 percent immediately afterward and had fallen to 20 percent one week later, even though they could use their own notes and a printed summary and were re-taking the same test.

In a comparison of over twelve hundred students, those who completed a year-long introductory economics course outscored students who never took it by only 20 percent at course end, 15 percent after two years, and 10 percent after seven years.

Faculty report a recurring cluster of symptoms of failing instruction: attendance near 50 percent by mid-semester in lower-division courses, unread assignments, low energy in discussion, students focused on grades rather than learning, ever-larger textbooks forcing more coverage, lost joy in teaching, and feeling unsupported when they try to change.

In an extensive study of student reaction to instruction, students' most common criticism targeted teachers relying primarily on lecture and workbook exercises to transmit information, the absence of interaction, and the lack of hands-on learning.

Students in that study were not self-directed learners, lacked confidence in figuring out a problem on their own, sensed they were not learning as much as they should, and believed many college teachers do not care about them or their learning.
Students disengage from learning they do not want to do or see no reason for doing.
Students report feeling fragmented, because their courses do not connect to one another, and isolated, because they have little course-related interaction with other students inside or outside class.

Although teachers commonly expect two hours of out-of-class study per class hour, which would be about thirty hours a week for a full-time load, studies of actual study time repeatedly find most students spend six hours or less per week across all their courses combined.
Course design is the right place to integrate new teaching ideas and is the single most significant change most teachers can make to improve the quality of their teaching and of student learning.
A significant learning experience has both a process dimension and an outcome dimension, and each dimension has two defining features, so a course must be judged on both rather than on either alone.
The process features of a significant learning experience are that students are engaged in their own learning and that the class has a high energy level.

The outcome features of a significant learning experience are significant and lasting change in the students that persists after the course and after graduation, and learning with high potential value in students' later lives.

Significant learning offers value along at least one of three axes: enhancing the individual's own life, enabling contribution to the communities the learner belongs to, and preparing the learner for the world of work.

A college education depends on three ingredients — good curriculum, good instruction, and faculty who interact well with students — and if any one is done badly the quality of the whole educational experience drops significantly.
Among the three ingredients, instruction quality is the critically important one: exciting course titles and kind faculty cannot compensate for instruction that is not done well.

Faculty will only invest time in learning new ways of teaching if they judge there is a potential benefit with sufficient value and sufficient likelihood to justify the effort, because nearly all faculty already feel fully loaded with teaching, research, and service.

The motivational basis for a teacher to change comes from surfacing their own inner dream of what their teaching could be, which is usually significantly different from their everyday classroom experience.

A workable way to elicit a teacher's real goals is a dreaming exercise: ask them to imagine a perfect situation with no student-compliance constraint, then ask what they would want to be true of their students one or two years after the course that is not true of others.
condition: used at the start of a course-design workshop or design process

statement: When asked about their dreams for students, teachers reliably name outcomes far beyond content coverage — real-life application, deep curiosity, lifelong learning, joy of learning, integrated rather than compartmentalized thinking, creative problem solving, communication skill, community building, resilience, mentoring, and critical thinking.
Having teachers render their dream in an artistic form and then share it in small groups enlarges and enhances the dream, because peers add complementary goals to it.
condition: in a facilitated group workshop setting

statement: Faculty are unlikely to decide to change without institutional support, meaning time, encouragement, instructional-development centers that supply ideas, and reward.

Institutions that keep an Industrial Age factory model are at a growing competitive disadvantage because they are insufficiently flexible, focus on processes and outputs such as graduates rather than on outcomes such as significant learning, and operate at high cost.

Traditional institutions are losing their monopoly on postsecondary learning to corporate universities, for-profit providers, and online universities, so the decisive competitive requirement becomes the ability to offer a high-quality learning experience better, sooner, and at lower cost in time, effort, and money.

Four interacting forces are driving structural change in higher education: information technology, the emergence of new educational providers, globalization of course and degree offerings, and new kinds of students.

Traditional measures of institutional excellence are inadequate because they measure resources and inputs rather than what students actually learn and how much they grow between entrance and graduation.

National reports since the 1980s have urged institutions to produce demonstrable improvement not only in student knowledge but in students' capabilities, skills, and attitudes, which is an explicit call for courses to go beyond content learning.

Professional accreditation bodies have moved beyond technical competence and now require graduates to demonstrate general professional skills such as effective communication and broad professional perspectives such as understanding an engineering solution's global and societal impact.
condition: in accredited pre-professional programs such as engineering under ABET 2000

statement: Employers and major studies converge on a list of critical competencies graduates need: conscientiousness and dependability, principled ethical action, oral and written communication, interpersonal and team skills, critical thinking and complex problem solving, respect for people different from oneself, adaptability to change, and the ability and desire for lifelong learning.

A survey of 140 college teachers found 75 to 80 percent said they value and act to promote critical thinking, but only 19 percent could clearly explain what critical thinking is, only 9 percent were clearly teaching for it on a typical day, and only 8 percent could name the criteria and standards by which they judge student thinking.

Claiming to teach a competency is weak evidence that it is being taught; the operational test is whether the teacher can define the competency and state the criteria and standards used to evaluate student work against it.

The shift from an instruction paradigm to a learning paradigm redefines mission from improving instruction quality to improving learning quality, success criteria from quality of entering students to quality of exiting students, and structures from covering material to specific learning results.

Under the learning paradigm the faculty role changes from primarily lecturer to primarily designer of learning methods and environments, and productivity is measured as cost per unit of learning per student rather than cost per hour of instruction per student.

The goal should be stated as producing significant learning, not merely producing learning, because the learning-paradigm formulation alone does not specify the quality or durability of what is learned.

The new teaching paradigm treats knowledge as jointly constructed by students and faculty, the student as an active constructor and transformer of knowledge, and the mode of learning as relating rather than memorizing.

The new paradigm shifts assessment from norm-referenced grading on the curve with multiple-choice items and end-of-course ratings, to criterion-referenced grading against predefined standards using performances and portfolios with continual assessment of instruction.
The new paradigm rejects the assumption that any expert can teach, holding instead that teaching is complex and requires considerable training.

People learn only from activities that are interesting and comprehensible to them; when an activity is not satisfying in that sense, only inefficient rote memorization is available and forgetting follows.

Students take either a deep approach to learning, seeking personal meaningful understanding, or a surface approach, content to reproduce presented information; teachers must therefore attend to the quality of learning their teaching and assessment produce, not only to how much is learned.

Role-playing, simulation, debate, and case studies give students an experience with psychological and social as well as intellectual dimensions, and are a clear alternative to teaching as dispensing information.

Writing can be used as an integral part of the learning process to enhance the process and quality of student learning, not only as an after-the-fact assessment device such as term papers and essay exams.

Small groups can create powerful learning about the subject, the problem-solving process, oneself, working with others, and cross-cultural awareness, but only given the right kind of structure and assignments.
condition: given appropriate group structure and assignment design

statement: Assessment can be built into the learning process itself: frequent, usually ungraded feedback lets students improve the quality of their learning and lets teachers gauge which teaching strategies are working.

In problem-based learning the problem comes first: students meet an open-ended, ill-defined problem and must make a preliminary analysis, gather data, judge the relevance of new information, propose a solution, and assess its quality.
Evidence indicates students learn to analyze and solve problems much more effectively under problem-based learning than under a curriculum that front-loads two years of facts before any application.

Service learning adds a dimension of quality by pairing a course topic with a related community activity that combines service to others with the chance to observe significant community problems firsthand.

Teaching decomposes into four aspects — knowledge of subject matter, design of instruction, teacher-student interaction, and course management — of which the first two happen mainly before the course begins and the last two after it begins.

Subject-matter knowledge is not the major bottleneck to better college teaching, because graduate school and faculty selection already select strongly for it, though some faculty would benefit from rethinking what a beginning learner rather than an expert needs.
Teacher-student interaction skill ranges from poor to excellent across faculty, so improving it is a major advance for a significant percentage of teachers but not the primary problem for the rest.

Of the four aspects of teaching, faculty knowledge about course design is the most significant bottleneck, because few college teachers have training in it and most simply follow their discipline's traditional practice, lacking the conceptual tools to rethink their teaching and learning activities.
When students do not prepare before class, redesigning the course to give students a reason to do the reading is a better response than adding penalties or giving a pep talk.

When students are bored, redesigning the course to replace lecturing with more active learning has greater potential to raise learning quality than polishing lecturing skill or adding cutting-edge research content.

When students pass exams but cannot retain knowledge into later courses, redesigning the course to give more experience using what was learned is better supported by research than tougher tests or a refresher course, because application opportunities deepen understanding and retention.

Learning to design courses is the missing link that integrates new teaching ideas, solves major teaching problems, gives teachers a route to their own dreams, and gives institutions a direction for improving curricula and instruction.

A good course meets five criteria: it challenges students to significant kinds of learning, uses active forms of learning, has a teacher who cares about the subject, the students, and teaching and learning, has a teacher who interacts well with students, and has a good system of feedback, assessment, and grading.

Challenging students to significant learning is the single most important of the five criteria: if it is achieved the learning experience was good regardless of other weaknesses, and if the five criteria are not met the teaching is poor regardless of other strengths.

Bloom's cognitive taxonomy arranges six kinds of learning hierarchically — evaluation, synthesis, analysis, application, comprehension, and knowledge as recall — and has been used both to formulate objectives and to test learning.

Bloom's cognitive taxonomy does not readily yield several kinds of learning now demanded — learning how to learn, leadership and interpersonal skills, ethics, communication, character, tolerance, and adaptability — because these go beyond the cognitive domain and even beyond cognitive learning itself.
Learning is defined as change in the learner: no change means no learning, and significant learning requires a lasting change that matters in the learner's life.

A language for learning goals must work across a wide range of disciplines and learning situations and satisfy the needs of faculty, students, administrators, disciplinary associations, and employer groups alike.
The taxonomy of significant learning has six categories: foundational knowledge, application, integration, human dimension, caring, and learning how to learn.

Foundational knowledge means understanding and remembering specific information, ideas, and major perspectives, and its special value is providing the basic understanding that other kinds of learning require.

Application learning covers new kinds of action that may be intellectual, physical, or social — critical, creative, and practical thinking, skills, and managing complex projects — and its special value is making other kinds of learning useful.

Integration is seeing connections between specific ideas, between whole realms of ideas, between people, or between realms of life such as school and work, and its special value is giving the learner a new form of intellectual power.

The human dimension is learning something important about oneself, such as a new self-image or self-ideal, or about others, such as why they act as they do, and its special value is informing students about the human significance of what they are learning.
Caring is a change in the degree or kind to which a student cares about something, expressed as new feelings, interests, or values.
Caring supplies the energy for learning: when students care about something they gain the energy to learn more about it, and without that energy nothing significant happens.

Learning how to learn covers becoming a better student, learning a mode of inquiry such as the scientific method, and becoming a self-directing learner; its special value is enabling students to keep learning in the future with greater effectiveness.
The taxonomy of significant learning is not hierarchical but relational and interactive: each kind of learning relates to the others, and achieving one enhances the possibility of achieving the rest.
Because the kinds of learning are synergistic, teaching is not a zero-sum game: a teacher does not have to sacrifice one kind of learning to achieve another.

Concrete synergies illustrate the interaction: helping students apply course concepts to solve problems makes it easier for them to get excited about the subject, and helping them relate the subject to other subjects makes it easier for them to see its significance for themselves and others.
A learning experience can be deemed truly significant when the course promotes all six kinds of learning.

A course's learning goals should include content mastery but also go beyond it, because including more than foundational knowledge makes the learning experience inherently more worthwhile and more interesting for learners.
Using a combination of significant learning goals rather than a single kind creates interaction effects and synergy that greatly enhance students' achievement of significant learning.

A generic set of significant learning goals can be stated as: by the end of the course students will understand and remember key concepts, know how to use the content, be able to relate the subject to other subjects, understand its personal and social implications, care about the subject, and know how to keep learning about it after the course ends.

General-form course goals deliberately leave the specific concepts, relationships, and uses of content unspecified, on the expectation that they will become clear as students work through readings, lectures, and application exercises.
condition: when the teacher prefers to state goals in general terms

statement: Course-specific learning goals are written as statements of what students will be able to do after the course is over, with one or more concrete goals under each of the six taxonomy categories.

A worked example of category-specific goals for a world regional geography course pairs foundational goals such as holding a mental map of the world with caring goals such as wanting to keep learning about other places, and learning-how-to-learn goals such as interpreting the geographic significance of information encountered in future.
Each of the familiar curricular goals in the college-teaching literature expresses one kind of significant learning, and none of them captures the whole of significant learning on its own.

Teaching factual knowledge is insufficient; a teacher's responsibility includes helping students grasp the underlying conceptual structure or logic of the subject, because a powerful command of foundational knowledge is more than a large collection of poorly related facts.

Goals commonly listed under learning how to learn include self-regulated or deep learning, learning a discipline's mode of inquiry, and self-directed intentional learning with a learning agenda and reflective practice.

Goals commonly listed under the human dimension include leadership, ethics and character building, self-authorship, multicultural sensitivity, teamwork, citizenship, service to others, and environmental ethics.

Goals commonly listed under integration include interdisciplinary learning that connects disciplines and perspectives, learning communities that connect people, and connecting learning with living and working.

Goals commonly listed under application include critical thinking, practical thinking for problem solving and decision making, creativity, managing complex projects, and performance skills such as language, communication, technology operation, fine arts, and sport.

Conceptual understanding means understanding a subject's concepts well enough to explain and predict with them, which is a different target from being able to perform the calculations in routine exercise problems.
Nearly all kinds of significant learning rest on an in-depth understanding of some subject matter, which is why that layer is labelled foundational knowledge.
Application learning has three distinct meanings that should not be conflated: developing particular skills, learning to manage complex projects, and learning to engage in various kinds of thinking.

Most skills have criteria that distinguish competent or expert performance from novice performance, and the goal of skill-focused learning is to move learners along that continuum toward higher competence.
What distinguishes managing a complex project from other application learning is the complexity itself: the student must organize and coordinate several tasks as parts of one major project.

An authentic complex project can be built by having students produce and pitch a real proposal to a real client, which forces them to learn subject content, information gathering, modelling tools, and the politics and marketing needed to sell the idea.

A complex research project develops general project-management ability because students must sequence subtasks: focusing the topic, finding sources, extracting key ideas, and organizing them into a coherent paper or presentation.

Teachers and writers who say they want students to learn to think are often referring to very different things, because the term is complex and attractive enough that people use it as a label for whatever learning they favour.

Thinking is best treated as the general concept with three distinct subcategories — critical, creative, and practical thinking — rather than using critical thinking as the umbrella term, so critical thinking is one of three rather than the whole.
Critical thinking is analyzing and evaluating something, so explicit criteria play an especially important role in it.
Creative thinking is imagining and creating a new idea, design, or product, and is judged by novelty together with fit to the context.

Practical thinking is using and applying something to solve a problem or make a decision; its product is a solution or decision and the paramount criterion is the effectiveness of that solution or decision.
The three kinds of thinking can be operationalized as three differently-shaped questions on the same course topic, so a teacher can check which kind of thinking an assignment actually asks for.
To think critically students need both the relevant conceptual understanding and criteria for assessing the quality of interpretations, explanations, and predictions.
Practical thinking can be exercised with hypothetical, simulated, or real problems, and the ability transfers to students' personal, social, and work lives.

Interdisciplinary learning is justified because most of the world's big problems are bigger than any single discipline, so graduates must be able to view a problem from two or more disciplinary perspectives and work with people who hold them.

Interdisciplinary learning can be delivered at several scales — one teacher presenting multiple disciplinary perspectives, team teaching, coordinated courses, interdisciplinary programs, or a whole college curriculum — all aiming at a more holistic understanding of a problem.

Learning communities pursue integration by connecting diverse people as well as diverse disciplines, using devices such as residential arrangements, linked course sets taken by the same cohort, and bringing outside people in or sending students out.

An alternative community structure puts the subject at the centre with teacher and students arranged around it learning about it together, creating a different relationship among teacher, students, and subject.

Academic work can be connected to other realms of life through oral-history interviews with family members, internships and real-world work alongside coursework, service learning, and journals in which students note personal events reflecting the subject.
Learning about self and others differs from learning about people in the abstract, and the difference is the existence of a real relationship.

Learning about the Self takes two forms: a changed self-image, which is understanding who one is now, and a new self-ideal, which is a picture of the person one wants to become; either can happen intentionally or as a by-product of formal education.

Authentic project work can produce a new self-image and self-ideal simultaneously, as when a student doing real professional work is recognized as professional by peers and consequently decides to enter that profession.

Longitudinal research supports self-authorship as a valid teaching goal: college teachers can do more than they currently do to help students internally define their own beliefs, identity, and relationships.

Self-authorship rests on the premises that knowledge is complex and socially constructed and that the Self is central to knowledge construction, so students need a strong sense of identity before they can take responsibility for constructing their own knowledge.

Cross-cultural learning about others can arise from group work when a team notices a member's participation pattern, learns the cultural reason behind it, and redesigns its own procedure to accommodate it.
Direct community-service experience followed by written reflection can change how students see and subsequently interact with people in less fortunate circumstances.

The human dimension of learning parallels emotional intelligence, which splits into personal competence — self-awareness, self-regulation, and motivation — and social competence in interacting with others.
Learning about Self and learning about Others are reciprocal: teaching one almost inevitably produces the other, so a teacher who designs for one kind will likely get both.

Human-dimension learning is applicable in all or almost all disciplines, including the natural sciences, because even a technical field's major figures, motivations, and working relationships are content students can learn about themselves and others through.

When teachers are asked what they most want students to get out of a course, a frequent answer is that students should get excited about the subject or about learning itself, which is a caring goal — a change in what students value.
Caring outcomes can be targeted at five distinct foci: the phenomena studied, the ideas studied, the student's own Self, the Others encountered in the class, and the process of learning itself.
Caring about the process of learning itself is the most powerful of the caring foci, because students then care not only about phenomena and ideas but about learning more of them.

Because the volume of knowledge in every subject keeps growing, the only strategy with any hope is to identify the fundamental knowledge of a subject, ensure students master that, and then teach them how to keep learning after the course ends.

Learning how to learn has three valid and distinct meanings — learning to be a better student, learning to inquire and construct knowledge, and learning to be a self-directing learner — and each leads to different recommendations for teachers.
Self-regulated learning targets three dimensions of a student's learning: observable behavior, motivation and affect, and cognition.

Practitioners report five moves that shift students toward a deep approach to learning: developing their concept of learning and knowledge itself, developing metacognitive awareness and control, providing space and freedom to explore personal interests, making assessment demands explicit so students see that only full understanding is acceptable, and changing teaching methods to be more active and interactive.
Training students in study skills alone does not have the same effect as changing their orientation to learning.

Because the nature of knowledge differs by domain, how one adds to that knowledge also differs by domain, so students must be taught the inquiry method specific to each domain rather than a generic one.

Inquiry teaching holds that a science education should teach how scientific inquiry works, not only the results of other people's inquiry, which in practice means helping students learn to formulate questions and then seek the information that answers them.

The goal of education can be framed as producing a change in the meaning of experience rather than a change in behavior, which directs teachers to help learners reflect on experience and construct more powerful meanings.

The Knowledge Vee makes explicit that any knowledge claim has a theoretical or conceptual dimension and a methodological dimension, and that inquiry requires alternating between the two in an escalating search for knowledge claims.
When students learn to construct knowledge on their own their efforts lead to meaningful learning rather than rote learning.

Concept mapping — asking students to diagram the relationships among the concepts of a unit — prompts them to make sense of what they learned, to see that others may organize the same concepts differently, and to link new concepts to prior understanding.
Learning how to learn in the self-directing sense involves two general steps: diagnosing one's own learning needs and designing a learning plan.

Because adults learn on their own all the time, the teacher's role for adult learners is facilitator of learning rather than transmitter of knowledge, and the self-directing learner's key capability is critical reflection on alternative ways of understanding an experience.
condition: with adult and self-directing learners

statement: Self-directed learning must be distinguished along two axes — as goal versus method, and in life versus in the student role — yielding personal autonomy, autodidaxy, self-managed learning, and learner-controlled activities as four different targets.

A pick-a-topic independent study with a report back to class promotes self-directed learning only as a method inside the student role; without critical reflection on the process it does not build self-managed learning, and without asking what else the student should learn beyond the topic and why it does not build autodidaxy or personal autonomy.
exception: unless the activity is accompanied by critical reflection on the learning process and by the broader question of what to learn next and why

statement: A teacher can promote fuller self-directed learning by making use of learners' existing knowledge structures, encouraging deep-level learning, increasing questioning by the learners, developing their critical thinking, enhancing reading skills, and enhancing their monitoring of their own learning.

Learners are often not ready for mature self-direction and may progress through four stages — dependent, interested, involved, self-directed — with the teacher's role changing significantly at each stage.

Professional education should not separate studying the principles of good practice from applying them, because good professionals are reflective practitioners who reflect on what they are doing while doing it, and the curriculum must support learning both tasks simultaneously.
condition: in professional schools

statement: Under the content-centered paradigm a teacher answers what students should learn by listing topics; under the learning-centered paradigm the teacher answers by naming kinds of learning.
The content-centered paradigm expands a course along one dimension only, adding topics, and is driven by continuous new research and ever-larger textbooks into a coverage race the teacher cannot win.
The learning-centered paradigm keeps attention on important content but expands the course into multiple dimensions of learning rather than more content.

The coverage objection is answered by facts teachers already accept: no course covers everything students will need, talking faster each year is neither effective nor attractive, and research indicates cramming more material into a course does not produce learning that lasts.

Taking a long-term view of learning means identifying the most important topics in the course and simultaneously promoting multiple kinds of learning, so that students are more likely to keep learning after the course is over.

The learning-centered paradigm does not abandon content: content is renamed foundational knowledge and other kinds of learning are wrapped around it, so acquiring knowledge becomes the basis for further learning rather than the sole purpose of the course.

Faculty dreams for their students map onto the taxonomy's non-content categories rather than onto content coverage, so the learning-centered paradigm brings faculty closer to their own goals than the content-centered one.

Defining teaching goals in terms of the taxonomy of significant learning does not by itself improve the quality of student learning; the goals must be realized through designing the learning experience.
Unless a course is designed properly, all the other components of effective teaching will have only limited impact.

The list-of-topics approach builds a course by naming eight to twelve topics from the teacher's own knowledge or a textbook's table of contents, working up a lecture on each, and adding a midterm and a final.

The list-of-topics approach is attractive because it takes thirty to forty-five minutes, but it organizes information while ignoring how that information will be learned, so it typically supports only foundational knowledge, which has a relatively short half-life.

In integrated course design the teacher takes responsibility for deciding what would constitute high-quality learning in the given situation and then designs that quality into the course and the learning experience.

Designing any learning experience requires answering five key questions in order: what the important situational factors are, what the full set of learning goals should be, what feedback and assessment to provide, what teaching and learning activities will achieve the goals, and whether all components are connected and mutually supportive.
Feedback and assessment should be designed before teaching and learning activities, because settling assessment first greatly clarifies which teaching and learning activities are needed.

Backward design proceeds in three time-reversed moves: imagine one or two years after the course and ask what learning should still be there and have value, then move to the end of the course and ask what students would have to do to convince the teacher they achieved it, then move into the course and ask what students need to do to be able to do well on those assessments.
Working out what students would have to do to prove they achieved a learning goal clarifies the real meaning of that goal.
A course can be designed successfully in either order, activities first or assessment first; backward design is preferred on experience rather than because the other order fails.

The three primary components — learning goals, teaching and learning activities, and feedback and assessment — must reflect and support each other; the model's core proposition is that they be integrated, not merely present.
Covering the content is a statement of what the teacher does, not what students do, so it is not a learning goal and must be restated as what students will be able to do.
A straight lecture course with only a midterm and final is disconnected from a critical-thinking goal, because students get no practice and no feedback on thinking even if they do learn the content.
A diagnostic for a badly designed course is to trace each stated learning goal to the activity that practises it and the assessment that measures it, and name the missing links.

Integrated course design has twelve steps in three phases: an initial phase building strong primary components (situational factors, learning goals, feedback and assessment, teaching and learning activities, integration check), an intermediate phase assembling a coherent whole (thematic course structure, teaching strategy, overall scheme of learning activities), and a final phase of remaining tasks (grading system, debugging problems, writing the syllabus, planning evaluation of the course and the teaching).
The twelve steps build on each other, so the early steps must be finished and done properly before the later steps are attempted.
Skipping or superficially doing the situational-factors step increases the chance of a course that does not work for the students, does not meet the curriculum's needs, or does not fit the teacher.

The situational-factors checklist has six groups: the specific context, expectations of external groups, the nature of the subject, characteristics of the learners, characteristics of the teacher, and the special pedagogical challenge.
Only some situational factors matter for any given course, but going through the whole list systematically is what surfaces the ones that do.
Specific-context questions are always important: class size, course level, length and frequency of meetings, and delivery mode all bear on key design decisions.

External expectations that constrain a course include what society needs from graduates in the subject, state or professional accreditation requirements, and institutional or departmental curricular goals such as writing across the curriculum, major recruitment or filtering, and licensing-exam preparation.
Whether a subject is convergent, aiming at a single correct answer, or divergent, aiming at multiple valid interpretations, must be reflected in how the course is designed.

Whether the subject is primarily cognitive or also involves significant physical skills, and whether the field is stable, changing rapidly, or contested between competing paradigms, are design-relevant properties of the subject.
When a discipline is contested between old and new paradigms, some courses in the curriculum should inform students of the controversy and help them develop a thoughtful response of their own.
condition: when the field is undergoing a paradigm or method controversy

statement: Learner factors that change the design include students' life situation and work or family responsibilities, their life or professional goals, their reasons for enrolling, their prior experience, knowledge, skills, and attitudes toward the subject, and their learning styles.

Students arrive with different affective states toward different subjects — high fear or anxiety in subjects such as maths or statistics, anticipation in others — and this prior feeling is a design input.

Some students work well in online and distance delivery and others do not, so the finding can be used both to advise students on enrolment and to decide how much student support to build into the course design.
condition: for online or distance-delivered courses

statement: The teacher is a situational factor too: prior experience with the subject, whether this is the first or last time teaching it, and whether the subject sits at the edge of the teacher's competence all affect preparation time and the level of risk that is safe in choosing a teaching strategy.

A teacher should honestly assess their own interaction, course-management, and design skills: if these are still basic, keep the course design close to the comfort zone; if they are well developed, take on more challenging goals and more powerful strategies.

A teacher's tacit philosophy of teaching is worth examining and revising over the long term, but in the short term when designing a given course it should be taken as given and the design shaped accordingly.
condition: when designing a specific course under time constraint

statement: How much the teacher actually cares about the students and how exciting they find the subject are personal factors that must be taken into account in the design process.
After reviewing situational factors, ask one integrating question — what is the special pedagogical challenge of this course — because meeting that challenge makes success for the students likely.

Special pedagogical challenges are often about a student preconception rather than about content: fear that a subject is unintelligible, belief that it is merely common sense already known, or a single dominant episode crowding out the rest of the field.

Situational information can be collected with survey questionnaires and achievement tests as well as informal discussion, which is worth doing where assumptions tend to conflict with real understanding of the situation.
A thorough situational analysis often suggests the answers to the next design questions — the learning goals, the meaningful forms of feedback and assessment, and the appropriate activities.
Content expertise is the wrong tool for setting learning goals; it belongs later, in creating the course structure and the learning activities within it.
Only after describing the intended learning with the taxonomy or an equivalent formulation can a teacher select the teaching and learning activities and the feedback and assessment that support it.

The procedure for formulating learning goals is to ask, for each of the six kinds of learning, what that kind of learning would mean in the context of this specific course, and answer at least the most important question in each set.

Framing the goal question as what should be true of students a year or more after the course focuses on lasting impact and prevents the teacher from writing down course activities in place of desired outcomes.

Each learning goal should begin with a verb, and the verb should be as concrete and specific as possible, because that is what clarifies for both teacher and students what students should be able to do.

The goal-setting prompts per category are: which key facts, terms, concepts, and perspectives to understand and remember; which kinds of thinking, skills, and complex projects to learn; which connections to recognize within the course, across courses, and to personal, social, and work life; what to learn about oneself and about interacting with others; what changes in feelings, interests, and values; and how to be a good student, inquire in the subject, and become a self-directing learner with a learning agenda and plan.

Learning goals across all six categories can be written for any discipline, including highly technical ones, as shown by parallel goal sets for microbiology, art history, and statistics under the same six headings.
Foundational-knowledge goals should be limited to what is genuinely important for students to hold in long-term memory one to three years later, not everything the course introduces.

A course may legitimately introduce far more material than its retention goals name; the worked example keeps only certain terms, one framing concept, and the primary categories as what should survive years later.

Application goals are derived by asking which situations students are likely to be in one to three years later where the course learning is relevant, and what they should be able to do in those situations — evaluate, analyze, create, design, or calculate.

Integration goals require choosing which kind of connection matters for this subject — to everyday life, to other realms of study, or to closely related subjects — since all are valid but the teacher must decide.

Human-dimension goals are set by asking whether students should see themselves in some new way, for example as carrying a new responsibility for social leadership on the topic, and whether they should gain a new understanding of interacting with others in relation to the subject.
Accepting a human-dimension goal commits the course to more than theory and content: students must learn how the theories and content affect their own lives and their interactions with others.
If a teacher wants students to value the subject more highly, that should be written down as an explicit course goal rather than left as an unstated hope.
A single course can address all three forms of learning how to learn — being a better student, inquiring in this subject matter, and self-direction — provided the goals are selective and focused.
condition: if the goals are kept selective and focused

statement: Each taxonomy category has a characteristic verb set — remember/understand/identify for foundational knowledge; use/judge/calculate/critique/create/manage/solve/analyze for application; connect/relate/integrate/compare for integration; come to see themselves as, understand others in terms of, decide to become for the human dimension; get excited about, be more interested in, value, be ready to for caring; read and study effectively, frame useful questions, set a learning agenda, create a learning plan for learning how to learn.

The more of the six kinds of significant learning a course sets as goals and genuinely supports, the better each individual kind of learning happens, so five or six goals produce fuller learning in each than one or two.
condition: provided each goal is really supported by activities and assessment, not merely stated

statement: The mechanism behind the more-is-better effect is designing powerful learning activities that make students aware of what they are learning and how it all relates, not the mere listing of extra goals.

A teacher's own deep dreams for students should be translated into explicit course goals during goal formulation, since the language of significant learning lets them be stated in a controlled and focused way.
Many teachers reduce feedback and assessment to two midterms and a final, and both teachers and students experience the resulting grading and exam-taking as the most distasteful part of the course.

A main reason exams are onerous for both parties is that teachers hold too limited a view of feedback and assessment; the view must be expanded toward educative assessment just as the view of goals must be expanded toward significant learning.
The aim of grading and assessment design is procedures that support learning rather than hinder it.
Audit-ive assessment serves only to audit student learning as a basis for the grade; it is backward-looking, checking whether students got what was covered over the preceding weeks.
A course whose only feedback and assessment are two midterms and a final is by definition operating under the audit-ive perspective.
The primary purpose of educative assessment is to help students learn better, going beyond recording the results of learning while still supplying a valid and fair basis for grades.
Educative assessment has four components: forward-looking assessment, criteria and standards, self-assessment, and FIDeLity feedback.
FIDeLity feedback is feedback that is frequent, immediate, discriminating in the sense of resting on clear criteria and standards, and delivered lovingly.

Implementing the four components of educative assessment gives teacher and students a clearer picture of whether learning is happening correctly, which in turn lets students begin monitoring and evaluating their own learning — a prerequisite for becoming self-directing learners.
Assessment results can simply be announced, but feedback must be a back-and-forth dialogue, because the giver needs a response to know the message was understood.
Feedback need not come only from the teacher; good teachers also generate it from other students and occasionally from an outside expert brought in for the purpose.

Students need practice at self-assessment inside the course, because the criteria and standards are new to them and because after the course the learner is the one primarily responsible for judging whether their own work is worthwhile.

Criteria and standards are not one component among four but the precondition for the other three: feedback, forward-looking assessment, and self-assessment cannot be done properly without clear and appropriate criteria and standards.

Backward-looking assessment asks whether students got topics X, Y, and Z; forward-looking assessment asks students to imagine a situation where people actually use that knowledge and to use X, Y, and Z to act in it.

Assessment must be anchored in authentic tasks because those supply valid direction, intellectual coherence, and motivation for day-to-day knowledge and skill development; assessment is authentic when testing is anchored in the kind of work people actually do rather than in easy-to-score responses to simple questions.

An authentic assessment task is realistic, requires judgment and innovation on an unstructured problem rather than following a routine, and asks the student to do the subject by exploring and working within the discipline rather than reciting content.

An authentic task replicates a real context with its particular constraints, purposes, and audiences, whereas typical school tests are contextless; real contexts are messy and murky and therefore demand good judgment.

An authentic task assesses the efficient and effective use of a whole repertoire of knowledge and skill on a complex task, because conventional test items are isolated elements of performance like sideline drills and performance is always more than the sum of the drills.
exception: drill tests still have a place for practising isolated elements

statement: Authentic assessment gives students appropriate opportunities to rehearse, practise, consult resources, get feedback, and refine performances and products; the secure secret test still has a role but must coexist with educative assessment if performance is to improve.
exception: the conventional secure test that withholds questions and resources retains a limited role

statement: Learning should be focused on realistic meaningful tasks through cycles of performance, feedback, revision, and new performance, so students learn to use information, resources, and notes to perform effectively in context.

A backward-looking item can be converted to a forward-looking one by wrapping the same content in a decision scenario with a client, constraints, and a recommendation, so students must select which information matters, compare cases, and defend a best choice.

A forward-looking task works partly because the needed information was never presented in that form in the text or in class, forcing students to decide which information is relevant and to articulate the reasoning behind their answer to defend it.

Exercising — repeating a taught protocol over homework problems with slightly different parameters — provides useful practice and familiarity in the early stages of learning but is not the same thing as forward-looking assessment.
condition: exercising is appropriate in the early stages of learning a protocol

statement: Students find more intellectual excitement and motivation when challenged to use new knowledge on realistic tasks they can relate to than when repeating exercises.
The key question for developing forward-looking assessment is what the teacher is preparing students to do, phrased operationally as: having studied and learned X, is the student ready to do Y?

A learning portfolio assessed by both a faculty member and a practising professional, judged against the single question of readiness to practise, is a working instance of institution-level forward-looking assessment.

All assessment measures the quality of something and therefore requires a yardstick, so a course needs a clear and appropriate rubric of criteria and standards; students need to know what constitutes high-quality performance in what they are learning.

A four-year longitudinal collection of every writing assignment and returned paper for over a hundred students found that in the majority of assignments and returned evaluations, the criteria and standards used to judge the writing were not clear even to the researcher.
Empirical evidence shows faculty frequently omit explicit criteria and standards, so the obvious-seeming need for them is in practice a common failure point rather than a solved problem.

Primary Trait Analysis builds a rubric in four steps: get clear about the objectives for the assignment, identify the traits that will count in the evaluation, construct a two- to five-point scale per trait with descriptive statements of good and poor versions, and try the scale out on a sample of students or colleagues and revise.
A standard on a rubric scale is written as a description of what performance at that level looks like, not as a bare numeric label, in both science and humanities examples.

Criteria are derived from the course learning goal: an application goal naming three verbs, such as design, construct, and assess, yields three criteria clusters, each of which then gets its own multi-point standards describing levels of quality.

Working through learning goals into explicit criteria and standards gave one professor the clarity and tools needed for a range of assessment tasks, showing the process has value beyond the rubric artifact itself.
Good assessment procedures require the teacher to make clear, for themselves and for their students, which criteria will measure student performance and what the standards are for each criterion.

The ability to assess the quality of one's own work does not develop automatically; it is a skill students must be helped to develop if they are to be self-directed learners and effective performers later.

Self-assessment capability is built in three ordered steps: acquire or develop the relevant criteria and standards, practise applying them to other students' work, then apply them to one's own work and improve on the basis of that assessment.
Students do not begin a course knowing what distinguishes high-quality from mediocre work, and it is not self-evident to a novice, so the criteria must be supplied or built rather than assumed.
Telling students the criteria works, but having students brainstorm and refine the criteria themselves is the better option where possible.
condition: where the situation allows students to generate criteria

statement: Peer review of draft work is a training device for self-assessment: to give another student feedback, a student must first form and then apply a sense of what constitutes good work.

A gallery-review protocol — teams post their solutions, all teams circulate and judge, then mark the best and flag a concern in writing, and each flagged team answers — makes tacit criteria explicit and drives in-depth comparative analysis.
Comparing several teams' different solutions to the same problem forces students to ask which plan would work best and why, which develops criteria tacitly before they are written down.

A self-grading protocol can be made workable by publishing the criteria with the assignment, having students submit a self-declared grade with justification, accepting it when it is within one level of the teacher's, and requiring a conference and a re-justification when it differs by more.

A self-assessment task can be designed so honesty is the winning strategy: grade the quality of the evidence and argument in the student's self-appraisal rather than the flattery of its verdict, so a well-argued modest claim scores high and an unsupported strong claim scores low.
Feedback is inherently evaluative but also helps the learner improve, which puts the feedback provider in the role of a coach.
Feedback differs from assessment in two ways: feedback does not become part of the course grade, and feedback is conducted in dialogue with the learner whereas assessment is announced to the learner.

A feedback dialogue should include the teacher's evaluation, what the student thought of the work and which criteria the student was using, and how the teacher's criteria were applied, so the teacher can confirm the student understands the criteria and self-assessment can begin.

Frequent feedback means every class where possible, or at least weekly, from the teacher or fellow learners; feedback only via two midterms and a final is insufficiently frequent for high-quality learning.

Immediate feedback comes close in time to the learning activity, ideally in the same class, because with a week or more of delay students stop caring why the answer was good or bad and only ask what they got.

Discriminating feedback names which criteria were met and which were not; a bare OK or a letter grade is neither informative nor discriminating, whereas telling a student the organization was good but the use of evidence and reasoning was poor is.

Feedback delivered without a caring relationship gets filtered by students into instructions for obtaining a grade rather than information for improving capability; empathy and personal understanding make students more likely to internalize the fuller meaning of feedback.

Educative assessment has multiple goals at once: giving students and teacher valid information about performance, and supporting the student's ability and desire to keep learning, so the psychological effects of how feedback is delivered must be designed for.

Sustained motivation in learning requires both a scoreboard — quick, reliable feedback against clear criteria on whether this attempt succeeded — and applause — recognition of success by peers, the teacher, or an external assessor.

A repeatable practice cycle that combines performance, video capture, immediate multi-source feedback, written self-analysis, and a one-to-one coaching session before the next attempt implements scoreboard and applause concretely.

Under repeated practice with feedback, learners first act only in response to the instructor's corrections, then reach a point where the pieces come together and a success plus peer and teacher recognition makes them start caring about the whole activity, after which they become composed, take charge, and seek ways to get better on their own.

Graduates of an intensive practice-and-feedback preparation typically dip one or two steps in performance when first placed in a real setting with many unknowns, then after a short adjustment surpass their preparatory level.

Deliberately looking for what is good in a student's work rather than only what needs improving shifts the teacher-student relationship to a more positive footing and gives students a foundation identity to build from.

When authentic tasks set the bar high, students generally do not do well initially, so feedback should start by emphasizing encouragement and only gradually raise the bar toward honoring excellence while still providing a valid scoreboard.
condition: when students are early in learning a challenging authentic task

statement: Educative assessment procedures support and further the learning process itself while still giving teacher and learner information on how well the student is learning, so the two functions need not be traded off.

The remaining initial-phase work — choosing teaching and learning activities and checking integration — shapes the nature and quality of the learning experience to a major extent and deserves as much attention as the earlier components.
Selecting activities is framed as two separate questions: what the students will actually do, and what the teacher will do, to make significant kinds of learning happen.

The research literature on college teaching questions the effectiveness and adequacy of the lecture-discussion tradition and indicates students learn more and retain it longer when more active methods are used.
Active learning in its original formulation is anything that involves students in doing things and thinking about the things they are doing.
Active learning is best organized into three components — getting information and ideas, experiencing, and reflecting — with experience split into doing and observing.
Receiving information and ideas is a real and important part of learning but is very limited on its own; when the teacher's job is seen as covering the material, class time fills with teacher talk.
Intellectually mature students will reflect and make connections on their own, but that is an optional activity the teacher has not built into the learning experience, so it cannot be relied on.
Whatever the teacher wants students to be able to do with the subject after the course is over is what students need to be doing during the course.

Observing is watching or listening to someone else do something related to what is being learned, or observing the studied phenomena themselves, and it gives learners a chance to experience the reality of the phenomena.

A strong direct observing experience produces two discoveries at once: that the subject studied is real and significant, and that the course's analytical tools let the student make sense of what they encounter.

A new experience or idea automatically acquires an initial meaning that may stay unconscious and be limited, distorted, or destructive; the meaning can only be changed by pulling it to the conscious level and reflecting on what meaning it should have.
A goal of teaching is to make students meaning-making rather than meaning-receiving beings, which requires giving them time to reflect on the meaning of the experiences and ideas they acquire.

Some meaning-making must be done alone, but dialogue with others dramatically increases the chance of finding new and richer meanings, and collaborative meaning-making also creates the foundation for community.

The first principle for choosing learning activities is that an effective set includes activities from each of the three components of active learning: information and ideas, experiences, and reflection.

The second principle is to prefer direct forms of each of the three kinds of learning whenever possible; indirect or vicarious forms are sometimes necessary, but direct forms enhance the quality of learning.
exception: indirect or vicarious forms may be necessary when direct access is not available

statement: Every learning activity can be classified on a grid of three active-learning components by directness, which lets a teacher see which cells a course currently uses and which are empty.

Textbooks and lectures are the indirect form of getting information and ideas, because an intermediary has already organized and interpreted them; the direct form is having students read original sources and examine original data not yet analyzed by others.
A direct doing experience is a real action in an authentic setting, such as leading a real group in a real institution even briefly, or taking part in a real community deliberation on the subject.

Case studies, gaming, simulations, and role-playing are vicarious doing: students practise the very activity the course prepares them for, without the risks and consequences that a mistake would carry in the real setting.
Small groups solving discipline problems in class are practising the doing of that discipline, and role-playing translates ideas into human actions as another form of doing.

Direct observation can target the object being studied or the people interacting with it, depending on what the teacher wants students to learn; examples include watching a professional at work, field-noting behaviour in a public setting, and recording repeated observations of a natural phenomenon.

Indirect observation through film, literature, and oral history is less full and authentic but significantly broadens the range of phenomena students can access, reaching people, cultures, times, and places direct observation could not.
Without reflection after new information and new doing or observing experiences, students have learned something but have not made that learning fully meaningful to themselves.
Classroom discussion and term papers are the two common reflection activities, and debriefing a simulation or problem-solving activity is reflection on what new understanding the experience produced.

A rarer but potentially more important form of reflection is on the learning process itself, using a journal, a learning portfolio, or writing about critical incidents, in which students record what they are learning, how they are learning it, what role it plays in their life, and how it makes them feel.
Expanding the experiential dimension of student learning is probably the single most powerful change most teachers can make in their courses.

A rich learning experience is one in which students simultaneously achieve multiple kinds of significant learning, and the best experiences are those that support the several significant learning goals set earlier in the design process.

Rich learning experiences come in an in-class family — debates, role-playing, simulations, dramatizations — and an out-of-class family — service learning, situational observations, and authentic projects.

A multi-year cumulative simulated project in which each new component must integrate with what earlier courses already built makes the work steadily more complex and more interdisciplinary, and moves students beyond calculating prestructured problems.
A cumulative design project simultaneously builds technical competencies, deadline management on major projects, teamwork, public presentation, and integration of different kinds of knowledge.

An integrated core of theory courses plus a practicum in which student companies start, run, and close a real business in one semester, with mandatory community-service hours and profits donated, is a workable rich-learning design.

Over six years and twenty-four student companies in the integrated business core, none went bankrupt, early cohorts netted roughly one to two thousand dollars in sixteen weeks, and later cohorts averaged ten to twenty thousand, indicating cumulative learning across cohorts.
Over 50 percent of graduating seniors named the run-a-real-business program the most significant learning experience of their entire time in the college.

An early authentic practicum makes students see why the later courses in the curriculum are needed, because they use ideas at the same time as they learn them and so see the relationship between theory and practice.
A rich doing experience can work reliably even when students have had no prior formal instruction in the activity, as shown by a program that produced results year after year with unprepared cohorts.

An authentic project can be staged in three phases — gather extensive real information, work in teams to develop a proposal with a concrete model, and present it to the real decision-making body — which produced a proposal a city council adopted and voters funded.

A single authentic project yields factual and conceptual knowledge plus application of concepts to a specific problem, tool skills, intense collaboration, deadline management, self-confidence, the exhilaration of completing a major project, and interaction with unfamiliar kinds of people — all more or less simultaneously.

Rich learning experiences can be real or simulated, on campus or at a distance; the common requirement is a complex, challenging, context-rich doing experience that generates several kinds of learning simultaneously.
The operational design question for a teacher is what they can have students do that presents a complex, challenging, context-rich learning experience.

Lectures and textbooks are convenient but expose students mainly to secondary sources and secondary data; the more often students meet original authors and primary data, the sooner they learn to make sense of and use primary sources themselves.
exception: new learners still need a teacher or book to supply context for why an author or subject matters

statement: Lecturing consumes class time, a scarce and expensive resource requiring room, utilities, and the simultaneous co-location of expert and students, so shifting content delivery elsewhere frees class time for rich learning experiences that cannot easily happen anywhere else.

Unread assignments are sustained by a double-feedback loop: teachers cover the material in lecture because they expect students not to read, and students do not read because they see the material will be covered in class.

Breaking the unread-assignment loop takes a three-part response: do not lecture on material that was assigned as reading, hold students accountable for it in a visible way such as a quiz, and set up an in-class activity in which they must use what they read, which supplies the intrinsic reason to read.

Web-accessible primary material can give students better information than a textbook or even a laboratory in specific cases, such as a large image collection viewed from multiple angles, or original-language documents in multiple editions and translations for comparison.

Substantive writing is about the subject and deepens the writer's understanding of the topic; reflective writing is about the learning experience itself and makes the writer more self-conscious as a learner.

Reflective writing legitimately addresses personal questions — what am I learning, what is it worth to me, how did I learn best or with difficulty, what else do I need to learn — and this self-awareness starts students toward becoming self-directing and meaning-making learners.
Reflective writing scales across three forms of increasing extent: one-minute papers, regular journals or learning logs, and end-of-course or end-of-program learning portfolios.

A one-minute paper asks students at the end of a session to write a short answer to a prompt such as the muddiest point, the most important idea, the relationship between two topics, or what questions remain, which forces a mental review of the whole lesson.

Students initially give widely varying answers to a one-minute paper because they are unaccustomed to reflective thinking and to feedback on their sense-making, but with continued asking and responding they get much better at valid responses.

Course-long journals differ from one-minute papers in letting students connect and build on their interpretation of the whole learning experience, and work best when the teacher periodically collects, comments on, and returns them.

The learning portfolio is powerful because it simultaneously integrates and promotes all three main components of instructional design: significant learning goals, active learning activities, and educative feedback and assessment.
A learning portfolio generally has two parts: a narrative statement of the meaning of the whole learning experience and an appendix of material that illustrates and supports the narrative.

Portfolios work better when preceded by frequent smaller reflective writing during the course, because students become more capable of reflecting and accumulate a substantial body of material to organize at the end.
Knowing in advance that a learning portfolio is due prompts students to reflect along the way on what they should be learning and how well they are meeting the goals set for them.
A learning portfolio serves three audiences at once: it lets students communicate what they learned, supports their own self-assessment, and can feed institutional assessment.

A portfolio assignment can raise the credibility of the rest of the course, because students continuously look for connections to their future work and for material to include, and consequently interact more with the subject, each other, and the teacher.
Grade the care with which a learning experience is documented, not the quality of the experience reported, so students are not penalized for honest reflection.
condition: when grading reflective portfolios or learning journals

statement: Portfolios work best when students have practised weekly reflection during the course, and sharing entries in small groups lets students see similarities and differences in how they experienced the same course.

A reflective portfolio can be structured around three questions: what was learned about the content, how the learning fits the student's individual, social, and work life, and what the student learned about how they learn most effectively.

The taxonomy of significant learning works as a structuring device for a learning portfolio: one reflection prompt per category points students to the several possible meanings their learning experience may carry.

An institution can run portfolios at degree scale by defining a small set of central abilities that guide the whole curriculum and requiring students to document a level of proficiency on every one of them to graduate.
The right comparison for online learning is not against poor classroom teaching but whether high-quality online learning matches high-quality classroom learning.

A delivery mode should be evaluated by asking whether each of the three components of active learning can be satisfactorily fulfilled in it, which gives a meaningful basis for judging its potential quality.

For access to information and ideas, online delivery is at least equal to and possibly better than classroom teaching, because anything in a textbook or lecture can be put on a site, and sites update faster and can carry rich illustration, sound, and moving images available anytime anywhere.
