Online delivery supports reflection adequately, and electronic dialogue has two specific advantages: students who hold back in live discussion contribute more freely, and everyone has more time to compose their thoughts.

The weak link in online learning is providing significant doing and observing experiences; the two available responses are to assign direct authentic experience outside class or to use indirect forms such as case studies, simulations, and stories.

Hybrid courses reflect the strengths and limits of each mode by using the online component for content access and discussion and reserving reduced live class time for experiential learning such as case studies and simulations.

The single biggest improvement most teachers can make is to give students more doing and observing experiences related to the subject; direct experiences are the most powerful, but indirect and vicarious forms remain very valuable when direct ones are not feasible.
exception: where direct experience is not feasible, indirect and vicarious forms are used instead

statement: A strong combination for in-depth reflective writing is one-minute papers plus weekly journals plus an end-of-term learning portfolio.

Two changes to the information component pay off across the whole design: move students' initial exposure to content outside class to free in-class time for rich learning experiences, and keep looking for ways to put students in contact with original authors and primary data.
Lectures and secondary sources retain value as a basis for students' study of a topic; the recommendation is to relocate and supplement them, not to eliminate them.
Integration is a check-and-change-as-necessary operation performed on each connection between components, not a design step that produces new content.

Integration against situational factors asks whether the course decisions are consistent with what was learned about the situation, testing for invalid presumptions about student knowledge or attitude, a course structure at odds with the teacher's own beliefs and values, and conflicts between student goals and teacher goals.

Component integration is checked with a three-column worksheet: list every primary learning goal, then for each name the assessment procedure that will show whether it was achieved, then name the specific learning activities students need to achieve it.
The goal-assessment-activity worksheet exists to prevent the easy trap of giving lip service to important learning goals while teaching in a way that does not actually support them.
Assessing non-content learning goals often requires new and more innovative forms of assessment rather than familiar paper-and-pencil tests.

The model supplies explicit criteria for judging a course design: in-depth situational analysis, learning goals spanning several kinds of significant learning, educative feedback and assessment, active teaching and learning activities, and integration and alignment of all components.

A thematic course structure is built by identifying the most important concepts, issues, topics, or themes of the subject — usually at least four and no more than seven — and arranging them in a sequence.

Topics may be sequenced chronologically, simple to complex, or fundamentals first with derived topics after; the goal is a sequence in which topics build on one another so students can integrate each new one with the preceding ones.
A good course structure lets the teacher design assignments that grow progressively more complex and challenging, dealing with more interactions among topics as the term proceeds.

The test for a good topic set is whether a student who understands each of those topics has a good grasp of the subject's essential content and a foundation for future learning; subtopics live under them but the chosen topics span the course's primary dimensions.
Each topic needs an introduction followed by opportunities to apply and use its concepts in assignments, and time per topic need not be equal across topics.

A teaching technique is a single discrete activity such as lecturing, discussion, lab work, small groups, essays, or case studies; a teaching strategy is a particular combination of learning activities in a particular sequence.
The aim of a teaching strategy is a combination and sequence of activities that work synergistically and build a high level of student energy that can be applied to learning.
Teachers face two tasks — getting students to master the content and getting them to learn how to use it — and the first is chiefly a means to the second.
Most courses leave little time for teaching students to use the content because class time is consumed covering it, so the solution is to move initial content learning to out-of-class activities.

A teaching strategy can be laid out on a castle-top template that alternates boxes for class sessions with boxes for the between-class intervals, making the planned in-class and out-of-class sequence visible so the designer can judge whether it builds energy as it unfolds.
Small groups used as an independent activity inserted into an otherwise unchanged course are being used as a technique, not a strategy.

The team-based learning cycle runs: students read the material on their own, take a readiness test individually and then as a group, spend substantial class time on practice application exercises in small groups, then take a test measuring both content understanding and ability to use it, then repeat for the next topic.
The Readiness Assurance Process brings nearly all students up to a moderate level of content understanding quickly, which is what frees class time for application work.

Working through the repeated cycle with frequent immediate feedback converts small groups into cohesive learning teams whose members become committed to the team's work and can then take on very challenging learning tasks.

Team-based learning covers information-and-ideas in the Readiness Assurance Process and doing in application exercises, and its missing reflective-dialogue component can be added easily via periodic journals and learning portfolios.

In problem-based learning the first thing students receive is a realistic problem in case-study form rather than a body of information, ideally one they might actually encounter in later personal or professional work.
Problem-based learning reverses the professional-curriculum tradition of studying content for the first two years and only meeting clinical-type problems in the third.

Students in problem-based learning work through a fixed question sequence: which systems or topics are involved, what we already know, what we do not know, how to learn about it, how to use that understanding to analyze and diagnose, and what solution seems appropriate.
The what-we-do-not-know step is especially important because it is how students identify the learning issues they need to work on.

Learning to work through the right questions in the right sequence is itself a major part of what problem-based learning teaches, because those questions are what practitioners confront continually in their work.

The problem-based learning cycle alternates in-class and out-of-class work: groups receive the problem and decide what information is needed, individuals seek it out between classes, groups apply the new information to the original problem, students review solutions, and groups present solutions to the teacher and class.

An alternative learning-cycle strategy runs six ordered stages: motivate the mind and lower fear of mistakes, acquire information in the learner's preferred modality, search out meaning rather than facts so it enters long-term memory, trigger memory with association or categorization or story, exhibit what is known to someone else as elaborative rehearsal with a social dimension, and reflect on what and how one learned.
That six-stage strategy does not yet have an extensive track record in higher education, though it has been used with reported success in public schools and corporate training.

The overall scheme of learning activities is produced by identifying the course's main topics, choosing an instructional strategy that spans one to three weeks, and repeating that strategy for each main topic, adjusted to the course's time structure.

Good course design needs differentiation in two ways: variety in the type of learning activity from day to day within each topical block, and a pattern of growing complexity and challenge across the sequence of units.
A course whose class sessions all do more or less the same thing has a low level of differentiation.

Integration is needed at two scales as well: individual activities connect toward the conclusion of each topical unit, and each new unit connects with the preceding topics toward the conclusion of the whole course.
Schedule the term by deciding first how the course should begin, then how it should end, and only then laying out the middle around the instructional strategy and topic sequence.
Leave blank or unscheduled time in the course schedule, so that overruns, cancelled sessions, and mid-course creative additions can be absorbed without breaking the design.
A grading system must be both fair and educationally valid, and remains necessary because nearly all institutions still require grades even when the course uses educative assessment.

The list of graded items should be diverse, because students learn in different ways and differ in how they best show what they know, so a system resting on one or two exams penalizes students who could demonstrate ability another way.

The graded items should reflect as much as possible the full range of learning goals and activities; not every learning activity needs grading, but an activity the teacher genuinely wants students to do must be reflected somehow in the course grade.
exception: not all learning activities need to be graded

statement: The relative weight of each graded item should reflect its relative importance, so that for example a culminating project spanning all the course's realms of learning outweighs a weekly quiz.

A worked grading system spreads points across basic individual activities, major individual activities, and group activities, including a journal and a culminating group project, with weights matched to importance.

Before implementing a design, review it for operational problems that can be corrected in advance, such as an assignment that allows too little time to complete or too few copies of required reading for simultaneous access.

A syllabus should carry enough information for students to do what the teacher wants plus the policies that set the ground rules: management information, course goals, the structure and sequence of activities with due dates, required reading, grading procedures, and course policies on attendance, late work, make-ups, and academic misconduct.
Evaluating the course and one's own teaching must go well beyond looking at the means of end-of-course student ratings.

Collect information from students at midterm as well as at the end, because formative assessment lets the teacher address major student concerns while there is still time for those students to benefit from the change.

Assessing teaching quality should draw on multiple sources: student questionnaires, structured interviews with the class or a sample, audio or video recording of a session, analysis of patterns of correct and incorrect test responses, and observation by a colleague or instructional consultant.

An outside observer contributes distinct insight because they carry neither the teacher's nor the students' workload during the session and can apply knowledge of the subject and of teaching to identifying what is going well and what could improve.

Evaluation questions for students or observers should focus on four aspects: whether the course goals are being achieved, how effective particular activities and the overall strategy are, whether feedback and assessment procedures are helpful and fair, and how effectively the teacher interacts with students.
Once goals extend to the human dimension, caring, and self-directed learning, students must be treated as subjects and essential partners rather than as objects the teacher acts upon.
condition: when the course's goals go beyond foundational knowledge and application

statement: Involving students means at minimum sharing the goals and teaching strategy with the class, and for the course to run well students should add their own goals, help select the forms of feedback and assessment useful to them, and take part in rethinking which strategies work for them.
The teacher owns the game plan the way a coach does, but the plan must be understood by the whole team and may need modifying from ongoing dialogue, since the points are scored by the players.

Keeping dialogue open about the design — explaining the plan and the reasons for it, then interacting with students about the course throughout — produces good student suggestions and makes the course a shared, collaborative experience.

A single unifying theme, integrating question, or graphic helps students see the central focus of a whole course and guides which information and questions are needed for each new case the course studies.
Teachers should shift attention from how much content is enough to how the course content should be organized, and a good course graphic is a valuable way to communicate that organization.
A unifying question, theme, or graphic helps students make the connections between the course's goals, its teaching and learning activities, and its feedback and assessment.

Poor student motivation is a symptom, not the root problem; the root problem is usually poor course design — low-level learning goals, audit-ive assessment, and passive forms of learning — and better design will eliminate or diminish many common teaching problems.

The integrated course design model is intended to be simple, holistic, integrative, practical, and normative, the last meaning it supplies specific criteria for judging whether a given design is a good design.

The twelve design steps can be remembered as twelve questions: where are you, where do you want to go, how would you know if you got there, how are you going to get there, who and what can help, what are the major topics, what will students need to do, what is the overall scheme, how are you going to grade, what could go wrong, how will students know the plan, and how will you know how it went.

The model asks for seven changes: set more ambitious learning goals, enlarge the kinds of learning activities used, create rich learning experiences, provide multiple opportunities for in-depth reflection on the learning process, find alternative ways to introduce content, create a coherent and meaningful course structure, and select or create a dynamic instructional strategy.

The underlying principle is to incorporate as much significant learning, active learning, and educative assessment as possible, then place all of it inside an effective instructional strategy operating within a coherent course structure.

A flow experience occurs when what a person feels, wishes, and thinks are aligned; they become totally absorbed, all psychic energy runs one direction, and self-consciousness and the sense of time disappear.
Flow cannot be created at will; it happens to a person, but some activities make it more likely and those are called flow activities.
Flow activities have three characteristics: goals that are clear and compatible, immediate feedback making it clear how well one is doing, and a right balance between high challenge and high skill.
Flow acts as a magnet for learning through a challenge-skill cycle: a high challenge forces new skills, greater skill readies the person for new challenges, and the cycle repeats.

Setting the right level of challenge requires accurate information about what students can and cannot do at the start, so the challenge stretches them a bit but not too far, and about how this particular set of students learns.

The four design components map onto the conditions for flow: situational analysis sets the challenge level, significant learning goals supply clear compatible goals, criteria-based feedback with student involvement supplies immediate meaningful information, and paired challenge-and-support activities keep skill matched to challenge.
A teacher must complement challenging activities with other activities that help students develop the skills needed to meet those challenges, rather than issuing the challenge alone.

Teachers cannot manufacture flow but can design instruction that makes flow conditions likely, which then sets in motion a self-reinforcing cycle in which students realize a need for more challenge and more learning.
Changing how one teaches is not a matter of changing everything, only some things, which makes the change tractable even though ingrained patterns are hard to alter.

Significant learning is demonstrably achievable rather than aspirational, because innovative teachers are already achieving parts of it, as documented across a sample of published course descriptions.

Very few published course descriptions include in-depth comment on feedback and assessment, so that component could not be analysed across the sample — an evidence gap in the documented practice, not necessarily in the practice itself.

Teachers in the sample were not following this book's model yet arrived at goals, activities, and results consistent with it, which is convergent support for the model rather than a demonstration of it.

Students can become better students without class time spent on study skills, if the course structure puts them in a position of having to learn a lot of material on their own; downstream instructors then observe them organizing for effective learning faster than peers.

Having students mid-programme ask what they are learning, what else they could learn, and what they should be learning, and reflect on the implications, seems likely to improve their subsequent learning, though the cited case did not report whether it did.

Courses that teach inquiry have students formulate their own questions and then work on answering them, which requires learning to search for and identify relevant information and analyze it to solve the problem.

Teaching inquiry requires two moves together: give students practice conducting inquiry as a doing experience, and give them constructive feedback on how well they are conducting the process of inquiry itself.

How knowledge is constructed differently by discipline can be taught by having students analyze the same collected material through several disciplines' methods and then discuss, at the end of each unit, both what was learned and how it was learned.
Learning logs in which students record what they are learning, what they could or should be learning, and how they are learning can definitely increase students' self-awareness as learners.

Self-awareness is not enough for self-direction: the next step is to have students look forward and build a learning agenda of what else they need or want to learn, plus a plan of specific actions such as reading, searching, consulting an expert, observing, or attempting the thing themselves.

A workable self-direction sequence is: have students survey the range of topics in the field, pick the three most important to them and argue why, then close the course with a portfolio section stating what they will do next, naming both the learning agenda and the plan of action.

Students in that course rated the portfolio, and especially the forward-looking final section, as one of the most valuable assignments, and many reported implementing their learning agendas within a year or two after the course.
Courses that successfully build caring follow a two-step pattern: first connect students with their own feelings about the topic, then have them take an action informed by that connection.

In the caring sequence the first step is usually an indirect observing experience carrying stories — film, novels, role-play, or a visitor's account — though direct observation during community service also works, and the second step is a doing experience in which students create something, propose an action, or reshape ideas.

A simulation can be made feasible by relaxing an unrealistic constraint — for instance requiring students to work out everything that would have to be done rather than actually completing the physical result — without losing the engagement the scenario creates.

Caring-building designs pair an affective encounter with a consequential product for a real audience — an anthology sold for relief funds, a decision about how the material will affect one's future professional practice, or a public exhibition taken into schools.
Human-dimension learning is promoted by making students more self-aware and other-aware in relation to the subject being studied, and activities aimed at either usually produce both.

Self-awareness is heightened by placing students in an imaginary situation or simulated role and then having them reflect in a learning log on how it makes them feel, comparing the new perspective with their prior thoughts, feelings, and beliefs.

Other-awareness is heightened by bringing in the stories of others through an indirect observing experience such as film or literature and then having students discuss with classmates what those events mean for the people involved.
Combining activities aimed at learning about self with activities aimed at learning about others produces an especially strong impact.

A structured debate designed to make students argue views that differ from their own, paired with a learning log on their own experience of the topic, produces other-awareness and self-awareness simultaneously.

Deliberately selecting readings that represent multiple cultural viewpoints alongside the canonical ones, and pairing them with learning logs and discussion, lets students understand others' perspectives and reflect on how they want their own Self to grow and change.

Human-dimension goals can be embedded even in a skills course by having students set short- and long-term goals about who they want to become, discuss progress with the teacher, and pair up to create something the rest of the class will use.

A language course can embed linguistic competence in a larger cultural theme by running each unit in three stages — students first look inward at their own experience and knowledge of the theme, then explore the target culture's expressions of it through authentic contemporary material — gaining both cultural understanding and the four language skills.

Integration learning is generally accomplished in a two-part sequence: first students learn about each subject being connected, then they give focused attention to making the connection, either comparing similarities and differences or examining the interaction between them.

The connecting half of integration work runs on thinking, writing, and reflecting plus small-group or whole-class discussion, and sometimes a special doing project — it is that second step, not the first, in which integration actually occurs.

Integration can target different objects: comparing how several disciplines construct knowledge, connecting scientific knowledge with policy issues and the student's own values, or connecting beliefs with artefacts across cultures and across past and present.

Application learning follows one consistent pattern across courses: students engage in a doing activity giving repeated practice at the target ability, then receive feedback, preferably prompt and criteria-based.
Eighty percent of the selected courses that promote significant learning involved work on application learning, defined as a kind of thinking, an important skill, or managing a complex project.

Each kind of thinking gets a characteristically different activity: repeated critical assessment of published articles for critical thinking, creating a realistic invented case or story for creative thinking, and diagnosing a designed problem with incomplete information for practical thinking.

A complex-project assignment must be genuinely open-ended and multi-task — soliciting content, designing and laying out a product, promoting it, and choosing a recipient for the proceeds — for project-management learning to occur.
Courses that add other kinds of significant learning free the necessary time by moving initial exposure to content out of class, without abandoning the foundational-knowledge goal.

The key to getting students to do the reading before class is devising the right in-class activity: students must know the prior reading is absolutely necessary for the in-class work and that the in-class work is valuable; when that holds, the majority will do the out-of-class work.

Content can reach students in forms other than lecture and textbook — current periodicals in the target language, documentary film that records phenomena directly, dramatic film that portrays them realistically, and field or lab work where students gather their own data.

In the vast majority of these courses the foundational-knowledge activity is linked in a structured, sequenced way to activities promoting other kinds of learning, and that linkage supplies the educational energy for multiple kinds of learning.
With reading assignments quickly followed by application exercises, lecture can shrink to an occasional ten- to fifteen-minute explanation of the concepts students had difficulty with on their own.

Foundational knowledge can be deliberately delayed until students have developed a strong internal sense of what they need to know and why, by first surfacing their own beliefs and assumptions and having them generate the key questions before the literature is introduced.

A long class block can be sequenced as discussion of the previous week's problem, then new foundational knowledge presented by the teacher, then group work on a new problem applying it — introducing content and immediately using it within the same session.

Students can acquire foundational knowledge through their own research and through discussions led by other students, with progressively more responsibility for choosing their own topics across successive cycles.

The procedures for promoting each kind of learning reduce to short recipes: for inquiry, practise with feedback plus analysis of how knowledge is created; for caring, connect to feelings then act; for the human dimension, create a connection then reflect on its impact; for integration, learn the parts then think about the connection; for application, repeated practice plus feedback; for foundational knowledge, use out-of-class time, vary the form of content, and link content to other activities.

Beyond foundational knowledge and application, the available assessment procedures are valid but not as consistently reliable as one would like — a multiple-choice test can reliably indicate foundational knowledge whereas journal writing is a valid but not always reliable indicator that caring has increased.
Some assessment procedures are appropriate for feedback but not for the grade: caring and human-dimension goals are highly desirable yet may be unsuitable as a basis for assigning the course grade.

Assessment procedures matched to each learning kind include personal reflections, learning portfolios, and performance in problem-based learning for learning how to learn; standardized interest, attitude, or value questionnaires for caring; before-and-after self-confidence instruments and teammate reports for the human dimension; concept maps, interdisciplinary cases, and capstone projects for integration; and simulations, demonstrations, team projects, and case studies judged against clear criteria for application.
Assessing application learning means having students do the very thing you want them to learn to do and then assessing what they do against clear criteria and standards.
Improvement requires innovation and innovation inevitably carries risk, but avoiding innovation condemns a teacher to stagnation and an inability to grow professionally.

Resolve the innovation-risk dilemma deliberately: size up the political situation and one's own tolerance, decide first how much risk is affordable, then choose the amount and kind of innovation that promises significant learning gains without exceeding that level.

Risk is perhaps the greatest barrier for teachers who want to use more active learning, and it has two sides: how students will react — unwilling participation, less content covered, or learning less well — and how the teacher will feel — not in control, lacking the skills, or seen by others as not fulfilling the proper teacher role.

Three strategies lower the risk of trying a new teaching activity: choose a lower-risk activity such as a brief paired task during a lecture rather than a role-play, choose an activity taking less in-class time, and structure the activity carefully by anticipating where it could go and setting boundaries.
What a teacher who wants to improve needs is not to make a change but to change continually, which requires a major restructuring in how they think about teaching and about themselves as a teacher.

Adult consciousness can be read at three working orders: third-order acts on what external authority says one should do, fourth-order engages in self-authorship of one's own meaning, and fifth-order deliberately authors continuous change in the Self.
Research indicates most new college teachers begin by emulating teachers they admired as students and doing the opposite of those they disliked, taking their authority from their own former teachers.

Teachers usually find their own style after a few years, which corresponds to authoring their own teaching style and sense of Self as a teacher; the further step is recognizing the need to keep learning new ways, making small changes continually and major changes periodically.
Award-winning teachers with mature, student-approved lecturing styles have abandoned them after becoming uneasy that student learning was poor even though their teaching was called good.
The decisive shift in those cases was the criterion for good teaching moving from the teacher's own comfort level to the quality of student learning.
Teaching well is a journey rather than a destination, so an excellent teacher never arrives and must keep asking how to take their practice to the next level.

Human-dimension and learning-how-to-learn goals are applicable even in a hard-science course: that science is a human enterprise with noble and petty personalities, that students should form a self-image as people who can do serious science, and that they must learn to work with others because that is how major research is done.

Setting a learning-how-to-learn goal in a discipline can force a prior question the teacher has never had to answer explicitly — what counts as knowledge in this field — and that question must be settled before the design can proceed.

A course should emulate as closely as possible what students will actually be doing in their subsequent work, which is the argument for replacing cookbook exercises with the tools and projects practitioners really use.

A four-column worksheet listing goals, feedback and assessment activities per goal, and teaching and learning activities per goal produces a design that is more ambitious than the original yet internally cohesive and demonstrably doable.

A teacher who already knows the full topic list still benefits from the course-structure step, because it forces identifying which are the major topics that absorb the subtopics and laying out a thematic structure for the whole course.

A repeatable four-phase strategy for a lab science course runs: examine the concept and device, measure the properties of that device, use the device to measure a physical property, then use that measurement to create knowledge about a further property.

Layering the strategy that way walks students through the multiple layers of inquiry involved in creating knowledge in the discipline: learn the instruments, use them to collect data on phenomena, then use that data to infer principles and patterns.
Teachers can badly overestimate students' incoming knowledge, which surfaces only when a real task is posed early — so posing that task at the start doubles as a diagnostic.

Asking a teacher what they had hoped students would do in response to a diagnostic task yields a good description of the intended end-of-course capability, and clarifying that ultimate goal is what allows the course to be refined.
A simulated client organization that periodically sends project requests turns open-ended design assignments into a playful but realistic frame that replaces cookbook exercises.

Having students design a teaching and learning unit for the students one level behind them forces them to reason about goals, activities, and feedback for others, which simultaneously makes them more conscious of those same issues in their own learning.

The design-a-unit-for-juniors project also made students review and deepen their knowledge of the introductory concepts and solidify their own subject knowledge while producing something genuinely useful to other students.

Reflective dialogue can be built into a technical course as periodic short writing on the course and its activities, shared with classmates, closing with an extended end-of-course essay in learning-portfolio form.

A workable first self-assessment exercise is to have all groups display their artifacts, hold a whole-class discussion to generate the assessment criteria and procedure, have every group assess every artifact against them, and base the grade on both the group assessments and the instructor's.
Assessment work is felt as relevant when the artifact being judged is one students must themselves rely on in every later exercise of the course.

Asking students mid-semester what they think, explicitly requesting honesty, and then visibly listening and responding, makes students see themselves as part of the experiment and become supportive of solving the course's problems.

Learning goals often need revisiting mid-course: listening to what the teacher really wants students to be able to do can reveal that the primary goal is a single application statement, and stating it precisely is what unlocks the criteria and standards work.

Criteria can be generated by asking the teacher to describe how a student who cannot do the task well behaves and then how a student who can do it well behaves; the contrast between those two descriptions supplies the criteria, and each criterion then gets a short scale of quality standards.
Clearer criteria and standards benefit both parties at once: students self-assess with more focus and clarity, and the teacher assesses performance with more confidence and focus.

A redesign can be evaluated by assembling colleagues with expertise in educational assessment and data analysis and gathering student performance data, students' perceptions of their own performance, and student assessment of the course.

In the documented redesign, students self-rated a majority of four or five on a six-point scale across nine kinds of significant learning, and their open comments named foundational, application, integration, and caring gains.

Students in a redesigned course reported learning-how-to-learn gains of all three kinds — how they personally learn, how knowledge is created in the discipline, and what they must do next to keep learning — which is evidence the three meanings are separately observable in student reflection.
Students perceive a significantly redesigned course as unlike an ordinary course and advise that their prior expectations about course format be dispelled as soon as possible.

The features that made a redesigned course feel different to students were more meaningful goals, extensive group work, a high level of hands-on projects, and frequent student involvement in generating and responding to ongoing assessment.

Even with good departmental seminars and access to a design coach, the teacher still had to translate the general ideas into specific activities in a specific course; the model does not remove that translation work.

Dialogue with an outsider is powerful in a redesign because the outsider brings different expertise and, not being a student or coteacher, can ask probing questions about what terms mean, about plans, and about possible problems.
Where no instructional consultant exists on campus, a fellow faculty member interested in creative and innovative teaching can fill the outside-dialogue role.
condition: on campuses without an instructional-development consultant

statement: A change effort should start from the four primary components at a level appropriate to the teacher: experienced teachers can begin with ambitious goals and innovations, while less experienced ones should first get clear about what their goals really are, even traditional ones, and about the relationships among situation, goals, feedback, and modifications.

A redesign can and often must start from a draft design that is not fully worked out, accepting the uncertainty of beginning with ideas still in nebulous form, provided the best available thinking is in place on goals, feedback and assessment, and activities.
Redesign requires sustained monitoring and searching through the term rather than a one-time design act.

Once the basic components of a good design are in place, a significant improvement in one component can produce synergistic improvement in the others — in the documented case, clarifying the fundamental application purpose and its criteria and standards was the breakthrough.
condition: when the other primary components are already in place

statement: A skills-based professional curriculum still needs all six kinds of learning to reach its application goals: foundational knowledge of the instruments and techniques, integration of parts into the whole, self-understanding and interaction with others, caring and professional attitude, and knowing how to keep improving.

Practice in a performance curriculum should gradually increase in complexity across one-on-one, small-group, and large-group settings, taking on more of the full responsibility as the programme progresses.

A reflective teaching journal with entries after every class, begun with hopes, fears, and self-evaluations, can serve as a reflective tool across a whole undergraduate career and as a record of professional development that later feeds a portfolio.

A full authentic-assessment package for performance learning combines real performance situations, recording, frequent oral and written teacher feedback, peer feedback, written self-assessment against the recording, and clear specific criteria and standards.
Graduates of a heavy practice-plus-feedback programme finish with high self-confidence because they know they can perform, having already done it many times.

A multi-programme study relating two kinds of doing experience and two kinds of reflective feedback to graduates' rated first-year teaching performance found each of the four activities individually related positively to high-quality performance.

In that study the major impact appeared only when the four learning factors were combined: on a 10-to-50 rated scale the low and medium exposure groups averaged 25 to 28 while the high-exposure group averaged 40.

The combined use of significant learning goals, active learning methods, and extensive educative feedback and assessment made a measurable difference in graduates' readiness to perform professionally, supporting the claim that the components must be combined rather than adopted singly.

A service-learning course reaches human-dimension goals only by supporting the other kinds as well: foundational knowledge of the social phenomenon, critical and creative thinking and complex-project management, integration across institutions, value change, and self-consciousness about how new experience shapes knowledge.

A strong service-learning design pairs living and working alongside the community with substantial theoretical reading and with journals, reflective essays, and frequent discussion, so students reflect on both the subject and their own learning process.

Having students give something back to the host community — for instance presenting what they learned through theatre — adds a rich learning experience requiring collaboration, critical thinking, and creative form-finding.

An authentic setting supplies meaningful feedback on performance naturally and frequently, which peers and instructor supplement and which students then use for self-assessment through reflective journals.

Both convincing case studies share the same signature: ambitious significant learning goals, powerful active learning, meaningful educative assessment, and in particular the two general strategies of rich learning experiences and extensive reflective dialogue.

Substantial teaching change has been achieved both by teachers with problems they wanted to solve and by already-good teachers committed to becoming better, and in both cases students became more engaged and the teachers rediscovered the joy of teaching.
Faculty are the ones in charge of the courses and curricula that constitute the core of educational programmes, so until the faculty changes nothing significant has happened to programme quality.
Faculty can teach mindlessly out of habit, following their usual patterns without taking or being able to take the time to examine the quality of what they do or to learn better alternatives.

Faculty who do rethink their teaching get little encouragement, because colleagues rarely talk about teaching except to complain about students, and do not compare new ideas or celebrate one another's successes.
The prevailing definition of faculty work as teaching, research, and service provides no in-load time for professional development in teaching, so that work must be done on overload.

Motivated faculty are easily overwhelmed by the volume of literature on college teaching and need a conceptual framework of the big picture to tell which ideas are major and which are supporting detail.
Students who have not thought about their own learning may object when a teacher changes the game and creates new rules and expectations, so student resistance is a foreseeable cost of innovation.
Even a successful teaching innovation can meet a faculty culture that is indifferent or jealous, or that attributes the effort to pandering to students or to neglecting research.

Faculty need six conditions to change: awareness of their own need to learn and change, encouragement signalling that others value their development as teachers, time for learning and course revision, resources such as consulting, support groups, reading, and workshops, cooperative students who are mindful about good learning and teaching, and formal recognition and reward for both the effort and the success.

The six faculty-support conditions are mutually reinforcing, so all six must be improved to have a major impact on faculty's ability to change, which requires coordinated effort across the organizations involved.

Colleges and universities are the priority target for change because they exert immediate direct influence on teachers and because faculty working together have a reasonable chance of changing them, but accrediting bodies, funders, disciplinary associations, and teaching journals supply support institutions cannot supply alone.

How a college or university is organized and operates is the single most significant factor affecting how well its faculty can change and improve their teaching, so effective instructional development depends on effective organizational development.
If only one aspect of institutional operations changes while the other dimensions stay the same, the original change will not last and the institution will revert to business as usual.
Institutions should start from the educational needs of individuals and society rather than from ideas that grow out of their existing structure and resources.
Few institutions have a clear set of educational goals, and most faculty and students cannot state their institution's goals; departments may have goals while the whole institution does not.

Students take courses from the whole institution and the whole institution defines their general education, so when there is no coherent educational purpose at institutional level students experience their education as fragmented, isolated, and unrelated.

Three fundamental goals students and society have always had for education are enhancing the quality of individual lives, preparing people to contribute to the multiple communities they belong to, and preparing people for the world of work.
Institution-wide educational goals should meet three criteria: learning-centered, inclusive of a broad range of educational needs, and specific enough to be measurable.
It is impossible to design programs that generate a good education until the institution knows what it means by a good education.

Institution-wide goals can be defined as a stable list of abilities every graduate must demonstrate, with a stated proficiency threshold — for instance moderate proficiency in all eight and high proficiency in four.

A less specific institutional goal statement can still be sufficient to drive substantial organizational change, as when a research university reframed itself as a student-centered research university after concluding it had been funding research on the backs of undergraduates.

Institutions commonly publish attractive general-education goal statements while their actual delivery programs are the standard distribution requirements plus a major, with no structure capable of achieving the stated goals.
An across-the-curriculum goal needs a curricular structure that provides multiple opportunities to achieve it and connects those experiences; a single related course does not deliver it.
A curriculum that states ambitious goals also needs a strong faculty development program so the faculty know how to implement it.

An institution should work backward from the learning it wants in graduates by asking which learning experiences students need, where in the curriculum each skill, knowledge, and attitude will be acquired, and how curricular learning will be coordinated with extracurricular, co-curricular, housing, and student-organization experiences.

Beyond freshman- and senior-year reflection courses, a course running continuously through the undergraduate programme may be needed to let students reflect on and connect their learning experiences across time.

Institution-wide abilities can be operationalized by marking in the catalog which abilities each course develops, so students choose courses by ability coverage as well as subject, and by requiring portfolio courses documenting achievement of each ability.

Most institutions rely on discipline-based departments as the only delivery unit, and because those units control recruitment, support, evaluation, tenure and promotion, and course offerings, the result is strong departmental programs and weak coherence in institution-wide programs.

Institutions can counter departmental entrenchment either by replacing departments with cross-disciplinary field groups organized around shared research and teaching interests, or by keeping departments and giving every faculty member a second membership in a unit organized around one of the institution's educational abilities.
An institution can also leave its overall structure alone and instead expand a teaching and learning center to support faculty and students.

Most institutions have policies and procedures that, without intending to, create major barriers to serious faculty work on changing educational programs; the two with the strongest impact are policies on faculty work and on the evaluation of teaching.
Very few institutions assess their graduates against the learning the institution intended, relying instead on individual courses or on department-level assessment of majors.

Quality assurance is needed for both an external audience, the public that supports institutions and needs assurance in exchange, and an internal one, the institution itself needing to know whether its own goals are being achieved.

Institutional quality assurance requires three moves: formulate educational goals for all graduates in language meaningful to the public, make assessment against them an institution-wide rather than per-department responsibility, and develop procedures that go beyond current quality-assurance practice.

A public-facing goal set for all graduates was proposed as high-level communication, computational, and technological literacy; informational abilities to gain and apply new knowledge as needed; the ability to reach informed judgments and function in a global community; and the readiness to address specific problems in complex real-world settings.

Institution-level outcome assessment can be run by a dedicated office that collects information on graduates' performance for years after graduation against the institution's stated abilities, asks for evidence of each ability, and asks graduates which parts of the curriculum promoted it and which need improvement.

Institutional quality evidence comes at three levels: testimonial and facilities imagery, then general outcomes such as retention, graduation rates, and accreditation, then whether graduates as a group actually demonstrate the specific learning outcomes and whether that resulted from the programs.

Institution-wide assessment completes the link between an institution's educational goals and its programs, and can also expose whether the organizational structure and the policies and procedures are working.

Institutional effectiveness requires five aligned components: significant measurable educational goals, programs capable of implementing them, an organizational structure that supports those programs, policies and procedures that support the people implementing them, and institution-wide assessment; omitting any one greatly diminishes the institution's ability to provide quality programs.
The entry point for the whole change sequence is the first component: developing a focused set of educational goals that is important, appropriate to the institution, and measurable.

Organizations that succeed at change are the ones making a multidimensional response, attributed in one documented case to near-perfect alignment of vision, mission, structures, rewards, dollars, and decisions up and down the organization.
Faculty commonly report that their institution rewards publications and teaching courses but not improving them, so evaluation procedures actively discourage a highly desirable activity.
Annual faculty evaluation on most campuses consumes a lot of everyone's time and generates negative feelings on both sides while being used for nothing beyond very modest pay raises.

The core dysfunction is that institutions have more work than faculty to do it, ask faculty to do everything on the false assumption that faculty time is infinitely elastic, and then evaluate on publication counts and one or two global student-rating averages — which breeds resentment and narrows what faculty will spend time on.

Institutions should rethink two questions about faculty work: what the institution really needs its faculty to be doing, and how to encourage them to do that in a way that meets institutional and faculty needs at the same time.

Professional development should be added as a fourth expected area of faculty work alongside teaching, research, and service, because faculty competence is the foundation on which all of higher education rests and must be continually expanded.

A worksheet naming the major areas of faculty work and explicitly including professional development, used both in setting yearly expectations and in reviewing the year, prompts faculty and administrators to ask which areas of development would most enhance the quality of faculty work.

Within teaching, the capabilities faculty might develop include basic skills such as lecturing, leading discussion, and making tests, plus designing courses, designing curricula, interacting with students, and responding to changes in the institution and in higher education.

A faculty-activity worksheet should apportion 100 percent of time across four areas — teaching, research and creative activity, service, and professional development — with each area unpacked into its concrete activities.

Professional development for faculty should cover four competence areas — teaching, research, service, and professional self-management — with self-management including time and stress management, work-life balance, negotiation and conflict resolution, and prioritization.

Adding professional development to the expected faculty activities initially worsens the workload problem, so it must be paired with realistic time estimates and with joint faculty-department expectation setting.

Start time allocation with teaching and professional development, because teaching has a fixed time character and a minimum must be protected for development, then divide what remains between research and service.

The 20 Percent Rule estimates that an ordinary three-credit course taught well consumes 20 percent of a term's time: three contact hours plus about six hours of preparation and grading per week, nine hours against a forty-five-hour professional work week.

The 20 percent baseline should be adjusted up for workload-increasing features such as high enrollment or frequent writing assignments and down for workload-decreasing ones such as a graduate assistant or fewer credits, with separate allowances for supervising assistants and advising.
A course taught for the first time is a new preparation and its workload should be doubled, which is almost always overlooked in workload planning.

Two new preparations in one semester consume about 80 percent of a faculty member's work time before advising, service, and research, which is the major reason new faculty are so overloaded and stressed.
New-preparation overload stifles creative teaching and promotes a teaching style of passive learning, easy grading, and lower-level learning.
Time set aside for professional development should never be less than 10 percent, rising to 15, 20, or even 25 percent during a major career change.
condition: higher share during a major career change

statement: An explicit time worksheet gives both the faculty member and the department a realistic view of how much time remains for research and service, and a basis for adjusting expectations when an unexpected opportunity arises.
Setting expectations and assessing faculty work should be an explicit collaborative endeavour between the faculty member and the department, since the root of assess means to sit down together.

Benign neglect of expectation setting forces faculty to decide the trade-offs alone because they have more to do than can be done, which is why the trade-offs should instead be decided jointly at the front end of the work year.

The recommended procedure is: at the start of the year the faculty member lists all major activities they would like to undertake, the chair or executive committee examines the list against departmental needs, adjustments are negotiated then with all affected parties present, and the resulting agreement — revisable during the year — becomes the basis for the end-of-year assessment.

Front-loaded joint expectation setting gives faculty a clearer sense of how to spend the year, gives the department a mechanism for ensuring priorities are covered and ownership assigned, and pressures both sides to get clear about their real priorities.

In a two-year departmental pilot, the reported benefit was that evaluation-time discussion shifted from arguing over a rating decimal to asking which activities would be most valuable next year and what resources would support them.
The same pilot pushed the department to get serious about its own priorities and let individual faculty pursue professional development in-load rather than as overload or on the run.

Heavy reliance on student ratings persists because institutions do not know what other criteria to use; departments and teachers must evaluate teaching without a shared vision and language for what good teaching and good learning are.

Absent shared criteria, the default criterion becomes how well students like the teacher or course relative to others, reducing evaluation of a complex activity to the mean of one or two global questions.
Evaluating teachers on global liking diverts their attention from student learning to student approval.

The primary criterion for evaluating teaching should be whether a major proportion of the students had a significant learning experience; teacher expertise, lecturing ability, and rapport are important but secondary.

Evidence of student learning for evaluation should come from both parties: the teacher supplying samples of student work showing the types and range of learning, and students reporting on end-of-semester questionnaires and, where assigned, in learning portfolios.

The taxonomy of significant learning supplies the language for interpreting and assessing multiple kinds of student learning in a teaching evaluation, by asking whether student work shows evidence beyond foundational knowledge.

A learning-centered evaluation uses the institution's evaluation procedures to direct faculty attention to increasing the quantity and quality of student learning, and gives a basis for choosing professional development likely to improve it.
Good evaluation also needs process and context information, because the point is the relationship between the quality of student learning and both the teacher's activities and the teaching context.

Evaluating the process of teaching reduces to two questions — was the course well designed, and did the teacher interact well with students — with the first answered from course materials such as the syllabus, sample activities, and exams.

The integrated-course-design criteria double as evaluation criteria for course materials: whether the teacher analysed the situation in depth, focused goals on significant learning, used educative assessment, used activities reflecting active learning, and used an effective teaching strategy.

Student questionnaires should ask questions grounded in a conceptual framework of good teaching — whether the teacher provided stimulating questions and ideas, seemed to care whether you learned, and made you feel included and comfortable — rather than global liking.

Context factors such as class size, physical character of the room, and time and day of the class can make teaching harder or easier, and the simplest way to gauge their influence is to ask the teacher and the students whether specific factors helped or hindered.

When the evaluation system is driven by whether teaching promotes significant learning, the same question propagates through design, in-course reflection, the teacher's own end-of-term assessment, and the evaluators' judgment.

A campus office staffed by professionals familiar with faculty questions, conversant with the literature on college teaching, and skilled at working with faculty individually and collectively greatly increases how fast faculty can learn what they need.
An estimated 30 to 40 percent of institutions awarding undergraduate degrees have some kind of faculty development program, a share that appears to be steadily increasing.

The financial case for a faculty development program is that it increases the capability of the institution's single most costly and important resource, and the vast majority of new faculty arrive with no formal preparation for their instructional responsibilities.

A review of 210 award-finalist faculty development programs found their activities fell into three groups: improving teaching, redesigning courses, and changing the institution's learning environment.

Within those three groups, effective programs improve teaching by applying knowledge about cognition and learning, targeting particular student or faculty groups, and developing a personal vision of teaching; redesign courses to adapt to new technologies and new curricula; and change the environment by creating learning-centered colleges, focusing on student learning outcomes, and instituting incentives and rewards for teaching.
Institutions can create structural room for faculty development, for instance by scheduling a class-free day every week that is used for workshops, many led by the institution's own faculty.

Students often become anxious and resistant when a teacher changes the rules of the game, preferring a known challenge to an unknown one even when the new way is meant to be better, and that resistance discourages faculty from innovating.
Institutions must educate students as well as faculty about better ways of teaching and learning, because doing either alone gets only half of what is needed.

Leaving responsibility for shifting student attitudes to the individual innovating teacher does not work, because students are unlikely to acquire positive attitudes about new teaching from one of their many teachers; institution-wide mechanisms are needed.

Student-side education can run through freshman-year or ongoing learning courses and through the student affairs office, and should engage students in the question of what they can do to help their teachers create significant learning experiences for them.

Students with more sophisticated ideas about significant learning and good teaching would make it easier for faculty to build powerful learning experiences and would rate innovating teachers highly rather than penalizing them.

The four institutional recommendations work in combination: professional development inside the evaluation system supplies incentive and time, learning-centered teaching evaluation focuses attention, a development center supplies ideas, and prepared students supply cooperation and reward.

A definition of good teaching is better developed at national level and adopted locally, because a local committee working under a content-centered tradition will struggle to find a definition that applies across disciplines.

In public education, national bodies produced credible criteria for identifying excellent teachers independent of level and subject matter, after which districts funded programs encouraging teachers to meet them.
Research indicates teaching by board-certified teachers produces deeper and more coherent student learning than teaching by those who applied for but did not receive certification.

National higher-education organizations could jointly develop a sophisticated but not overly complex definition of good teaching plus criteria and identification procedures, whose credibility would let individual institutions adopt it as a target for their faculty.

Certification against national teaching standards would need an evaluating body outside the institution, perhaps at state or regional level, after which the percentage of an institution's faculty meeting the standards becomes a quality measure.

A credible national instrument intended for internal improvement can become a public quality signal once high-scoring institutions publicize their scores, as happened with a national student-engagement survey.

Accrediting agencies are potentially among the most powerful sources of change in higher education, because institutions must have accreditation and society relies on those agencies to certify programme quality.

Accreditor pressure made most institutions take assessment seriously, but the resulting effort focused on student progress through the system — graduation progress, readiness skills, satisfaction — rather than on higher-order learning skills, affective development, or professional skills.

Online and virtual institutions force the quality question because seat-time hours on a physical campus can no longer serve as the criterion, pushing supporters and critics alike back to what students really need from a college education and how one can tell they are getting it.

An accreditor has three options for judging quality: measure inputs and process such as faculty credentials, library holdings, and endowment; take the institution's own goals at face value and check it meets them; or set out general principles of quality learning and ask whether students achieve them and whether programs support them.
Input-and-process accreditation ignores whether the resources are used effectively, and taking the institution's own goals at face value gives no assurance that the goals selected are significant.

A multi-sector policy conference concluded that for purposes of quality assurance the paramount issue for every college or university is the performance of its graduates, naming technical competence, the ability to gain and apply new knowledge, flexibility and adaptability, and the ability to address specific problems in complex real-world settings.

Learning-centered accreditation is already feasible, not hypothetical: an engineering accreditor requires programmes to show evidence that students achieve twelve named kinds of learning applicable across all engineering majors and that courses and curricula support them.

A regional accreditor's principles moved toward evidence of learning by requiring institutions to identify and assess expected outcomes, to evaluate program and learning outcomes per program, to identify general-education competencies and evidence graduates attained them, to weigh documented teaching excellence when judging faculty qualification, and to evidence ongoing professional development of faculty as teachers.
A conceptual framework for learning-centered quality assurance must be broad, flexible, and intuitive enough to be acceptable to a wide range of constituents.

Requiring evidence of significant learning would push institutions into the multidimensional response — re-examining educational goals, organizational structure, programs, and policies, and collecting information on what students actually learn.

Funding agencies shape faculty behaviour through award criteria, so requiring proposals to show how the activity would promote one or more kinds of significant learning would be a powerful stimulus for faculty to learn about learning outcomes.

A funder requirement that education proposals include a strong assessment plan, paired with published examples of good plans, demonstrably drove faculty to learn evaluation concepts and then apply them to their unfunded educational work as well.

Funder guidelines could require proposals to name the kind of significant learning to be enhanced and to incorporate the principles of effective instructional design: thorough situational analysis, clear significant learning goals, active learning, and educative assessment.
Disciplinary associations exert enormous influence on faculty attitudes and practice because faculty work for recognition under those associations' professional norms and use their resources.

A comprehensive disciplinary-association effort on teaching would sponsor research on effective teaching, provide forums for sharing theory, findings, and innovative practice, offer skill-building workshops for teachers, publish synthesized good-practice materials, and address local policy issues such as how teaching should be evaluated and what role professional development should have.

Disciplinary leaders who ignore the general college-teaching literature risk limiting themselves to refining, restating, and reifying the traditional forms of teaching already dominant in their discipline.

A disciplinary statement on excellent classroom teaching that addresses only content, disciplinary thinking, classroom environment, and evaluation of student performance omits active learning, reflective writing, small group work, classroom assessment techniques, authentic assessment, learning portfolios, and self-evaluation of teaching — factors now known to matter for high-quality learning.

The productive pattern is a leader inside a discipline who takes ideas from the general field of college teaching and translates them into terms and cases meaningful to that discipline's faculty, sustained at workshop scale over years.

Because teachers in every discipline must decide what they want students to learn, a cross-disciplinary taxonomy gives them a shared language for defining course goals and raising their sights on intended learning.
An analysis of pedagogy articles in disciplinary journals found the vast majority focus on technique — how to structure one assignment or activity — which honours reflective practice but is limited.

Technique-only pedagogy articles are limited in three ways: authors show no awareness the technique has been written about elsewhere, do not note it could be used in other disciplines, and give little rationale or context, which limits transferability to other teachers.

Published course descriptions were often so focused on the teaching activity that they gave limited information about the teaching situation, only tangentially identified learning goals, and almost never described the feedback and evaluation components.

Authors writing about their teaching should situate the technique inside their instructional strategy and course design, which still permits writing about the technique while letting readers see its relationship to the other components.

Journal guidelines for course-description articles should ask for the important situational factors, the types of learning promoted, the teaching and learning activities and how they were assembled into a strategy, the feedback and assessment procedures used, and the criteria used to judge the quality of student learning.

Meeting the six faculty needs requires coordinated effort across institutions, funders, accreditors, disciplinary associations, and journals, because no single group can change all six conditions by itself.

Awareness is the hardest of the six needs because it comes first, and it requires faculty to get the message multiple times from multiple sources that competence in teaching and course design is expected.

An institution's claim that it takes teaching seriously must be backed by more than public rhetoric: it must examine and where necessary change its educational goals, programs, organizational structure, policies and procedures, and institutional assessment.

Encouragement requires a departmental and institutional culture in which identifying as an effective teacher is admirable, being open about one's teaching problems and experiments is acceptable, and colleagues informally celebrate each other's teaching successes.

Departmental colloquia or college-wide conferences on teaching let faculty discuss that part of their role, and knowing colleagues treat high-quality teaching as a challenge worthy of sustained thought is itself motivating.

Responsibility for faculty time lies primarily with the institution: add professional development to the traditional expectations, then have each faculty member hold a realistic discussion with the chair or executive committee about allocating time across the four areas.

Support for faculty learning comes in three complementary layers: campus centers offering consulting, workshops, classroom observation, group discussion, and reading; disciplinary associations supplying the language and examples for a particular subject; and journals supplying a stream of emerging ideas and their applications.
Learning is accomplished by students, not teachers, so effective teaching requires students who are knowledgeable about and capable of fulfilling their part of the effort.
Formal structures for students to learn about and reflect on what constitutes good teaching and learning should run throughout the college experience, not only at the beginning and end.
Recognition of teaching must go beyond a few teaching awards based on haphazard criteria if it is to have a major impact on sustained improvement.
Improving recognition of teaching requires two things: clarifying the criteria that define excellence in teaching, and expanding the opportunities for faculty to receive that recognition.

Excellence in teaching should be judged on three criteria: the learning-centered question of whether the teaching produced significant student learning, plus two process factors, course design and teacher-student interaction.

Using learning-centered criteria requires the institution and faculty first to agree on what constitutes significant student learning, and faculty then to find ways to document the degree their students achieved it under whichever framework was agreed.

High-profile awards are inherently limited to very few people, so institutions should instead define criteria and standards applicable across disciplines and promptly recognize and reward every faculty member who meets them, with an appropriate title and if possible a financial award.

Threshold-based teaching recognition could create friendly interdepartmental competition over the percentage of faculty designated effective teachers, paralleling existing competition over grant money and publication records.

Disciplinary teaching awards could also be made learning-centered and look for evidence of good course design and teacher-student interaction, which would build a disciplinary culture that understands and values exemplary teaching.

Almost all the needed supporting actions are already happening somewhere across institutions and organizations; what is missing is the leadership and vision to connect the separate events into a coordinated effort.

Some learning challenges are cyclical, recurring for every generation across the life stages — walking and talking, adolescent relationships and responsibility, adult work and family, mid-life meaning and leadership and letting go, and late-life physical limits, leisure, and mortality.

Other learning challenges are linear and change with time — technology, health-care choices, adolescent life, environmental impact, organizational effectiveness, retirement decisions — so for these one cannot simply learn what one's ancestors knew but must engage in entirely new learning.

People learn in three general ways: individual informal learning from everyday experience, individual intentional learning in self-organized adult learning projects, and formal structured programs organized by others.
Much of what people learn about themselves and others comes from their own interpretation, and sometimes misinterpretation, of everyday events.
Research documents that a large majority of adults routinely identify particular things they want to learn and then find specific ways to learn them, which is the adult learning project.

Formal learning is becoming more consequential as professions mandate or encourage continuing development, individuals seek seminars for personal life issues, and organizations invest in employee training, which makes the effectiveness of those programs critically important.

People differ profoundly in their sense of themselves as learners: passive learners let parents, teachers, or friends dictate what and how they learn and lack a clear sense of what they need to learn, so their learning does not transform their life.

Proactive learners take responsibility for seeking out what they need to learn: they know who they are and what they want to do, derive from that what they need to learn, and have or can develop appropriate learning strategies.
Better teaching has a dual meaning: helping students learn something significant about the subject, and helping them develop a strong proactive sense of themselves as learners.
Without teaching that builds intentional learners, schools will keep producing graduates who know how to pass courses but who continue through life as second-rate learners.

The guide-on-the-side metaphor rightly marks the limits of lecture-centred teaching and student responsibility for learning, but it depicts the teacher as more passive than good teachers actually are, since they are proactive and reactive at once and operate in an interdependent team.

The teacher-as-helmsman metaphor casts teaching as coordinated teamwork toward a challenging shared destination: the teacher steers and coordinates while each student must understand both their individual role of studying and learning and how to work with others.
The difficulty of the learning a group takes on is a joint decision of leader and group, and the harder route is more demanding but more exciting and rewarding when carried off.

For a challenging learning effort the teacher must discover what each individual and the group are collectively capable of, and students must discover what they, their peers, and the leader are capable of and how working together raises all those capabilities.
More ambitious learning goals lead only to frustrated expectations unless they are linked to more powerful learning experiences in the course.

Integrated course design works by incorporating and organizing existing potent ideas such as active learning and educative assessment, and then increasing their impact by connecting and integrating them.
A good design creates the possibility of a significant learning experience but still has to be implemented; the design is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

An institution's five support steps are: keep the institution internally in alignment, make professional development an integral part of faculty work and establish centers to serve it, have leaders especially department chairs who help faculty find that time, evaluate teaching in a way that focuses faculty on student learning, and build mechanisms to educate students about good teaching and learning so they cooperate with innovating faculty.
A shared definition of good teaching must be meaningful across a broad spectrum of disciplines and teaching situations yet specific enough to distinguish good teaching from mediocre teaching.

Journals on college teaching would have more impact if editors, authors, and reviewers related each article to major ideas in the general college-teaching literature, broadened the focus from specific techniques to teaching strategies, and reported all key design components and their relationships.

Course design alone is insufficient: good teaching and learning also require good interaction between teachers and students, approachable through teacher credibility, leadership, and the spiritual dimension of teaching.
An audience continuously judges whether a speaker is credible and attends to the speaker's ideas only if the judgment is favourable, otherwise spending their mental energy elsewhere.
Factor-analytic communication research yields models of speaker credibility with three, four, or five factors; the three-factor version names competence, trustworthiness, and dynamism.
Students decide whether to buy into a teacher's course according to whether they perceive the teacher as competent, trustworthy, and dynamic.
