statement: Creation requires arranging elements into a coherent pattern or structure that was not clearly present in the starting material.
condition: When distinguishing creation from reproduction or analysis

statement: Assess creation of a communication by whether the learner develops an organized product that effectively conveys ideas, feelings, or experience to others.
condition: When the target product is written or spoken communication

statement: A created plan should propose an ordered course of work that satisfies the constraints and requirements of the task.
condition: When planning itself is the intended product

statement: Evaluation is a qualitative or quantitative judgment of material or methods against criteria appropriate to a stated purpose.
condition: When distinguishing evaluation from unsupported preference

statement: Distinguish evaluation based on internal evidence, such as logical consistency and accuracy, from evaluation against external standards or comparable exemplars.
condition: When designing or interpreting an evaluative task
exception: A robust evaluation may deliberately combine both sources of criteria.

statement: Creating abstract relationships can involve formulating an explanatory hypothesis and revising it as new factors or evidence emerge.
condition: When the learner must construct a relation not supplied in advance

statement: Instruction is the full set of events that affect a learner so that learning is facilitated; these events may be external (printed pages, a teacher's talk, a picture, a television program) or partly internal when the learner manages them as self-instruction.
Teaching is only one form of instruction, so instructional design must cover events not set in motion by a teacher rather than being scoped to teacher behaviour alone.
Instruction must be planned rather than haphazard if it is to be effective; a lesson design sits inside a topic design, which sits inside a course or curriculum design.
The purpose of designed instruction is to activate and support the learning of the individual student, whatever the setting (tutorial, classroom, adult interest group, on-the-job).

Instructional design should be aimed at aiding the learning of the individual, not at mass change in opinion or capability and not at diffusion of information across a society; learners may be grouped, but learning occurs within each member.
Planned instruction is not expected to make individuals more alike; the authors hold that diversity among individuals is enhanced because each person is helped to develop in his or her own direction.

Instructional design has two distinct phases: an immediate phase (preparing a lesson plan hours before instruction) and a long-range phase (sets of lessons, topics, courses, or a whole instructional system).

Immediate and long-range instructional planning are best performed as separate tasks rather than mixed together, because attempting both while teaching 20 or 30 students is too large a job for one person and leads to neglect of essential teaching functions.
condition: when one person also carries a full teaching load
exception: teachers can and should undertake long-range design on their own or as part of a team, best done during nonteaching periods

statement: The teacher's immediate planning task is greatly eased when the products of careful long-range design are supplied as textbooks, teachers' guides, audiovisual aids, and other materials.

The authors reject the view that education is best as an unplanned nurturing environment: they believe unplanned and undirected learning is very likely to leave many individuals unable to derive personal satisfaction from living in society.
A fundamental reason for instructional design is to ensure no learner is educationally disadvantaged and that all students have equal opportunity to use their talents fully.

Instructional design should be conducted as a systems approach: a sequence of steps beginning with analysis of needs and goals and ending with an evaluated system of instruction that demonstrably meets the accepted goals.
Decisions at each step of the systems approach should be based on empirical evidence to the extent such evidence allows.
condition: to the extent that empirical evidence is available

statement: In a systems approach each step's decisions become the inputs to the next step, and each step is additionally checked against evidence fed back from subsequent steps to indicate the validity of the system.

Designed instruction must be based on knowledge of how human beings learn: it is not enough to state what abilities should be developed, one must examine how they can be acquired, and materials must reflect how the student is intended to learn the content rather than only what the author knows.
A learning situation has two parts: one external to the learner and one internal, the internal part deriving from the learner's stored memories from previous learning.
A learner who experiences the external part of a learning situation but lacks the required internal capabilities recalled from memory will not learn what is being presented.

The conditions of learning are the relationships, both external and internal to the learner, that make learning occur; anyone intending to make learning occur must deliberately arrange both sets of conditions.
Only the parts of learning theory that pertain to controlled events and conditions — the events an instructor can actually do something about — are the parts relevant to designing instruction.
The principle of contiguity states that the stimulus situation must be presented simultaneously with the desired response.

When a model or prompt stands between the intended stimulus and the response — for example a printed letter left in view while a child is asked to print it — contiguity has been established with the wrong stimulus, and the intervening stimulus must be removed in stages so the intended cue becomes contiguous with the response.
condition: when the practised stimulus differs from the stimulus named in the objective

statement: The principle of repetition states that the stimulus situation and its response need to be repeated or practised for learning to improve and retention to become more certain.

Modern learning theory casts much doubt on repetition working by strengthening learned connections, and there are many situations in which repeating newly learned ideas improves neither learning nor retention.
It is perhaps best to treat repetition not as a fundamental condition of learning but as a practical procedure (practice) that helps ensure the other conditions for learning are present.

The historical principle of reinforcement (Thorndike, 1913) holds that learning of a new act is strengthened when that act is followed by a satisfying state of affairs, and this remains a live theoretical issue with considerable supporting evidence.

For instructional purposes the Premack (1965) form of reinforcement is preferred: a new act A is most readily learned when it is immediately followed by an old act B that the learner likes and performs readily, with the opportunity to do B made contingent on doing A.
condition: the contingent activity must be one the learner already likes and performs readily

statement: Instructional design methods should define the learning purpose of each design step as far as possible; beyond that point the detailed craft of print, pictures, and sound has its own technologies and other considerations take over.
Instructional design efforts should meet intellectually convincing standards of quality, and those standards need to rest on scientific research and theory about human learning.

Contiguity, repetition, and reinforcement are valid controllable instructional events, but applying all of them still does not guarantee an efficient learning situation; instruction must additionally account for the wider set of conditions of learning.

Internal conditions of learning are the previously learned capabilities the learner brings to the task, and these internal capabilities appear to be a highly important set of factors in ensuring effective learning.

To take account of external and internal conditions, instructional design starts from a model of learning as information processing: stimulation activates receptors, is held briefly in a sensory register, and is transformed by selective (feature) perception into patterns entering short-term memory.
Short-term memory storage lasts less than about 20 seconds unless the information is rehearsed.
condition: unless the material is rehearsed

statement: Short-term memory has a limited capacity — perhaps as few as four separate items held in mind at once — and because short-term storage is a stage of learning, that capacity limit strongly affects how difficult a learning task is.

A task that forces intermediate results to be held in short-term memory (such as mentally computing 29 x 3 via 30 x 3 then subtracting) is considerably harder to learn than an otherwise similar task that does not (such as 40 x 3).

Information passes into long-term memory by semantic encoding, where it becomes meaningful and largely propositional, and can be returned to short-term (working) memory by retrieval, where retrieved items may combine with others to produce new learning.

Observable performance is produced when retrieved information passes to a response generator and activates the effectors; that performance is what lets an external observer tell the stimulation has had its expected effect and learning has occurred.

Executive control and expectancies activate and modulate the flow of information during learning: a learner's expectancy of what he or she will be able to do can affect how a situation is perceived, encoded, and transformed into performance, while executive control governs the use of cognitive strategies.

The internal processes in an act of learning are: reception by receptors, registration by sensory registers, selective perception into short-term memory, rehearsal to maintain it there, semantic encoding into long-term memory, retrieval back to working memory, response generation to the effectors, performance in the environment, and control of these processes by executive strategies.

External events can be made to influence the internal learning processes, particularly selective perception, rehearsal, semantic encoding, and retrieval — for example emphasising features in a diagram aids selective perception and opening a passage with a topic heading aids semantic encoding.

Instruction is best conceived as a deliberately arranged set of external events designed to support the learner's internal learning processes; these events, individually and collectively, constitute the external conditions of learning.

The events of instruction, in roughly this order, are: gain attention; inform learners of the objective; remind learners of previously learned content; present material clearly and distinctively; guide learning; elicit performance; provide feedback; assess performance; and arrange varied practice for retention and transfer.
condition: the ordering is approximate rather than fixed

statement: Each event of instruction is chosen to support a specific internal learning process — gaining attention supports reception, stating the objective establishes expectancies, recall of prior content supports retrieval from long-term memory, distinctive presentation supports selective perception, and guidance supports semantic encoding.

Beyond external events, the conditions of learning include specific memory contents present in working memory, retrieved from long-term memory when the learner is reminded of or asked to recall previously learned content.
Prior memory contents that contribute to new learning are best differentiated into five categories of previously learned capabilities, each exhibited in a corresponding kind of performance outcome.

The five kinds of learned capability are intellectual skills (carrying out symbolically controlled procedures), cognitive strategies (control over one's own learning processes), verbal information (facts and organised knowledge of the world), attitudes (internal states influencing personal action choices), and motor skills (organised skeletal-muscle movements for purposeful action).
Previously learned capabilities fall into the same five categories as the capabilities to be newly learned, so the taxonomy applies both to prerequisites and to outcomes.

Concentrating instruction on only one or two of the five capability types is insufficient: verbal information alone is a highly inadequate instructional goal, intellectual skills alone do not equip learners with cognitive strategies for independent learning, cognitive strategies need information and skills to work on, and attitudes need a substrate of information and intellectual skills — so multiple aims for instruction must be recognised.

An intellectual skill cannot be acquired by being looked up or supplied through verbal communication: it must be learned, recalled, and put into use at the proper time, which is why skills rather than facts anchor the design framework.
Essentially flawless performance of an intellectual skill can be established in a short time, unlike cognitive strategies, which appear to need months of refinement.

Intellectual skills become highly interrelated and build cumulative internal intellectual structures: learning one skill aids the learning of higher-order skills, and the resulting transfer effects broaden intellectual competence across subject areas.

An intellectual skill can always be defined in operational terms — related to a class of human performances the successful learner can carry out — which makes it relatively easy to observe reliably that the skill has been learned.

Choosing intellectual skills as the primary point of reference for instructional design rests mainly on practical considerations — they must be learned rather than told, are acquired over short periods, accumulate through transfer, and are readily observable — not on a claim that they matter most.
The conditions under which learning occurs depend on what is being learned, so instructional design must attend to conditions that differ by learning outcome rather than applying one uniform method.

Systematic design must first establish a rationale for what is to be learned by returning to the original sources of the recognised need, then build the system step by step from a base of information reflecting the identified goals.

In the systems approach the prospective outcomes of each planning stage are checked against the goals adopted by those who manage the system as a whole, and technical knowledge is kept consistent and compatible at each decision point.

Deriving an instructional system begins by investigating needs, agreeing goals through a responsible group, and weighing available resources together with the circumstances that constrain instructional planning.

Instructional sequences are planned by determining the capability type to be learned, inferring its necessary learning conditions, and tracing backward from the outcome to identify the subordinate prerequisite objectives that must be met first — because the information and skills recalled for a task must themselves have been learned earlier.

Performance objectives identify the planned outcomes of learning as instances of human performance that can be reliably observed and assessed, and they fall into the five categories of learned capability.

Lesson-level planning takes the lesson's performance objectives as its first reference, then arranges the external conditions most effective for the desired learning, taking learner characteristics into account because these determine many of the internal conditions, and selecting media accordingly.

Assessment procedures follow directly from the statements of instructional objectives, which describe the domains from which observations or test items are drawn, and should give criterion-referenced (objective-referenced) measurement of learning outcomes.

Evaluation is applied first to the design effort itself to find needed revisions (formative evaluation), and only at a later stage to seek evidence of the learning effectiveness of what has been designed (summative evaluation).
An instructional system is an arrangement of resources and procedures used to promote learning; any institution whose express purpose is developing human capabilities may be said to contain one.

Instructional systems design is the systematic process of planning instructional systems and instructional development is the process of implementing those plans; both are components of instructional technology, the systematic application of theory and organised knowledge to design and development.

The process of designing an instructional system has features in common at all levels of the curriculum despite differences in size and scope, so the same design process applies to a national curriculum project, a course, a unit, or a single lesson.

Every stage of any instructional systems design model can be categorised into one of three functions: identifying the outcomes of the instruction, developing the instruction, and evaluating its effectiveness.

An instructional designer must distinguish instructional goals from non-instructional goals, because some desirable states of affairs (for example adequate medical care, or employee motivation and job satisfaction in industrial courses) cannot be reached by instruction.
Global instructional goals must be made more specific before systematic instruction can be designed to attain them.

A need is a discrepancy or gap between a desired state of affairs (the goal) and the present state of affairs, so needs can only be determined after goals are stated and the present state has been analysed.

Training needs in business or industry may be derived from a job analysis or from productivity data for a department, with the discrepancy between desirable and present performance identifying the need.

Perceived or felt needs are not the result of any documented gap, yet they are sometimes the basis for curricular decisions, and the prevailing view is that the general public should be involved in determining instructional goals.
Instructional analysis and learner analysis may be conducted in either order or simultaneously; they are not strictly sequential stages.

The purpose of instructional analysis is to determine the skills involved in reaching a goal; for a procedural goal a task (procedural) analysis yields a list of the steps and the skills used at each step.

An information-processing analysis reveals the mental operations used by someone who has already learned a complex skill and supports inferences about the internal processes involved; it may require having a learner talk through a procedure to check whether appropriate skills and strategies are being applied.
For each decision and action revealed by an information-processing analysis, the designer must estimate whether the intended learners already enter with that capability or must be taught it.

Task classification — categorising each learning outcome into a type of learning — lets the designer check that no intended purpose of a unit has been overlooked and identifies the conditions most effective for that outcome type.

Classified target objectives can be grouped into course units as an instructional curriculum map, which is then reviewed to check that the necessary verbal information, attitudes, and intellectual skills are all present in the unit.
A learning-task analysis is appropriate for objectives that involve intellectual skills; it reveals the subordinate enabling objectives for which teaching-sequence decisions must be made.
condition: applies to intellectual-skill objectives

statement: A designer may need to apply any or all of the analysis types — procedural, information-processing, task classification, and learning-task analysis — when designing a single unit of instruction.

Analysing entry behaviours determines which required enabling skills learners already bring, so the designer can choose where to start instruction knowing it will be redundant for some learners and necessary for others, and can identify learners who need remediation instead.

It is usually not sufficient for a designer to guess the skills of an intended audience; the better procedure is to interview and test the target population until enough is known to design the instruction appropriately.

Learner abilities and personality traits are usually considered less readily alterable through learning than skills, and they affect general qualities of instruction such as media and pacing, whereas possession of particular skills and verbal knowledge has quite specific effects on instructional content.

Instruction for learners low in verbal comprehension would best de-emphasise verbal presentations such as printed text, and learners high in anxiety may learn better from leisurely paced instruction that permits choice of optional next steps.
condition: where the learner ability or trait has been measured

statement: Needs and goals must be translated into performance objectives specific and detailed enough to show progress toward the goals.

Working from general goals to increasingly specific objectives serves communication at different levels: some audiences such as parents or a board of directors want only goals, while teachers and students need detailed performance objectives to know what to teach or learn.

Because different types of learning outcome require different instructional treatments, the designer must determine the conditions of learning needed for each acquisition, and specifying performance objectives is what makes that determination possible.

Once objectives are stated in performance terms the curriculum can be analysed for sequence, completeness, and prerequisite-skill requirements, and the size of the delivery system and development schedules can be estimated and coordinated across the design team, teachers, media producers, and teacher trainers.

Objectives should be stated as observable, measurable performances rather than as content outlines or teacher activities, so that student performance can be measured to determine when the objective has been reached.

Performance objectives function to show whether the instruction relates to the goals, to focus lesson planning on the appropriate conditions of learning, to guide development of performance measures, and to assist learners in their own study.
Objectives, instruction, and evaluation are the three anchorpoints in planning and must be checked for agreement with one another.

Objectives must guide instruction and evaluation rather than the reverse, so objectives are determined before lesson plans or evaluation instruments — a sequence followed by almost all instructional design models.

Designing assessment before lessons is recommended because a novice is more likely to stray from the objectives when writing tests than when preparing lessons, and a designer who has just written lesson material may inadvertently test content rather than performance; an experienced designer may instead develop lessons first.
exception: an experienced designer may choose to develop lessons before performance measures

statement: Performance measures serve diagnosis and placement (confirming prerequisites and pinpointing missing skills so unnecessary instruction is avoided), in-lesson checks that detect and remediate misunderstandings before continuing, and end-of-unit documentation of progress.

Formative evaluation provides data for improving instruction while materials are still being formed and reformed; summative evaluation determines the success and worth of the course in its final form when no further changes are planned.

Planning performance measures before lesson materials keeps the tests focused on what the learner must be able to do rather than on what was read or what the teacher did, so that assessment detects acquired skill and not mere recall of the presentation.

An instructional strategy is a plan for assisting learners with their study effort for each performance objective, taking the form of a lesson plan for teacher-led instruction or production specifications for mediated materials; it is developed before the materials so that instructional activities are tied to the objectives.

Instructional systems design applies to teacher-led group-paced instruction as well as to self-contained modules; the process differs in whether the resulting guide is written for the teacher or for the student.
It matters little whether the events of instruction are performed by teachers or by materials, so long as they are successfully performed.
The events of instruction apply to all domains of learning outcome, although the details of how each event is implemented imply somewhat different conditions of learning by domain.

Different media have different capabilities for providing the various events of instruction — teachers excel at learning guidance and feedback, while videotape can present stimulus situations a classroom teacher could not otherwise supply — so media should be assigned event by event and objective by objective within the chosen delivery system.

Strategy planning is where the designer combines learning and design theory with experience of learners and objectives; creativity in lesson design is what separates the art of instructional design from its science, and the work is most often done as part of a team.

The danger in selecting existing materials is that teachers sometimes choose them for convenience, in effect changing the objectives to fit the available materials, so that students learn content unrelated to the instructional goals.

Commercial materials are typically referenced by content rather than by objective and rarely address the events of instruction they provide, so existing materials should be checked against objectives and supplemented for the objectives they miss.

Four material-selection principles hold: the more innovative the objectives the larger the share of materials that must be developed; developing materials for a particular delivery system is almost always more expensive than selecting available ones; expense can be saved by integrating available materials into a module that covers all desired objectives; and the teacher's role shifts with the delivery system and completeness of materials because the teacher must supply whatever events are missing.

Deciding at the outset to develop all new materials is usually justified when a central concept, method, theme, or body of content must be preserved intact (often in experimental programs), whereas deciding to maximise use of existing materials is usually driven by cost.

Formative evaluation proceeds in three levels: one-to-one trials with representative learners, a small-group tryout with six to eight students, then a field trial of the revised instruction with a whole class.

One-to-one trials surface structural and logistic problems and can be run by interviewing the learner or having him talk through his thoughts; it has been estimated that a few one-on-one evaluations could improve the effectiveness of instructional materials by 50 percent.

The small-group tryout focuses on how students use the materials and how much help they request, which is used to make the lesson more self-sufficient and gives a more representative estimate of large-group effectiveness than one-on-one scores.

Formative evaluation is one of the most frequently overlooked stages because it comes late and takes significant effort, yet using systems feedback to correct the system is the essence of systems philosophy — instructional design without formative evaluation is incomplete.
Formative evaluation data may call for revision or review of products derived from any of the earlier design stages, not only the materials stage.

Summative evaluation is normally conducted only after the system has passed through its formative stage and is no longer under point-by-point revision, and if wide use is expected it must be conducted under an equally varied range of conditions.
condition: when wide deployment across varied settings is expected

statement: For an educational product to be judged exemplary, the evidence of effectiveness must be valid and reliable, the effects must be of sufficient magnitude to have educational importance, and it must be possible to reproduce the intervention and its effects at other sites.

Designing instruction for a total educational system adds stages beyond the nine-stage course model: analysis of resources, constraints, and alternate delivery systems; curriculum scope and sequence; teacher preparation; field testing and revision; and installation and diffusion.

A delivery system includes everything necessary to let a particular instructional system operate as and where intended, and the delivery decision directly constrains the personnel, media, materials, and learning activities available to reach the goals.

If new goals appear out of reach of every available delivery system, no further planning is possible until goals are changed, resources or constraints are changed, or another delivery system is conceived; ignoring this leads to piecemeal planning and waste such as unused equipment, unusable laboratories, disrupted activities, and goals missed for want of prerequisite experiences.
condition: when the goals exceed every available delivery system

statement: When resources and constraints force goals to be achieved within an existing delivery environment, the key question is whether that existing delivery system is capable of providing the environment needed for learning the new skills.

If a new instructional system requires skills beyond those current teachers already possess, the special training to supply those skills must itself be designed as part of the instructional systems design process.
condition: when the new system demands skills in-service teachers lack

statement: Workshops are one common mode of teacher preparation, but visits to a school where the system is running as a pilot are an important alternative because teachers need to perceive that the new system will work in their own environment.

In an interpretive study of schools adopting individualized instruction, most teachers felt they needed a year of experience beyond their initial training before they preferred the new system to their prior practice.

Teachers must be prepared before materials are distributed for a new unit of instruction to be adopted, and the more input teachers have along the way the more likely the materials will fit the existing system and be adopted.
A new system is ready for widespread adoption only after an acceptable degree of merit has been shown in one or more summative evaluations.

Installation requires final adjustment of practical matters — storage differences between buildings, fitting time schedules to existing patterns, and duplication and distribution of expendable materials — and above all awareness of the nature of the system the innovation enters, because new technology is often perceived as a threat and blocked by the very people who should use it.
A frequent problem is securing enough adoptions of a new instructional system to amortise development, marketing, and the often-overlooked maintenance costs.

If diffusion is a goal of a development project it must be considered early in the design process, because a publisher's operating procedures can constrain the final product or delivery system and force the instructional goals, needs, or system objectives to be rethought.
condition: when diffusion is among the project's goals

statement: The instructional systems approach is a process of planning and developing instruction that draws on research and learning theory and uses empirical testing as the means of improving the instruction.
All design models focus attention on the same three anchor points of instruction: performance objectives, materials, and evaluation instruments.

The key steps of lesson planning are: classify the lesson objectives by learning type, list the needed instructional events, choose a medium capable of providing those events, and write prescriptions incorporating the appropriate conditions of learning for how each event will be accomplished — with events allocated among learner, materials, and teacher.

The instructional design process is iterative: earlier stages must be revisited and their products reworked in light of findings uncovered during later stages, so design proceeds by working back and forth rather than straight through.
Each design objective should be stated in testable form so that the success of the design can itself be evaluated.
The best way to design instruction is to work backward from its expected outcomes, beginning with identification of the human capabilities to be established.
Educational goals are those human activities that contribute to the functioning of a society, and of an individual within it, and that can be acquired through learning.

Structuring education as subject matters is a gross simplification of educational goals: a subject name such as English stands in for the many different human activities performed with language, and the simplifying condensation loses information at each stage.

A goal is better stated as a category of human activity than as an abstract noun — 'performing those activities that will maintain health' rather than 'health', 'carries out the activities of a citizen in a democratic society' rather than 'citizenship'.
The human capabilities that make an educational goal's activities possible are the proximate goals of instruction; the educational goal itself is the distal outcome.

In a complex society instruction cannot be planned separately for each educational goal; the designer must instead identify the human capabilities that contribute to several different goals at once, such as reading comprehension or performing arithmetic operations.
condition: in a highly differentiated and specialised society

statement: Course titles and topic designations are ambiguous — the same title can mean different things at different grades or cover different content — and this ambiguity is a real source of difficulty for students planning programs of study.
Ambiguity in what a course means is readily avoided by describing the course in terms of its objectives rather than its title or topics.

A single course usually carries several objectives of different kinds — for example describing historical context, evaluating sources, and showing a positive liking for the study of history — and the most important difference among them is that each requires a different plan for its achievement.
Instruction must be differentially designed so that each objective within a course is attainable, rather than one uniform treatment being applied across the course's objectives.

Instructional planning is vastly simplified by assigning learning objectives to the five categories of human capability, because each category leads to a different class of performance and requires a different set of instructional conditions, while within a category the same qualities of performance apply regardless of subject matter.
exception: useful subcategories exist within each of the five categories

statement: Observed learning outcomes are performances made possible by internally stored states of the learner called capabilities; the capability is inferred, the performance is what is observed.

Intellectual skills let individuals interact with their environment through symbols or conceptualisations, ranging from composing a sentence to finding the stresses in a bridge, and they form the most basic and pervasive structure of formal education.

Learning an intellectual skill is learning procedural knowledge — knowing how — and contrasts with verbal information, which is knowing that something exists or has certain properties; a learner can acquire either without the other, so the distinction must be maintained even when one unit teaches both.

A learned intellectual skill functions as a component of further learning: acquiring the rule for using a metaphor contributes to more complex skills such as writing illustrative sentences, describing scenes, and composing essays.
To verify that an intellectual skill has been learned one must observe a category of performance — several specific instances of applying the rule — rather than a single instance.
Cognitive strategies are the capabilities that govern a learner's own learning, remembering, and thinking — controlling behaviour when reading to learn or when getting to the heart of a problem.
Cognitive strategies are expected to improve over a relatively long period as the individual engages in more studying, learning, and thinking, rather than being acquired on a single occasion.

Intellectual skills are essential but not sufficient for solving a novel problem: the learner must also apply a previously practised cognitive strategy, such as working backward from the goal, as the mode of seeking a solution.
condition: the strategy must have been previously learned and practised

statement: Most commonly occurring cognitive strategies are domain specific — strategies for retaining information from reading, for solving arithmetic word problems, for composing effective sentences — while some, such as inference or induction, are more general.

A general strategy such as induction apparently requires a number of experiences in widely different situations before it becomes dependably useful, and learners can carry it out without having been told the target concept or taught how to induce.

Once acquired, a cognitive strategy such as induction can be applied across enormously varied situations whose performances resemble each other only in involving that strategy — provided the requisite intellectual skills and information have also been learned.
condition: provided the requisite intellectual skills and verbal information are present

statement: Verbal information is declarative knowledge — knowing that — and is the kind of knowledge a learner is able to state.

Verbal information is stored as the gist of paragraph-length passages and recalled in that form, not necessarily memorised verbatim; much of it is also learned incidentally rather than from formal instruction.

A large stock of subject-matter facts may not be a defensible primary goal of instruction, yet learning those facts is an essential part of learning the subject because the information must be available for the learner to apply a rule to a particular case.

One major function of verbal information is to provide the learner with directions for how to proceed in further learning; a rule cannot be applied to a specific situation unless the relevant facts are recalled at that moment.

Verbal information also enables transfer of learning: possessing information about one domain makes an analogy to another possible, after which cognitive strategies and intellectual skills can be brought to bear and new knowledge generated.

Whether verbal information has been learned is determined by observing whether the learner can communicate it — normally by asking for an oral or written statement, and in the early grades by simple oral questions or by pointing to pictures and objects.

The function of a motor skill as a capability is simply to make the motor performance possible, and such performances can themselves enter into further learning — printing letters is used when learning to write words and sentences.
Acquisition of a motor skill can be reasonably inferred only when the learner performs the act across a variety of contexts — different tools, surfaces, and sizes — not from a single instance.
An attitude is a learned, persisting internal state that amplifies a positive or negative reaction and modifies the individual's choices of action toward a class of objects, persons, or events.
Attitude strength is indicated by the frequency with which a person chooses the item across a variety of circumstances, not by whether the choice is made on any single occasion.

A change in attitude is revealed as a change in the probability of choosing a particular course of action, so attitude outcomes must be assessed as shifts in choice frequency over time rather than as a single measured state.

Direct observation of choices over an extended period is prohibitively time-consuming, so attitude inferences are usually drawn from self-reports; because students can see the intent, self-reports can misrepresent reality, and only with proper precautions do they support the inference that an attitude was learned or modified.
condition: only when proper precautions against transparent-intent responding are taken

statement: Many attitudes are acquired outside school and many are not appropriately within a school's instructional function, so attitude objectives must be scoped rather than assumed universal.
The five categories of capability cut across course content, and the primary reason for distinguishing them is that each makes possible a different kind of human performance.

An objective's capability type can be read from its wording: solving problems of velocity and acceleration names intellectual skills, designing an experiment to test a stated hypothesis implies cognitive strategies used in a novel situation with little guidance, and valuing the activities of science names an attitude.
The five capability categories each require a different set of learning conditions for efficient learning, which is the second important way they differ.
Instruction should always be designed to meet accepted educational goals, and the ideal planning condition exists when goals are matched to societal needs.
Human activities derived from societal needs, when analysed, yield a set of capabilities that would probably not correspond simply to the traditional subject-matter categories of the curriculum.
Learning outcomes cannot reliably be identified from the topical titles of courses; they are identified as the varieties of learned capability that make different types of performance possible.

A designer who claims to care only about producing creative thinkers is fooling himself: with the exception of motor skills, all the capability categories are likely to be involved in planning any course — no course exists without information, none leaves attitudes untouched, and none exists without intellectual skills.
exception: motor skills are not implicated in every course

statement: Intellectual skills are central to structuring a course of study for two reasons: they determine what the student can do and so define the course's learning outcomes, and they are cumulative — building on each other predictably — which makes them the most useful model for sequencing course structure.

A complete mapping from the most general educational goals down to specific course objectives has probably never been done for any curriculum, so designers must define course objectives in the absence of that connecting network.

A capability taxonomy is used to evaluate the scope of objectives a course intends, to group similar objectives and cut the work of designing a total instructional strategy, to inform the sequence of course segments, and to plan the internal and external conditions of learning each group requires.

Grouping a course's objectives into the five capability categories lets the designer assess adequacy of coverage per category while exploiting the fact that the conditions of learning are the same for every objective within a category.

There is no better guide to applying learning principles to instruction than first asking what is to be learned, because the answer places the objective in one of the five capability classes and thereby fixes the conditions required.

Intellectual skills can be categorised by complexity — the intricacy of the mental process inferred to account for the performance — and these complexity categories cut across and are independent of subject matter.

Intellectual skills form a prerequisite ladder: problem solving requires recall of simpler rules and defined concepts, rules require concrete concepts, and concrete concepts require previously learned discriminations.
A designer may assume lower-level prerequisites are already in place, but if that assumption is wrong instruction must be designed so learners catch up on the simpler intellectual skills first.
condition: when the assumed prerequisite turns out not to be held

statement: Rule-governed performance implies an internal capability that makes behaviour regular; the learner need not be able to state the rule for the rule to have been learned.

A discrimination is the capability of making different responses to stimuli that differ along one or more physical dimensions, in the simplest case indicating that two stimuli are the same or different.

Relevant discriminations are usually assumed to have been learned early in life, but that assumption sometimes fails for adults and specialists — whether the learner actually hears a foreign-language phonetic contrast, sees a microscopic boundary, or distinguishes two wood grains must be checked, not presumed.

Every type of intellectual skill should be described by three components of the learning situation: the performance to be acquired, the internal conditions (capabilities recalled from memory and integrated into the new capability), and the external conditions that supply stimulation.

Discrimination learning depends on contiguity (the response must follow the stimulus within a short time), differential reinforcement for right versus wrong responses, and repetition — with additional repetitions needed when several discriminations must be learned at once.
condition: more repetition required when multiple discriminations are learned simultaneously

statement: A concept is the capability of identifying a stimulus as a member of a class sharing some characteristic, even when the members otherwise differ markedly; a concrete concept identifies an object property or attribute and requires recognition of a concrete object.

Whether a concrete concept has been learned is tested by asking the learner to point to two or more members of the same object-property class; the particular pointing response — choosing, checking, circling, grasping, or naming — is of no consequence provided the learner can perform it.
condition: provided the learner already knows how to make the pointing response

statement: Object positions such as above, below, beside, and in front of qualify as concrete concepts because they can be pointed to, even though a position is necessarily relative to another object.

Discriminating between two particular figures supports only the conclusion that the learner can tell them apart; testing whether the concept has been learned requires identification of several instances that differ widely in irrelevant qualities such as size, colour, and border thickness.

Concrete concepts are prerequisites for concepts acquired by definition: a learner who cannot concretely identify the referents of the words in a definition cannot in any complete sense know the meaning of the defined concept.

To teach a concrete concept, present instances varying widely in their non-relevant characteristics and include negative instances, so that correct performance is shown by both selecting members and rejecting non-members.
The internal condition for learning a concrete concept is that the relevant discriminations must be recallable — the learner must already be able to tell the underlying physical variations apart.

A defined concept is learned when the individual can demonstrate the meaning of a class of objects, events, or relations by classifying an instance in accordance with the definition, which is a different mental process from reciting the definition as memorised verbal information.

Many concepts such as family, city, or justice can only be acquired as defined concepts and cannot be pointed to; some defined concepts share a name with a corresponding concrete concept whose meaning overlaps but is not identical.

Asking a learner what a term means is always subject to the ambiguity that he is repeating a verbalisation without knowing the meaning, which is why the criterion is to demonstrate a concept rather than to state or define it.

Demonstrating a defined concept requires identifying each component concept in the definition and showing an instance of the relation among them — for boundary line: identifying an area, identifying a line marking its limits, and showing that a moving object stops at the line.

An assessment item that lets a learner reach the answer by plugging values into a formula does not show that a defined concept has been attained; the better item requires identification of the component concepts and their relation, for example asking for two different sets of conditions that could produce a given acceleration.
The internal condition for acquiring a concept by definition is that the learner can retrieve every component concept in the definition, including the concepts representing the relations among them.

A verbally stated definition is sufficient to induce learning of a defined concept provided the learner's internal conditions are met — that is, provided the component concepts, not merely the words, can be retrieved.
condition: provided the learner can retrieve the component concepts rather than only the words

statement: A rule has been learned when the learner's performance shows regularity across a variety of specific situations — responding to classes of objects with classes of relationships — rather than a particular fixed stimulus-response pairing.

Sorting items by a fixed label is insufficient evidence of rule-governed behaviour because it may only show learning of concrete concepts; evidence of a rule requires a relational regularity that cannot be described as a particular stimulus-response pairing.

Possessing a rule does not mean being able to state it: a student who can recite a law may be unable to apply it to a concrete problem, and children construct oral sentences long before learning any grammatical rule.

A defined concept is not formally different from a rule and is learned in much the same way: it is a classifying rule, while rules in general also cover relations such as equal to, greater than, before, and after.
A rule is demonstrated by showing that it applies to one or more concrete instances, so rule assessment items must require application rather than restatement.
In rule learning the instructor must assume the component concepts, including relational concepts, have been previously learned and are readily recalled by the learner.

The purpose of the verbal communication used to teach a rule is to remind the learner of the component concepts to recall and to cue their arrangement in the correct order — not to teach a formal verbal proposition representing the rule, and it need not be phrased precisely.

The external conditions for rule instruction vary in how much learning guidance they supply: minimal guidance is what is meant by emphasising discovery, and extensive detailed verbal communication de-emphasises it.

Studies of discovery learning suggest that small amounts of learning guidance have advantages for retention and transfer of the rules learned, and discovery techniques often use pointed questioning that leads the learner to the proper ordering of component concepts.

Higher-order rules are complex combinations of simpler rules, often invented to solve a practical problem or class of problems; solving such a problem yields a new rule that generalises to other problems with similar formal characteristics.

The rules combined during problem solving must have been previously learned and recallable, though the solver cannot necessarily verbalise them and need not have learned them in a formal course on the subject.
The essential condition that makes an episode a problem-solving event is the absence of learning guidance from any external source: the guidance is supplied by the problem solver alone.
Because a learner cannot possibly acquire all the rules needed for every situation, concepts and rules must be synthesised into new complex forms to cope with new problems.

Problem solving should be treated as an activity that combines previously acquired concepts and rules, not as a generic skill: ability to solve mathematics problems does not automatically transfer to solving an automobile's mechanical problems, and problem solving in a task class is improved by adding intellectual skills relevant to those tasks.

Acquisition of a higher-order rule is confirmed when the learner can demonstrate its use in other physically different but formally similar situations — that is, when the rule shows transfer of learning.
The external condition for problem-solving learning is a real or represented problem situation not previously encountered, with verbal cues at a minimum or absent entirely.
A cognitive strategy is a control process — an internal process by which learners select and modify their ways of attending, learning, remembering, and thinking.
Learner strategies can be classified by control function into rehearsal, elaboration, organising, comprehension-monitoring (metacognitive), and affective strategies.
Rehearsal strategies are the learner's own practice of the material — repeating names in an ordered list for simple tasks, and underlining main ideas or copying portions of text for complex ones.

Elaboration strategies deliberately associate the item to be learned with other readily accessible material — an acoustic-link image for foreign vocabulary, or paraphrasing, summarising, note taking, and generating questions with answers for prose.

Organising strategies arrange material into a framework — sorting words into meaningful categories, tabulating relations so spatial cues aid recall, or outlining and regenerating the organisation of prose ideas as comparison, collection, or description.

Comprehension-monitoring (metacognitive) strategies are the learner's capability of setting learning goals, estimating success against them, and selecting alternative strategies to meet them; students have been taught to generate their own statements and questions to guide and control prose comprehension.

Affective strategies are used to focus and maintain attention, control anxiety, and manage time, and they can be taught by making students aware of how they operate and giving them ways to practise their use.

Cognitive strategies can be mapped to the information-processing stage each supports: highlighting, underlining, advance organisers, adjunct questions, and outlining for selective perception; paraphrasing, note taking, imagery, outlining, and chunking for rehearsal; concept maps, taxonomies, analogies, and schemas for semantic encoding; mnemonics and imagery for retrieval; metacognitive strategies for executive control.

Chunking strategies reduce the number of separate items held in short-term memory by organising them into more general categories, which matters because short-term capacity is limited to approximately seven separate items.

Semantic encoding makes information meaningful by tying it to previously learned schemas or establishing new ones; concept maps are especially helpful where the existing structure is weak or nonexistent, whereas analogies work only by linking new information to existing structures.
condition: analogies require an existing structure to link to

statement: Which cognitive strategy a learner selects in an unstructured environment is governed by goal schemas — the learner's expectancies and goals — so a student studying for a test will probably use a different strategy than one preparing to teach the same skill.

Embedding a strategy in instructional materials is not the same as teaching the strategy: an embedded strategy performs a function for the learner, whereas a learned strategy lets the student perform that function for himself.

If the goal is for learners to acquire cognitive strategies as outcomes, the designer must account for the conditions necessary to learn those skills, just as for any other type of learning outcome, rather than merely supplying the strategy inside the materials.
condition: when cognitive strategies are themselves an intended outcome

statement: Whether learners who construct an outline acquire something different from learners who study with a prepared outline — and what test would reveal the difference — remains an open question requiring empirical research.

What differentiates a cognitive strategy from other intellectual skills is the object of the skill: concepts and rules are oriented toward environmental objects and events, while cognitive strategies take the learner's own cognitive processes as their object.

Enthusiasm for teaching students how to think should be tempered by two facts: genetic factors not amenable to education play an important part in creative thought, and the internally organised nature of cognitive strategies means instruction can affect their acquisition only indirectly.

Because instruction affects cognitive strategies only indirectly, designing for them means arranging favourable conditions — opportunities for their development and use: to learn to think, the student must be given opportunities to think.

A described learning-strategies training system begins with direct instruction of strategies such as comprehension monitoring, problem solving, and control of affect, then practises the same strategies across varied learning situations over an extended period using distinctive cues — incorporating spaced and varied practice, considered desirable for higher-order strategies.

Cognitive-strategy performance cannot be observed directly and must be inferred from performances that call on other intellectual skills, or elicited by asking learners to think aloud while learning, remembering, or solving problems.

Cognitive strategies themselves often have a very simple internal structure, such as underline main ideas or divide the problem into parts, even though the prior knowledge they operate on must be retrievable.

Strategies can be suggested verbally or demonstrated in simple form — even young children respond to a suggestion to classify word lists into categories — or can arise from discovery, but favourable conditions always depend on providing opportunities for practice.

Metacognition is the internal processing that uses cognitive strategies to monitor and control other learning and memory processes; a learner who becomes aware of and can describe such strategies is said to possess metacognitive knowledge.

Of the two views on where metacognitive strategies come from — direct communication of metacognitive knowledge plus practice, versus generalisation from many specific task-oriented strategies after varied problem-solving experience — the weight of evidence appears to support generalisation, and the authors adopt it.
Strategies for highly novel problems are often the primary interest of educational programs, yet knowledge of how to ensure their learning is the weakest part of the field.

Documented adult strategies for verbally stated problems include inferring transformed conceptions of the givens, classifying rather than randomly choosing action sequences, hill climbing toward the goal, identifying contradictions showing the goal is unattainable, breaking the problem into parts, and working backward from the goal statement.
condition: most obviously applicable to algebraic or geometric brain-teaser problems

statement: Three currently irreconcilable models of problem-solving instruction exist: that general skills can be taught directly and will generalise; that general skills develop only indirectly by generalisation from task-specific strategies; and that direct instruction in general strategies establishes only weak, broadly generalisable strategies that help very little.
There is dependable evidence that task-specific strategies, such as strategies for solving mechanical problems or constructing geometric proofs, can readily be acquired.

Expert-novice studies generally indicate that experts do not necessarily use better problem-solving strategies than novices but approach problems with larger and better organised knowledge bases containing both verbal information and intellectual skills — which should temper the value assigned to teaching general problem-solving strategies.

The varieties of intellectual skill are distinguishable by the class of performance they make possible, the internal and external conditions necessary for their occurrence, and the complexity of the internal process they establish in memory.

The frequency of each skill type varies widely by school subject: discriminations are common in printing letters, reading music, and beginning foreign language but rare in history, while composition work draws mainly on defined concepts and rules because the simpler skills were learned years earlier.

Analysing a subject down to every skill type is not always practical because a grade-level presentation may legitimately assume simpler learning is done; but where simple skills are genuinely new — such as the discriminations required to use a microscope or spectrophotometer, or to judge wood textures — they must be learned before the concepts, rules, and problem solving that are the course's main aims.
condition: when the simpler prerequisite skills are genuinely new to the learners

statement: A structure of intellectual skills representing the path of greatest learning efficiency exists in theory for every subject, but it is known only vaguely, and the efforts of teachers, curriculum specialists, and textbook writers to represent it must on the whole be characterised as partial and inadequate.
A method for describing learning structures must itself be subject to empirical verification, revision, and refinement.

Mapping learning structures does not routinise or mechanise learning: a map shows starting points, destinations, and alternative routes but does not dictate how the journey is made, and the learning journey requires a different set of internal events for each individual.

A learning structure describes accepted goals and the subordinate steps toward them; it does not prescribe how an individual student must learn, since in a fundamental sense there are as many learning styles as there are individuals.
Cognitive strategies have not been broken into subcategories as intellectual skills have, and future research may show that this can and should be done.

Instruction is typically designed to encompass several objectives of different capability classes in a given unit and to achieve a suitable balance among them, rather than pursuing one outcome type at a time.

Knowing the conditions of learning for each capability type supports two design tasks: accounting for the prior learning the new learning presupposes, and planning the external conditions needed to attain that outcome type.

Verbal information is theorised to be stored as networks of propositions conforming to the rules of language, and is also called declarative knowledge to emphasise the performance capability it implies.

Large amounts of information are learned outside school from books, magazines, newspapers, radio, and television without special instruction — provided the audience possesses the basic intellectual skills for interpreting those communications.
condition: provided the recipient has the intellectual skills to interpret the communication

statement: Planned instruction in a body of information is undertaken because incidental media exposure yields learning that varies greatly across individuals, whereas a planned course aims at certainty that all students learn the information deemed essential.

Two reasons justify demanding high certainty of information learning: some information must be recalled repeatedly to pursue further study efficiently within a subject, and some is continually useful throughout life for giving and receiving communications.

The curriculum-design problem for information is distinguishing what is essential — for which certainty of learning is a concern of formal education — from what is personally interesting but not essential; there is no reason to limit information a learner wishes to acquire out of interest.
Information organised into bodies of meaningfully interconnected facts and generalisations is what is called knowledge, and specialists in a field store their information in that organised form.
General cultural knowledge serves communication, particularly for citizenship, and may contribute to the individual's sense of identity in relation to the society he belongs to.

A more critical proposed function of general knowledge is that it is the vehicle for thought and problem solving — thinking broadly is carried by the associations, metaphors, and analogies of language within shared bodies of knowledge — although evidence about this is incomplete.

Verbal information presented for learning varies in amount and organisation, and for design purposes three learning situations should be distinguished: learning labels or names, learning isolated single facts, and learning organised information.
Learning a label is acquiring the capability of making a consistent verbal response that names an object or object class; information in this form is simply a short verbal chain.

Learning a name as a label is distinct from learning the meaning of that name: the learner knows a label when he can supply the name of a specific object, but knows the concept only when he can identify examples and nonexamples that define and delimit the class.
Name learning is easy for one or two objects but difficulty increases rapidly when many names for many objects must be learned at once, as when a set of trees, leaves, or cabinet members is assigned.
condition: when several or many names must be acquired simultaneously

statement: Label learning is a useful activity even when it amounts to memorising, because among other uses it establishes the basis for communication between learner and teacher or learner and textbook.

Mnemonic techniques markedly aid the learning of sets of names — embedding a word pair in a made-up sentence usually brings remarkable improvement in paired-associate learning, and the keyword method uses learner-generated images to cue retrieval of foreign-vocabulary equivalents.
A fact is here defined as the verbal statement expressing a relation between two or more named objects or events — not the referent it describes.

Learned facts matter for two reasons: some are essential to everyday living, and others are used in further learning, as when the value of pi is needed for a circumference or a valence for a chemical equation.

The designer has an obligation to decide, for the many facts in a course, which are of such infrequent use that they should be looked up, which are referenced often enough that learning them is efficient, and which are fundamental enough to be remembered for a lifetime.
The performance indicating a fact has been learned is stating, orally or in writing, a relation having the syntactic form of a sentence.

The internal condition for acquiring and storing a fact is that an organised network of declarative knowledge be accessed in memory and the new fact related to it; that network may differ for each individual learner.

The external conditions for teaching a fact are: present a cue reminding the learner of the larger knowledge network, present the fact, suggest the association to be acquired, optionally elaborate with related facts and imagery, and provide for rehearsal or spaced review.
The key to remembering bodies of knowledge appears to be organising them so they can be readily retrieved, and organising during learning aids later retrieval by supplying retrieval cues.

The more highly organised a learner's previously acquired information, the easier it is to acquire and retain any new fact that can be related to that structure — as the periodic table aids recall of element properties or a framework of historical periods aids recall of events.

Connected prose appears to be retained in a way that preserves meaning but not necessarily the detailed component facts, with general ideas recalled better than specific ones and details often reconstructed by the learner from a schema representing the gist.

Retrieval cues for organised information must be as distinctive as possible to avoid interference among stored propositions; distinctiveness is increased by memorable stimuli such as rhymes, by reducing confusion with similar ideas, and by organising component ideas into tables or spatial arrays.

Elaboration enhances retrieval because adding related information to new ideas adds more retrieval cues, which may be environmental (using parts of a room to recall a speech's sequence) but are more often retrieved from memory as words, phrases, or images.

Telling learners what to look for or what to remember before learning begins can activate a cognitive strategy; this may be done directly, through questions inserted in a text, or through an advance organiser — a brief passage given beforehand that orients the learner to what is to be remembered.

Repetition markedly affects remembering of both isolated facts and larger bodies of information, but its effective employment is providing spaced occasions for the learner to recall what was learned — the retrieval processes are apparently the most important factor in remembering.
condition: repetition must take the form of spaced retrieval, not mere re-presentation

statement: Students' attitudes toward attending school, cooperating with instructor and peers, attending to communications, and toward the act of learning itself are of great significance in determining how readily they learn.

Whatever their content, all attitudes resemble each other in formal properties: each functions to affect approaching or avoiding, and therefore some general principles of learning apply to acquiring and changing attitudes.

An attitude is defined operationally as an internal state that affects an individual's choice of personal action toward some object, person, or event; it is inferred from behaviour and is not the behaviour itself.
An attitude cannot be inferred from a single instance of behaviour; the inference requires a number of instances of the same general class across different situations, each of which is a choice.

An attitude question phrased at a broad group level is too general to be answered sensibly; the answerable question names a specific personal action, such as working with, living near, or sitting beside, because it is the choice of action that the attitude affects.

Attitudes should be measured in terms of the personal actions chosen — by direct observation of choice proportions over repeated periods where possible, and otherwise by questionnaire self-reports of choices in described situations, because many relevant choices occur outside the observable setting.
condition: direct observation only where the choices occur within the observable environment

statement: Persuasive communication alone does not establish or change an attitude, according to a great deal of evidence: repeated maxims, emotional appeals, and carefully reasoned chains of argument all often have equally poor effects.

The methods of instruction used to establish desired attitudes differ considerably from those applicable to intellectual skills and verbal information, and much about the conditions favouring attitude change is yet to be discovered.

Classical conditioning can establish an attitude of approach or avoidance toward a class of objects, events, or persons, so some attitudes students bring to school may originate in earlier conditioning experiences.

Arranging contingencies of reinforcement is a direct attitude method usable in school: when a preferred activity is made contingent on the new performance, the learner acquires a liking for the new task as well as learning it.
condition: the contingent activity must already be preferred by the learner

statement: Success in a learning accomplishment is likely to lead to a positive attitude toward that activity, as when learners come to like skating once they achieve some success or to like classical music once they can recognise its forms and themes.

Human modeling is the indirect attitude method of great importance and widespread utility: it operates through another human being, real or imagined, and can be delivered in person, on television, in film, or through printed literature.
A human model must be someone the learners respect or identify with, and should be perceived as credible and powerful, or the modeling will not establish the attitude.
condition: the model must be respected, credible, and perceived as powerful

statement: Modeling requires that the learner observe the model making the desired choice of personal action AND see that the action leads to satisfaction or pleasure for the model — the step Bandura calls vicarious reinforcement.

The internal conditions for attitude learning by modeling are that respect for or identification with the model already exist (or be established first), and that the intellectual skills and knowledge related to the modelled behaviour have been previously acquired — though such prerequisite knowledge does not itself engender the attitude.
exception: prerequisite knowledge alone does not produce the attitude

statement: The external conditions for modeling an attitude form a four-step sequence: present the model and establish its appeal and credibility; have the learner recall knowledge of the situations the attitude applies to; have the model communicate or demonstrate the desired choices of personal action; and show the model obtaining pleasure or satisfaction from the outcome.

Role playing is a form of human modeling in which the actor models action choices after an imagined rather than an actual person, and class discussion of social or personal problems also models attitudes, with the discussion leader acting as the model.

Teachers need to appreciate their human-modeling role given the large proportion of time students spend in their presence; it is likely that the teachers students later remember as good teachers are the ones who modelled positive attitudes.
When an attitude is the intended outcome, first give learners information about the possible alternative choices, because a common obstacle is that learners do not know the options available.

Give learners the pros and cons of the desired choice: current behaviour persists because it has positive consequences or is habituated, so the costs and long-term benefits must be made explicit, especially when short-term benefits of competing behaviours are stronger.
condition: especially where the desirable consequences are long-term

statement: Provide relevant models for the desired behaviour: do as I do outperforms do as I say, and the more salient the model is to the learner the greater the likelihood the choice behaviour is adopted.

Ensure the environment supports the desired choice behaviour — the opportunity to perform it must actually exist — and treat an unmodifiable environmental conflict as evidence that the desired behaviour is not viable.
condition: if the environmental conflict is unmodifiable the objective is not viable

statement: Fit the desired behaviour into a larger framework of values where possible, because attitudes reflect values and people who see themselves as important members of a company or class make different choices than those who feel unimportant.
condition: where such a value framework exists to connect to

statement: Identify and teach the skills that make the desired choice behaviour possible: a learner cannot choose an action he lacks the skill to carry out, such as choosing low-cholesterol food without being able to identify which foods contain cholesterol.

Recognise and reward the choice behaviour when exhibited, and take care not to inadvertently punish it — rewarding work with more work breeds resentment, so the reinforcement schedule should make the student want to do more.

Because affective behaviour passes through awareness, acceptance, and valuing and is relatively resistant to change, let learners set their own goals, report their own progress, and periodically re-evaluate those goals, which builds confidence as they move toward the desired behaviour.

Use simulations, role playing, collaborative processes, or other involving experiences in which the benefits of the desired behaviour become obvious; these complement rather than replace modeling experiences.

Do not inadvertently pair a behaviour targeted for change with an unrelated one; because habituation and attitudes form behaviour complexes, the most important behaviours must be identified and prioritised for instructional intervention.

Motor skills are learned capabilities whose performance outcomes are reflected in the rapidity, accuracy, force, or smoothness of bodily movement; the terms perceptual-motor and psychomotor carry no useful added meaning.

Practised motor skills appear to give rise to a centrally organised motor program, but increased smoothness and timing are held to depend on feedback that is both internal (a perceptual trace of stimuli from muscles and joints, used as an error reference) and external (knowledge of results).
As practice proceeds, improvement in a motor skill comes to depend increasingly on internal feedback and less on externally provided knowledge of results.
A motor skill divides into part skills that occur simultaneously or in temporal order, and learning the total skill requires learning both the component part skills and their integration.

The executive subroutine that organises a motor skill is not itself motor: it is a procedure conforming to a procedural rule, and this rule-governed component controls which movement is executed first, second, and so on.
Many studies comparing part-skill practice with whole-skill practice have produced no clear answer: it depends on the skill, sometimes part practice helps and sometimes not.
Both the executive subroutine and the part skills must be learned: practice on either without the other has repeatedly been shown to be ineffective for learning the total skill.

Motor skills are best learned by repeated practice, there is no way to avoid practice if accuracy, speed, and smoothness are to improve, and practice continues to yield improvement over very long periods of time.

The external conditions for motor-skill learning are: communicate the executive subroutine (by verbal instruction, a checklist of the movement sequence, or pictures and diagrams), then have the learner practise the movements with accompanying informative feedback.

Verbal information, attitudes, and motor skills differ in the outcome performance each makes possible: verbally stating facts, generalisations, or organised knowledge; choosing a course of personal action; and executing a bodily movement.
