The key condition differs by outcome type: for verbal information, external cues relating the new information to an organised prior network; for attitudes, direct reinforcement of action choices or vicarious reinforcement through modeling; for motor skills, practice with frequent informative feedback after the executive subroutine is learned and part skills integrated.

Verbal information, attitudes, and motor skills are not less important than intellectual skills; the categories differ in the internal conditions that must be assumed and the external conditions that must be arranged, not in their importance to instructional programs.

Intellectual skills stand in enabling prerequisite relations to each other, whereas prior learning has merely supportive effects on verbal information, attitudes, and motor skills — a distinction with particular implications for determining instructional sequence.

The design strategy gives first priority to intellectual skills as central planning components: identify the intellectual skills, analyse and identify their prerequisites, then add at appropriate points the cognitive strategies those skills make possible.
exception: where the primary objective is verbal information, an attitude, or a motor skill, the analysis instead reveals the supportive effects of prior learning

statement: Instructional design must reduce the enormous diversity of learner characteristics to a number small enough to make planning feasible, identify the dimensions that carry different implications for instruction, and then provide a design for those learner variations shown to make a difference in learning results.

The learner characteristics that matter to instructional design are those affecting the whole information-processing chain: sensory input, internal processing, storage and retrieval, and the organisation of learner responses.

Innately determined learner qualities such as visual acuity need be considered in instruction only under extreme conditions — leading to avoidance of fine print or fuzzy projected images — rather than driving general design.
condition: only under extreme conditions of sensory demand

statement: Working-memory capacity, indicated by an immediate memory span of seven plus or minus two items, and the speed of retrieving and identifying learned concepts may both have innate limits.

For genetically determined learner characteristics, instructional design cannot aim to alter the quality by learning; it must instead be designed to avoid exceeding human capacities — using words, sentences, diagrams, and other communications that stay well within working-memory capacity rather than testing its limits.
Long words in early decoding tasks and long sentences for readers generally place demands on working memory that may exceed its capacity limits.
The large set of learned learner characteristics is precisely what constitutes the internal conditions of learning for each capability type, and these have critical effects on new learning.
An intellectual skill is believed to be stored as a production of the form IF <goal or condition> THEN <action>, which is why stored sets of intellectual skills are called procedural knowledge.

A complex rule is composed of simpler rules and concepts that are usually learned as prerequisites, and when the complex skill is retrieved it readily activates those simpler prerequisite skills because they are actual components of it.
A cognitive strategy is a production that governs the selection and use of intellectual skills, so it can only be used when the underlying intellectual skills are already known.
condition: the underlying intellectual skills must already be in place

statement: A typical cognitive strategy is structurally simple yet broadly general within its domain — a self-editing strategy that adds phrases answering when, how, where, and why applies to virtually any sentence but is not relevant outside sentence revision.

Declarative knowledge is stored as individual propositions or as networks of propositions organised around central ideas, and elements of such a network connect at various points with productions (intellectual skills).

Retrieval from long-term memory works by spread of activation: contacting one proposition brings interconnected propositions to mind, which accounts both for apparently random association and for the flexibility of reflective thinking.

What is stored for an attitude appears to include the choice of personal action as exhibited by a human model, a representation of a standard of conduct for the self reflecting the model's standard, and a feeling of satisfaction from direct or vicarious reinforcement.

Attitudes are strongly influenced by situational factors and appear to be stored within propositional networks organised by situation, so an attitude such as neatness may apply to one situation and not to another; reviving the memory of a situation revives the attitude with it.

Conditions become right for the attitude-revealing choice of personal action when the memory of the admired model and the model's action choices is retrieved together with the situational factors appropriate to each.

The core memory of a motor skill is a centrally located motor program established by practice, which attains automaticity and becomes only incidentally responsive to variations in external stimulation and kinesthetic feedback.

When a motor skill has been unused for many years the executive subroutine is likely to remain intact even though the performance becomes hesitant and rough — a person still remembers how to finger a clarinet after years of disuse.

What is stored in long-term memory can be conceived as propositions (declarative and procedural), images, and motor programs, organised into interconnected networks that can be searched and retrieved to serve an activity or further learning.

A schema is an organisation of memory elements representing a large set of meaningful information about a general concept, with common features called slots whose values are filled in by newly learned information.

Schemas differ across individuals in comprehensiveness and in the details stored in their slots, and these differences have particular importance for planning instruction whose content relates to those schemas.

Learners arrive at a lesson with schemas already in memory that the new instruction fills out with more elaborate content, so a designer should anticipate which schemas the learners bring to the topic.
A learner's schema may carry an attitude as well as knowledge — an air-pollution schema is likely to include an attitude influencing personal choices such as votes on related legislation.

On the view that schemas control perception, an individual sees a stimulus only in reference to a schema, which directs attention to what is relevant and gives the event meaning — implying learning is a highly personal act.
exception: where schemas are formed by growth in a fairly homogeneous society, individuals may possess and activate similar process schemas

statement: Process schemas can differ by culture: the same term evokes a different procedure where a different algorithm was taught, as with subtraction taught with borrowing in the United States and without it in Australia.

Because individuals possess different knowledge and process schemas, what is obvious to most students may make no sense to another; careful analysis of that individual's schema may reveal missing prerequisite skills or knowledge, and the instructional solution is to teach those prerequisites before the primary intervention.
Abilities measured by psychological tests tend to be stable characteristics persisting over long periods and are not readily changed by instruction or practice aimed at them.
Personality traits such as introversion, conscientiousness, impulsiveness, and self-sufficiency are likewise persistent and not readily influenced by instruction aimed at changing them.

Whether it is more useful to measure general ability or a number of differential abilities remains unanswered: differential-ability scores correlate positively with each other and low-to-moderately with general intelligence measures, so they are not truly distinct from one another.

Well-known differential abilities and their measures include reasoning (nonsense syllogisms), verbal comprehension (printed prose), number facility (speeded arithmetic), spatial orientation (rotated figures), associative memory (object or number pairs), and memory span (immediate recall of digit lists).

Aptitude treatment interaction research tests the hypothesis that a given instructional treatment differs in effectiveness for learners scoring high versus low on a trait, and such relations have been shown for several achievement-related traits.

Documented aptitude treatment interactions include learners with high achievement motivation achieving better when instruction permits considerable learner control, and anxious students learning more when given the option of reviewing videotaped instruction than when viewing the same tapes in groups without review.

Locus of control distinguishes students who attribute learning results to external factors such as luck from those who attribute them to their own effort, and internal attribution may account for aptitude treatment interaction findings on this trait.

Prior learning affects new learning through two channels with different design implications: learned capabilities and schemas exert direct, specific effects that are retrieved into the new learning, whereas abilities and traits do not enter the new learning directly but influence the ease with which learning processes are carried out.

Which kind of effect prior learning exerts depends primarily on the objective of the new learning, so the analysis of prior learning must be organised by the expected outcome type of the new learning.

For a new intellectual skill, the analysis of prerequisite component skills can be expressed as a learning hierarchy, and the absence of any skill in a subordinate box markedly decreases the ease of learning the superior skill connected to it.
Prerequisite skills must be learned to mastery to be most effective for new learning, presumably because thorough learning makes them easier to recall and therefore more accessible.
Ease of retrieval also depends on the number of cues available to the memory search, so embedding prerequisite skills within the organised network of a schema may be expected to benefit instruction.

Abilities affect new learning indirectly by contributing strategic techniques for processing the task and its material — numerical facility eases mathematics processing, verbal comprehension eases connected prose, spatial orientation eases figures and spatial arrays — in contrast to learned capabilities and schemas, which enter the new learning substantively.

Traits also have indirect effects on skill learning: very anxious learners may be reassured by frequent feedback during practice and so learn more readily than under infrequent feedback, while learners with high achievement motivation may thrive on discovery learning where low-motivation learners perform poorly.

On one account, abilities and traits give rise to an aptitude complex that engenders purposive striving; with intellectual abilities this affects the quality of learning and with personality traits the quantity (effort and persistence), and their combination determines learner engagement and hence achievement.

Instructional design can take abilities and traits into account in two ways: circumventing a lack of aptitude (for example easily read text plus elaborate learning guidance for learners low in verbal comprehension), or developing aptitude through instruction and practice in cognitive strategies.
A conservative view of aptitude development is that cognitive strategies applicable to specific task domains are readily learnable, but generalisable strategies may require many years to develop.

The prerequisites of a cognitive strategy are often very simple and well known, and the more general the strategy the simpler its prerequisites — a working-backward strategy needs only identifying the problem goal and placing steps in backward order.

A schema can supply the retrieval cues for a cognitive strategy and its prerequisites, and a strategy may be retrieved because the whole schema of a previously encountered problem is recalled and reveals the analogy.

Where the aim is aptitude development, instruction may begin with a task using a partially developed ability and proceed to develop it further; a successful demonstration of training in spatial visualisation has been conducted.

Learning new verbal information requires intellectual skills of language — synonyms and metaphors in word meanings, rules of syntax, and logical sequencing of ideas — and these basic comprehension skills strongly affect how readily declarative knowledge is acquired and how much is ultimately available in long-term memory.
The greater the elaboration of prior knowledge — the larger and more intricate the complex of ideas retrievable — the more readily new verbal information is learned and remembered.

Designing verbal-information instruction requires determining what schemas the prospective student already has, because new information is best learned with a readily accessible schema whose slots the new content can fill.

Verbal comprehension has been shown in many studies to predict the ease with which new verbal knowledge is acquired, and if only one ability test score could be obtained for a group about to learn verbal information, verbal comprehension would be the one to choose.

Acquiring a new attitude may require retrieval of specific intellectual skills that make the choice actionable — estimating chemical concentrations for a safety attitude, or calculating caloric intake for a dietary one.
When a human model is used, previously learned information must be available that identifies the model as a familiar, respected person and attests to his or her credibility.

The essential verbal information for attitude learning takes the form of schemas representing the situations in which the attitude will be displayed, and the attitude is most effective when those situational schemas can be readily recalled at the time of learning.

Traits such as sociability and external locus of control may possibly affect how easily a learner acquires an attitude communicated by a model, but little evidence is available and these relationships are judged not to be of great significance.

Two kinds of prior learning matter for a new motor skill: the previously learned part skills that are components of the total skill, and the procedural rule (an intellectual skill) that Fitts and Posner identified as an early cognitive learning stage.
Whatever degree of skill practice yields, the procedure must always be followed for skill improvement to occur.
Correlations between abilities such as speed of movement, motor coordination, and spatial visualisation and motor-skill learning are usually found to be low to moderate.

Motivation is a hypothetical construct explaining the initiation, direction, intensity, and persistence of goal-directed behaviour; it cannot be measured directly and is inferred from observed student behaviour.

Causes of motivation are classified as extrinsic or intrinsic; understanding which internal factors motivate people lets a designer build in questions that arouse curiosity or opportunities for social interaction and approval.

Not all individuals are motivated by the same things — a situation may motivate one learner and not another because of prior learning, experience, or expectations — yet motivation researchers have described principles generalisable enough to warrant use in designing materials.

The ARCS model organises motivational design into four categories — attention, relevance, confidence, and satisfaction — each implying design questions such as capturing interest, letting learners set their own goals, providing practice with a high degree of success, and rewarding good performance.
The objective of attending to motivation within instructional design is to get students to give the time and intensity of effort necessary to learn the required knowledge and skills.

Design procedure by learner characteristic: stimulate retrieval of prerequisite intellectual skills; provide for retrieval of cognitive strategies when available; stimulate recall of propositions and of the meaningful context or situational schema; activate previously acquired positive attitudes for motivation; and recall essential part skills for motor learning.
Instructional design procedures should include provisions for detecting the presence of relevant schemas and activating them by questions, advance organisers, or other devices.

Instruction should be adapted to learner differences in abilities and traits only to the extent feasibility permits — for example easily read text for learners low in verbal comprehension, and detailed learning guidance with frequent feedback for highly anxious learners.
condition: to the extent that feasibility considerations permit

statement: Where instruction is verbal in nature, ease of verbal comprehension is of particular importance in the design.
condition: when the instruction is verbal in nature

statement: Performance objectives are in practice written during the process of task analysis — to clarify target objectives and classify the skills to be learned so further analysis is possible — rather than strictly after it.
Because instructional design technology corrects and revises instruction based on empirical testing, the desired outcomes must be stated clearly and unambiguously.

A performance objective is a precise statement of a capability that, if possessed by the learner, can be observed as a performance; before developing any instruction the designer must be able to answer what the learners will be able to do afterward that they could not do before.

Precisely defined objectives serve two needs at once — communicating the purposes of instruction and evaluating it — by ensuring that what is evaluated and what is communicated as the intended outcome carry a common meaning, and by specifying the domains from which achievement-test items are drawn.
The test for overcoming ambiguity in a course-purpose statement is to ask how one would know when the purpose has been achieved.

Course-purpose statements may communicate general goals successfully to fellow teachers yet remain too imprecise for unambiguous communication of content and outcomes, because they do not tell how someone could observe what has been accomplished without having been present during the lesson.

An objective is precisely described when it communicates to another person what would have to be done to observe that the stated lesson purpose has been accomplished; it is imprecise if the reader cannot think of how to carry out that observation.

Mentalistic wording such as realises that most plant growth requires sunshine fails the precision test, whereas demonstrates that sunshine affects plant growth states in a general way what observation is required.

The five-component objective specifies the situation, the type of learned capability, the object of the performance, the specific action the learner takes, and the tools, constraints, or special conditions associated with the performance.

A capability cannot be observed directly, only inferred from satisfactory performance on a task that employs it, and the particular action exhibited is often confused with the capability itself — which is why the five-component objective carries two verbs, one defining the capability and one the observable action.

One purpose of unambiguous objectives is to let the designer determine which conditions of learning must be built into the instructional materials, which is why the five-component form is more specific than other authors' definitions.

The situation component must specify the stimulus situation the learner faces, because what the student actually does is highly dependent on it — whether a letter is typed from longhand copy, from an auditory message, or from notes changes the task.

The objective may also need to describe the environmental conditions under which the behaviour will be performed on the job: unimportant for many learned behaviours, but critical for others such as donning a gas mask.
condition: when the performance environment materially changes the task

statement: An objective phrased only as an observable behaviour is ambiguous about which capability is intended — typing a business letter could mean copying from a draft or composing one — and including a learned-capability verb removes that ambiguity.

The nine standard learned-capability verbs are: discriminates, identifies, classifies, demonstrates, generates, adopts, states, executes, and chooses — covering discrimination, concrete concept, defined concept, rule, higher-order rule (problem solving), cognitive strategy, verbal information, motor skill, and attitude.
Including the learned-capability verb in the objective both communicates the intended behaviour more clearly and makes the conditions of learning appropriate to that outcome type readily applicable.
The object component names the content of the learner's performance, and the action verb describes how the performance is to be completed and hence what would be observed.
Never use one of the nine learned-capability verbs as the action verb, because doing so creates confusion when the objectives are later sequenced.

Special tools or constraints named in an objective are conditions placed on the performance, not the skill being acquired, and like the situation they may imply further prerequisite skills that must be learned before the target skill can be adequately evaluated.
Writing a five-component objective is itself a problem-solving task whose first sub-problem is deciding what type of learning outcome the instruction aims to produce.

Discrimination objectives always require seeing, hearing, feeling, smelling, or tasting sameness or difference between stimuli, and the action is an indication of same or different such as pointing or circling.

Whether the performance environment must be specified in a discrimination objective depends on whether the real setting makes the discrimination harder — an operating kitchen full of competing food smells is a harder setting than an isolated one.
condition: where competing stimuli in the real environment raise task difficulty

statement: A concrete-concept objective uses identify and can be satisfied by any of several acceptable actions — describing, pointing to, touching, selecting, or recognising pictures — since a learner may know the concept without being able to describe it.

Identifying anything requires that the learner first discriminate the critical physical attributes, so a concrete-concept objective presupposes the underlying discriminations in whichever sensory modality is available to the learner.

A defined concept is a rule that classifies objects or events by expressing the relationships among the concept's attributes and its function, so its objective verb is classify and the learner must classify an instance by reference to the definition.

A defined-concept objective can be observed in several ways: describing or illustrating the concept by reference to its definition, selecting the instances that conform to the definition from descriptions that do and do not, or applying the concept properly in a sentence.

A rule objective uses demonstrate and must be specific enough about the object that the class of stimulus situations is unambiguous — short division of three-digit by one-digit numbers with no remainder, not merely division — so the task components can be described and the right instruction designed.
Most rules are complex because they require previously learned concepts and rules — short division requires multiplication and subtraction, which in turn require addition.

Rule-using and problem-solving objectives are distinguished by asking demonstrate what rule versus generate what rule: if learners are given the rule and asked to apply it the outcome is rule learning, and if they must generate a new rule or synthesise existing ones it is problem solving.

When writing a problem-solving objective the instructor should focus on what the learner is constructing — the higher-order rule expressing relationships among other rules and concepts — rather than on the process of problem solving.

Problem-solving objectives are hard to write mainly because problem-solving skills are usually not formally taught: most teachers present problem situations and then verify whether the student has the skill.

The verb for cognitive-strategy objectives is adopt, and the objective should not hand the learner the strategy — it implies the learner will select an already known technique; a learner who truly originates a strategy is doing problem solving (generating a strategy).

Verbal-information learning must be distinguished from verbal-chain learning: individuals can learn and recall extremely long verbal chains verbatim without comprehending the words, whereas verbal information consists of semantically meaningful propositions.

Because a verbatim answer may be a rote verbal chain, requiring the learner to state the information in his own words or to use it in a different question is what proves it was stored as meaningful propositions.
exception: verbatim recall does not by itself prove the information is not meaningfully stored

statement: A task is a motor-skill objective only when precision, timing, and coordination of muscular performance are genuinely involved; where the learner already has the requisite motor skills and is merely following a procedure, the outcome is rule learning.

An attitude objective uses choose and must state the situation precisely, because situational factors determine the choice — choosing to vote when convenient is a different objective from choosing to vote even when inconvenient.

Many cognitive objectives have affective components, and a designer who specifies them will attend to the context in which the skill is presented, making the new skill meaningful to the learner and building in as much reinforcement as possible.

A criterion of performance need not be included in the objective statement, for two reasons: the necessary criteria are likely to differ by capability type so a uniform criterion would be an error, and criterion setting is a measurement question best considered with assessment procedures.
exception: if the criteria are already known when the objective is written they may be included under tools, constraints, and special conditions

statement: The mastery level specified for a skill that is prerequisite to further learning may have to be higher than for a skill that is not prerequisite to anything.
condition: when the skill is a prerequisite for subsequent learning

statement: An objective statement exists for unambiguous communication of intent, so not all five components need be written out if the intent is already unambiguous — but any component left implicit is left open to interpretation.
condition: only where the shorter statement is genuinely unambiguous

statement: Turning a vague purpose into an objective starts with the designer asking what kind of capability is actually wanted, then rejecting candidate performances that would be satisfied by a lesser capability.

Understanding a concept such as an electric circuit is not shown by stating what it is (that could be mere verbal information) nor by distinguishing instances from non-instances (the learner may be cueing on a surface feature such as an open wire); it is shown by using the rule in one or more specific situations.

A purpose worded as taking personal responsibility concerns whether students tend to act on all appropriate occasions without specific direction, which makes it an attitude objective about choices of personal action rather than a skill objective.
Identifying the major characters in a play is a defined-concept objective: the learner classifies each character by defining that character's relationship to the plot, not by naming them.

Asking a learner to paraphrase a difficult passage in simpler terms is a problem-solving objective — a whole set of problems in which subordinate rules (synonyms, defining, figures of speech) are applied to generate higher-order rules — and the higher-order rules cannot be specified exactly in advance because the solution path is unknown.
A concept that cannot be denoted by pointing must be treated as a defined concept, so recognising a metaphor is a classify objective performed by reference to the definition.

For rule-using skills such as interpreting charts, particular attention must be paid to describing the situation, because more complex instances may require several intellectual skills or a combination of them.
Objectives defined this way reveal the fine-grained nature of instruction: there may be scores of objectives for a single course topic and several for each individual lesson.

Once each of a lesson's objectives has been classified by capability type, the designer can decide whether an original intention was overlooked or under-represented, whether the lesson has a suitable balance of expected outcomes, and whether the instructional approach matches the objective's type in each case.

A lesson normally has a primary objective without which it would hardly be worthwhile, plus supporting objectives of other capability types that must be learned first — an intellectual-skill lesson is typically supported by information, cognitive-strategy, and attitude objectives.

Judgments about correspondence with original intentions and about balance of objectives are made at the topic and course level as well as the lesson level, and are made possible by categorising objectives into capability types.

When instructional materials do not state their objectives, the teacher must infer what they are and design the lesson so the textbook's objectives are supplemented by others; determining the categories of expected outcomes matters as much for the teacher as for a design team.

Because an objective describes what must be observed to verify the desired learning, it more or less directly describes the assessment situation the teacher can set up, and can equally serve as the basis for teacher-made tests or for student self-tests.
Performance objectives serve both as guidelines for developing the instruction and as the basis for designing the measures that determine whether the objectives were reached.

Instruction often produces unintended or unexpected outcomes, judged desirable or undesirable only when later observed, so the planned objectives are the basis for evaluation without being the whole of what occurs.
Care is needed in choosing action verbs that both suit the learned capability inferred from the performance and describe the nature of the performance itself.

Different communications of the same objective — for teachers, students, and parents — can be derived from one precisely formulated definition, which also ties those same meanings to the construction of tests.
Design begins from the question of what students will be doing after they have learned, not what they will be studying.

Two kinds of objectives are involved in design: target objectives to be attained at the end of a course, and enabling objectives that must be attained during it because they are prerequisites to the target objectives.
The analysis procedure begins with the target objectives and then works top-down to determine what enabling objectives are prerequisite to attaining them.
The process of task analysis is the same for a course as for a lesson; only the scope of the analysis and the number of steps differ.

A statement of course purpose must describe what the student will be like after the instruction, not what he does during the course: providing experience with apparatus describes activity, whereas stating apparatus names or assembling apparatus for experiments describes learning.

Course purposes should be stated as expected current outcomes rather than distant ones: acquiring a lifelong respect for a subject is not a realistic outcome of a single course, though nothing is wrong with the lifelong goal itself.
At the course-purpose stage it is not necessary to formulate specific five-component objectives, though many of the same guidelines apply to defining purposes.
There are two major classes of task analysis: procedural task analysis (also called information-processing analysis), and learning-task analysis.

A procedural task analysis breaks a task into the steps the learner must perform, and must include mental steps such as recalling an item or deciding between forms as well as observable ones — which is why it also accounts for the intellectual skills that are components of the total task.
Because choices differ from actions, the analysis diagram must distinguish kinds of steps — conventionally a trapezoid for input, a rectangle for an action, and a diamond for a choice or decision.

Information-processing analysis yields two things: a clear description of the target objective including the steps of the procedure, which lets the designer specify the sequence for presentation to the learner; and the revelation of individual steps — especially internal decision steps — that would not otherwise be obvious.
A decision step exposed by information-processing analysis is itself a specific skill that must be acquired if not already known, and so becomes one of the target objectives making up the total task.

After the information-processing analysis, the component skills are written as five-component objectives, which requires classifying them by learning-outcome type and thereby makes the learning-task analysis possible.

A prerequisite is a task learned prior to a target objective that aids or enables its learning; the same task may be a target objective for one lesson and an enabling objective for a later one, and prerequisites may have been learned years earlier, immediately before, or within the same lesson.

Prerequisite objectives should be classified as either essential prerequisites — actual components of the total skill, without which the target cannot be learned or performed correctly — or supportive prerequisites, which merely make the new learning easier or faster.

Whether a component skill was acquired through formal instruction or incidentally is irrelevant to systematic design; what matters is that essential prerequisites be acquired before the target objective, early or late in the course of instruction.
Essential and supportive prerequisites differ considerably in character for each task category, which is a major reason for performing task classification before attempting to identify prerequisites.

A target objective that is an intellectual skill is typically composed of two or more simpler subordinate skills that must be learned before the target skill is put together, whether long before or within the same lesson.

Superficially similar problems can conceal distinct prerequisite rules: subtracting whole numbers by borrowing decomposes into subtraction without borrowing, several borrowings in nonadjacent columns, successive borrowing in adjacent columns, and borrowing across zero.

Carrying learning-task analysis down through successively simpler components of a target skill yields a learning hierarchy — a diagram of progressively simpler enabling intellectual skills, each itself composed of subordinate skills.

The most important questions answered by a learning-task analysis come from any two adjacent levels of the hierarchy, because when the design interest is one intellectual skill the enabling skills of primary relevance are its immediate prerequisites.
A fully worked-out learning hierarchy has two main uses: guiding the design of an instructional sequence, and guiding student and teacher in planning instructional assignments.

Sequential steps and subordinate skills must be kept distinct: the steps are what a person does in sequence when exhibiting the learned performance, whereas the subordinate skills are what the person must learn, in a sequence beginning with the simplest.

Subordinate skills are derived by asking of any intellectual skill what simpler skills a learner would have to possess to learn this skill, then repeating the same question of each skill so identified.

The analysis stops at a pragmatically determined point where, given knowledge of student characteristics, the lowest-level skills are judged already known; this stopping point varies with the learners' educational background, so the same target skill yields a deeper hierarchy for less prepared students.
condition: the stopping point depends on the specific learner population

statement: Empirical hierarchy validation showed that information-type capabilities such as stating that the slope of a position-time graph is velocity were helpful but not essential prerequisites, contrasting markedly with the genuinely essential intellectual-skill components.

Verbal information supports intellectual-skill learning by aiding the verbal communications of instruction — often as labels for the concepts in a rule — and by providing a context of retrieval cues for the skill.
The design error to avoid is not mixing intellectual skills and information during instruction — which is normal — but confusing the two types of learning as target objectives.

Cognitive strategies may speed the learning of intellectual skills, make them easier to recall, or aid transfer to novel problems, but empirical evidence of the effectiveness of that support is as yet scanty and still needed.

The attitudes a learner holds toward a subject are presumed to strongly influence the ease with which it is learned, retained, and used, and a review of the literature shows attitude learning strongly related to the learning of cognitive skills.

Capabilities such as information and attitudes are not learned by putting together subordinate parts as intellectual skills are, so their prerequisites tend to be supportive rather than essential and they do not form learning hierarchies.

The prerequisite map by outcome type is: intellectual skills need simpler component skills (essential) plus attitudes, cognitive strategies, and verbal information (supportive); cognitive strategies need specific intellectual skills; verbal information needs meaningfully organised sets of information plus language skills; attitudes sometimes need intellectual skills and verbal information; motor skills sometimes need part skills and procedural rules.
The essential prerequisites for cognitive strategies appear to be very basic mental abilities such as forming visual images or dividing a verbally described situation into parts.

There is disagreement over how far the prerequisites of cognitive strategies depend on innate maturation versus learning, but on either account the effect takes place over a considerable period of intellectual development.
To learn and store verbal information the learner must already possess the language skills of forming propositions in accordance with rules of syntax, which are usually learned fairly early in life.

Verbal information is most readily learned and retained within a larger context of meaningful information, and that context — learned immediately before or long previously — deserves to be classified as a supportive prerequisite.

Acquiring an attitude may essentially require prior intellectual skills and specific verbal information — for example comprehending a printed food label plus information about ingredients before a truth-in-labelling attitude can be acquired.

Attitudes are mutually supportive: a related attitude eases adoption of another, and in general the degree to which a human model is respected affects the readiness with which the model's attitude is adopted.

Knowledge of the situations in which the choice of personal action will be made contributes to the ease of attitude acquisition, so an attitude is more readily acquired when the learner knows the specific social situations where the temptation arises.

For motor skills, part skills function as essential prerequisites when the most efficient learning comes from practising them separately and later combining them, and a separately learned executive subroutine (procedural rule) is likewise an essential prerequisite.
condition: when separate part practice is in fact the more efficient route for that skill

statement: Instructional curriculum mapping represents the functional relationships among objectives by starting from the target objective and asking what other objectives — essential or supportive — relate to its attainment.

In an instructional curriculum map, objectives from the same domain are connected with solid lines and a cross-domain link is marked with a symbol; what matters is not the particular symbol but that the domain shift be recognised, because it implies different conditions of learning will be needed.
Instructional curriculum mapping makes it possible to see where there are holes in the instruction and where there are extraneous dead-wood objectives that do not relate to any target objective.
Verbal-information objectives that are supportive rather than essential need not be prerequisites of each other, but may still be taught in a contextual supportive sequence.

Entry skills are prerequisites — essential or supportive — that the learner is expected to hold before the lesson and that will not be taught during it; drawing them below a dotted line in the hierarchy or map makes it possible to construct a pretest for readiness.

Task classification exists to provide the basis for designing the conditions necessary for effective instruction, since each of the five outcome categories carries different implications for the conditions of learning.
The most obvious sequencing principle follows the order from simple prerequisite skills to complex target skills, which take longer to accomplish.
Cognitive learning theory holds that one very important determinant of what students will learn, and how fast, is what they already know.

Elaboration theory proposes macrolevel sequencing in which the student first meets an epitome — a few general, simple, fundamental ideas — then successively more detailed elaborations, with content organised simple to complex and general to specific.

The elaboration pattern of overview, elaboration, summary, and synthesis — with each round reviewing the overview and delineating relationships between new and earlier ideas — is repeated until the desired level of coverage is reached.
A course should be organised from the top downward, from general to more specific objectives, using the functional relationships among the types of learning.

Intellectual-skill objectives are the usual starting point for sequencing because of their importance as curriculum components and because more is known about sequencing relationships among them than among other capability types; objectives from other domains are then woven in insofar as they support those skills.
exception: if the terminal objective is not an intellectual skill but an attitude, the intellectual skills supportive of that attitude must be identified instead

statement: Courses differ enormously in definiteness: a CPR course has consensus on objectives, mastery criteria, and teaching time with relatively few objectives, whereas a computer-literacy curriculum is broader with less agreement on terminal objectives and far more of them.
Time is a very important part of planning instruction, and the amount available must be carefully considered when setting course and unit objectives.

Even the largest course can be described at five levels of performance outcome: lifelong objectives, end-of-course objectives, unit objectives, specific performance objectives (the level appropriate for task analysis), and enabling objectives.

A lifelong objective states what learners will continue to do after the course — enrolling in further study and choosing to apply, modify, or originate the learned methods — and is distinct from the end-of-course objective, which states the performance expected immediately after instruction.

How complete the instructional events designed into a lesson need to be depends on the sophistication of the learners, because it depends on which events the learners are expected to provide for themselves.

The learning sequence often should differ from the performance sequence: a complex skill needed early in a procedure may be more easily learned after skills used later, as when writing good test items becomes easier once five-component objectives can be written, even though on the job the item comes first.
condition: when a skill used early in performance is easier to learn after later-used skills

statement: The sequence problem arises at four distinct levels — course, topic or unit, lesson, and lesson component — and it is important to distinguish among them because quite different considerations apply to each.

Course-level sequence decisions must ensure the prerequisite information and intellectual skills for any topic have been learned earlier — adding fractions after multiplying and dividing whole numbers, graphing relations after measuring variables, the concept of culture before comparing family structures across cultures.

Course and curriculum sequences are typically represented in scope-and-sequence charts that lay out the topics of a course or set of courses in a matrix, which is a good first step in defining different levels of skill across content topics.

A scope-and-sequence matrix crossed with outcome types is especially useful for surfacing the affective outcomes that would otherwise be omitted — in a computer course most outcomes are intellectual skills, but in the social-issues unit the attitude outcomes are the most important ones.

Where two units' intellectual-skill objectives are fairly independent their teaching order is not critical, whereas units whose skills are prerequisite to the next must be sequenced accordingly — so a course-level map should distinguish ordered from unordered units.

Topic-level objectives must be stated in performance terms; wordings such as understand the procedure or appreciate the equipment are too ambiguous and may imply different performance objectives to different people.

At the unit-planning level the outline should be kept broad with only the major objectives specified, because each unit objective may have a great many subordinate essential and supportive prerequisites and the detail can get out of hand.
Course, unit, and lesson maps stand in a globe-to-country-to-state-map relation: each successive level shows less scope and more detail.
A lesson occupies a given period of time and lesson length varies by audience — shorter for a small child than for an adult because attention span is shorter.

Designers sometimes aim for one learning outcome per lesson because each outcome type requires different learning conditions, but since teaching a single objective may take very little time it is not feasible to give every objective its own lesson, so specific objectives are grouped.

It is more important to plan lessons around the order in which the performance objectives are best learned than to worry about mixing outcome types in one lesson; once objectives are grouped by functional relationship and available sitting time, integrating the necessary conditions of learning becomes straightforward.

Lesson sequencing within a unit should follow the prerequisite relationships among objectives, requiring that new learning is supported by previous learning, that a learning analysis confirms sequential order, that the sequences are complete, and that objectives irrelevant to the learning task are eliminated or taught at a different time.

Sequencing principles differ by outcome type: each new intellectual skill must be preceded by prior mastery of its subordinate skills; problem-solving situations should involve recall of previously acquired relevant intellectual skills; for major verbal-information subtopics the order of presentation is not important but new facts should be preceded by a meaningful context; attitudes require establishing respect for the source first and mastery of any intellectual skills before the choice situation; and motor skills need intensive practice on critical part skills plus practice on the total skill, with the executive subroutine learned first.
Verbal information relevant to a new intellectual skill, or to the choices in an attitude objective, should either have been previously learned or be presented in the instructions.

Building a lesson map requires asking both what the learner must know to learn the new skills and what these learners already know that matters for it; the answer to the second question defines the lesson's entry skills.

The designer must begin with information about the audience and make explicit assumptions about the skills they bring, which usually requires a fairly detailed analysis of the intellectual skills involved in the lesson because that analysis is the organising factor for sequencing.
If constructing a lesson map reveals that the skills cannot be taught in a single instructional period, the map should be divided into two lesson maps each representing one period.
condition: when the mapped skills exceed one instructional period

statement: When a proper sequence of prerequisite skills is established, intellectual-skill learning becomes easy for a teacher to manage and highly reinforcing for learners, who repeatedly find they can suddenly do something they could not do before — the opposite of drill and rote recitation.

Being simpler is not enough to make a skill a prerequisite: a prerequisite is integrally related to the skill above it, such that the superior skill cannot be performed if the prerequisite is unavailable to the learner.
The test question for identifying a prerequisite is what skill the learner must have to learn this new skill, the absence of which would make that learning impossible.

A first attempt at listing prerequisites is checked by examining the demands the new skill makes and identifying where the learner could go wrong; the specification should completely describe the previously learned skills needed to acquire the new skill most readily.
If learners already know each subordinate skill, learning the target objective is easy and rapid, sometimes with the immediacy implied by the word discovery.

When a learner struggles with a new intellectual skill the first diagnostic question should be which prerequisite skills that person failed to learn — not what genetic deficiency or what general intelligence the learner has, because those questions lead to solutions that merely remove the learner from the learning environment.

Responsible diagnosis attempts to discover what the learner needs to learn; the answer is very likely a prerequisite intellectual skill identified by the learning hierarchy, for which instruction can readily be designed to get the learner back on track.

A lesson with a procedural-rule primary objective typically also needs verbal information about the varieties involved and attitudes such as carefulness, precision, and hazard avoidance, and a curriculum map traces the interrelationships among these different kinds of objectives.

Learners' differing goals for the same subject imply different lesson objectives and different combinations of objectives, so provision for multiple objectives begins with consideration of the goals of the particular instruction being designed.

Integrating different objectives into learner goals requires more than an external instructional map: it requires the learner to acquire a higher-order cognitive structure — a goal schema — that represents the goal.

When learning several objectives integrated in a goal, learners must retrieve prior verbal information and prerequisite skills, apply the encoding procedures suited to each objective type, associate retrieval cues with the rules and propositions acquired, and keep in mind how the new material will be displayed or used.
Maintaining a mental set about how the learning will be used is crucial for transfer — for applying what has been learned to the learner's goals.

The purposive external activity the learner is aiming at is called an enterprise, and the goal is its internal cognitive representation; each such pursuit is an activity with a purpose, not simply an activity.

A goal schema relates the goal to its prerequisites — verbal knowledge as labels, concepts and rules, cognitive strategies, and attitudes — and includes a scenario or script, a progression of verbal information relating learned knowledge to the enterprise, which reminds learners where they have been and where they are going.

Common enterprise types include denoting (elaborative identifying that goes beyond labelling to demonstrate the rules in an entity's definition), manifesting (showing others the steps in a procedure or process, typically needing narrative plus rule demonstration), and discovering (problem solving or finding a novel process, integrating intellectual skills and verbal information).

Provision for activating the goal should be made well toward the beginning of instruction, carried out within the second event of instruction as a verbal statement of the goal and its relation to prerequisite skills, knowledge, and attitudes, plus a verbal scenario relating what is to be newly learned to the goal.
The verbal communications that establish a goal schema are relatively simple yet adequate, and should be related as far as possible to the individual learner's prior experience and motivation.

An established goal schema functions metacognitively: it monitors new learning to keep it on track and free of distraction, rejects attention to irrelevant events, aids retrieval of prerequisite knowledge when performance is required, and supports mindful abstraction that enhances transfer.

Course-level topic sequencing is typically done by common-sense logic: one topic precedes another because it describes earlier events, because it is a component part, or because it provides a meaningful context for what follows.

It is not always necessary to list complete performance objectives at every intermediate planning level; choosing representative samples of objectives within each outcome domain is a workable method, though the fuller procedure can be followed and is sometimes desirable.

A new skill is learned most readily when the learner can recall the subordinate skills that compose it; once the intellectual-skill sequence is designed, learning of other capabilities is interjected at appropriate points, before, during, or after.

Instruction is the set of events that acts upon and involves the student during a lesson; in a basic sense these events are a set of communications, most typically verbal but for young children gestures or pictures.

The sole aim of instructional communications is to aid learning, not to inform; keeping firmly in mind that anything beyond facilitating learning is mere chatter is the best guard against a teacher talking too much.
Much teacher communication is essential for learning: sometimes a fairly large amount is needed, on other occasions none at all.

Any or all of the events of instruction may be supplied by the learner when self-instructing — not only with programmed materials but when studying textbooks, doing laboratory exercises, or completing projects.

Skill at self-instruction increases with learner age and experience, so lesson events require far more teacher activity in the first grade than in the tenth, and learners progressively become self-learners who manage their own learning with skills and strategies.
The events of instruction should not be viewed as invariably required for every lesson and every learner; a judgment must be made about how much self-instruction the learner can undertake.

To design instruction at the level of the individual learning episode, the desirable characteristics of instructional events must be derived from what is known about the learner's internal processes rather than invented.

The internal processes of a single act of learning are attention, selective perception, rehearsal, semantic encoding, retrieval including search, response organisation, feedback that sets reinforcement in motion, and executive control processes that select and activate cognitive strategies modifying any of the others.
Retrieved information may be transformed directly into action by a response generator or recalled to working memory where it combines with incoming information to form new learned capabilities.

Instruction is possible because the internal processes of learning, though largely self-activating, can also be influenced by external events — selective perception by highlighting, underlining, or bold printing, and semantic encoding by externally supplied meaningful information.

The events of instruction are designed to let learners proceed from where they are to the capability named in the target objective; they sometimes arise naturally from interaction with the materials but mostly must be deliberately arranged by a designer or teacher.

The exact form of the instructional events cannot be specified in general for all lessons but must be decided for each learning objective, with the chosen communications designed to have the desired effect in supporting learning processes.

Each event of instruction maps to a learning process: gaining attention to reception; informing the learner of the objective to activating executive control; stimulating recall of prerequisites to retrieval into working memory; presenting the stimulus material to selective perception; providing learning guidance to semantic encoding and retrieval cues; eliciting performance to response organisation; providing feedback to reinforcement; assessing performance to retrieval plus reinforcement; and enhancing retention and transfer to retrieval cues and strategies.

The events of instruction do not invariably occur in the listed order — that is only their most probable order — and by no means are all of them provided for every lesson, since their role is to stimulate internal processes, not replace them.

In design practice the list of instructional events becomes a checklist, against which the designer asks whether these learners need support at this stage for this task; an event already obvious to the learner, or one experienced self-learners supply themselves, may be omitted.

Attention can be gained by stimulus change or, more fundamentally, by appealing to the learner's interests; because every student's interests differ, no standard content can be prescribed and skill at gaining attention rests on insightful knowledge of the particular students.
Partially or wholly nonverbal communications — a demonstration of a novel physical event, or an unusual scene on film or television — are often used to gain attention for school lessons.

A good preplanned lesson gives the teacher one or more options for attention-gaining communications, and individualised instruction lets the teacher vary their content and form to match individual interests.

The learner should know what performance will indicate that learning has been accomplished; where the aim is obvious no special communication is required, but many school objectives are not obvious — reciting a passage verbatim is a different objective from stating its major ideas.
condition: unless the objective is already obvious or already known to the learner

statement: The student should not have to guess what is in the instructor's mind: it is probably best not to assume the student knows the lesson objective, since the communication takes little time, prevents the student getting off the track, is consistent with the frankness of a good teacher, and helps the teacher stay on target.

Objectives written to communicate unambiguously to teachers and designers must be translated into words or pictures the students themselves can readily understand before being communicated in a lesson.

The speculation that communicating an objective keeps students from pursuing other objectives they formulate themselves has never been observed and is highly unlikely; the basic purpose of the communication is simply to answer the student's question of how he will know when he has learned.

When multiple objectives serve an enterprise, the objective-informing event is elaborated to build a goal schema: the learner is told what purposeful activity the new learning is aimed at — passing a test, teaching others, applying it practically, solving a problem — and a scenario relates the single objectives to that goal.
condition: when the lesson pursues multiple objectives serving an enterprise

statement: Because most new learning is the combining of previously learned ideas, the component concepts and rules must be highly accessible at the moment of learning, and their accessibility is ensured by having them recalled just before the new learning takes place.
Recall of previously learned capabilities is stimulated by asking a recognition or, better, a recall question, and a chain of such questions can lead the learner toward the new rule.

The stimuli presented must be those involved in the performance that reflects the learning — oral French questions for answering oral French questions, verbally stated problems for solving verbally stated problems — because neglecting to use the proper stimuli can leave the learner having acquired the wrong skill.
exception: a differently-stimulated task may legitimately be used earlier as a subordinate skill

statement: Stimulus presentation should emphasise the features that determine selective perception — italics, bold print, underlining, heavy outlining, circling, or arrows on the essential features of a picture or diagram.

In establishing discriminations, distinctive features are emphasised by enlarging the differences between the objects first and reducing them later — large shape differences before small ones, distorted letter forms before the true smaller contrasts.

Learning concepts and rules requires presenting a variety of examples that differ in irrelevant properties; the importance of this can hardly be overemphasised for young children, and failing to vary examples produces the classic case of a child who recognised verticality with a pencil but not with a table knife.
For rule learning, knowing the formula and all its component concepts is not enough — the learner must work a variety of examples to ensure he understands and can use the rule.
Retention and transfer are likely to be enhanced by presenting problems stated in words, in diagrams, and in combinations of the two over a period of time.

Concepts and rules may be taught inductively or deductively: for concrete concepts it is best to present a variety of examples before the definition, whereas for older learners acquiring a defined concept a simple definition may best come first, followed at once by an example — provided the component concepts are already understood.
condition: the definition-first route assumes the learner understands the component concepts

statement: Learning guidance consists of hints and questions that do not tell the learner the answer but suggest the line of thought leading to the combining of subordinate concepts and rules into the new rule.

What the teacher or textbook literally says in providing learning guidance is not the important point; what matters is that the communication performs its function of stimulating a direction of thought and keeping the learner on track, thereby contributing to the efficiency of learning.

The amount of learning guidance should vary with the capability being learned: for an arbitrary matter such as a new object's name, telling the learner the answer is the correct guidance and indirect hinting wastes time; where discovery is a logical route to the answer, less direct prompting is appropriate and may yield more permanent learning.

Learning guidance is readily adapted to learner differences: highly didactic instruction with low-level questions appeals most to high-anxiety learners, low-anxiety learners respond to the challenge of difficult questions, and frequent pictures and oral communication aid poor readers while being inefficient for skilled ones.

Too much guidance may seem condescending to a quick learner and too little frustrates a slow one, so the best practical solution is often to release guidance a little at a time and let the student take as much as needed — one hint for a fast learner, three or four for a slower one.

In attitude learning the human model and the communications it delivers constitute the learning guidance, so the event takes a more complex form than for verbal information or intellectual skills while still serving semantic encoding.

Eliciting the performance asks the learner to show he can do it, first with the same example he has been working with, and the instructor normally follows with a second, new example to make sure the rule can be applied to a fresh instance.
Eliciting performance serves to convince the learners as well as the instructor that they know how to do it.

Learning is not necessarily complete once the correct performance appears: the after-effects of the learning event importantly influence exactly what is learned, so at minimum there should be feedback about the correctness or degree of correctness of the performance.

Some tasks provide automatic feedback — a thrown dart's distance from the bull's eye, a matched printed word that conveys an expected meaning — but many school tasks do not, and there feedback from an outside source such as the teacher may be essential.
condition: where the task itself does not supply automatic feedback

statement: There are no standard ways of phrasing or delivering feedback — a printed answer, a nod, a smile, a spoken word — because the important characteristic is not its content but its function of informing learners about the correctness of their performance.

A single observed performance may be due to chance or guessing, so asking the learner to do it again with a different example raises the reliability of the inference far beyond chance level, and a third example raises it further.

Validity of an observed performance requires two judgments: whether the performance in fact accurately reflects the objective, and whether it occurred under conditions free of distortion such that the learner could not have memorised or remembered the answer from a previous occasion.
The informal one-to-three observations made immediately after learning are of the same kind as formally planned assessments, and there need be no conflict or discrepancy between them.

For recall of knowledge, the meaningful context in which material was learned offers the best assurance of reinstatement, because the network of relationships it was embedded in supplies multiple retrieval cues.

Retaining intellectual skills requires course planning for systematic reviews spaced at intervals across weeks and months, each requiring the skill to be retrieved and used; these spaced repetitions contrast with the relative ineffectiveness of repeated examples given directly after the initial learning.

Transfer is best assured by setting new tasks requiring application of what was learned in situations that differ substantially from the learning situation — varying the whole situation, not merely the items within the same task format.

Cognitive strategies develop through variety and novelty in problem-solving tasks introduced systematically and interspersed with other instruction; when presenting a novel problem the general nature of the expected solution must be made clear, since a practical solution differs from an original one and the student's performance is easily affected by that difference.

The events of instruction apply to all five kinds of learned capability, but the specific form of events 3 (stimulate recall), 4 (present the stimulus), and 5 (provide learning guidance) differs sharply by capability type, whereas an event such as gaining attention need not differ.

For an intellectual skill: recall must retrieve the prerequisite rules and concepts to working memory, the stimulus is a statement of the rule or concept with examples emphasising the component concepts, and guidance presents varied examples in varied contexts plus elaborations furnishing retrieval cues.

For a cognitive strategy: recall task strategies and relevant intellectual skills, describe the task and the strategy and show what the strategy accomplishes, then describe the strategy with one or more application examples.

For verbal information: recall a familiar well-organised body of knowledge related to the new learning, display printed or verbal statements emphasising distinctive features, and elaborate the content by relating it to larger bodies of knowledge using mnemonics and images.

For an attitude: recall the situation and the actions involved in the personal choice and remind the learner of the human model, then have the model describe the general nature of the choice of personal action.

For a motor skill: recall the executive subroutine and relevant part skills, display the situation existing at the beginning of the performance and demonstrate the executive subroutine, then continue practice with informative feedback.

The invariant features of a single lesson are the instructional functions that must be carried out, not a standard routine set of communications and actions; even those functions are adapted to the situation, the task, the type of learning it represents, and the students' prior learning.

Every instructional function should be specifically considered in lesson planning even where it is ultimately not provided, and the events must be organised flexibly with primary attention to the lesson's objectives.

A worked computer-based lesson shows the nine events realised frame by frame: instructions with second-by-second change to gain attention, a paired contrast example to state the objective, questions recalling prior concepts, a definition with worked instances and explicit noninstances, learner-typed responses, item-specific feedback, a fresh set of instances and noninstances for assessment with mastery guidance, and varied-form instances plus spaced review questions for retention.

A concept lesson presupposes its place in a longer sequence: teaching the concept object assumes sentence, subject, and predicate are already learned, and for learners without that background instruction would have to begin with the simpler prerequisite concepts.
condition: where learners lack the prior concepts the lesson assumes

statement: The framework of instructional events leaves considerable opportunity for the designer's art to flourish; it constrains the functions, not the creative form of the lesson.

In middle and higher grades the events of instruction are increasingly controlled by the materials or the learners themselves: where successive units are structurally similar the objectives may be evident and need not be communicated, and for reasonably well-motivated students no special provision for controlling attention may be needed.
condition: where units are structurally similar and learners are reasonably well motivated

statement: Text-based homework depends on the learner's own cognitive strategies for the instructional events: the text may aid selective perception through bold print and headings and supply a meaningful context for encoding, but practising the appropriate performance and judging its correctness fall to the learner.

An important part of studying is practising the appropriate performance — restating information in one's own words, applying a new rule to examples, or originating solutions to novel problems — not merely reading.

Some instructional events are supplied by the teacher, some by the learner, and some by the materials; an older, more experienced learner may supply most of them by his own study effort while for young children the teacher arranges most of them.

Presenting the stimulus for discrimination learning requires conditions in which the stimulus differences become increasingly fine, whereas concept learning requires a variety of instances and noninstances of the class.

Learning guidance for rules includes examples of application, for verbal information is prominently about linking to a larger meaningful context, and for attitudes takes the distinctive form of a human model and the model's communication.
Media is used in a very broad sense: instructional delivery may be by a teacher's speech or a printed text as well as by technical materials such as sound and video recordings.

A completed lesson plan should contain a statement of the lesson's objectives, a list of the instructional events to be included, a list of the media, materials, and activities by which each event is accomplished, and notes on the teacher roles and communications required.

Available materials and media presentations are not indexed or catalogued by intended instructional objective, so the teacher must decide media during lesson planning by asking what medium is wanted for each intended outcome and where the specific materials will be found.

Available materials often deliver the desired content but not the other instructional events — a film may not present the objective, guide encoding, or pause for response and feedback — so the teacher must create those events separately or stop the film so questions and feedback can occur.

Because materials are usually not designed for the exact objectives adopted and rarely provide all the desired events, media selections cannot be made from catalogues alone — the actual materials must be previewed before final selection, and the lesson plan must state how they will be used and how the missing events will be accomplished.
Many published materials are carefully organised to present information in a logical order yet do not cover each instructional event appropriate for the particular objectives.

Published instructional modules increasingly direct both teachers and learners on how the materials and exercises reach the objectives and how to know the objectives have been reached, and though not always built on this specific event list they are usually designed to implement a systematic instructional strategy.

The features of the learning situation constrain which media can be effective, and the four decisive features are: teacher-delivered versus self-instructional communication; learners with versus without sufficient verbal comprehension for print; direct versus centrally broadcast delivery; and whether errors in the performance are serious.

When errors in the performance are dangerous, all media are eliminated except those on which the performance can be directly practised — the actual equipment or a simulator; a lecture or television program may set the stage but is inadequate for learning such a skill.
condition: when potential errors in the target performance are serious or dangerous

statement: Central-broadcast delivery severely limits media to those transmitting sound, pictures, or both and providing no interactive responding by the learner.
condition: when delivery is by central broadcast

statement: The learning-situation features yield six decision types — job competence (consequences of error), central broadcast, self-instruction with readers, self-instruction with nonreaders, instructor with readers, and instructor with nonreaders — each of which sets certain media aside as inappropriate while leaving several options.
As a general rule most instructional functions can be performed by most media, so media choice is rarely forced by function alone.

Media are often chosen in practice on availability, feasibility, and cost, but appropriateness for learning should be addressed first so that critical errors are avoided — no printed discourse for nonreaders, no radio broadcast alone for intellectual skills, no instructor lecture for training vehicle driving — with cost and availability deciding among the remaining learning-appropriate options.

Instructional media are defined as the physical means by which an instructional message is communicated, so a printed text, an audiotape, a training device, a TV program, and an instructor talking are all media.

The six learning situations exclude media as follows: high performance competence with serious error consequences allows only large equipment, portable equipment, or a simulator; central broadcast allows only TV and radio broadcast; self-instruction with readers and instructor with readers leave all media potentially effective; self-instruction with nonreaders excludes media using discursive printed passages or complex audio; and instructor with nonreaders excludes printed texts and complex instructor lectures.

A simulator reproduces the operating characteristics of real equipment, whereas a training device permits practice of skills or part skills without necessarily having the appearance or operating characteristics of the real equipment; a training aid merely exhibits a process the learner observes without interacting.
Verbal knowledge of all kinds is readily transmitted by radio and TV broadcast, and intellectual skills have been successfully taught by broadcast when provisions are made for student response.
condition: intellectual-skill teaching by broadcast requires provision for student response

statement: Computer-based instruction can be truly interactive, providing adaptive informative feedback according to whether learner responses are correct or incorrect, which makes it particularly well suited for learning intellectual skills.
condition: only when suitably designed for adaptive feedback

statement: Television is normally not learner-interactive but can be made so by combining a tape cassette or videodisc with a computer.

The instructor's media functions are the voice delivering speech, the action demonstrating procedures, and the delivery of informative feedback adapted to learner responding — in addition to the executive functions of planning and managing instruction.

Matching media characteristics to the learning situation is only the first step; the field must then be narrowed to the few media capable of supporting the instruction most effectively, with the final choice of one or two made on practical feasibility.
There is no one medium universally superior to all others for all types of desired outcome and all learners, a conclusion supported by research on media utilisation.

Media cannot be identified as particularly effective for a single school subject at a single grade level; both careful design work and media research suggest media are best selected for specific purposes within a single lesson.

A film may portray content effectively while leaving the teacher to inform the learner of the objective, offer learning guidance, and provide feedback — not because a film could not carry those events, but because most available films do not.
