Film is uniquely able to portray theoretical events such as atomic particles in motion, and to enlarge, condense, speed up, or slow down the portrayal of observable activities in nature or manufacturing.
Beyond the learning situation, media-selection models narrow choices using three categories of factor: physical attributes of the media, task characteristics, and learner characteristics.
Visual display capability is needed for teaching identification of concrete concepts such as shapes and objects and for spatial relationships such as locations and distances.
When printed text is otherwise appropriate, print on paper is one of the least expensive media.
condition: when printed text is otherwise appropriate for the outcome and learners

statement: Research findings indicate that colour does not increase the effectiveness of instruction except when it is an essential feature of what must be learned.
condition: except where colour is an essential feature of the content

statement: Real objects may sometimes be the most effective media, notably for learning motor skills and complex procedures.

Pictorial motion is virtually essential when the dynamic features of objects are part of the essential content, and its capacity to display the actions of living beings — particularly humans — realistically is of hard-to-overstate importance in motion pictures and television.
condition: when dynamic features are essential content

statement: When intellectual skills are being learned, precise feedback about correctness and incorrectness matters greatly to learning effectiveness, so the medium's interactive quality is the most obvious media difference for that outcome.
Pictures rather than verbal descriptions are an essential aspect of instruction when concrete concepts or rules involving spatial arrangements or spatiotemporal sequences are being learned.
condition: when the content is spatial or spatiotemporal

statement: Attitudes are best presented by media that can display a human model and the model's message about personal choices, which makes pictorial motion of human activity a major consideration for attitude media.

Whether learning-style differences exist and whether they interact with media has not been definitely established, and even if the styles were known it might not be feasible or economical to provide enough parallel media packages per lesson to accommodate them.

Reading comprehension is the learner characteristic about which there should be little question in media selection: low scorers will have difficulty learning from print and, because the ability correlates with oral language understanding, are also likely to learn poorly from semantically complex speech.

Two remedies exist for low reading comprehension: write the printed or oral passage low in reading difficulty using familiar words and short sentences, and use pictures and diagrams as far as possible for novel concepts, rules, and procedures — which convey such content more rapidly and efficiently to these learners than verbal expression.
condition: for learners low in reading comprehension ability

statement: Dale's cone of experience orders twelve media categories from direct purposeful experience through contrived and dramatised experience, demonstrations, study trips, exhibits, television, motion pictures, still pictures, radio and recordings, and visual symbols up to verbal symbols, in a somewhat age-related fashion.

For cognitive objectives the rule of thumb is to go as low on Dale's scale as needed to ensure learning for the group but as high as possible for efficiency, trading off slow-but-sure direct experience against fast-but-risky verbal symbols for weak readers.
condition: applies to cognitive objectives — information, intellectual skills, cognitive strategies

statement: For attitude objectives the age-media relationship inverts relative to cognitive objectives: a young child who needs direct experience with real objects for cognitive learning may acquire an attitude by hearing verbal statements from respected people, while changing an already established attitude may require real-life experiences for both children and adults.
condition: applies to attitude objectives

statement: Attitude formation and change occurs by classical conditioning, hearing persuasive communications, and human modeling, and different media are involved in each of these methods.

It is not clear whether family-background data are more useful for checking entering competencies (what learners need to be taught) or for selecting media (how they should be taught), though some indirect implications are likely — children of parents who do not or cannot read are less likely to have acquired a love of and skill in reading, other factors being equal.

The practicality of a medium depends on administrative features of the learning environment: school budget, class size, capability to develop new materials, equipment availability, teacher capability and availability for design work, availability of modular individualised materials, attitudes of principal and teachers toward innovation, and school architecture.

It is useless to plan a delivery system whose design and development resources are inadequate: available time, budget, and personnel determine both which media can be developed successfully and which design model and team management system are feasible.

Media must be acceptable to the users as well as affordable: attitudes toward media differ between urban and rural populations and among ethnic, socioeconomic, religious, and cultural groups, and some regions lack the technical skills or electric power for radio and television.

Cost may be the overriding factor in one circumstance while in another a required level of effectiveness is fixed first and costs considered after — military training designers separate objectives that must be completely mastered at any cost from less critical ones.

Designers should ascertain the intended user's status and intentions to avoid selecting unacceptable or impractical media, by visits or questionnaires — and perhaps best by making some users members of the design team, which also enhances the effectiveness of the whole design.

Consultants must avoid recommending a solution from their own country where it is ill-suited — in the total instructional approach as well as media — and translations of materials and even straightforward teacher-guide directions must be carefully reviewed for clarity, since what is perfectly clear to the writer may confuse the reader.

Practical media-selection questions include group size, viewing and hearing distance, how easily the medium can be interrupted for responding and feedback, adaptivity to responses, whether the stimulus needs motion, colour, still pictures, or spoken or written words, whether sequence is fixed or flexible and the instruction repeatable, which media carry most of the conditions of learning and instructional events, probable affective impact, obtainability and storability of hardware and software, disruption caused, backup availability, teacher training needs, budget for repairs, and cost versus probable effectiveness.
Having a backup plan or alternative lesson minimises the negative reaction when equipment fails or a medium proves unsuitable for the group size so that many cannot see or hear.

Media selection should begin by identifying the learning situation, because the most prominent differences among media relate to it; the choice then depends particularly on the type of learning outcome intended, as a multistep intellectual-skill procedure cannot be adequately taught by an instructor's lecture.

A media-selection model considers logistic factors (group size), learner variables (readers versus nonreaders), and task variables (task importance and outcome type), and the media it suggests are those able to deliver the events of instruction that provide the conditions of learning for that outcome type.

For a motor-skill outcome in self-instruction with nonreaders, only portable equipment and a training device survive, because these are the only two media that make possible the direct practice motor-skill learning requires.
condition: in the self-instruction-with-nonreaders situation

statement: If neither self-instructional medium can provide adequate feedback during practice, the selection routes to the instructor-based learning situation, on the reasoning that an instructor will supply the necessary feedback.
condition: when no available self-instructional medium can supply adequate feedback

statement: For an intellectual skill only media that interact with learner responses — computer instruction and interactive TV — qualify; motion picture, slide or videotape, and TV cassette are excluded because they do not permit the response interaction essential to effective intellectual-skill learning.

For an attitude outcome, motion pictures, slide or videotape presentations, and TV cassettes are effective because they can picture the situations the attitude applies to and realistically display a human model delivering the message.

For verbal information with nonreaders, audio alone (such as an audiotape recorder) is a reasonable choice unless visuals would help recall, in which case motion picture, slide or videotape, or TV cassette is chosen — since visuals often aid recall by elaborating the verbal information and adding visual cues.
condition: depends on whether visuals will help recall for this content

statement: The media-selection method bases its decisions on learning effectiveness derived from the five types of learning outcome, selecting the media best able to put into effect the conditions of learning appropriate for each outcome type.

By learning outcome, the media exclusions and selections are: intellectual skills and cognitive strategies exclude non-interactive media and printed discourse for nonreaders while selecting feedback-capable media plus audio and visual features; verbal information excludes only real equipment or simulators without verbal accompaniment and complex prose for nonreaders while selecting media able to present verbal messages and elaborations; attitudes take the same exclusions as verbal information while selecting media able to present realistic pictures of a human model and the model's message; and motor skills exclude media with no provision for learner response and feedback while selecting media making direct practice with informative feedback possible.

The media-selection model is deliberately fine-grained and analytical: exclusion rules prevent consideration of media inappropriate for learning and inclusion rules identify those best suited, after which the practical choice is made from a short list on feasibility, availability, and cost.

Every neglect of the consideration of how learning takes place may be expected to result in a weaker procedure and poorer learning results, which is why primacy is given to selecting media by their effectiveness in supporting the learning process.
Experienced designers may perform much of the media analysis in their heads because the steps in the problem solution have become familiar.

A design model must be adapted to the circumstances of the particular project — budget, time, personnel, facilities, equipment, supplies, and institutional characteristics of both the developing and using agencies — and the design team leader must also set task time periods, assign personnel, and monitor the management plan.

Media selection depends on the learning situation, the type of learning outcome, the learning environment, the conditions for development, the culture in which instruction is given, and practical factors — with primacy given first to the learning situation and its intended learners, and then to the kind of outcome expected.

Designing a lesson requires first ensuring the events of instruction are provided for, then classifying the lesson objectives and arranging the specific events in an appropriate sequence for attaining them, and only then writing the content of the events as instructional prescriptions.

Teachers often design as they teach, planning each lesson only in enough detail to be ready and improvising the rest, which is not entirely undesirable because it preserves flexibility to redesign on the spot in response to the situation and to learners.

Large-group instruction affords less precision of control: unpredictable student responses plus restricted planning time mean instruction is often carried out with only a moderate degree of control over the conditions of learning.

Small-group and individualised modes make greater precision possible by allowing self-pacing and self-correction adapted to each learner's entering competencies and learning rate, supported by branching in programmed, computer-assisted, or computer-managed materials or by frequent self-tests.
Individualised instruction takes account of student needs, beginning with an analysis of entry skills and prescribing subsequent instruction based on that individual's needs.

Self-paced instruction lets the learner spend as much time as necessary to achieve the objectives and is generally associated with mastery learning, in which achievement rather than time dictates the rate of progress.

Adaptive instruction constantly monitors the student's progress and changes the instructional content based on it, which entails complex record keeping and decision making usually facilitated by computers though it can be done manually for individuals or small groups.

A lesson plan in a teacher-based system may be somewhat incomplete because the teacher fills the gaps, whereas individualised or self-paced instruction must be more carefully planned and developed since immediate teacher help is often unavailable.

Both teacher-led and mediated lessons rest on the same four themes: classify objectives by a taxonomy of learning outcomes, sequence objectives to take account of prerequisites, include the appropriate events of instruction that apply to all domains, and incorporate into those events the particular conditions of learning relevant to the objectives' domains.

A learning hierarchy implies that the bottom row of skills should be taught first, then the next higher row, and so on: options exist among boxes within a horizontal row, but not in proceeding from the bottom row upward when a single sequence is adopted for a whole group.
condition: when one sequence must serve all learners in a group

statement: A student may succeed with a sequence that violates the hierarchy either because she already could perform some of the skills or because she had enough cognitive strategy to discover some of the rules without direct instruction.

Instruction should begin where each student is; in a group this can be done by arranging other activities for students who do not need part of the planned instruction, with sitting through it as review being an alternative that is not always the best solution.

A review of earlier skills may be needed at the start of each lesson to ensure ready recall for the new learning, though intellectual skills once learned are recalled well compared with facts or labels.

A hierarchy implies several possible effective lesson sequences: only the essential-prerequisite relationships must be maintained, and otherwise no particular order is implied, leaving room to insert instruction from other outcome domains.

Mastery must be taken with complete seriousness for intellectual skills: each prerequisite must be performable with perfect confidence before more complex skills are attempted, since any lesser degree of prerequisite learning yields puzzlement, delay, and inefficient trial and error at best, and failure, frustration, or abandonment at worst.
Because mastery of prerequisites is load-bearing, allowing the student to choose the sequencing is not likely to be the most efficient procedure.

Lesson planning on a hierarchy also supplies diagnosis: any lesson that requires prerequisite skills to be recalled yields diagnostic information, and where mastery is not achieved the assessment should be followed by assessment of the prerequisites and a relearning loop before the student proceeds.

One usually cannot specify a particular sequence of prior learning leading to a cognitive strategy, and students already possess strategies as automatized rules for processing information — so teaching a new strategy means getting them to modify an existing strategy or drop it and adopt the new one.

A sequence designed to improve cognitive strategies takes the form of repeated opportunities to apply them, interspersed with instruction having other outcomes and recurring over relatively long periods, so that gradual improvement is possible.
For metacognitive strategies it does not seem likely that observable amounts of improvement can occur within the time of a single lesson or two.

A taught cognitive strategy often takes the form of a sequence of steps — as in the survey, question, read, recite, review technique — whose step list and explanation serve as an executive subroutine, just as the movement sequence does for a motor skill, and the instructional activity is practising that subroutine.

The most telling indicator that a strategy has been adopted is a decrease in time and an increase in accuracy between the early applications while learning and the later ones after adoption, more informative than self-report or direct observation.
Adoption of a strategy implies it is now part of the learner's information-processing repertoire and can be applied efficiently and effectively.

The sequencing principles for verbal information differ by subtype — learning a set of names, learning an isolated fact, and learning the sense of a logically organised passage — with the meaningful context being the most important prerequisite throughout.

Prescribing particular encoding codes for the learner is generally found to be less successful than permitting the learner to use an encoding system of his own; what the learner mainly needs to have learned beforehand is how to encode, a metacognitive strategy.

Because label learning draws on whatever meaningful structures the learner already holds, no specific content of previous learning implying an instructional sequence can reasonably be recommended for it.
The imagery a learner uses for encoding may be entirely arbitrary — using the shops on a well-known street as associations for names having nothing to do with the shops.

Two sequencing procedures are available for factual information and both should probably be employed: prior presentation of an organiser passage naming the major categories of description, and prior use of questions or statements identifying the categories of fact for which learning is desired.

Prior experience with questions of a given kind about a sample passage facilitates the learning and retention of that kind of information, so the pre-questions should match the target category — names if names matter, dates if dates matter.

A schema is an abstract structure of information conceived as a set of expectations, whose slots the new information is integrated into; sequencing of organised knowledge should take account of the existing schemas the new knowledge can be subsumed under.

The teacher should structure new information so that it builds on what the student already knows; in correlative subsumption, new material similar to an existing schema is absorbed into it and the schema broadens.

Whether part skills or the executive subroutine dominate motor-skill sequencing depends largely on the complexity of the skill: identifying part skills for dart throwing would not yield a useful plan, while for a complex skill such as swimming part-skill practice is often valuable.
condition: depends on the complexity of the skill

statement: The executive subroutine is typically placed early in a motor-skill sequence, before the part skills have been fully mastered — an athlete acquires the approach, weight shift, and release sequence while performing each movement poorly.

Part skills may themselves have prerequisites — the concrete concept of a correct sighting picture is a valuable subordinate for target shooting — so a motor-skill plan must sometimes sequence the individual part skills as well.

An attitude cannot be established without the verbal information and intellectual skills that make up the personal action the learner is expected to choose — a positive attitude toward reading poetry presupposes knowledge of poems and the language skills to interpret them.

An attitude sequence begins with the intellectual skills and verbal information relevant to the attitude, then introduces the procedure that establishes the positive or negative tendency constituting the attitude itself.

Domain interactions in attitude learning can be analysed by audit trails that relate the attitude to be acquired to the other attitudes, verbal information, and intellectual skills that facilitate it, providing a guide for sequencing the experiences leading to attitude change.

When human modeling is used, an extra prerequisite step may be needed to establish or build up respect for the model — a pictured famous figure is more likely to be respected if the learner knows of that person's accomplishments.
condition: where respect for the chosen model is not already established

statement: The general purpose of the events of instruction is to arrange the external conditions of learning so that learning will occur, and although the events apply to all lesson types, the particular conditions that make each event effective differ by outcome class.

The conditions checklist pertains only to instructional events 3 (stimulating recall of prior learning), 4 (presenting the stimulus), 5 (providing learning guidance), and 6 (eliciting performance); the remaining events are handled generically.

Effective conditions for a discrimination lesson are recall of the responses, presentation of same and different stimuli with emphasis on distinctive features, and repetition of same and different stimuli with feedback.

Effective conditions for a concrete-concept lesson are recall of the discriminations of the relevant object features, presentation of several instances and noninstances varying in irrelevant qualities, and identification of instances by the student with feedback.
Effective conditions for a defined-concept lesson are recall of the component concepts, demonstration of the concept using its definition, and demonstration of a concept example by the student.

Effective conditions for a rule lesson are recall of the subordinate concepts and rules, demonstration of the rule using a verbal statement, and demonstration of rule application by the student; for a higher-order rule they are recall of the relevant subordinate rules, presentation of a novel task or problem, and demonstration of the new rule in the student's solution.

Effective conditions for a cognitive-strategy lesson are recall of the relevant rules and concepts, a verbal statement or demonstration of the strategy, and practice of the strategy in novel situations.

Effective conditions for verbal information are, for names, recall of verbal associations plus student encoding relating the name to an image or meaningful sentence plus use of the name in context; for facts and for organised knowledge, recall of the related meaningful context, performance reinstating the new material within that larger context, and using it by relating it to other facts and bodies of knowledge.

Effective conditions for an attitude lesson are recall of the verbal information and intellectual skills relevant to the chosen personal actions, establishment or recall of respect for the source (usually a human model), and reward for the personal action either directly or vicariously through the model.
Effective conditions for a motor-skill lesson are recall of the responses and part skills, establishment or recall of the executive subroutine (procedural rule), and practice of the total skill.

A lesson planning sheet should carry the objective and its outcome-domain classification, the list of instructional events to be employed, the media, materials, and activities accomplishing each event, and notes on teacher roles and activities as prescriptions for instruction; a script may then be written from it.

Even a single-objective lesson requires the teacher to attend to its prerequisites and provide for transfer to subsequent objectives, since its purpose is to supply part of the instruction for the unit's integrated goals.

Because the events follow the hypothesised sequence of internal processing it makes sense to present them in order, but they serve only as guidelines: not all need be included, strict linear order is not required, and the plan must reflect both the learners' sophistication as self-directed learners and the nature of the objectives.

It may be desirable to spend an entire period on a single instructional event — establishing motivation for a series of lessons, or clarifying the exact nature of the expected performance for a unit before instruction begins, which suits courses whose major outcomes are problem-solving skills.

A worked concrete-concept lesson realises the events as: varied figures on the board for attention; paired examples and nonexamples with this-is/this-is-not statements plus a pick-out question for the objective; presentation of the critical attribute contrasts for prerequisite recall; series of example-nonexample pairs with feature naming for guidance; a worksheet of mixed figures for performance; projected item-by-item review naming the present or absent critical feature for feedback; a similar test for assessment; and drawing the figure from varied starting lines plus finding it in real objects for transfer.
However crucial the events of instruction are to the design model, the way they are planned must reflect the best estimate of the students' capabilities and entering competencies.

The greatest difference between designing teacher-led and mediated instruction appears at the media step: mediated instruction requires the designer to attend to every instructional event and how it will be operationalised in the materials, whereas the teacher-led model can be less exact because the teacher fills the gaps.

The planning question for each event in both teacher-led and mediated design is the same — how will I accomplish this event with these students — and if the wanted material cannot be found another way to accomplish the event must be devised.

Designers building a mediated module go through the same event-by-event determination as the teacher; existing materials can sometimes be incorporated, but in most cases new materials must be produced.

Attention can be gained by presenting an anomaly the learners notice for themselves — text printed with no capitals, or a morning routine that ends with the screen going blank — and then asking what is unusual, rather than by announcing the topic.

For a defined concept, the guidance step contrasts the general case against the particular case in matched pairs (boy/John, building/World Trade Center) to show the definition being applied, before the learner produces instances.

The performance-eliciting items for a defined concept should deliberately span the hard conditions — sentences with no instance, one instance at the start, one embedded, multiple instances, and near-miss forms — rather than only easy positive cases.

Prerequisite recall for a rule lesson must supply the specific quantities and conventions the rule operates on — the standard voltage of the circuit, where the appliance wattage is printed, and what a fuse rating means — not merely the abstract formula.

Rule guidance should push the learner from a single application to a compound case that requires combining results and asking how the answer could be proved, rather than repeating the same one-step calculation.
Feedback on a rule involving a ratio should watch for the specific predictable error — inversion of the fraction — and remediate it, rather than only marking answers right or wrong.

A problem-solving objective should state the criterion of an acceptable solution in performance terms — covering at least a stated percentage while using the least material — so that competing solutions can be compared.

Prerequisite recall for problem solving enumerates the specific subordinate rules the solution will have to combine, and the problem is restated first in general terms and then with the specific constraining details.

Guidance during problem solving is given only when rules appear to be misapplied, taking the form of options and questions about the learner's own rule — what rule are you following here — and confirming good moves rather than supplying the solution.
condition: guidance is offered when the learner appears to be misapplying rules or sees no possible solution

statement: Assessment of problem solving presents a different problem of the same type, and transfer is assessed by varying the situation along several dimensions at once to test the generalisability of the student's solving.

The prerequisites for a verbal-information objective drawn from a historical text are gaining meaning from the sentences: the specific unfamiliar word meanings must be defined and the syntactic structures recognised before the passage is presented.
Learning guidance for organised verbal information has students number the discrete points in the passage and elaborate each to themselves by associating it with familiar ideas.

Verbal-information performance should be elicited without trying to repeat the passage word for word, and both feedback and scoring should verify learning and retention in terms of meaning units rather than verbatim wording.
Verbal information is remembered best when it is practised — used — so retention exercises should require the learner to apply the learned content to a new question rather than recall it again.
An attitude lesson should be scoped to an appropriate audience and run over time, with performance, feedback, and assessment events recurring weekly rather than concluding in one session.
condition: appropriate audience and an ongoing rather than single-session format

statement: In an attitude lesson the content should be delivered by a person serving as a human model who has actually made the choice, is admirable and believable, and describes the shift made, the resulting difference, and the satisfaction obtained.

Self-reports of choice behaviour are imperfect indicators of actual choosing, so attitude feedback confirms desired choices or movement toward them with praise or support, and assessment uses unobtrusive measures observed over weeks.
Attitudes are reinforced by support from the environment, so the individual's effort can be aided by arrangements such as regular meetings of a support group.

Transfer activities should move the learned capability into the learner's own production and into real-world instances — writing one's own sentences, drawing the figure from varied starting points, finding the shape in pictures of real objects, or competing on a practical constraint problem.

Multiple objectives are common because a single lesson is most often only part of a larger unit, and instruction should engage the student in a comprehensive purpose (an enterprise) that may require integrating verbal information, attitudes, concepts, and rules together.

An instructional curriculum map analyses an integrative goal into component objectives from differing domains and shows each objective's role in supporting attainment of the larger goal; maps drawn at several levels correspond to the levels at which sequencing arises.

The main difference in planning a multiple-objective lesson is that the designer must plan how to present the events of instruction for several objectives at once, which is done by grouping objectives and events into instructional activities.

An instructional activity is something the teacher does or has the student do that represents one or more events of instruction for one or more objectives — showing a film may both motivate and present content, and a team game may both motivate and elicit performance.

A lesson consists of one or more instructional activities occurring within a predetermined framework, most commonly a fixed period of time — and even a mediated lesson is generally planned to complete within an estimated period.

An objectives/time-line matrix lists the lesson's objectives vertically in teaching order against a time line, with cells holding the event numbers that occur as time progresses; events are then grouped, across or within objectives, into instructional activities.

The objectives/time-line matrix and the lesson-planning sheet are completed simultaneously, with the planning sheet listing the instructional activities rather than the bare events, and the events incorporated into those activities.

The guiding principle in building the matrix and planning sheet is to go from prerequisite skills to higher-order skills and to present the events through the activities in a sequence that facilitates information processing.

Reviewing skills from previous lessons serves two events at once: enhancing retention and transfer for the earlier skills, and stimulating recall of prerequisites for the current lesson's target objectives.

Verbal-information objectives may be taught first in a lesson not because they are prerequisites but because they supply a supportive context that aids transfer to the main intellectual-skill objectives.

It is sometimes helpful to treat a group of consecutive events for one objective — learning guidance, eliciting performance, and providing feedback — as a single instructional activity occurring over a short time.

A teacher has considerable latitude over which events to include, omit, or combine across objectives, but prerequisite-sequencing considerations favour presenting content for the supportive objectives first and the target objectives after.

The effectiveness of instruction depends on the ability of the media employed to provide the events of instruction in the manner required by the type of learning outcome and by learner characteristics.

That most media research shows no significant differences in learning may speak more to the research's failure to consider when media differences matter — that is, when the events being presented make a significant difference — than to whether such differences exist.

Writing the prescriptions before choosing media leaves designers wide latitude in media decisions — the open-media model — whereas a preselected medium forces the prescriptions to accommodate that medium's limits in providing the events.

Substituting videotape for a live teacher leaves the prescriptions largely unchanged, whereas mediating the same lesson as printed text requires them to change substantially — media decisions matter most around whether learners are readers and the consequent requirements for visual display, practice, and feedback.

Existing mediated materials have value to a teacher only in terms of the learning activities they apply to, so the teacher must study them carefully and particularly note the instructional events they do not address, so those events can be planned into the lesson.

In new development the instructional designer and the subject-matter expert work together to analyse the learning task, decide the delivery system, review existing materials for fit, and then determine how the remaining events and activities will be provided.

Lesson design cannot be reduced to a cookbook recipe and partakes of art as well as science, but the events of instruction provide a focus that aids both lesson construction and revision after formative evaluation.

Although intuition, ingenuity, creativity, and experience are all valuable in planning lessons, reference to the relevant conditions of learning sharpens instruction and prevents neglect of desirable instructional functions.

Every stage of instructional design is done the same way whether a team designs a curriculum or a teacher designs a course, up to lesson design — at which point teachers must consider what they personally bring and what role they will play, while designers of mediated materials must decide how to provide the needed activities in a preplanned lesson.

Placement tests determine which skills in a sequence each student has learned and can recall at the start of a term, revealing each student's pattern of mastery and nonmastery in order to identify the starting point for instruction.

Even a group that left the previous term with highly similar capabilities will not all be at the same starting point in a new sequence, because skills are forgotten and new information, skills, and attitudes are acquired in between.
The more suitable the provisions made for each learner, the more precise the instruction will be and the more likely students are to experience success.

Diagnostic tests are built from the prerequisite skills revealed by a learning hierarchy, because a probable reason for falling behind in group instruction is that earlier skills in the sequence were not mastered.

Remedial instruction on a diagnosed prerequisite may need to use methods and materials different from those originally used, in order to avoid a second failure at the same trouble point in the sequence.
condition: where the original methods already failed for that learner

statement: Progress checks should be used less often when a whole group is consistently progressing well and more often when a number of learners are having difficulty; brief checks both assure learners they are progressing and give the teacher dependable information for planning the next steps.

For evaluating instruction, total scores indicate the overall degree of success but item analyses showing which items are passed or failed by a majority are even more important, because item scores are what tell where the instruction needs improvement.

The principles for preparing performance measures are the same whether the test covers one prerequisite skill in a hierarchy, an entire topic, or a larger unit, so tests can be discussed in terms of validity for a single objective at any level.

Objective-referenced assessment means building tests that directly measure the human performances described in the course objectives, so that one can infer the intended capability was developed as a result of the instruction.

Normally a teacher pretests only the assumed entering capabilities and assesses the objective itself only afterward, but a convenient compromise is to let any student who believes he has already mastered the objective take that test as a pretest and skip the corresponding instruction if he passes.

The performance objective is the keystone in planning assessment: its verbs tell what the student should be asked to do, with the capability verb naming the intent of the objective and the action verb serving as the indicator that the intent has been achieved.

Objective-referenced assessment gives a direct rather than indirect measure of the objective, which eliminates the need to relate the measure to a criterion by a correlation coefficient as is required for indirect measures or tests built without explicit objectives.

Test validity is settled by answering whether the performance required during assessment is the same performance described in the objective; a clear yes makes the test valid, and it is desirable for more than one judge to make that judgment and to reach consistency.

Congruence-based validity assumes the objective statement is itself valid — that it truly reflects the purposes of the topic or lesson — so the consistency of specific objectives with the broader purposes may need rechecking, and inconsistencies often become apparent when objectives are transformed into tests.
condition: assumes the objective statement itself validly reflects the lesson's purpose

statement: Test is used generically to mean any procedure for assessing the performance described in an objective, covering written and oral testing as well as evaluation of student products such as essays, musical productions, models, or works of art.

Two objectives that share a surface performance can belong to different domains: composing and typing a letter requires the problem-solving capability of generating it, whereas typing a letter someone else composed requires only the motor skill.

Test items must use different examples from those used in teaching, so the correct response cannot be produced by copying a value or remembering a previously worked problem instead of by the intended intellectual process.

Performances that are useful in themselves — copying a letter, spelling the concept name, explaining how the concept may be used — do not necessarily reflect the intent of the objective, either as to the capability required or the action signifying it is present.

The five components of the objective statement provide the description of the test situation, so for many objectives and older learners changing only a few words converts the objective into directions for taking the test.
condition: for objectives written in the five-component form and learners not too young

statement: The more closely objectives follow the five-component outline, the fewer decisions remain in planning the test and the fewer directions must be given to the student; objectives written for the designer thus also define most of the test situation.
exception: both objectives and derived items must be restated in simpler terms for young children

statement: The more incomplete the statement of an objective, the more must be filled in when moving to the test situation, and the more the cautions about test construction are needed.

Do not substitute verbs that change the meaning of the capability or the action; particular care is needed not to shift from an answer the student must construct to one he merely chooses, selects, or recalls — an objective to generate a position and its defence cannot be tested by multiple choice.

Ambiguity from vague verbs is avoided by using the standard capability verbs, and careful attention is needed to fix unambiguous meanings for verbs such as summarize, describe, list, analyze, and complete.

Reviewing an objective in the course of writing its test sometimes reveals that the objective itself needs changing — in which case it should be changed before planning the instruction and before using it as a lesson objective or as test directions.

Unless a change is deliberate, the situation, object, tools, constraints, and both verbs should stay congruent between objective and test, since large changes may make the test call for capabilities not yet taught.
exception: except where simplification of the student's directions requires it

statement: In the worst mismatch the objective, the teaching, and the examination each specify a different domain of learning outcome — objectives calling for appreciation, teaching delivering facts, and the examination requiring use of concepts and rules — producing maximum incongruence among the three anchor points.
Tests should not be made either easier or more difficult than the objectives: the aim is accurately representing the objective, not estimating how to make the test sufficiently difficult.

Objective-referenced tests should not try to achieve a wide score range or a normal distribution, because their purpose is to discover which objectives each student has learned, not to discriminate one student's score from another's.
Grading on a normal curve tends to fix the academic goals of teachers and students at inappropriately low levels and reduces both teacher and student motivation.

The practice producing those effects is group-paced instruction: when both pace and mode of instruction are fixed, each student's achievement becomes primarily a function of aptitude, whereas letting mode and rate vary makes it likely more students succeed.

It is easier to let the rate of learning vary than to predict which mode will most benefit each student, and economic limits mean a different mode cannot be provided for every student; modularised individualised instruction largely solves the rate problem and partly the mode problem.

Mastery learning holds that under proper conditions perhaps 90 to 95 percent of students can master most objectives to the degree now reached only by good students, abandoning the idea that students merely learn more or less well in favour of finding out why students fail and remedying it.
condition: if the proper conditions can be provided

statement: Resolving a student's learning problem usually requires one of three measures: more time for learning, different media or materials, or diagnosis to determine the missing prerequisite knowledge or skills.

A remedial decision for an intellectual-skill objective is best made by administering a diagnostic test over the subordinate capabilities, or by oral testing to find where in the teaching sequence the failure to learn first began.

For a known slow learner, diagnostic tests of subordinate competencies can be used as the performance assessments so that each capability is known to be mastered before the next is attempted, detecting small failures before they accumulate into failures of whole lessons, topics, or courses.
condition: for learners known to progress slowly

statement: Defining mastery for a test also defines the criterion of success for that objective, and recording how many students reach it shows whether the instruction for that objective met its design objective.

A frequently used course design criterion is that 90 percent of students achieve mastery of 90 percent of the objectives, though other percentages may be used and sometimes three criteria are set with one indicating minimal acceptable success and the others higher degrees.
The same objective-referenced test results serve to promote students, to drive formative evaluation showing where the course needs revision, and — where the school requires it — to assign grades.

Scoring a problem-solving product requires a prepared list of features it should include, because no verbatim key is possible and mechanical scoring is not feasible; where several teachers share the objective they should jointly define the criteria and how many rules must be synthesised, marking some mandatory and others optional.

A problem-solving test is not scored on a count such as eight of ten correct: the criteria may be qualitative as well as quantitative, applying the checklist requires judgment rather than clerical matching, and agreement among teachers applying it is what determines the measure's reliability.

The situation part of the objective statement defines the class of situations from which particular test items are drawn, so an objective that says given a verbal statement implies a different item form from one that says given a diagram.

The purpose of using multiple test items is to avoid measurement error from idiosyncratic features of a single item; convention suggests ten or twenty items for an arithmetic rule, but sequential-analysis assumptions have been shown to permit mastery decisions on as few as three correct items.

A defined-concept item that has the learner construct a diagram is less dependent on verbal ability, whereas an item that asks for a spoken definition is subject to distortion — unless one is entirely convinced the subordinate concepts are mastered, the response may have to be interpreted as a memorised verbalisation.
condition: a stated definition counts only if the subordinate concepts are known to be mastered
exception: verbal statements, preferably in the learner's own words, are nevertheless often used as criteria for defined concepts

statement: Changing the response mode of a concrete-concept item changes its assumptions: pointing and naming assumes only that the oral responses can be made, whereas placing printed labels additionally requires that those words can be read.
A concrete-concept item counts as attained only when the student responds to every instance and to none of the non-instances in the set.
Discrimination tasks are purely perceptual: they do not require the learner to name the stimulus or identify its attributes, only to indicate same or different.

Cognitive-strategy indicators are indirect and require a longer chain of inference, because the same successful performance could have been produced by a different and less efficient strategy — so assessing a strategy needs added observations such as the order of the responses and the efficiency of the performance, or think-aloud verbal reports.

Mastery learning cannot readily be extended to the measurement of cognitive strategies, because what is assessed is the quality of the mental process rather than its presence or absence, and novel problems may have many solutions — so assessment becomes judging how good the solution is and a pass-fail decision is unlikely.

Originality is routinely judged without exact specified criteria — a doctoral dissertation is expected to make an original contribution and qualified people arrive at a consensus about its degree of originality — showing that judgment-based assessment of novel contribution is workable.

Productive thinking has been measured by items asking students to invent hypotheses, questions, and answers beyond the lectures and text — predicting consequences of an unusual event, writing an imaginative sentence using specified new concepts, stating a novel hypothesis, titling a data table, drawing conclusions from a graph — with reasonably adequate reliabilities from ten to fifteen items and two raters agreeing highly after short training.

Assessing the quality of thought as a learning outcome differs in aim and method from measuring creativity as a trait, and requires two things: the problem must require knowledge, concepts, and rules recently learned rather than acquired years earlier, and it must be assumed or preferably shown that all students already hold the prerequisite information and skills, so that no student's solution is handicapped by missing knowledge.

The fundamental distinction in information assessment is objective-referenced versus content-referenced measurement: the aim is to determine whether certain objectives were attained, not whether some content was covered.

Information objectives should state clearly which names, facts, and generalisations must be learned, differentiating the core content to be recalled from the incidental information in the book that some students may recall beyond the required level.

It would be a mistake to make information objectives so exhaustive that no time remains for objectives in other domains; the designer should deliberately identify the informational outcomes most likely to contribute to attaining objectives in other domains.
The lifelong goal of acquiring masses of information should not be allowed to interfere with attaining objectives in intellectual skills and problem-solving strategies.

Assessing verbal information typically means measuring quantity — how much the student knows about a topic — with items drawn from a domain that may be precisely defined as a specific passage or loosely defined as the declarative knowledge expected from lectures, text, and references.

Prose-analysis methods can distinguish main ideas from subordinate ones and raise the possibility of assessing the quality of knowledge, but the fuller meaning of depth of knowledge awaits research and theoretical development before such measures can be built.

Objective-referenced testing of information requires exact identification of what is to be learned and retained — whether a list of names or dates, or the substance of a passage — and making that equally apparent to the student, which is what makes learning for mastery feasible, fair, and reasonable.

Because what one wants to assess about an attitude is its strength, mastery cannot be identified for attitude objectives; strength is instead measured as the proportion of times the person behaves in a given way across a sample of defined situations.

An attitude objective can be framed as improvement rather than pass-fail — that each child will exhibit the target behaviour more times per month in May than in the previous October — with anecdotal records quantified as a count of positive actions or as the proportion of positive to total actions.

Occasions offering no opportunity for the behaviour either way should simply not be recorded, in recognition that some of the learner's time is spent in periods that afford no chance to act toward others at all.

The most serious limitation of attitude questionnaires is bias from students answering to win approval rather than reflecting their actual choices, and there appears to be no simple solution despite many investigations.

Best results from attitude self-reports appear when students are first assured the assessment is not an adversary process and that they need not report only what they think will be approved, with anonymous recording as an additional precaution for group administration.

A domain of attitude assessment items can be specified along several dimensions of the situation so that the set of personal-action choices is defined, yielding acceptable objective-referenced scores for attitudes.

Motor-skill standards usually refer to the precision of performance and often also to speed; since both improve with extended practice it is unrealistic to define mastery as learned or not learned, so a standard of performance must be decided upon.

Motor-skill standards are set at progressively higher levels for practice extending over longer periods — a beginning typing course may set thirty words a minute with a specified error limit where an advanced course expects forty or fifty.

Reliability has two primary meanings for objective-referenced measures: consistency of measurement across items aimed at the same objective, and dependability of the measurement on temporally separated occasions.

Because the purpose of assessment is to discover whether the learner can perform a class of operations rather than one particular instance, additional items belonging to the same class are used to ensure dependability of the measurement.

A single item supports no measure of consistency: a student may respond correctly because he happens to have memorised an answer, or incorrectly because some particular feature of the item misled him, so one item cannot support a confident conclusion of mastery.

The conclusion sought is not how many items are correct but whether the number correct dependably indicates mastery; two items can yield an uninterpretable half-right result, so three items seems a reasonable minimum with two of three correct giving confidence in the measurement.

Assessing a cognitive strategy may require several lengthy problem-solving tasks, because it is necessary to disentangle prior learning of information and intellectual skills from the quality of original thought and to make it unlikely a student could meet the criteria without a genuine generalisable capability.

Temporal dependability asks whether the demonstrated mastery would be the same on another day or was determined by how the student felt, a temporary illness, or an adventitious feature of the testing situation; it is determined by test-retest separated by days or weeks.

Norm-referenced tests compare each student's performance with a group or an established norm and typically measure a mixture of objectives over large segments of content rather than single identifiable objectives.
Because of their comprehensive coverage, norm-referenced tests are most useful for summative assessment over reasonably long periods such as midcourse or end-of-course examinations.

Because their items mix objectives that often cannot be identified singly, norm-referenced tests cannot readily serve diagnostic testing of prerequisite skills and do not give direct unambiguous measures of what has been learned against defined objectives.

Norm-referenced items often require intellectual skills, information, and cognitive strategies simultaneously, giving global rather than objective-specific assessments, which suits outcomes across a set of topics or a whole course.

Refining a test by item analysis discards items that most students pass and items that few pass, which makes the test increasingly measure problem solving and other cognitive strategies and, in part, intelligence rather than what was directly learned.

Little justification exists for norm-referenced tests when assessing the outcomes of individual lessons: used on defined objectives they are likely to miss the point entirely and to neglect both assessment of mastery of the specific capability and the diagnostic help that identifies missing prerequisites.

Standardised tests are generally norm-referenced: their items are not derived from particular objectives, are selected to produce the largest possible score variation, and so correlate rather highly with intelligence rather than with particular learning outcomes, and they rarely identify missing subordinate capabilities.

Standardised tests are quite inappropriate for detailed assessment of lesson outcomes with specifiable objectives; their most appropriate use is summative evaluation of total courses over several years, where they can give valuable information about long-term effects.

Objective-referenced tests serve four purposes: showing whether each student has mastered an objective and may go on, permitting early detection and diagnosis of failure to identify the needed remedial study, providing data for improving the instruction, and being fair evaluations because they measure the very objective the student was told to learn.
Testing what the student was told he was supposed to learn is consistent with the honesty of the teacher-learner relation.

Mastery levels can be defined as error-free performances for intellectual skills, motor skills, and information, but criteria of mastery are less clearly applicable to cognitive strategies and attitudes, where assessment deals with how well or how much.

When instruction is delivered to a group one must constantly bear in mind that learning still occurs within individuals, and the attempt in group instruction is to make each instructional event as effective as possible for every member.

Three group sizes matter for design: the two-person group enabling tutoring; the small group of roughly three to eight favouring discussion and interactive recitation in which members affirm or correct each other's performances; and the large group of fifteen or more where the lecture and individual recitation predominate.

The distinctions among group sizes are not hard and fast — a group of eight to fifteen may be handled by discussion, by lecture, or by division into small groups — and for very large groups the differing factors are mainly logistic, such as seating and acoustics, with large-group modes otherwise still applying.

What matters for understanding instruction's effect on learning is not the mode label — lecture, discussion, recitation — but the variations in what is actually done within each mode, so group instruction is better analysed by asking what arrangements are possible and most effective for each group size.

Group size is an important determinant of the learning environment because it determines which interaction patterns are attainable, and those patterns may influence learning outcomes through how students perceive them.

Interaction flows differ by mode: two-way between teacher and student in a two-person group; mutual with one student at a time while others merely receive in recitation; among students as well as with the teacher in interactive recitation and discussion; and one-way from teacher to students in the lecture.

Group size sets limits on the effectiveness of the events of instruction: attention can be precisely managed in a two-person group but only loosely in a large one, and the semantic encoding a lecturer suggests will be modified by each learner's own strategies.

Feedback that merely marks an answer correct or incorrect can be delivered to a large group with about the same precision as to a single student, but feedback that explains the causes of incorrect responding necessarily varies with the individual.

Diagnosis of entry capabilities is not itself an instructional event but makes the design of certain events possible, and such diagnosis is most successful when based on learning hierarchies, using simple tests or probes to reveal specific gaps in enabling skills.

Diagnosing gaps in enabling skills is not severely affected by group size — it can be done about as effectively with large groups as small — but designing and executing the instruction implied by that diagnosis is greatly affected by group size, which is the basic rationale for individually prescribed instruction.

Group size matters most for diagnosis of immediate prerequisites, because a different individual pattern of prerequisite capabilities may appear for each student — twenty different patterns among twenty students — which a tutorial handles easily and a class teacher finds a considerable challenge.
A two-person instructional group need not contain a teacher: peer tutoring and older-student tutoring succeed, and learning gains are reported about as often for the tutors as for the students.

In individualised systems teachers act as tutors when they follow a diagnostic prescription with oral instruction, so individualised instruction frequently combines self-instruction with two-person tutoring.

The primary reason the two-person group is considered ideal is the opportunity it provides for flexible adjustment of instructional events: stimulation can be increased if a first attempt fails, alternative encoding schemes can be tried in turn, and comprehension can be checked immediately and again after a lapse of time.

In tutoring, informing the learner of the objective gains flexibility from restating it in different terms or demonstrating an instance of the expected performance — and the event may be omitted entirely if the objective is already known.
condition: omit only when the student already knows the objective

statement: Tutoring's decisive advantage is on prerequisite recall: having diagnosed what is missing the tutor can fill the gaps first and only then require recall, which does much to ensure that learning proceeds smoothly.
In tutoring the number and varied features of concept instances can be chosen to fit the student's need as indicated by his immediately preceding performance.

Learning guidance is where adapting instruction to the needs of the learner has its clearest meaning: the tutor can try one means of encouraging semantic encoding after another until one is found that works best.

Feedback precision in tutoring is not primarily about timing but about the nature of the information: the learner can be told accurately what is right or wrong with his performance and given directions permitting correction.

A tutor can select retrieval cues that past experience shows work for a particular learner, choose just enough varied examples to aid transfer, and conduct as many spaced reviews as that student needs for long-term retention.

As manager of instruction the tutor decides which events to employ, which to emphasise, and which to assign to the learner's own control, with timing chosen to make each act of learning optimally efficient.

The evidence appears to show that tutoring's advantage does not come from the individual attention itself: tutoring works best when the instruction it makes possible is highly systematic, and the freedom of the two-person setting produces poor results if it leads to sloppiness.
The tutoring advantages appear to yield favourable achievement results often but not always, so the mode itself does not guarantee gains.

A tutoring episode proceeds by repeating, as necessary, the cycle of stimulating recall of prerequisites, presenting the stimulus, providing learning guidance, eliciting and assessing performance, and providing feedback — and if the learner performs correctly at once the tutor confirms and moves on rather than working through the steps.

When a tutored learner gives an incorrect response he is told the correct one and asked to repeat it, and the same procedure is then run for each successive component until the whole performance is correct.

The same tutoring steps apply to older students and adults except that greater dependence is placed on encouraging the student to institute the events himself; university-level tutoring is usually almost entirely self-instruction with the tutor confined to assessing performance and suggesting retention and transfer means.

Small groups are formed by dividing a class so that students at approximately the same point in learning a subject are taught together, because presenting print to pupils still struggling with oral language accomplishes nothing and forcing fluent readers through readiness exercises wastes their time.

Small-group instruction is best understood as multistudent tutoring: the teacher uses tutorial methods with single students by taking turns, managing the events for each individual but with evident loss of flexibility and precision.

An important feature distinguishing small-group from large-group instruction is that the teacher can diagnose each student's attainment of immediate prerequisites by questioning each in turn, approaching the precision of the two-person group.
A recall question directed to one student has the added effect of reminding the other students of material already available to them.

For presenting the stimulus material the loss of flexibility in a small group compared with tutoring is minimal, since emphasis by voice change or by making features prominent in pictures serves the whole group at once.

Learning guidance in a small group is either addressed to the whole group (behaving as in a large-group setting) or given student by student (as in tutoring, which costs more time the larger the group), and teachers commonly alternate between the two as judgment dictates while the event's function stays the same.

Discussion places a fairly high degree of dependence on the individual students' self-instructional strategies — adult discussion members largely decide for themselves what they want to learn and select it from what they hear or say.

Because eliciting each student's performance one by one consumes much time, the small-group teacher usually calls on one or two and assumes learning was equally effective for the rest — trading a precise determination of outcomes for a probabilistic estimate.
Feedback in a small group is precise only for the student called upon; for the others it is merely probable, depending on which of them made the same response covertly.
Oral questioning assesses only a sample of each student's performances rather than the whole repertoire, so a test covering the entire lesson or topic may later be given to the whole group.

In a small group the teacher's judgments about varied examples and spaced reviews are made by averaging the group's performance rather than with the precision available in tutoring; for older students and adults the conduct of discussion is itself a major means of enhancing retention and transfer.

In small-group recitation the varied examples used with different students serve the function of enhancing retention and transfer, on the assumption that students not called upon are responding covertly while learning.
condition: assumes uncalled students respond covertly

statement: Discussion is interactive communication in which one student speaks at a time to the whole group, the order of speaking is not predetermined, and students often respond to each other rather than to the teacher.
Three kinds of objective are appropriate for group discussion — subject-matter mastery, attitude formation, and problem solving — and a class discussion not unusually pursues more than one of them.

An issue-oriented discussion is opened with an incident illustrating the issue, then opinions are solicited and commented on, with the leader progressively sharpening and clarifying the issue by introducing different examples and encouraging statements from various members, often aiming at a consensus no member majorly disagrees with.

An attitude-forming discussion is a particular kind of learning guidance in which the group members and leader act as multiple human models, followed by performance as the individual student's choice of action and by feedback in the form of group consensus.

The problems that provide the most effective instruction in discussion groups are those with multiple solutions and those including attitudinal components, and presenting problems that capture student interest and emotional involvement enlists motivation.

A problem-solving discussion group depends very largely on students managing the instructional events for themselves — supplying their own recall of relevant knowledge and their own encoding and problem-solving strategies — with attitude change as a secondary though not less important outcome.

The teacher's communications to a large group do not differ in function from those to a two-person group, but because the cues for timing and emphasis come from many sources rather than one student there is a marked reduction in precision of managing the events.
Large-group instruction is inherently a probabilistic strategy: it can be effective on the average but cannot by itself be ensured effective for each individual learner.

The widely held college-teaching view that good communication is the teacher's job and profiting from it is the student's — leaving students to infer the objective, remind themselves of prerequisites, and choose an encoding — runs contrary to mastery learning, which requires managing events beyond the giving of information.
Mastery learning relates the quality of instruction to the occurrence of cues, participation, reinforcement, and feedback with correctives — a set closely resembling the events of instruction.

Instruction delivered to a large group is relatively imprecise because instructional readiness, motivation and alertness, appropriateness of the suggested encoding, and accessibility of relevant cognitive strategies all vary across the individuals in the group.

What a student fails to learn from a lecture he may recover later by applying his own encoding strategies to his notes, while another student may find that ineffective and prefer to process the information in its original oral form.
Occasional demonstrations and audiovisual media should be used to gain attention at the times when other critical instructional events are about to follow, rather than at arbitrary points.

Stimulating recall of prerequisites is both critically important and one of the hardest events to accomplish with reasonable probability in a large group, because calling on one or two students leaves the others — many hoping to avoid being called — without the necessary retrieval, and those students will probably not learn the objective.

The cumulative effects of failing to secure prerequisite recall are quite serious, so devices such as spot quizzes for the whole group are used to improve the event, which deserves a great deal of attention from instructional designers.

In a large group the suggested encoding — a picture or dramatic episode for a historical event — can be made generally effective for the group as a whole but cannot be adapted to individual members as it can in smaller groups.

Student response has a low degree of precision as an instructional event in a large group: a tutor expects several performances per lesson from the student, whereas the class teacher calls on one or two and covert responding by the others is not highly likely.

Quizzes are used to overcome the difficulty of eliciting performance and should be frequent to work as instructional events, but even daily quizzes cannot approximate the frequency with which a tutor asks for performance reflecting what was learned a moment earlier.

Because feedback is tied to the occurrence of performance, feedback in a large group occurs with low frequency and tends to be confined to results of tests covering a number of different objectives at once.

The more frequent and regular assessment followed by corrective feedback can be, the better the learning outcome; regularly scheduled quizzes after segments of study material are considered the most valuable feature of some computer-managed college courses, and computer assessment achieves a precision impossible for the teacher of a large group.
For retention and transfer in a large group the teacher can use the varied examples and spaced reviews found to work best on average, but cannot adapt these to differences among individual learners.

A lecture can inspire an audience with the lecturer's enthusiasm, relate the field of study to human purposes and student interests, and relate theory and research to practical problems — attaining these with the utmost economy, which explains its survival for over two thousand years of higher education.

The lecture's recognised strengths map onto instructional events: inspiring with enthusiasm means the lecturer functions as a human model establishing positive attitudes, relating the field to human living carries motivational effect, and relating research to practical problems supplies a context of cues aiding retention and transfer.

The weakest features of the lecture are its lack of control over the recall of prerequisites and over the eliciting of student performance with corrective feedback: the lecturer can remind and encourage but cannot ensure recall or require performance.

When the lecture is the sole mode of instruction there is heavy dependence on the student to institute the missing events himself, and quizzes and tests overcome this only slightly because they are typically both infrequent and coarse-grained in assessing specific objectives.

A teacher's question in a recitation class may serve different instructional events at different moments — stimulating recall of a prerequisite, eliciting performance, guiding encoding in the manner of guided discovery, or asking for application examples that supply cues for recall and transfer.

When recitation follows a homework assignment, control of attention, learning the objective, semantic encoding, and corrective feedback are all expected to be managed by the student while doing the homework — so good study habits become the determiners of effective learning.
condition: when recitation follows independent homework

statement: Large-class recitation forces an unresolvable choice — calling on the well-prepared students neglects those less able to guide their own learning, while calling on the less able bores those who have already learned — and in practice the events reach only a few students on any one occasion because time does not permit everyone a turn.
All too frequently students in large recitation classes learn to play the game of avoiding being called upon, which is the wrong game with respect to learning the lesson objectives.

Dividing a large group into small groups for part of its meeting time, or into smaller classes following a lecture, is a simple scheme for regaining a degree of precision in controlling instructional events that surpasses the large group.

Mastery learning supplements large-group teaching with diagnostic progress testing and feedback-with-correction: the course is divided into roughly two-week units with clearly defined objectives, a test after each unit diagnoses which objectives were and were not acquired, masters go on to self-instructional enrichment, and non-masters get small-group study, tutoring, or extra materials and are retested when they feel prepared.

Against conventional instruction in groups of thirty per teacher, mastery learning procedures raised achievement from the fiftieth to the eighty-fourth percentile (one standard deviation) and tutoring raised it from the fiftieth to the ninety-eighth percentile (two standard deviations).

The enhanced-prerequisites technique — helping students review and relearn the prerequisites they lacked — raised achievement from the fiftieth to the seventy-sixth percentile under otherwise conventional instruction, and to the ninety-fifth percentile when combined with mastery learning.

Enhanced cues meant supplying explanations of the concepts and rules being learned, and participation was encouraged by having students note the frequency of their participation and the problems they had understanding the instruction; both combinations produced substantial achievement increases, with the greatest effects beyond the ninety-sixth percentile when added to mastery learning.

Three tutoring-derived events can be employed satisfactorily in groups of about thirty and accomplish much of what tutoring is expected to give: ensuring review of prerequisites, employing student participation as part of learning guidance, and enhancing retrieval cues by elaborating concepts and rules through explanations.
These studies confirm the effectiveness of mastery-learning procedures, particularly those that inform students of correct and incorrect performances and permit restudy until success is achieved.

As group size increases, the effects of necessary instructional events on individual learners decrease from near certainty to lower probabilities, so learning outcomes come to depend increasingly on the self-instructional strategies available to the individual learner.

Diagnosis of entering capabilities is the feature that becomes hardest to manage as group size grows, and it matters most for stimulating recall of prerequisites — since students cannot recall what they never learned — so weak control of that event with larger groups may produce a cumulative deficit in learning.

Merely asserting a determination to adjust teaching to individual needs accomplishes little: teachers need a delivery system designed to achieve that purpose, because dividing time between individuals and groups leaves some pupils unoccupied and unable to progress for periods of time.

Besides tutoring there is a second solution to the two-sigma problem: instructional materials that address the student directly without depending on a teacher for delivery and that are tailored to individual student needs.

Early individualisation experiments failed largely because a total support system was lacking — no design technology, no marketing agency developing and diffusing the special materials — which left too great a burden on the teacher.

A delivery system for individualised instruction must assess entry skills, find each student's starting point in a carefully sequenced series of objectives, provide alternative materials and media including print and nonprint choices, let students learn at their own rates, and provide frequent convenient progress checks so students do not become bogged down with cumulative failures.
