Individualisation is accomplished in part by designing learning materials and media that can carry more of the support for more of the instructional events, so that every pupil can work each day on objectives within their own needs, capacities, prerequisite skills, and learning rate.
Three nationally diffused individualised-instruction systems declined in use or were discontinued when federal funding ceased, in spite of their proved effectiveness.

When a school's objectives coincide closely with those of an available system it seems wasteful to repeat the entire instructional design that has already been carefully done; schools may instead adopt with few modifications, modify heavily, purchase some components and develop others, or build from scratch.
condition: when the school's objectives closely match the available system's

statement: Few publishers have actually validated the effectiveness of materials sold as objective-keyed; usually they have simply added objectives and test items onto existing materials, a deficiency one state addressed by requiring publishers to validate effectiveness as a textbook-selection criterion.
Visits to two independent samples of schools using individualised systems found great variation in specific classroom application even though all were directed toward the same five purposes.

In a working individualised classroom, learners at very different points work simultaneously on their own objectives — some on visual letter discrimination with programmed booklets, some on letter names by machine, some in a small teacher-led group on word-attack skills, some with read-along tapes, some testing or self-checking — so that slow learners still experience success rather than failure during the hour.

The machinery that makes an individualised classroom run is that diagnostic and placement tests are keyed to a sequence of objectives, which are in turn keyed to the materials available for each objective, held in files the students have learned to use and return materials to.

Individualisation need not extend to the whole curriculum or the whole day: a school may individualise only reading and mathematics while teaching other subjects conventionally, and schedule common activities where all pupils can participate at a shared level.

Diagnostic and placement tests at the start of the year determine which objectives in the ordered sequence each student has already mastered and can recall, fixing the starting point, and frequent subsequent testing updates the record of prerequisite mastery for later objectives.

In reading and mathematics a single sequence of objectives is often adopted for all learners with materials and pace varying, whereas science and social studies often set core objectives for all plus enrichment or excursion objectives chosen by student interest.

Gaining attention presents fewer problems in an individualised program because each student is eager to begin a new objective after succeeding on the previous one, and it is rare that more than one student at a time is not actually working.

Attention is maintained by the systematic cycle of presenting a problem, requiring a response, and providing feedback built into the material; children encouraged to switch to a different activity when tired usually return to the task without prompting.

Informing the learner of the objective matters less for highly structured material, where the objective is often evident, than for loosely structured material, where the student needs the objective to decide which portions are most relevant for selective reading and review.
condition: the event is more important the more loosely structured the material

statement: Under individually paced programs the composition of small groups shifts constantly — five students at the same point one day may not be at a common point on another.

Careful sequencing makes recall of immediately prior learning highly probable and structured materials make initial mastery of prerequisites more probable, while frequent progress checks after each objective prevent the cumulative forgetting that would slow further learning.

The strongest feature of individualised programs may be the appropriate and precise management of presenting the stimulus, eliciting the response, and providing feedback — and that strength is primarily a feature of the materials, not the teacher.

The teacher's primary strengths in an individualised program lie in managing and monitoring the whole system in the classroom and in ensuring personal guidance is available when the provided materials and tests fail to function adequately for an individual learner.

Materials can carry encoding-level learning guidance as prompts, cues, and suggestions blended with stimulus presentation more precisely than a teacher can except in tutoring, while the teacher gives a more general guidance about which alternative materials and which enrichment objectives to choose.

An advantage of individualised delivery systems is that they give the teacher time to spend with individual pupils: once pupils learn the pretest-learn-posttest procedures and how to find materials, the basic system runs itself, though the teacher is not idle and students may have to wait, turning to enrichment activities meanwhile.

Individualised systems protect slow learners from inappropriate tasks and instruction and hence from failure, and free fast learners from the boredom of unnecessary instruction — but it is the teacher who must see that the arrangements are suitable for each learner.

Learners may self-test with an answer key for some objectives, but at least periodically — and more often than in large-group instruction — the teacher makes the assessment, using time freed from other instructional events.

Group instruction is often the suitable vehicle for retention and transfer within an individualised program: once several learners have been assessed at the same point, teacher-led discussion lets them hear each other's applications while progressing toward terminal objectives in attitudes or cognitive strategies.
condition: once several learners are assessed to be at the same point of progress

statement: It should not be concluded that individualised instruction is effective only for mature learners: because each lesson's appropriateness is assured and the instruction is precise, this form may be needed more by less mature learners, while adults and college students are expected to discern appropriate materials and supply many events themselves.

College-level individualised methods are not as fine-grained or precisely controlled as elementary ones: they combine large-group lectures, smaller quiz sessions, and independent study economically, use tests to route students to the most appropriate activity, and adopt mastery learning within the limits of academic-term policy.

College programs have students concentrate study where progress checks show the most work is needed, make less use of small-step materials, and provide laboratory assistants for individual tutoring when other methods fail — yielding a precision intermediate between large-group and elementary individualised programs at reasonable cost.

Independent study plans agree only the most general objectives and place no restriction on how the student prepares for a final examination, while self-directed study agrees specific objectives and supplies optional resources but still leaves the method entirely to the student.

In public schools learner choice of objectives is usually permitted only for enrichment exercises and only after required core skills have been mastered, often offered as an incentive to learn the core skills.

Self-pacing individualises only the rate: all students may use the same materials toward the same teacher-set objectives, which distinguishes it from student-determined instruction where the learner may control objective selection, materials, scheduling, pacing, self-evaluation, and abandonment of an objective.

Computer-adaptive or intelligent computer-assisted instruction paces the learner by pretest scores, performance history, and progress through the lesson, aiming to customise instruction via learner analysis, alternative presentation strategies, and a knowledge database, typically built on expert-system technology.

Expert systems structure knowledge or procedures as rules and can learn by asking an expert for a new rule when they cannot decide, but many barriers to their use exist — not least the complexity of even a relatively simple system.

Most of the looser varieties of individualised instruction place greater responsibility on students to provide the instructional events and permit greater freedom over objectives, which is why they have been used mainly with selected groups of students.

The unit of management scales with learner age: an objective for young children may be masterable in an hour or less so management centres on single objectives, while for older students a module may take a week or two and evaluation covers a cluster of objectives.

The frequency of formal progress checks, and of responding followed by feedback, tends to decrease with the age of the learners, adjusted either by how the self-instructional materials are designed or by how a module is assembled.

A module should contain or point to everything needed to pass the objective's test, including practice tests by which the student judges readiness and directions for locating and using any external materials, so the learner can proceed without another person's direction except when difficulties arise.

A module for children benefits from showing the learner both the target objective and the prerequisite capabilities to be acquired, either as a list or as a learning hierarchy, plus a suggested sequence of activities derived from the enabling objectives and making provision for retention and transfer.
The total menu of modules should be designed to meet the needs of fast learners as well, not solely those of slow learners.

Contingency-management programs use a preferred high-reward activity as an inducement to study, often by contracts in which the student spends starting points to negotiate time for a module and earns points for completing it within the period, which can then be spent on free time or preferred activity.

Because the capabilities a child will need to reach his goals and solve problems not yet foreseen by today's adults cannot be determined exactly, emphasis needs to be placed on intellectual skills and problem-solving strategies rather than simply on presently known facts.

Research studies have identified few intellectual and personality characteristics that can be related to success with specific forms or media of instruction, so the common appeal to individual learning styles rests on a phrase whose specific meaning is not entirely clear.

Where one material works better for a learner the cause may be differing entering capabilities matching the content, or the fact that the instructional events appropriate to that individual occur more fully in that material, or design features such as small versus large steps, inductive versus deductive, and concrete versus abstract.

Providing several versions of a module is often worthwhile — one with simpler vocabulary, one with shorter sentences, one pairing an outline or advance organiser with technically complex presentation — but the alternative-module concept raises an economic question that research on the size of the advantage is needed to answer against cost.

For young learners and lengthy modules it is unwise to wait until a test to give feedback: feedback after small increments of study is usually desirable, and it is a built-in feature of text-based and computer-programmed instruction.
condition: for young learners and lengthy modules

statement: The effectiveness of one-way media such as television or film can be improved by building in explicit provisions for learner response and feedback, which also signal when diagnostic testing, remedial instruction, or restudy of the module is needed.

A televised or live lecturer can pose a question after a brief segment, pause for the viewer to write or think of an answer, then give feedback; questions used with live lectures have been found to benefit learning and usually retention as well.
Classroom devices that immediately record students' multiple-choice answers for the teacher let the lecture be reprogrammed on the spot.

When a module is brief or the learner typically succeeds readily, a parallel form of the formal test can supply feedback after learning is completed; some self-testing with corrective feedback can usually be devised for each module.
condition: when the module is brief or the learner usually succeeds

statement: Built-in self-testing enhances learning and saves the teacher's time for individual remedial teaching when all other means fail — a valuable activity for which teachers have too little time under conventional group instruction — with the added bonus of time to guide thinking and give individual feedback when most needed.

Materials and procedures may properly be less highly structured for college students and experienced adults: performance checks come after a rather long period of study whether the module carries one broad objective or many specific ones.
condition: for adult and college-level learners

statement: Directions for adult learners may be greatly abbreviated — a list of resources or simply a pointer to the library and laboratory — with the objective itself serving as the main source of directions.
Adult learning materials may be highly structured as a programmed text, semistructured as an outline or laboratory guide, or unstructured as in library research on a topic.

Adult unit evaluation is usually based on the appropriateness of the procedures employed, competence in reporting and interpreting data, and ability to defend a rationale for the completed product or study — supported en route by advisor feedback on draft plans and preliminary reports and by direct instruction on subordinate capabilities such as writing and finding sources.

Modules may specify group activities, in which case a class chart of each pupil's progress is used to form groups of students at the same point; they may also serve as directions for laboratory or field exercises or for independent learning not based on instructional materials.
Modules need not be restricted to cognitive objectives; affective and motor-domain objectives can be devised equally well.

In shop courses all needed cognitive learning can be completed before a skill is practised on the equipment, which saves the cost of duplicate machines and avoids injury and damage by ensuring the trainee knows the safety precautions and correct procedures before gaining access.
Simple training devices can be used for parts of the total task, reserving the more expensive complex simulator for consolidating skills and practising emergency procedures in a safe environment.

A computer-supported individualised system stores each student's prior study, progress, and performance record and prints daily information on which objectives were completed and which activities begun or completed, constituting the essential information base for planning individual programs.
A module of about two weeks is a collection of activities representing closely related objectives, composed of teaching-learning units each carrying a single objective.

A teaching-learning unit opens with the learning objective telling the student what is to be learned, then lists the learning activities and references, self-test questions, and discussion questions, with pictorial techniques used in the early grades to convey the objective and activities.

On completing the unit's activities the student should be able to do what the objective calls for and is then ready for the performance test; if performance is satisfactory he moves to a new unit, and if not the teacher suggests additional work.

Teacher directions accompanying each unit communicate the objective, the plan of student activities, the materials needed, and the test directions, letting the teacher see at a glance what needs planning and which instructional modes — small-group work, partners, tutoring — may be required, so options can be advised to the student.

An instructional guide supplies direct instruction to the student where it is unavailable in published sources, often making it possible for the student to develop an intellectual skill necessary for further progress within the unit.

Materials in modular form arrive in smaller chunks than in traditional instruction, so the material for a single objective must be either physically separate from other objectives' material or clearly identified and indexed to match its objective and test.

Whatever the module's materials consist of, a system must exist by which student, teacher, and aides can locate them quickly — either an indexing system or separate physical packaging — with a numbering system convenient for planning, record keeping, locating, and storing.

A per-student planning sheet is needed when students have some freedom to choose objectives, whereas a single class sheet suffices for planning, monitoring, and record keeping when all students start at module one and progress as far as time permits.
condition: depends on whether students choose their own objectives

statement: Maintaining an individualised system is a substantial ongoing task — sufficient stocked supply of each module, restocking expendable portions after each use, and cross-referencing new material to objectives and test items — and it is this maintenance that sometimes appears to spell the downfall of individualised instruction, with lack of maintenance a probable major factor in past discontinuations despite adequate development funding.

All teachers need special training to conduct and manage individualised instruction and cannot be expected to function adequately, let alone enthusiastically, without it — and such training may at first make a teacher feel that his most cherished functions are being usurped and that he is reduced to a librarian or clerk.

Even with appropriate training not all teachers will like the individualised approach — some will not relinquish the familiar role while others tired of repeating the same lesson welcome the change — but once trained and experienced most come to prefer it, usually after one year.

Monitoring progress means knowing both what each student is undertaking to learn and how fast and how well each is progressing, and a module counts as finished only when the student has met a minimum standard on a test or other evaluation of the objective.

For product evaluation a grading or criterion sheet listing the features to look for, with points per feature or a count of satisfactory features, is preferable to a single overall judgment — it improves the evaluation and serves a diagnostic function by showing the student where improvement is needed.
The same criterion sheet given to the student at the onset of instruction informs him what is expected, suggests how it may be done, and states how the product will be evaluated.

Oral evaluation, though less standardised than written testing, often probes more deeply and can be combined with planning the next work or the remedial work needed, making it convenient and effective with an individual student.

A teacher usually knows more about each student's progress under a well-designed individual plan than under group instruction, one reason being that in individualised instruction every student responds to every question.

Assessment throughout an individualised program serves four purposes: initial placement at an approximate level for first assignments, assessment of mastery of each module and completion of enrichment objectives, diagnosis of difficulties to identify needed assignments, and measurement of yearly progress across the curriculum.

Day-to-day mastery assessment should be likened to the informal probing every teacher does rather than to formal testing; what distinguishes it is not formality of administration but the preestablished criteria the teacher or student uses to judge when mastery has been achieved.

When a student hits a difficulty a brief diagnostic test is administered, indicating which prerequisite skills and information were inadequately learned or forgotten and therefore which next or review assignment will re-establish the necessary competence.

Attitudes such as cooperation, helping, and control of aggressive acts may be assessed by teacher checklists completed at periodic intervals, while broader citizenship attitudes may be assessed by questionnaires.

An individualised system starts rough and improves with experience: at first there is slack time while pupils wait for help and the teacher feels harassed by too much to track, but gradually the pupil becomes a more skilled independent learner and the teacher reaches a calm, easy pacing.

Combining flexible scheduling with individualised instruction across a whole school lets a student concentrate heavily on one subject one day and range across many the next, which relieves schooling of much of the boredom of an identical daily schedule.

The teacher's day in an individualised system is spent on advance planning sessions with one to six students, reviewing progress and test results, giving next assignments, individual diagnosis and remedial instruction, schedule changes, and small-group sessions for students at approximately the same point.

Students and aides maintain the materials files once taught the filing system, and aides administer and score tests, keep records, help students find materials, tutor, and back up the teacher — their role being to help implement the plans agreed between teacher and student.

Discipline problems tend to be minimised in individualised instruction because personal attention motivates toward success, the method is designed to produce success which is itself rewarding, and less whole-class teaching leaves fewer opportunities for a student to capture the group's attention — all of which lessen the traditional adversary relationship between teachers and students.

An individualised system discourages public confrontations in which neither side wishes to back down and removes the temptation for a teacher to use sarcasm or ridicule of poor work, quietly reminding the teacher that the goal is learning rather than platform performance or crowd psychology.
Contingency management arranges successions of student activities so that an initially nonpreferred activity is followed by a preferred one, thereby reinforcing the former.

Used properly, contingency management establishes and maintains orderly behaviour aimed at productive learning, instils a positive liking for learning and its accomplishments, and captures interest in problem-solving activities as sources of satisfaction for mastering the intellectual skills involved.
condition: when used properly

statement: The teacher must learn to identify differences in the interests, likes, and dislikes of individual students and use these in selecting the specific contingencies that will produce a task-oriented learning environment.

Because the materials largely take over the role of instruction in an individualised system, the instructor's role changes to manager and maintainer of the system; teachers initially resist this but usually come to prefer it with experience.

Satisfactory performance of individualised systems depends on maintaining the appropriate procedures, and it is the lack of continuing support for these routines that typically makes such systems fail.
Most research on computer-assisted instruction has shown it to be at least as effective as other modes of delivery.

The main problem facing individualised instruction continues to be the development of materials and the maintenance of the system, and new technologies may demand an entirely new teacher role — instructional designer-developer — for which conventional lecture-and-discussion training does not prepare teachers.

Equipment ease of use is not the bottleneck for new media in individualised instruction — a teacher can learn to operate a videocamera recorder in fifteen minutes — the problem lies in training teachers how best to use such equipment to support and maintain the system.
Advanced technological conceptions for solving the two-sigma problem will require reconstruction of teacher training curricula if they are to have lasting effects on instruction.

The history of technological solutions to educational problems does not provide grounds for unusual optimism; what should be emphasised is that the technology has been proved effective, leaving cost of access and maintenance as the remaining problem.

Individualised instruction is designed by the same planning processes as conventional group lessons — performance objectives, learning hierarchies, sequencing, instructional events, and conditions of learning all apply — and it is the delivery system that primarily distinguishes module design from lesson design.
Modules are more distinctly self-instructional than conventional lessons because more of the needed instructional events and conditions of learning are designed into the materials themselves.

Because module materials do more of the direct teaching, individualised instruction depends less on the teacher as provider of information and places more stress on counselling, evaluating, monitoring, and diagnosing.

A single module should include at minimum a performance objective, a set of materials and learning activities whether self-contained or external, a method for self-evaluation of mastery, and a provision for the teacher to verify the learning outcome.

Individualised instruction typically provides more frequent feedback and more frequent progress checks than conventional instruction, and as a minimum the learner sets his own pace even where objectives are required.

Managing individualised instruction requires four things: a way to index and store modules, a way to schedule modules for each learner, a way to monitor pupil progress, and a way to assess performance.

Learning is affected by many variables besides instructional quality — learner perseverance, time allowed (opportunity), subject-specific aptitude, general ability to understand, and quality of instruction — each of which affects the time a learner needs or actually spends.

Most design models emphasise improving instructional quality through formative evaluation, but evaluating instruction also requires considering learner motivation and environmental variables such as the opportunity to spend the time needed.
Planning of evaluation should not be undertaken as a final step: designing the evaluation requires the same instructional-planning principles used throughout the design process.

Evaluation of a lesson, topic, course, or system should answer three questions: to what extent the stated objectives have been met, in what ways and to what degree it is better than the unit it supplants, and what additional possibly unanticipated effects it has had and whether these are better or worse.

Goal-free evaluation examines the effects of an educational innovation and assesses the worth of those effects whatever they are, rather than confining itself to the stated objectives — so a change in teacher attitude counts as one of the effects rather than merely an unanticipated outcome.

A comprehensive evaluation of a new educational product covers need, market, field-trial performance, consumer appropriateness, comparison with competitors, long-term performance, process fidelity, side effects, causation, statistical and educational significance, costs and cost effectiveness, and extended support.

Judging a new educational product's worth is a complex matter based on various kinds of information, with the judgment on each factor recorded on a profile graph that then supports a systematic overall judgment of appropriateness and worth.
The CIPP model treats evaluation as a continuing process in which information is first delineated, then obtained, then provided, with the primary purpose of guiding decision making.

Each CIPP stage guides a different decision: context evaluation determines problems and unmet needs for planning decisions, input evaluation weighs alternative solutions' strengths and feasibility for structuring decisions, process evaluation covers the educational processes actually set in motion for implementing decisions, and product evaluation assesses how well the course is working for the recycling decision to continue, drop, or modify.

Planning an evaluation requires answering what program is to be evaluated and what population it serves, what the audience's main concerns are, how the information will be used, what type of study will be conducted, and what questions will be addressed.

Goal-free evaluation is best treated not as a substitute for but as a valuable supplement to goal-based evaluation, with formative evaluation serving decisions about program development and summative evaluation providing a basis for accountability.

Formative evaluation collects evidence during development and uses it to form the program itself, leading to decisions about revision, whereas summative evaluation leads to decisions about program adoption and continuation.

Formative evaluation can expose practical infeasibility rather than ineffectiveness — a lesson requiring an organism that cannot be kept alive in ordinary conditions — in which case the specific difficulty may allow a simple substitution, or may force a rewrite or abandonment.

When a topic falls short of its objective, examining where the mistakes cluster localises the fault to a subordinate objective — a designer finding errors centred on identifying noun gender is led to revise or add a lesson on that prerequisite.
Formative evaluation proceeds in three stages, each a tryout of the material with a different sample of potential students representative of the target audience.

In one-to-one testing the evaluator sits with one student and watches performance closely, while a subject-matter expert made thoroughly acquainted with the objectives and the performance indicators addresses the validity of objectives and the accuracy and clarity of materials and items.

One-to-one testing surfaces four kinds of defect: errors in estimating students' entry capabilities, lack of clarity in the instruction, unclear test questions and directions, and inappropriate expectations of learning outcomes.

Small-group testing pretests the skills to be taught, presents the instruction, administers a posttest, adds an attitude questionnaire, and may ask students to discuss the instruction and the tests — beginning to answer whether learning occurred and how much, by comparing pretest and posttest scores.

The field trial gives the revised pretest and posttest around the instruction with an appropriate sample of the intended audience, surveys attitudes of both learners and participating instructors, and observes the adequacy of the materials, their directions, and the instructors' performance in using them.

The field trial is the critical test of the instruction's feasibility of use and effectiveness, yielding student and instructor behaviour and attitudes for a near-final revision, with achievement gains under near-typical conditions of crucial importance.

Feasibility can be decided from reports of the difficulties instructors or students had conducting the lesson, whereas effectiveness is a more complex judgment resting partly on whether materials were used and procedures carried out as intended, partly on attitudes incidentally established, and most importantly on the extent to which student test performance succeeded.

Formative evaluation is most cogently concerned with whether the stated objectives have been met — that is the essential evidence for revision — while comparison with a supplanted unit and observations of unanticipated effects may also feed the revision decision when available.
Evidence from observational records, questionnaires, and tests is used across the formative stages to decide whether a lesson should be kept as is, revised, reformulated, or discarded.

Summative evaluation is undertaken when development is in some sense completed rather than ongoing, to permit conclusions about how well the instruction worked and to let schools decide about adopting and using it.

Summative evaluation addresses the summed effects of a set of lessons making up a larger unit: individual lessons are evaluated as components rather than as separate entities, though the evidence may still reveal defects in particular lessons for use in the next revision.

The main decision summative evidence supports is whether a new course is better than the one it replaced and should therefore be adopted; if it is merely no better, considerations other than effectiveness such as cost determine the choice.

A convincing adoption case combines several strands of evidence at once — objectives met, examination scores against the prior year, student attitude, teacher-reported working conditions, and cost no greater than the old course.
condition: provided the new course does not cost more than the old

statement: Summative evaluation is far more formal than formative: attitude measures use carefully constructed questionnaires so they can be validly compared with the previous year's students, and mastery of each objective is systematically assessed to give a quantitative indication of the whole course's accomplishment.
Obtaining evidence of learning outcomes requires collecting data on input measures and process measures as well as on the measures that directly assess outcomes.

Outcome measures span all five capability types: mastery tests for intellectual skills, novel-situation exercises assessing the quality or efficiency of problem-solving thought, tests of specified facts or of breadth of knowledge for information, observations against a performance standard for motor skills, and probability-of-choice self-report questionnaires for attitudes.

Summative measures are interpreted primarily by comparison with similar measures from an alternative mode of instruction — usually the unit being replaced, sometimes two new units against each other — which requires data-collection methods able to demonstrate that all other things are equal, by no means an easy thing to do.

Whether the new unit's own objectives were met is a minimal condition in a summative study, because failure to meet them obviously affects the conclusions that can be drawn from any comparison with an alternative unit.
It is always of some importance to explore whether newly designed instruction has had unanticipated effects, since a topic teaching one subject may turn out to affect attitudes in an unrelated area.

Outcome measures often must be separately developed for an evaluation effort, though in some instances the required tests, observation schedules, or questionnaires are commercially available or adaptable.

Because the capabilities an evaluation measures are affected by factors in the educational setting other than the instruction itself, those other variables must be controlled or otherwise accounted for before valid conclusions about instructional effectiveness can be drawn.

Process variables are the operations actually carried out to put the instruction into effect — whether the specified type and frequency of teacher questioning occurred, whether the prescribed skill sequence was followed, whether the specified feedback was consistently given.

One cannot simply assume the process variables the designer intended will occur as expected: designers of individualised programs have frequently found the specified operations are not being executed as intended, so assessing process variables is essential — particularly on a first tryout.

Well-designed instruction provides for whatever action ensures the program operates as planned, such as training teachers in the required operations, but these efforts are not always fully successful.

Instructional entities vary greatly in how far they specify process variables — a textbook may imply a sequence through its chapter organisation while leaving the events of instruction entirely to the teacher or learner, whereas a designed topic may specify both the subordinate-skill sequence and the particular events.

Regardless of how far the design prescribes process variables, they must be taken into account in a well-planned evaluation, because the outcomes observed may be substantially affected by how the program was operated whatever its designed intentions.

Process variables are typically assessed by systematic classroom observation performed by an observer rather than the teacher, using a checklist or observation schedule normally designed specially for that evaluation study.

Support variables include classroom and library materials, availability of a quiet place to study, the classroom climate's encouragement of achievement, and parental reinforcement of favourable attitudes toward homework; the class is large and not enough is known to rank their relative importance confidently.

Support variables differ from process variables in that they do not directly influence the process of learning but determine the general environmental conditions — the opportunities for learning — during the times when process variables exert their effects.

A process variable can be fully satisfied while a support variable still differs: the teacher may allot the specified independent-study time, yet one student pursues it in a quiet place uninterrupted and another in an open corner of a noisy classroom.

Support variables require assessment methods matched to each variable — questionnaires for what parents do about homework, counts of books and reference sources for material availability, systematic observation schedules for classroom climate, and readily available records for class size or pupil-teacher ratio.

Of all variables likely to determine learning outcomes the most influential is probably the student's aptitude for learning: no combination of improved methods, process arrangements, and best possible support can influence outcomes as much as aptitude does.

Many studies have shown aptitude for learning as measured by intelligence tests may account for as much as fifty percent of the variation in learning outcomes across verbal information, intellectual skills, and cognitive strategies.

Aptitude has multiple determinants — genetic inheritance, prenatal environment, prior learning, and opportunities to learn — but as it enters an evaluation study it is an input variable that can only be measured, not manipulated.
To assess an instructional program's effectiveness, controls must be instituted that separate the influence of the students' entering aptitudes from the effect of the instruction itself.

Some evaluations should treat the prerequisite learner characteristics rather than general aptitude as the input variable — as when an adult basic-skills program asks about effectiveness independent of the students' entering skills.
condition: when the evaluation question concerns effectiveness independent of entering skills

statement: Measures correlated with intelligence — previous school grades, especially in reading comprehension and mathematics, or family socioeconomic status — are sometimes useful as aptitude proxies but are not to be preferred over measures that assess learning aptitude as directly as possible.

When reporting whether objectives were met, the students' aptitude level should be stated — average score and a dispersion measure — because the same course may meet a much larger share of its objectives with a higher-aptitude group than a lower-aptitude one.

The aims of evaluation may best be accomplished by trying the instructional entity out in several different schools, each with a somewhat different range of student learning aptitude — and likewise across schools differing in their support characteristics.

Making a comparison requires demonstrating that the two groups of students were equivalent to begin with; equivalence in aptitude is most likely when successive classes in the same school drawn from the same neighbourhood serve as the comparison groups.

Randomly assigning students to classrooms within a school requires definite administrative arrangements to ensure randomness — it cannot be assumed — and matching schools on student aptitude is an alternative, though all such designs need careful management for valid comparison.

Statistical control partials out aptitude effects by asking what the effect of instruction alone would be if aptitude were held constant rather than variable, which is of considerable value given how prominently aptitude influences outcomes.

No study evaluating learning outcomes can provide valid evidence of instructional effectiveness without a way of controlling the aptitude variable, whether by measurement, random assignment, comparison of aptitudes, or statistical means.

Even within one school, two aptitude-equivalent classes can differ in support variables — classroom climate, whether the teacher is liked or disliked, and how many students seek new learning opportunities — so equivalence on these must be demonstrated or handled statistically before concluding the new instruction is better.

The same instructional program can lead to markedly different operations — one teacher encourages students to invent a way of finding the answer while another requires them to do only what the exercise book describes — and equally marked effects may appear in the outcome measures.

A process-variable divergence is read differently by evaluation type: in formative evaluation it shows the need for additional teacher instructions or training, whereas in summative evaluation the results from the two groups must be treated separately to disclose the effect of that variable.

Process variables are more amenable to direct control than support or aptitude variables: a noisy environment may be unchangeable, but teachers found not to be using the specified operations can be instructed so the next trial starts with a desirable set of process variables.

Unanticipated outcomes are equally likely to be caused by process variables — favourable attitudes may stem from one teacher's human modeling rather than from the program — so equivalence of process variables must be demonstrated before attributing such effects to the instructional entity.

Randomisation is the best way to control variables in an evaluation study because it controls not only the specific variables identified but also others not singled out for measurement because their potential influence is unknown.

Randomising procedures are usually difficult to arrange in practice because schools do not customarily draw students randomly from a community or assign them randomly to classes or teachers, so aptitude, support, and process variables must usually be identified and measured instead.

All four classes of variable — aptitude, support, process, and outcome — are typically measured in any evaluation study whether formative or summative; what differs between the two roles is the interpretation of those measures.
A single study can serve both roles at once: a systematic formative evaluation of an instructional system also obtained initial data for summative purposes.

Where aptitude scores are unavailable across participating schools, socioeconomic status may be used as a correlated stand-in initially and verified later by administering standardized aptitude and readiness tests.
condition: where direct aptitude measures are not initially available

statement: The same aptitude data serve different purposes by role: formative evaluation needs to know the classes span a range of aptitudes representative of the system's intended usage, whereas summative evaluation needs equivalence of that variable between experimental and control groups.
Comparison groups should be requested from each participating district to be as equivalent as possible in the characteristics of both teachers and pupils.

A study's coverage should be reported honestly against its intended population: even a large multi-state sample representing a great majority of elementary schools may have omitted whole categories such as inner-city schools.

Teacher characteristics — level of formal education, amount of education in the subject's methods, and years of experience — can stand in for support variables on the inference that a typical range of teacher backgrounds produces a range of differential opportunities for learning.

Support measures of greater relevance to summative evaluation — availability of reading materials, encouragement of independent reading — may go unmeasured in a study, and where partial evidence exists it can reveal enormous individual variation such as a range from zero to over a hundred books read.

Feasibility of program parts can be measured by asking teachers to judge the appropriateness of materials for fast, medium, and slow learners, and such judgments led to elimination or revision of a number of program elements.

Teachers' estimates of how effective a lesson was are indirect evidence about process variables, weaker than direct indicators such as how many exercises were attempted, how long was spent on each, and what feedback was given — but they may be the best obtainable when the materials do not make the intended process variables evident.
condition: when the program does not make its intended process variables explicit

statement: Outcome differences between experimental and control groups become interpretable only once the groups have been shown reasonably equivalent on aptitude and support variables, with statistical tests confirming the differences are significant at an acceptable probability level.

Evidence of learning outcomes obtained during formative work should be treated as no more than initial indications of success, with further studies conducted to evaluate outcomes in a summative sense.

Where a school's entering classes are shown to have essentially the same aptitude and socioeconomic status year after year, it becomes reasonable to compare this year's experimental class with last year's class under the previous program.
condition: only where entering-class aptitude and status have been shown stable across years

statement: Support variables need not be measured individually when the same school facilities and the same teachers serve both groups and socioeconomic status is equivalent, since the school and home support variables can then be assumed equivalent.
condition: when facilities, teachers, and student socioeconomic status are demonstrably the same

statement: The process variables under study should be deliberately contrasted between groups and the contrast verified by classroom observation, while other process variables are held equivalent by using the same teachers for both groups.

When aptitude, support, and process variables are shown or reasonably assumed to affect both groups equally, the outcome measures can be expected to reflect the effect of the instructional change in an unbiased manner.

Every evaluation presents different circumstances and compromises must sometimes be made for inadequate outcome measures, difficulty achieving group equivalence, or events affecting one school and not others; part of the evaluator's job is judging the severity of these and how they must be taken into account to reach convincing evidence.

When the experimental school's aptitude exceeds the control's, the effects of instruction cannot be expected to show up at all: most if not all of the outcome difference is attributable to the aptitude difference, because that variable is so powerful.

If only the support variables differ, or only the process variables differ, the outcome difference may be caused by the instruction, by that variable, or by both in an unknown proportion — no attribution to the instruction is warranted.

Only when aptitude, support, and process variables have all been shown equivalent by one method or another can the outcome difference be attributed to the instruction itself — and that situation is what summative evaluation studies aim for.
Formative evaluation is undertaken while the unit is being developed to provide evidence on feasibility and effectiveness for revision, seeking that evidence from observers, teachers, and students.

Summative evaluation concerns effectiveness once the program is developed, and the evidence it seeks is mainly student performance measured on the kinds of capabilities the program was intended to establish.

Support variables are the conditions in the home, school, workplace, and community that affect opportunities for learning, whereas process variables arise from the manner in which the instruction is operated in the class or school.

Randomised assignment of students, schools, or communities can equalise the influencing variables, but more frequently statistical means must be used to establish the equivalence of the groups compared.

If two courses are to be evaluated to determine which is better, evaluation logic requires control over the other variables so that ideally everything is equivalent except the instructional programs themselves.
A first principle of instruction is a basic method: a relationship that is always true under appropriate conditions regardless of the program or practice used to implement it.
condition: under appropriate conditions

statement: Learning from a given instructional program is promoted in direct proportion to how fully that program implements the first principles of instruction.
The first principles of instruction can be implemented in any delivery system and using any instructional architecture.
First principles of instruction are prescriptive and design-oriented (about creating learning environments and products), not descriptive or learning-oriented (about how learners acquire knowledge).
When an instructional program or practice violates or fails to implement one or more first principles, learning and performance decline.
condition: when a program violates or fails to implement a first principle

statement: The most effective learning products and environments are problem-centered and engage the learner in four distinct phases: activation of prior experience, demonstration, application, and integration.
Much instructional practice concentrates on the demonstration phase alone and neglects activation, application, and integration.
Principle 1 (Problem-centered): learning is promoted when learners are engaged in solving real-world, whole-task problems.

A problem for problem-centered instruction is a whole task representative of what the learner will face after instruction; this contrasts with topic-centered instruction that teaches task components in isolation before introducing the real-world task.
Principle 2 (Activation): learning is promoted when relevant prior experience is activated as a foundation for the new knowledge.
Principle 3 (Demonstration): learning is promoted when the instruction demonstrates (shows) what is to be learned rather than merely telling information about it.
Principle 4 (Application): learning improves when learners must put their new knowledge or skill to work solving problems.
Principle 5 (Integration): learning is promoted when learners integrate (transfer) the new knowledge or skill into their everyday life.
Learning is promoted when learners are shown the whole task or problem they will be able to complete after the module, rather than given only abstract objective statements.
The first problem in an instructional sequence should be a worked example that shows learners the type of whole task they will learn to complete.

Learning is promoted when learners are engaged at the problem and task level, not only the operation or action level; effective instruction should engage all four levels of performance (problem, task, operation, action).

Learning is promoted when learners solve a progression of increasingly complex problems that are explicitly compared to one another; solving a single problem or receiving little-to-no guidance (sink-or-swim) is not effective for mastering a complex problem.
condition: for complex problems or skills

statement: Learning is promoted when learners are directed to recall, relate, describe, or apply relevant past experience as a foundation for new knowledge; a simple recall of information, or an information-oriented pretest given when learners feel they do not know the material, is seldom effective for this activation.
condition: when learners have relevant prior experience

statement: When learners lack relevant prior experience, learning is promoted by providing relevant concrete experience that can serve as a foundation before introducing the new material.
condition: when learners lack sufficient relevant prior experience

statement: Learning is promoted when learners are provided or encouraged to recall an organizing structure or mental model for the new knowledge: provide a structure when the learner's existing mental model is insufficient, and encourage the learner to activate their model when it is adequate.
condition: depending on whether the learner's existing mental model can adequately organize the new knowledge

statement: Motivational themes that are irrelevant to the instructional content activate inappropriate mental models, increase cognitive load, and can interfere with learning rather than promote it.
exception: when the theme is relevant to the content it can serve as a useful organizing structure

statement: Knowledge to be learned exists at two levels, information (general) and portrayal (specific case); instruction is far more effective when the information is demonstrated through specific portrayals such as examples or cases than when information is presented alone.

Superficial substitutes for instruction are by themselves seldom effective: tell-and-ask presentation (information followed by a few remember-what-you-were-told questions) and a few multiple-choice questions labeled as practice do little to promote learning.
Presenting examples is more effective than presenting information alone, and presenting examples in addition to practice promotes better learning than practice alone.

Learning is promoted when the demonstration is consistent with the learning goal: examples and nonexamples for concepts, demonstrations for procedures, visualizations for processes, and modeling for behavior.

The consistency criterion should be applied first for both demonstration and practice: if the presentation or application is inconsistent with the intended learning outcome, it does not matter whether learner guidance, media, feedback, or a problem sequence are present.

Learning is promoted by appropriate learner guidance during demonstration: directing learners to the relevant information, using multiple representations, and explicitly comparing multiple demonstrations.

Attention-focusing guidance should be provided early in instruction and then gradually faded as instruction progresses, so learners increasingly direct their own attention to the relevant information.
condition: fade as instruction progresses

statement: Merely presenting alternative or multiple representations is not sufficient; learners must be explicitly directed to compare the different representations in order to tune their mental models to a broader perspective.
Media aid learning when each medium serves a genuine instructional role and the different media forms do not compete for the learner's attention.

Gratuitous illustrations make little or no instructional contribution and may interfere with learning; some multimedia combinations (e.g., text and a graphic) compete for attention and increase cognitive load, while complementary combinations (e.g., audio and graphics) support one another and promote more effective learning.
Practice and the posttest should align with the stated or implied objectives, and the appropriate kind of practice differs by the kind of knowledge or skill being taught.
Guide problem solving with appropriate feedback and coaching — covering how to detect, correct, and avoid errors — and taper that coaching off (scaffolding) as the learner's competence grows.
condition: coaching gradually withdrawn as the learner's competence grows

statement: Feedback is a necessary condition for learning and has long been recognized as the most important form of learner guidance.

Learning is promoted when learners are required to solve a sequence of varied, divergent problems; applying knowledge to only a single problem, or a non-divergent set of examples, is insufficient for learning a cognitive skill.
Learning is promoted when learners are given an opportunity to publicly demonstrate their newly acquired knowledge or skill.
Reflection aids learning when learners get to think about, discuss, and defend what they have newly learned.
Learners benefit when they can invent and explore their own personal ways of putting the new knowledge or skill to use.
The durable motivation for learners is learning itself and observing their own progress; glitz, animation, multimedia, and games have only a temporary motivational effect.

Integration culminates in creation: learning is promoted when learners modify, revise, synthesize, and refocus the new knowledge to make it their own and carry it into the world beyond the instructional environment.
Across a wide range of instructional-design theories and models, the same fundamental first principles recur even though the vocabulary used to state them differs between theorists.
Every instructional theory and model reviewed incorporates some of the first principles, but no reviewed theory or model includes all of them.
No instructional theory or model reviewed includes principles or prescriptions that are contrary to the first principles of instruction.
Reviewed theories differ mainly in vocabulary, implementation detail, and which principles they emphasize, not in the underlying first principles themselves.

Some reviewed theories include additional prescriptions not covered by the first principles (for example different kinds of intelligence, or collaboration), which represent areas for further investigation.
Even when learners have preferences for particular learning styles, effective instruction requires engaging them in the whole cycle of learning phases rather than only their preferred activities.

Demonstration through modeling has two forms: behavioral modeling, which shows how to perform the activities, and cognitive modeling, which articulates the reasoning a learner should use while performing them.
Scaffolding can be supplied in distinct ways: adjust task difficulty to fit the learner, restructure the task to compensate for missing prior knowledge, or offer alternative assessments.

For problem-solving learning, the problems posed should be interesting, relevant, and engaging, and ill-defined enough that some aspects are emergent and definable by the learners rather than fully specified in advance.
condition: for ill-structured or problem-solving learning domains

statement: Problem progression should start with tasks the learner already knows how to perform and gradually add difficulty until the learner is no longer able to perform alone.

In whole-task practice, just-in-time information presentation is used to support the recurrent (consistent) aspects of the task, while methods that promote elaboration support the non-recurrent (variable) aspects.

The design of information presentation (demonstration) should be subordinate to, and integrated with, the design of whole-task practice, so that demonstration and application form an integrated whole rather than distinct phases.
Collaboration is best treated as one way to implement activation and integration rather than as a separate first principle of instruction.

Effective instruction requires systematic analysis of intended outcomes, the environment in which learning will be used, and learner characteristics, together with evaluation and refinement throughout development.
A generic systematic instructional-design process can remain current because its analysis steps can incorporate emerging technologies, theories, discoveries, and procedures.
Use performance analysis and needs assessment to identify institutional needs and performance requirements that instruction must address.
Analyze the performance context to uncover constraints and technologies that should shape the instructional design.
Analyze current learners rather than relying on assumed learner characteristics.
Compare available delivery options so that media and teaching methods can be combined efficiently and cost-effectively.
Learn instructional design by applying each model step to a small, authentic instructional goal rather than by memorizing the model in isolation.
condition: When developing proficiency with the instructional-design process.

statement: Use evaluation criteria and rubrics at each design step to assess and revise intermediate instructional products.

Treat purposeful instruction as an interacting system of learners, instructors, materials, activities, delivery mechanisms, and learning and performance environments rather than improving components in isolation.
A change to one instructional-system component can alter other components and the resulting learning outcomes.
Investigate the complete instructional system before attributing weak outcomes to learner ability, motivation, background, or persistence.
condition: When learning outcomes fall below the desired level.

statement: An instructional system needs a defined goal, coordinated components, outcome feedback, and a mechanism for modifying the system when the goal is not reached.
Instructional systems are dynamic because they contain human components, so they require continuing monitoring and adjustment.
Integrate preparation, implementation, evaluation, and revision as parts of one instructional process.
Do not interpret the boxes and arrows in an instructional-design model as proof that real design work must proceed linearly.
exception: Concurrent or repeated cycles are often appropriate during planning, development, implementation, and revision.

statement: Use an instructional-design model as a scaffold while developing proficiency, then adapt its sequence and methods to the multidimensional problem at hand.
condition: When the designer has sufficient experience to judge adaptations responsibly.

statement: Express an instructional goal as the new information and skills learners should master by the end of instruction.
Derive candidate instructional goals from performance analysis, needs assessment, observed learning difficulties, job analysis, practical experience, or other documented requirements for instruction.
Analyze an instructional goal by identifying the steps used to perform it, the subordinate skills required for complete mastery, and the entry skills learners need before instruction.
Analyze learners, the learning setting, and the eventual performance setting in parallel with the instructional goal because these findings shape the instructional strategy.
Write each performance objective to specify the skill learners will demonstrate, the conditions of demonstration, and the criterion for successful performance.
Design assessments to measure the performances stated in the objectives and align the assessment demands with the type of skill being learned.
Select assessment formats that fit the outcome, including objective items, alternative assessments, live performances, attitude measures, or portfolios that document progress over time.
condition: When more than one assessment format could measure the objective.

statement: Derive the instructional strategy from the goal analysis, learner and context analyses, objectives, and assessments rather than choosing activities independently of prior design decisions.
Include preinstructional activities that focus attention and stimulate motivation in the instructional strategy.
Present new content with examples or demonstrations that make the target performance observable.
Provide active practice and informative feedback as integral parts of the instructional strategy.
Use follow-through activities both to assess learning and to connect newly learned skills to their real-world applications.
Base instructional-strategy decisions on relevant learning theory and research, media characteristics, the content, and learner characteristics.
Decide whether to develop original materials by considering the type of learning outcome, the availability of relevant existing materials, and available development resources.
condition: When choosing between original and existing instructional materials.

statement: Formatively evaluate a draft through one-to-one evaluation, small-group evaluation, and a field trial because each stage reveals different information for improvement.
condition: After a usable draft of the instruction exists.

statement: Interpret formative data by linking learner difficulties on objectives to specific deficiencies in the instruction.
condition: When revising after formative evaluation.

statement: Use formative evidence to reexamine the goal analysis, entry-skill and learner assumptions, objectives, assessment items, strategy, and materials, not merely to edit the presentation surface.
condition: When formative evaluation exposes learning difficulties.

statement: Revise earlier design decisions continuously as later analysis and evaluation produce new information, rather than treating revision as a single final phase.
Conduct summative evaluation only after instruction has undergone formative evaluation and sufficient revision to meet the designer's standards.
condition: When judging the absolute or comparative value of completed instruction.

statement: Use summative evaluation to determine whether instruction solved the problem it was designed to solve and whether learning transfers to the intended performance setting.
condition: When evaluating completed instruction.

statement: Make instructional design empirical and repeatable by collecting performance data, identifying components that fail, and revising them until the instruction meets its goal.
Document lessons from evaluated instruction so they can guide adaptation for different learners, contexts, audience sizes, and media.
condition: When instruction is expected to be reused or adapted.

statement: Define precisely what learners should know or do after instruction because vague outcomes make subsequent planning and implementation unclear.
Align desired outcomes, learner characteristics, instructional activities, and assessments when planning standards-based instruction.
condition: When instruction must satisfy defined standards or accountability requirements.

statement: Select instructional activities that directly create the conditions needed for the targeted knowledge and skills; activities should not be only loosely related to the outcome.
Identify both prerequisite capabilities learners need before instruction and enabling capabilities they must acquire during instruction.
Use assessments that measure the capabilities described in the objectives, then use the results to improve the next delivery of the instruction.
Design for the environment in which learners will use the new capability so that instruction supports transfer to real performance.
Choose instructor-led, mediated, individual, or group delivery within the design process according to the learning problem rather than assuming a delivery mode in advance.
Instructional analysis and strategy appear to influence success more strongly than delivery mode alone.
condition: Across delivery modes that can support the required instruction.

statement: Distinguish the process of designing instruction from decisions about how the resulting instruction will be delivered.
Use multidisciplinary design teams when specialist expertise is needed, and manage interpersonal collaboration because the product depends on integrating those specialties.
condition: When a project requires content, technology, evaluation, and management expertise that one designer does not possess.

statement: A practitioner with limited planning time can apply the full design process to a small amount of instruction or selectively use relevant steps for other needs.
condition: When day-to-day instructional responsibilities make full-detail design infeasible for every lesson.

statement: Master the complete design model before selecting only fragments of it, because full-model experience supports sound judgment about which parts fit a particular need.
condition: When a practitioner intends to tailor or abbreviate the process.

statement: Use examples from multiple contexts to practice recognizing the abstract design process independently of the example subject matter.
condition: When teaching or learning instructional-design transfer.

statement: Generic instructional-design practices can support different learning-theory orientations when expert designers translate their theoretical commitments into decisions about goals, learners, and learning environments.
condition: When the practices are applied by designers capable of making theoretically coherent adaptations.

statement: Select and refine an instructional goal by analyzing the problem and need, their context, available design and development resources, and the clarity of the proposed goal.
Confirm that a performance problem can be addressed efficiently through instruction before treating it as an instructional goal.
condition: When converting an organizational or social need into a design project.
exception: Do not prescribe instruction when the primary cause is non-instructional.

statement: Distinguish broad organizational or social outcomes from instructional goals; define an instructional goal only when people need new capabilities to contribute to the broader outcome.
Do not accept a predefined content outline as sufficient evidence of an instructional need without checking whether the content remains relevant and adequate to the actual performance problem.
condition: When goals originate in standards, policies, manuals, or existing curricula.

statement: Check for non-instructional causes such as weak accountability, poor incentives, obsolete tools, or organizational culture before adding training.
condition: When a gap in desired performance has been identified.

statement: Do not let a subject-matter expert define instruction merely by replicating the expert's own knowledge or by using unobservable outcomes such as knowing and understanding.
condition: When an expert is asked to originate instructional goals.

statement: Confirm or redirect an administratively mandated training goal through analysis and negotiation when the mandate leaves room to do so.
condition: When an authority has prescribed training without demonstrating that the proposed goal addresses the performance need.
exception: A legal, contractual, or safety requirement may constitute a valid nonnegotiable mandate.

statement: Begin performance improvement without presuming what people must learn, what an instructional package must contain, or whether instruction is needed at all.
condition: When responding to an organizational performance problem or opportunity.

statement: Combine performance analysis with content review, subject-matter consultation, and mandate review when those sources provide relevant evidence; the goal-identification approaches are not mutually exclusive.
Conduct front-end analysis before instructional design to validate instructional needs and compare instructional and non-instructional ways of meeting them.
condition: Before committing resources to the design of instruction.

statement: Use performance analysis to define a performance problem, observe it, gather and interpret evidence about its causes, and identify possible corrective actions.
Make the training-versus-nontraining decision an explicit result of performance analysis, not an assumption built into the analysis request.
Approach performance analysis with open-mindedness, objectivity, causal inquiry, multiple perspectives, and willingness to revise conclusions when compelling evidence appears.
Suspend judgment about a preferred solution until pertinent evidence and contrary views have received a fair hearing.
condition: During performance analysis.

statement: Internal instructional designers need to cultivate deliberate critical-thinking habits because organizational membership can make impartial performance analysis more difficult.
condition: When analyzing a problem inside one's own organization.

statement: Relate the initially voiced problem to a core organizational outcome before evaluating proposed interventions.
condition: When framing a performance analysis.

statement: Verify an operational need by comparing an established organizational target with actual outcome data.
condition: When an operational goal and measurable actual performance are available.

statement: Verify a job-performance need by comparing relevant performance standards with employees' actual performance.
condition: When job performance is plausibly linked to the operational outcome.

statement: Separate external constraints outside local management's control from internal factors that local management can change.
condition: When identifying causes of a verified performance gap.

statement: Supplement performance statistics with direct observation, record inspection, and input from people who work inside the problem context.
condition: When diagnosing the causes of a performance problem.

statement: A performance analysis should produce a clear account of the organizational result gap, desired and actual employee performance, evidence about causes, and candidate cost-effective solutions.
Compare the cost of instruction with alternative interventions because instruction can be one of the more expensive ways to address a performance problem.
condition: When selecting among plausible performance solutions.

statement: Prefer a coordinated set of workflow, tool, staffing, job-aid, and training changes when analysis shows that multiple system factors contribute to the gap.
condition: When no single cause accounts for the performance problem.

statement: Evaluate proposed performance interventions after implementation before escalating to a more expensive or permanent solution.
condition: When lower-cost interventions can be tried without unacceptable risk.

statement: Do not prescribe instructor retraining when practitioners already possess the needed capability but schedules, tools, or other contextual constraints prevent them from applying it.
condition: When analysis shows a performance opportunity but no knowledge or skill deficit.

statement: Proceed to needs assessment and instructional design only for the portion of a performance solution that requires new or refreshed skills.
condition: When performance analysis identifies instruction as all or part of the solution.

statement: Define a need as the measurable discrepancy between a desired status and the corresponding actual status.
Operationalize both the desired standard and actual performance precisely before claiming that a need exists.
Do not initiate change or new instruction when actual performance meets or exceeds the desired standard.
condition: When a valid comparison shows no performance discrepancy.

statement: Start needs assessment with gaps in organizational results rather than with presumed deficiencies in an internal process such as teacher knowledge.
condition: When deciding how to spend organizational resources on performance improvement.

statement: A defensible training-needs assessment establishes a realistic performance standard, measures current performance with multiple relevant data sources, and describes the resulting capability gap.
condition: After performance analysis identifies training as a plausible intervention.

statement: Use the training-needs assessment to state both a job-performance standard for tracking intervention success and an instructional goal for starting design.
condition: When the identified discrepancy includes a knowledge or skill gap.

statement: An interim instructional goal may appropriately address only part of the gap between actual and desired performance.
condition: When closing the entire gap in one intervention is not appropriate or feasible.

statement: Avoid unnecessary instruction because it consumes resources, burdens learners with pointless activity, and can damage stakeholder attitudes toward training.
Triangulate training-need evidence through interviews, focus groups, direct observation, and performance data from the actual setting rather than relying mainly on surveys.
condition: When documenting a training need.

statement: Use job analysis to gather, analyze, and synthesize current descriptions of what people actually do in a job.
condition: When job performance must inform training, support, staffing, evaluation, or job redesign.

statement: Build an initial task inventory from observation of experienced performers and from performers' own accounts of their work, then group related tasks into duties.
condition: During job analysis.

statement: Have subject-matter experts and job incumbents verify that proposed tasks are genuinely part of the job before prioritizing them.
condition: After creating an initial task inventory.

statement: Prioritize job tasks using evidence about whether they are performed, their frequency and time share, their criticality to job success, and their difficulty.
condition: When selecting tasks for further analysis or training investment.

statement: Pilot test a task-analysis survey and revise it before distributing it to a representative sample of job holders.
condition: When survey data will be used to prioritize tasks.

statement: Reserve detailed task analysis for high-priority or otherwise critical tasks because the work is complex, labor-intensive, and time-consuming.
condition: When detailed task decomposition is not required for every job task.

statement: For each task selected for detailed analysis, identify its component elements, relationships among elements, tools and performance conditions, and standards for success.

Use performance analysis to establish the broad problem, needs assessment to isolate the performance deficiency, and job or task analysis to refine the learner performance and context before finalizing the instructional goal.
condition: When the project begins with an organizational performance problem.

statement: Replace vague goal terms about internal states with observable behaviors that would demonstrate successful goal achievement.
condition: When a goal uses terms such as awareness, appreciation, knowing, or sensing without observable performance.

statement: Clarify a broad goal by generating candidate demonstration behaviors, selecting those that best represent achievement, incorporating them into the goal, and checking that the revised performance still satisfies the original intent.
condition: When the initial goal is meaningful but not operationally specific.
