statement: Involve multiple knowledgeable stakeholders in clarifying a goal to expose the range of implied behaviors and reach consensus on what successful performance means.
condition: When a broad goal permits materially different interpretations.

statement: A complete instructional-goal statement identifies the learners, the performance they will demonstrate, the performance context, and the tools available in that context.
Verify that a real and sufficiently large target audience exists and that representative learners will be available for developmental tryouts.
condition: Before finalizing an instructional project.

statement: Iteratively reevaluate the instructional goal as front-end, learner, and context analyses reveal new information.
Evaluate a candidate instructional goal for logical connection to a documented organizational need, feasibility in its context, and shared clarity among stakeholders.
condition: Before committing to detailed instructional analysis.

statement: Do not make a large development investment in content likely to become obsolete soon unless a critical short-term need justifies the cost.
condition: When evaluating content stability and development feasibility.
exception: A sufficiently critical short-term need can justify developing instruction for unstable content.

statement: Assess whether the project has sufficient subject expertise, design and technology personnel, time, budget, delivery capacity, and access to representative learners.
condition: When determining whether an instructional goal is feasible.

statement: Choose the best strategy for mastering the required skills before setting instructional duration, while recognizing that early learning-time estimates are uncertain.
condition: When schedule constraints are being negotiated.

statement: Use results from repeated tryouts to improve estimates of the time learners require to achieve instructional goals.
condition: After empirical learning-time data become available.

statement: Retain the full set of positive and negative demonstration behaviors generated during goal clarification because it can inform later instructional analysis even when only a subset appears in the final goal.
condition: When a broad goal has been operationalized through behavioral brainstorming.

statement: Continue refining a goal until the behaviors expected within each broad performance category are sufficiently specific for consistent interpretation.
condition: When an initial restatement remains open to materially different interpretations.

statement: Account for the real performance context while clarifying the goal because that context has direct implications for instructional strategy.
Check existing courses, internships, and other learning opportunities before adding new instruction so the organization neither duplicates coverage nor assumes a capability is taught when it is not.
condition: When a curriculum-level capability gap is reported.

statement: Triangulate curriculum needs using evidence from recent learners, current learners, faculty, and external practitioners who employ graduates.
condition: When evaluating whether a professional program develops a needed capability.

statement: Match the size and format of an instructional intervention to the importance and scope of the verified capability gap rather than defaulting to a full-length course.
condition: When deciding how much curriculum to allocate to a goal.

statement: An acceptable instructional goal is a clear general learner outcome, grounded in an identified problem and needs assessment, that instruction can achieve more effectively than available non-instructional alternatives.
Describe meaningful variation in learners' prior education, progress through a curriculum, prior experience, existing capability, and motivation before designing instruction.
condition: When the target group is heterogeneous.

statement: Use familiar and transparent subject matter when teaching an unfamiliar design process so learners can attend to the process rather than simultaneously mastering new content.
condition: When examples are intended to teach transferable design concepts.

statement: State an instructional goal in terms of what learners will do, not in terms of what an institution or instructor will provide or assign.
Use observable and measurable learner behavior in the goal and state any material limitations on that behavior.
Ask colleagues and intended learners to interpret a draft goal, then revise it if their understanding of the required performance differs from the designer's intent.
condition: When checking goal clarity.

statement: When a goal exceeds the available instructional time, divide it into logical major performances and select the part with the best fit to the need and constraints.
condition: When the complete goal cannot reasonably be taught in the available time.

statement: When a goal is too small for the available instructional period, examine related entry skills and logical next skills to expand the scope coherently.
condition: When additional instruction is warranted and time is available beyond the current goal.

statement: Do not begin detailed goal analysis until the instructional goal is behaviorally clear and plausibly fits the intended instructional duration.
Begin goal analysis only after the instructional goal clearly states what learners will be able to do.
Classify the goal as an intellectual skill, psychomotor skill, attitude, or verbal-information outcome before selecting an analysis technique.
For intellectual and psychomotor goals, identify the major performance steps and arrange them in the most efficient executable order.
condition: When the goal performance consists of an ordered procedure.

statement: Write each major goal-analysis step so it includes both the action performed and the relevant content.
For verbal-information goals, identify major information clusters and organize them by an inherent relationship such as chronology, part-to-whole, simple-to-complex, or familiar-to-unfamiliar.
Treat the first goal-analysis diagram as a draft and evaluate it for steps that are extraneous, incorrectly sized, or misplaced in the sequence.
condition: After producing an initial goal analysis.

statement: Identify subordinate skills that must be learned because they enable or positively transfer to higher-level performance.
condition: When decomposing the capabilities needed to achieve a goal.

statement: Classify a goal as an intellectual skill when learners must manipulate symbolic information or perform a cognitive operation on previously unencountered examples.
Differentiate intellectual-skill demands among discriminating examples, classifying concepts, applying rules, and solving problems because these levels imply different prerequisite structures.
condition: When analyzing an intellectual-skill goal.

statement: Treat a concept as mastered only when the learner can classify new examples using defining characteristics, not merely recall a label or familiar instance.
condition: When specifying or assessing concept learning.

statement: Treat rule application as a performance requiring learners to use the component concepts and relationships on varied inputs.
condition: When specifying or assessing rule learning.

statement: Distinguish well-structured problems with defined data, processes, and answer criteria from ill-structured problems with missing information, multiple viable processes, and no single correct solution.
Consider elevating an intellectual-skill goal to a higher level when learners are capable of more transferable concept, rule, or problem-solving performance.
condition: When reviewing whether a proposed goal is appropriately challenging and useful.

statement: Classify a goal as psychomotor when success depends on learning and skillfully executing a nontrivial physical action, even if substantial cognition accompanies it.
exception: Trivial physical manipulation does not make an otherwise cognitive task psychomotor.

statement: Classify a goal as attitudinal when instruction is intended to influence whether learners choose a particular course of action.
Evaluate an attitude through the observable intellectual, physical, or verbal behavior that expresses the learner's choice, while recognizing that the disposition may emerge only over time.
condition: When assessing an attitudinal goal.

statement: Do not infer that learners will choose a behavior merely because they know how to perform it.
condition: When a goal includes ethical, social, health, or other discretionary action.

statement: Classify a goal as verbal information when learners need to recall a specific response to a specific prompt without manipulating the information to solve or apply a rule.
Analyze cognitive strategies that organize and regulate thinking as high-level intellectual skills similar to ill-structured problem solving.
condition: Within this instructional-analysis framework.

statement: Narrow an instructional goal when a precise analysis of what must be learned is needed, because smaller goals are generally easier to analyze accurately.
condition: When the original goal is too broad for useful performance decomposition.

statement: Analyze an intellectual or psychomotor goal by describing exactly what a competent performer does from the start of the goal through completion.
Infer and represent essential mental operations in an intellectual-skill analysis even when they cannot be observed directly.
condition: When covert cognition determines the performer's observable actions or results.

statement: When performance branches after a decision, identify both the criteria for making the decision and every alternative procedure learners may need to execute.
condition: When different decision outcomes lead to different next actions.

statement: Choose goal-analysis step size according to learners' age, experience, and learning proficiency; less prepared learners generally require smaller steps.
condition: When deciding how much performance to combine in one analysis step.

statement: Analyze learners and contexts alongside the goal so the performance decomposition is realistic for the intended population.
State every goal-analysis step with an action verb and an observable outcome or product.
When reading or listening is part of performance, specify what learners must identify, produce, or otherwise demonstrate from what they receive.
condition: When an input activity has no directly observable result by itself.

statement: Represent a decision as a branch only when at least two different subsequent skills or procedures depend on its outcome.
condition: When diagramming a goal analysis.
exception: A selection followed by the same next action does not require a decision branch.

statement: Teach a decision criterion as a subordinate skill only when intended learners are not already able to apply it reliably.
condition: When a decision point depends on a discrimination or judgment.
exception: If learners already possess the decision skill, it can be stated as an expected action without new instruction.

statement: Use arrows and branch labels to make the actual flow, optional paths, and possible returns to earlier steps unambiguous; step numbers alone do not necessarily express execution order.
condition: When representing a nontrivial goal-analysis flow.

statement: As a rough diagnostic, expect about five to fifteen major steps for one to two hours of instruction; substantially fewer may be underspecified and substantially more may indicate excessive detail or an overlarge goal.
condition: When reviewing the granularity of an initial goal analysis.
exception: The range is only a general heuristic and should yield to learner and task evidence.

statement: Represent a verbal-information goal as major topic clusters without procedural arrows because recall does not itself imply a performance sequence.
condition: When the goal requires recall rather than rule application or problem solving.

statement: For an attitudinal goal, analyze the observable behavior expressing the choice using the method appropriate to that behavior's intellectual, psychomotor, or verbal-information domain.
Use the intended assessment as a prompt for discovering what learners must do to perform the goal.
condition: When the major performance steps are difficult to identify.

statement: Perform the goal yourself and record both actions and decisions as evidence for an initial goal analysis.
condition: When the designer can competently perform the goal.

statement: Compare accounts from multiple competent performers because differences can reveal valid alternative methods or missing steps.
condition: When validating a goal analysis.

statement: Triangulate goal-analysis evidence through direct observation, expert interviews, job incumbents and supervisors, and authoritative manuals or procedures.
condition: When a defensible performance decomposition is needed.

statement: Question the authority of informal how-to resources before using them as evidence for a goal analysis.
condition: When consulting publicly posted demonstrations or instructions.

statement: Observe expert performance in the jobsite and consult job-performance standards because performance-context evidence is directly relevant to goal analysis.
condition: For professional or technical training.

statement: Use rapid prototyping when instruction and a new product must be developed concurrently and stable detailed performance documentation is not yet available.
condition: When delaying product introduction for a complete conventional analysis would impose an unacceptable time-to-market cost.

statement: Do not omit performance steps merely because they seem obvious to a subject-matter expert; evaluate their difficulty from the intended learner's perspective.
condition: When expert familiarity makes a task appear deceptively simple.

statement: List the steps learners use to perform the goal, not the explanations and activities an instructor would use to teach it.
condition: During goal analysis.

statement: Exclude background, topics, and skills that are valued by the designer or expert but are not required to perform the goal.
condition: When reviewing a goal analysis for relevance.

statement: Review a goal analysis for clear content, comparable learner-appropriate step sizes, explicit relationships and sequence, inclusion of only main performance steps, and absence of redundancy.
condition: Before using the analysis as the foundation for subordinate-skill analysis.

statement: Ensure that all main steps together constitute complete goal performance and that no individual main step is equivalent to the whole goal.
condition: When checking the scope of a goal-analysis decomposition.

statement: Choose a learning-outcome taxonomy for the practical guidance it provides about analysis, subordinate skills, and instructional strategy, not merely for its familiarity.
condition: When selecting a taxonomy for instructional design.

statement: Treat mappings between broad cognitive taxonomies and specific learning types as approximate because many cognitive categories combine several kinds of skill.
condition: When translating a goal between Bloom-style and Gagné-style classifications.

statement: Accept modest variation in the wording and decomposition of a goal analysis when alternatives represent the same complete performance accurately.
condition: When comparing independently produced analyses of the same goal.
exception: Differences that omit, add, or reorder essential performance cannot be dismissed as wording variation.

statement: Use an explicit organizing scheme for verbal information when the content has no natural chronology, such as part-to-whole or a spatial progression.
condition: When verbal-information clusters have no inherent execution order.

statement: Provide repeated physical practice for psychomotor goals so learners can calibrate the translation of mental plans into accurate movement.
condition: When mastery depends on force, timing, coordination, or other physical calibration.

statement: Use the product from each major performance step as a sequencing clue when it becomes input to a subsequent step.
condition: When determining the natural flow of a goal analysis.

statement: Use the completed goal analysis as the framework for identifying the subordinate capabilities needed for each major step.
condition: After the major steps and their relationships are validated.

statement: Treat purposeful instruction as an interacting system of learners, instructors, materials, activities, delivery mechanisms, and learning and performance environments rather than optimizing isolated parts.
A change to one instructional component can alter other components and the resulting learning outcomes.
Technology and delivery-system investments may fail to improve learning when the design of the learning experience and other instructional components are neglected.
condition: When technology is introduced without a corresponding systems analysis of instruction.

statement: An instructional system should have a defined learning goal, mutually dependent components, an outcome-feedback mechanism, and a revision process that continues until performance reaches the goal.
Instructional systems involving human characteristics are dynamic and require continuing monitoring and adjustment.
condition: When learner or instructor characteristics materially affect system performance.

statement: Use assessment results as feedback about the whole instructional system and revise implicated components when achievement is unsatisfactory.
condition: When measured achievement falls below the intended learning outcomes.

statement: Evaluate the contribution of every instructional component instead of attributing success or failure to a single component such as learner motivation or ability.
Design preparation, implementation, evaluation, and revision as one integrated process in which results determine whether and how the instruction changes.
Instructional-design models are simplified representations of practice and should not be mistaken for literal descriptions of how design work always proceeds.
Although model diagrams may appear linear, experienced instructional-design work commonly uses iterative, concurrent, or repeated cycles of planning, development, implementation, and revision.
exception: A novice may initially follow the represented sequence more literally as a learning scaffold.

statement: Use an instructional-design model as a scaffold while learning, then adapt sequence, shortcuts, and solution strategies as experience supports sound contextual judgment.
condition: When the designer has enough expertise to understand the consequences of departing from the model.

statement: Connect analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation so each step receives relevant prior outputs and supplies information needed by subsequent work and system improvement.
Express an instructional goal as the new information and skills learners should master by the end of instruction.

Derive instructional goals from relevant performance analysis, needs assessment, observed learning difficulties, expert job analysis, practical experience, or other requirements rather than assuming a solution in advance.
Analyze a goal by identifying the steps used to perform it, the subordinate skills needed for mastery, and the entry knowledge, skills, and attitudes learners need before instruction.
Analyze learners, the learning setting, and the eventual performance setting in parallel with the instructional goal because their characteristics shape later strategy decisions.
Write performance objectives from the instructional analysis and entry-skill description, specifying the skill, the conditions of demonstration, and the criteria for successful performance.
Design assessment tasks to be parallel with the objectives and to measure the same kind of skill the objectives describe.
Select assessment forms according to the target performance, using objective items, alternative assessments, live performance, attitude measures, or portfolios as appropriate.
condition: When different learning outcomes require different forms of evidence.

statement: Base the instructional strategy on the instructional goal, analyses, objectives, and assessments rather than selecting activities independently.

An instructional strategy should address motivation and attention, content presentation with examples or demonstrations, active practice with feedback, assessment, and connection of learning to real-world use.
Adapt the strategy to learning theory and research, content, learner characteristics, and the capabilities of the selected media, then use it to plan logistics, management, materials, and activities.
Choose between developing original instruction and selecting existing materials based on the learning outcomes, the relevance of available materials, and available development resources.
Conduct formative evaluation on a draft to identify instructional problems and improvement opportunities before treating the instruction as complete.
condition: After a usable draft of the instruction exists.

statement: Use one-to-one evaluation, small-group evaluation, and field trials because each produces a different kind of information for improving instruction.
condition: When evaluating a developed instructional product or adapting the same techniques to existing materials or classroom instruction.

statement: Interpret formative data by linking learner difficulties on objectives to specific deficiencies in the instruction.
condition: When formative evidence shows difficulty achieving an objective.

statement: Use formative evidence to reexamine the goal, instructional analysis, assumed entry skills and learner characteristics, objectives, test items, strategy, and materials—not merely to edit surface features of the instruction.
condition: When the evidence calls underlying assumptions or alignments into question.

statement: Treat revision as continuous reassessment informed by later design and evaluation work rather than as a single final step.
Conduct summative evaluation only after formative evaluation and sufficient revision have brought the instruction to the designer's standards.
condition: When judging the absolute or relative value of completed instruction.

statement: An evaluator independent of the original designer may be better positioned to conduct summative evaluation of instructional value.
condition: When independence is important to the summative judgment.

statement: Summative evaluation should test whether instruction solved the problem it targeted and whether learning transfers to the intended performance setting or to materially different learner contexts.
condition: When effectiveness beyond the original training event or audience matters.

statement: Preserve the model's logical input-output sequence for novice designers while allowing iterative evaluation and revision at every step.
condition: When designers are initially learning the discipline.
exception: Experienced designers may adapt the model to project resources and constraints.

statement: Systematic design is empirically testable and replicable because it collects performance data, identifies failures, and revises instruction until it meets its objective.
Lessons from evaluated and revised instruction can often guide adaptation across learner populations, settings, audience sizes, and media.
condition: When the original instruction has been systematically developed and evaluated.

statement: State intended learner outcomes precisely because ambiguous outcomes make subsequent planning, implementation, and evaluation unclear.
Maintain tight alignment among learning outcomes, learner characteristics, instructional activities, and assessments.
Identify both prerequisite capabilities needed to begin instruction and enabling capabilities that must be acquired during it.
Delivery mode alone is usually less determinative of instructional success than the quality of analysis and the instructional strategy.
condition: Across otherwise viable instructional media and groupings.

statement: Treat instructional medium, instructor involvement, and individual-versus-group delivery as design decisions, not predetermined assumptions.
condition: When selecting the most effective feasible delivery approach.

statement: A multidisciplinary instructional-design team can combine content, technology, evaluation, and management expertise to produce work no individual specialist could produce alone.
condition: When the project scope benefits from multiple specialties.

statement: Learn the full systematic process before selectively applying only parts of it, because mastery supplies the judgment needed to choose appropriate components for constrained instructional work.
condition: When day-to-day responsibilities make full application impractical.

statement: Define an instructional goal as a clear capability learners will demonstrate as a result of instruction.
Select and refine an instructional goal by examining the problem and need, their context, available design and development resources, and the clarity of the goal statement.
An incorrectly identified instructional goal can yield polished instruction that fails to address any real organizational or learner need.
Distinguish broad social or organizational outcomes from instructional goals; create an instructional goal only when achieving the broader outcome requires people to acquire new capabilities.
condition: When a broader institutional outcome is the starting concern.

statement: Do not infer that a performance problem is a content deficit merely because a curriculum, policy, or manual specifies content to teach.
condition: When using an existing content outline to identify a goal.

statement: Validate content standards against current organizational and social needs because standards may be outdated or may never have been adequate solutions.
condition: When standards or frameworks are used as the basis for instruction.

statement: Check noninstructional causes such as accountability, incentives, tools, and organizational culture before prescribing more instruction.
condition: When a performance problem is initially framed as a knowledge or content gap.

statement: Subject-matter experts may overemphasize transmitting what they know and formulate vague goals about knowing or understanding rather than observable learner performance.
condition: When experts identify goals chiefly by reflecting on their own learning and expertise.

statement: Confirm or redirect administratively mandated training goals through analysis and negotiation when latitude exists.
condition: When an authority mandates training without demonstrated prior analysis.
exception: A goal mandated by law, contract, or safety requirements may be valid by definition and leave little or no latitude for redirection.

statement: Begin performance-improvement work without presuming what people must learn, what an instructional package must contain, or whether instruction is needed at all.
condition: When responding to an organizational problem or opportunity.

statement: Combine performance analysis with review of content outlines, subject-matter expertise, and genuine mandates when each supplies relevant evidence.
Conduct front-end analysis before designing instruction to validate instructional needs and compare alternative ways to meet them.
A robust front-end analysis may include performance analysis, needs assessment, job analysis, and explicit evaluation of the proposed instructional goal.
condition: When project scale and risk warrant the relevant analyses.
exception: A bounded novice design exercise may use a reduced front-end process.

statement: Analyze a performance problem through careful definition, observation, data gathering, and interpretation before deciding whether the remedy is training or an operational change.

Effective performance analysis requires open-mindedness, objectivity, causal inquiry, multiple perspectives, fair treatment of contrary evidence, suspended judgment, and willingness to revise conclusions.
Internal performance analysts must deliberately cultivate critical distance because organizational membership makes objective analysis and contrary conclusions harder.
condition: When the analyst belongs to the organization experiencing the problem.

statement: Trace a voiced problem to a core organizational outcome, its operational goals, actual results, job-performance standards, controllable and uncontrollable contributing factors, and candidate solutions.
condition: When structuring a performance relationship analysis.

statement: Use operational records, performance statistics, direct observation, work artifacts, and input from affected workers to understand a performance problem.
condition: When the problem has multiple possible contributors.

statement: The output of performance analysis should state the organizational result gap, desired and actual employee performance, evidence about causes, and feasible cost-effective solutions.
Prefer a coordinated multicomponent remedy when analysis shows that process, tools, staffing, information routing, and skill gaps jointly cause the performance problem.
condition: When evidence identifies several interacting causes.

statement: Include cost in solution selection because instruction is often more expensive than viable noninstructional alternatives.
condition: When several solutions could address the verified cause.

statement: Allow implemented remedies enough time for evaluation before escalating to additional staffing or training, while using temporary mitigation if service risk requires it.
condition: When the initial remedies can be tested without unacceptable operational harm.

statement: Frame a performance problem as a measurable gap between a core organizational outcome's desired and actual status, then trace that gap to job-performance standards and contributing factors.
condition: When applying a performance relationship map.

statement: Separate external constraints outside local control from internal factors that local management can change before selecting remedies.
condition: When diagnosing contributors to an operational or job-performance gap.

statement: Map each verified cause to a corresponding remedy, which may include workflow redesign, logistics changes, performance support, training, or staffing.
condition: When analysis reveals multiple controllable contributors.

statement: Verify that an external assessment validly represents the target standards before treating low scores as evidence of a learner-performance gap.
condition: When test results initiate a performance analysis.

statement: Observe the actual learning setting and follow-up activities to determine whether learners receive enough time, practice, and application opportunities to meet the assessed standard.
condition: When poor assessment performance might reflect instructional implementation rather than staff knowledge.

statement: Consult the practitioners closest to a performance problem to distinguish capability gaps from schedule, resource, workflow, or implementation constraints.
Staff training will not correct poor learner outcomes when staff already possess the required knowledge and pedagogy but lack time or organizational support to apply them.
condition: When implementation constraints, rather than staff capability, cause the performance gap.

statement: Integrate targeted instruction with problem scenarios, guidance, embedded assessment, remediation, and enrichment when learners must move from recall to application.
condition: When the target standard requires applying information or concepts to solve problems.

statement: Define a need as the measurable discrepancy between an established desired status and observed actual status.
Do not interpret a report of current conditions as a need until a desired standard and a quantified actual level make the discrepancy explicit.
condition: When stakeholders initially describe only what is happening now.

statement: If actual performance meets or exceeds the desired standard, there is no discrepancy and no need for new instruction on that basis.
condition: When desired and actual status have been measured comparably.

statement: After performance analysis identifies training as a viable remedy, conduct a learning-needs assessment to set realistic performance standards, measure current performance, and specify the capability gap.
condition: When instruction is one of the selected solutions.

statement: Use subject-matter expertise, operational records, observation, interviews, and direct assessment together to establish desired and actual performance for a learning-needs assessment.
Translate a verified learning need into both an operational performance standard for tracking results and an instructional goal describing learner performance, context, tools, and independence.
An interim instructional goal that closes only part of a performance gap may be appropriate when full closure is not yet feasible.
condition: When constraints make the entire desired-performance gap an unrealistic initial target.

statement: Start needs assessment from gaps in organizational or learner results rather than from an assumed deficit in an internal process such as teacher competence.
Unnecessary instruction wastes development resources and can create negative attitudes among learners and managers when it does not solve a real problem.
Supplement surveys with interviews, focus groups, direct observation, stakeholder collaboration, and performance data gathered in the setting where training is considered.
condition: When identifying and documenting training needs.

statement: Use job analysis to gather, analyze, and synthesize current descriptions of what people actually do as a baseline for job redesign, performance support, and training decisions.
condition: When roles or technologies are changing or job performance must be clarified.

statement: Build an initial job-task inventory from observation of experienced workers and self-reports by job incumbents, then group related tasks into duties.
condition: When beginning a job analysis.

statement: Have experts and job holders verify whether listed tasks belong to the job before using the inventory to set priorities.
condition: After an initial task inventory has been assembled.

statement: Prioritize job tasks using evidence about whether incumbents perform them, their frequency and time demand, their criticality to success, and their difficulty.
condition: When deciding which tasks deserve deeper review or training resources.

statement: Reserve detailed task analysis for high-priority or critical work because decomposing tasks is labor-intensive and time-consuming.
condition: When detailed analysis is needed for job redesign or critical training.

statement: For each task selected for analysis, identify its component elements, relationships among elements, tools and conditions, and standards for successful performance.
Derive instructional goals through a narrowing chain from organizational performance analysis to specific needs assessment and, where necessary, curriculum, job, or task analysis.

Clarify a vague goal by listing observable behaviors that would demonstrate achievement, selecting the best indicators, rewriting the goal around them, and checking that the behaviors collectively satisfy the original intent.
condition: When a goal uses internal-state terms such as awareness, appreciation, or understanding without observable performance.

statement: Use several knowledgeable contributors to surface alternative interpretations of a broad goal and reach consensus on the behaviors that count as success.
condition: When an important goal is meaningful but initially underspecified.

statement: A complete instructional goal should identify the learners, the capability they will demonstrate, the performance context, and the tools available in that context.
Confirm that a real target audience exists and characterize its current skills, abilities, and motivation before committing to instructional development.
condition: When clarifying an instructional goal and project feasibility.

statement: Analyze whether performance occurs independently or collaboratively, under supervision or in the field, and with memory, software, job aids, or other tools because these conditions determine which skills instruction must include.
condition: When defining the performance context.

statement: Account explicitly for political influence, vested interests, economics, and technical or academic considerations when evaluating a proposed instructional goal.
condition: When goal selection occurs in a real organizational context.

statement: Treat front-end analysis as iterative formative evaluation: revise the goal whenever new information changes understanding of the problem, learners, or context.
Approve an instructional goal only when it is congruent with organizational needs, feasible in its development and delivery context, and clear to stakeholders.
Link a proposed instructional goal persuasively to a documented performance gap or organizational opportunity and explain how use of the new capability will change that result.
condition: When seeking client or decision-maker support.

statement: Do not invest in extensive instructional development for rapidly expiring content unless a critical short-term need justifies the cost.
condition: When content is likely to become obsolete soon.
exception: A sufficiently critical short-term need may warrant the investment.

statement: Ensure the design team has enough content expertise, instructional-design capability, technology support, and delivery personnel for the proposed goal.
condition: When assessing project feasibility.

statement: Novice designers should initially work in a familiar subject area so they can learn the design process without simultaneously mastering unfamiliar content.
condition: When a learner is first acquiring instructional-design skills.
exception: Experienced designers may work effectively in unfamiliar domains through collaboration and substantial content learning.

statement: Treat teamwork and willingness to learn the content as core designer capabilities when the design domain is initially unfamiliar.
condition: When instructional designers depend on subject and technology specialists.

statement: Assess feasibility using content stability, expertise, staffing, design and delivery time, budget, and access to enough target learners.
condition: Before finalizing an instructional goal.

statement: Development time and learner mastery time are difficult to predict accurately because both depend on many project and learner factors.
Select the best feasible strategy for mastery before forcing content into an arbitrary duration, then refine learning-time estimates from instructional tryouts.
condition: When scheduling instruction and estimating its duration.
exception: Hard organizational limits may still require shortening or lengthening the instruction.

statement: Secure access to representative learners for rough-draft tryouts because formative learner evidence is required to implement the full systematic design process.
condition: During instructional development.
exception: If representative learners are unavailable, the designer must alter the process and reconsider whether the stated need and project are viable.

statement: Check that goal approval rests on a clearly identified problem, a documented performance gap, a plausible instructional solution, and acceptance by those authorizing the work.
condition: When evaluating congruence with organizational needs.

statement: Evaluate goal clarity by checking that it identifies observable learner action, content, intended learners, performance context, and available performance tools.
Replace internal-state wording in a fuzzy goal with observable action and decompose broad performance categories into interpretable stages or components.
condition: When a goal describes knowing, valuing, or another unobservable state.

statement: Define ambiguous qualities by generating both positive and negative behavioral examples for each stage of the target performance.
condition: When qualities such as friendly, courteous, effective, or professional remain open to interpretation.

statement: Ask organizational stakeholders to add, remove, and clarify candidate behaviors before selecting those that best represent the goal.
condition: When operationalizing a broad or value-laden goal.

statement: Retain the full set of generated behaviors as input to later instructional analysis even when the concise goal statement uses only the most representative subset.
condition: After clarifying a fuzzy goal.

statement: Continue clarifying a goal until its categories specify actual behaviors sufficiently for different designers or instructors to interpret success consistently.
condition: When an initial rewrite still leaves room for materially different interpretations.

statement: Use the intended performance context to shape instructional strategy, particularly whether learners will have communication aids, supervision, colleagues, or repeated practice available.
Review existing curricula, courses, internships, and prior commitments before adding instruction so the solution fills a real gap without needless duplication.
condition: When a curriculum-level capability gap is reported.

statement: Corroborate a curriculum need using evidence from graduates, current learners, faculty, and employers or other external constituents.
condition: When determining whether a capability is both missing and important.

statement: Match instructional scope to the verified need; a bounded capability gap may warrant a short module or mini-course rather than a full course.
condition: When the goal is important but too limited to justify a larger curricular unit.

statement: Characterize variation in learners' prior education, sequence position, experience, existing skill, and motivation because a shared goal may serve a heterogeneous audience.
condition: When clarifying the audience for an instructional goal.

statement: Plan repeated authentic practice when the target capability is refined primarily through use and the performance context provides little formal support.
condition: When learners must develop an interactive performance skill with few job aids.

statement: State an instructional goal in terms of what learners will do, not what an organization, instructor, or delivery process will provide.
Replace vague verbs such as understand or learn with an observable performance and specify the relevant content and tools.
condition: When a goal does not reveal how achievement will be demonstrated.

statement: A statement describing an instructional activity is not a usable instructional goal when it omits the capability learners are expected to acquire.
Make the goal performance observable and measurable enough to determine whether learners reached it, and state any limits on the performance.

Select instructional goals with attention to content expertise, content stability, development effort relative to importance, access to tryout learners, known learning difficulty, availability of existing materials, and the structure of the content.
Ask colleagues and intended learners to interpret a drafted goal and revise it if their interpretation of the required behavior differs from the designer's intent.
condition: When checking goal clarity.

statement: If a goal exceeds available instructional time, divide it into logical major parts and select the part best matched to the need and constraint.
condition: When the original goal is too large for the available instruction.

statement: If a goal is too small for the intended instructional period, examine prerequisite and immediately subsequent skills and expand the goal only with relevant adjacent capabilities.
condition: When the original goal underuses the available instructional time.

statement: Begin goal analysis only after the instructional goal clearly states what learners will be able to do.
Classify a goal as an intellectual skill, psychomotor skill, attitude, or verbal-information outcome because the domain determines the appropriate analysis and instructional methods.
For intellectual and psychomotor goals and most attitude goals, identify major performance steps that include both action and relevant content, then sequence them efficiently.
condition: When the target performance unfolds through a sequence.

statement: For verbal-information goals, organize recall topics by a meaningful inherent relationship such as chronology, whole-to-part, simple-to-complex, or familiar-to-unfamiliar.
condition: When the goal requires recalling related information rather than performing a procedure.

statement: Treat the first goal-analysis diagram as a draft and revise steps that are extraneous, misplaced, too small, or too large.
condition: After producing an initial performance or information framework.

statement: Instructional analysis should identify both the major steps used to perform a goal and subordinate capabilities that enable learning of higher-level skills.
Classify a performance as an intellectual skill when learners must manipulate symbolic information, apply knowledge to unfamiliar examples, or solve a problem rather than merely recall information.
Analyze intellectual skills as a progression from discriminating features, to recognizing concepts, to applying rules, to combining rules and concepts in problem solving.
condition: When diagnosing the level and prerequisites of a cognitive performance.

statement: Distinguish well-structured problems, which have defined data, a preferred process, and a correct answer, from ill-structured problems, which have incomplete information, ambiguous goals, multiple processes, and several adequate solutions.
Consider raising an instructional goal to a higher intellectual-skill level when doing so is appropriate for learner needs and the intended application.
condition: When the initial outcome demands less transfer or reasoning than learners need.

statement: Classify a goal as psychomotor when successful performance depends on learning and practicing a new, nontrivial physical action, even if substantial cognition accompanies it.
exception: A task involving only trivial button pressing or physical movement remains primarily intellectual if motor practice will not improve mastery.

statement: Classify an attitudinal goal by the choice learners should make and the direction in which instruction should influence that choice.
Evaluate an attitude through the intellectual, verbal, or physical behavior chosen under relevant circumstances rather than expecting direct observation of an internal disposition.
condition: When assessing whether instruction influenced an attitudinal choice.

statement: Knowing how to perform a behavior is necessary but not sufficient for choosing to perform it; attitudinal instruction must address the disposition to act.
condition: When the desired outcome depends on voluntary action.

statement: Classify a goal as verbal information when learners must recall and state, list, name, or describe taught information without symbolic manipulation.
Treat cognitive strategies for organizing and managing one's own thinking as high-level intellectual skills similar to ill-structured problem solving for instructional-analysis purposes.
condition: When analyzing metacognitive performance in this design framework.

statement: Size and scope a goal before analysis because smaller goals permit more precise identification of what learners must do and may require far less instruction.
condition: When beginning goal analysis.

statement: Analyze intellectual and psychomotor goals by describing exactly what a competent performer does step by step, including both visible actions and necessary mental operations.
When a performance includes a decision, teach both the criteria for making the decision and every alternative procedure learners may need after it.
condition: When different decision outcomes lead to different subsequent actions.

statement: Represent a decision as a branch only when its possible outcomes require at least two different next skills or paths.
condition: When diagramming a goal analysis.
exception: Do not create a branch when the same next action follows regardless of the selection made.

statement: Determine whether a decision skill requires instruction or can be treated as an entry capability by assessing what the target learners can already do.
condition: When a goal path depends on a discrimination or judgment.

statement: Set step granularity according to learner maturity and learning proficiency, using smaller steps for learners who need more guidance and larger combined steps for proficient learners.
condition: When deciding how much performance to include in each analysis step.

statement: Analyze learners and contexts in parallel with goal analysis because learner knowledge changes which steps and granularity are realistic.
Write every goal-analysis step with an action verb and an observable outcome or product.
Replace unobservable activities such as reading or listening with the information or performance learners must produce from what they read or hear.
condition: When the activity itself produces no directly observable result.

statement: Label decision points as explicit questions and show how each answer leads to its corresponding path rather than assuming step numbers alone convey execution order.
condition: When a performance branches.

statement: Make arrows, loops, branches, and continuation markers unambiguous because diagram layout and numbering need not equal actual execution order.
condition: When a goal analysis spans lines or contains repetition and alternatives.

statement: As a rough calibration, analyze one to two hours of instruction into about five to fifteen major steps, then revise if the analysis is too coarse, too detailed, or the goal is too broad.
condition: When estimating useful major-step granularity.
exception: Learner and task characteristics can justify a different number of steps.

statement: Represent a verbal-information goal as major topic clusters rather than a procedural flow, because recall does not inherently require sequential performance.
condition: When learners retrieve specific taught information without problem solving or decision making.

statement: Sequence verbal-information topics chronologically when possible and otherwise by meaningful spatial, complexity, familiarity, or content relationships.
condition: When organizing instruction for nonprocedural recall.

statement: Analyze an attitudinal goal using a procedural flow when the chosen behavior is intellectual or psychomotor, and using topic clusters when the demonstration is verbal information.
condition: When translating an attitude into observable performance.

statement: If a clearly stated goal is difficult to decompose, draft an assessment of the goal and trace the physical actions, mental operations, and decisions required to answer it.
condition: When major steps are not immediately apparent.

statement: Triangulate goal steps through designer self-performance, observation and interviews of competent performers, workplace consultation, job-analysis results, and authoritative manuals or procedures.
condition: When validating the completeness and accuracy of a goal analysis.

statement: Compare how several experts perform the same goal and resolve meaningful differences in the final representation rather than treating one expert's path as definitive.
condition: When multiple valid or potentially incomplete performance strategies exist.

statement: Question the authority of informal how-to resources before using them as evidence for a goal analysis.
condition: When consulting public videos or similarly uncontrolled sources.

statement: Use rapid prototyping and continual access to emerging product knowledge when training must be developed concurrently with new equipment or software and stable documentation is unavailable.
condition: When time-to-market requires product, manuals, and training to be produced in parallel.

statement: Do not omit steps merely because they seem obvious to a subject-matter expert; evaluate their difficulty from the uninformed learner's perspective.
condition: When an expert creates or reviews the goal analysis.

statement: Separate the steps a learner performs from the explanations or activities an instructor would use to teach them.
condition: When evaluating a goal analysis.

statement: Exclude background information, favored topics, and related skills that are not actually required to perform the goal, even when a designer or expert prefers to teach them.
condition: When determining the main performance steps.

statement: Evaluate major steps for observable action, clear content, learner focus, appropriate and comparable scope, importance, correct relationships and sequence, and lack of redundancy.
condition: Before accepting a goal-analysis diagram.

statement: No single major step should be equivalent to the entire goal; successful goal performance should require completion of the full set of necessary steps.
condition: When calibrating step scope in a procedural goal analysis.

statement: Use formative evaluation to locate weaknesses and prescribe revisions during development; use summative evaluation after completion to inform decisions about adopting, maintaining, or adapting instruction.
Distinguish learner assessment from instructional evaluation: assessment measures learner achievement, while evaluation judges instructional materials and processes.
condition: Within this instructional-design framework.

statement: Prefer an evaluator without a personal investment in the materials for summative evaluation because detachment supports balanced reporting of strengths and weaknesses.
condition: When an appropriately qualified external evaluator is available.
exception: A designer can serve effectively if able to adopt an objective stance and possesses the required evaluation expertise.

statement: Structure summative evaluation in two phases: expert judgment of the instruction and impact analysis in the performance setting.
condition: When deciding whether existing instruction has sufficient value for organizational use.

statement: Begin expert judgment by testing congruence between organizational needs and the goals of the instructional materials.
condition: During summative evaluation of existing instruction.

statement: Judge content accuracy and completeness against a validated goal analysis and its required subordinate skills.
condition: During the content-analysis portion of expert judgment.

statement: Judge whether the instructional strategy is appropriate for the learning outcomes and whether it supports transfer from the learning setting to performance.
condition: During design analysis in a summative evaluation.

statement: Evaluate impact by determining whether organizational needs were met, learners used the new capabilities on the job, and job performance or productivity improved.
condition: After learners have completed instruction and returned to the performance setting.

statement: Do not involve target learners in the expert-judgment phase; involve them in the impact phase after they have had an opportunity to perform in context.
condition: When using the two-phase summative-evaluation design described by the source.

statement: Collect impact evidence in the performance setting through unobtrusive observation, questionnaires, document analysis, and job-performance ratings.
condition: When these methods fit the impact questions and setting.

statement: Screen materials through expert judgment before investing in an impact study because instruction with unsound content or strategy may not warrant further evaluation.
condition: When expert judgment reveals material deficiencies.
exception: Decision makers may choose to continue for a documented organizational reason.

statement: Report summative findings to decision makers as evidence about instructional soundness, transfer, and organizational impact rather than as a direct revision prescription.
exception: Summative findings may still motivate later revision.

statement: Assess transfer as a joint result of instructional characteristics, learner characteristics, and workplace characteristics.
condition: When interpreting whether learned skills appear in workplace performance.

statement: Evaluate whether instruction links to prior knowledge and job needs, provides job-congruent practice and targeted feedback, and includes explicit transfer strategies.
condition: When judging instructional support for workplace transfer.

statement: Evaluate learner ability, special needs, self-efficacy, motivation, expectations, and perceived relevance when interpreting transfer outcomes.
condition: During impact analysis.

statement: Evaluate supervisory feedback, accountability, opportunities and cues to use the skills, implementation support, peer discussion, and social incentives when interpreting transfer outcomes.
condition: During impact analysis of the work environment.

statement: Use strategic plans, current organizational goals, stated needs, job analyses, and problem descriptions to test whether instructional goals address the actual work.
condition: During congruence analysis.

statement: Closer alignment among organizational goals, job tasks, and instructional objectives tends to increase managerial support and the likelihood of workplace transfer.
Compare the intended target learners with the organization's proposed participants on experience, ability, motivation, attitudes, and special needs.
condition: When evaluating whether existing instruction fits a new audience.

statement: Compare the total acquisition, implementation, maintenance, facility, and equipment requirements of instruction with the organization's available resources.
condition: During congruence analysis of existing materials.

statement: Share congruence findings with the appropriate decision makers, who determine whether the summative evaluation should continue and what it should include.
condition: After comparing needs, audiences, and resources.

statement: Engage a qualified content expert when the evaluator cannot independently judge the accuracy, currency, and completeness of the subject matter.
condition: During content analysis of unfamiliar material.

statement: Provide content experts with validated design documents as an explicit standard rather than asking for an unstructured general review of the materials.
condition: When source design documents are available.

statement: Convert the instructional-goal skill framework into a checklist or rating scale for judging whether materials and assessments cover the required capabilities.
condition: When conducting a structured content analysis.

statement: Review preinstruction, presentation, learner participation, assessment, and follow-through as a strategy template, adapting criteria to the outcome type and learner capabilities and motivation.
condition: During design analysis of instructional materials.

statement: Investigate logistics and management as possible causes of instructional problems even when the learning design itself appears sound.
condition: During expert judgment of existing instruction.

statement: Evaluate whether learners receive guidance and performance support that bridges the gap between instruction and job performance.
condition: During transfer-possibility analysis.

statement: Check whether learners can use guides, checklists, job aids, just-in-time resources, apps, or accessible support in the performance setting.
condition: When judging transfer support.

statement: Ensure required software and instructional resources operate in the intended work environments rather than assuming the training platform will be available at the jobsite.
condition: When digital tools are required for performance or transfer support.

statement: Verify that training adequately simulates critical job conditions and that workplace equipment, supervision, and environments are compatible with the newly learned performance.
condition: When estimating transfer feasibility.

statement: Establish that learners actually acquired the target capability before interpreting absence of workplace performance as a transfer failure.
condition: When the target behavior is not observed after training.

statement: Inspect posttest content and group achievement evidence rather than treating attendance records or satisfaction surveys as evidence that learning occurred.
condition: When assessing whether instruction produced prerequisite learning for transfer.

statement: Sequence expert judgment as congruence, content, design, and transfer-feasibility analyses, deciding after each stage whether further evaluation remains justified.
condition: When screening existing instructional materials.

statement: Dismiss materials from further consideration when they do not address the organization's need, regardless of their general production or instructional quality.
condition: When congruence analysis shows a material mismatch.

statement: Stop or explicitly reconsider the evaluation when content is materially incomplete, obsolete, or inaccurate before spending resources on downstream analyses.
condition: When content analysis fails its quality threshold.
exception: Decision makers may authorize continuation for a documented reason.

statement: Document expert-judgment questions, design, procedures, recommendations, and the rationale for each recommendation in the evaluation report.
Frame an impact study from the organization's perspective and write questions that address outcomes for learners, jobs, and organizational goals.
condition: When moving from expert judgment to workplace impact analysis.

statement: Tell participants clearly that the study evaluates specified training and materials rather than judging them or their organization.
condition: When introducing an impact study at a worksite.

statement: Build trust and arrange access before collecting data; unexpected visits or questionnaires can undermine participation and data quality.
condition: When conducting evaluation inside an organization.

statement: Tailor impact criteria and collection methods to the performance site while retaining core questions about skill use, organizational need, and observable impact.
condition: When designing a site-specific impact evaluation.

statement: Triangulate impact evidence from learners, peers or subordinates, supervisors or managers, and customers when each group can observe a relevant part of performance.
condition: When selecting impact-study respondents.

statement: Ask learners whether and how they use the new skills and, when they do not, what prevents use.
condition: During impact analysis.

statement: Include supervisors because they can report skill utility, support provided, organizational changes, performance records, and alignment with the original need.
condition: When supervisors observe or shape the target performance.

statement: Choose the timing and number of impact measurements according to the skill's installation time, the rhythm of the work, and the organization's decision needs.
condition: When planning when to collect workplace data.

statement: Compare multiple worksites to identify transferable implementation practices, common barriers, and whether weak outcomes are more plausibly linked to instruction or to a local context.
condition: When the same instruction is deployed across comparable locations.

statement: When most sites fail but a few succeed, study the successful sites' strategies and support before deciding whether to revise the instruction or its implementation guidance.
condition: When multi-site impact results are heterogeneous.

statement: If the full trained population cannot be studied, sample learners across relevant differences in ability, posttest performance, experience, motivation, goals, tenure, and job performance.
condition: When impact-study resources require sampling.

statement: Include the selected learners' supervisors and peers in the sample when their social and work environment may affect implementation.
condition: When sampling a subset of trained employees.

statement: Select each data-collection instrument by tracing a study question to the evidence needed to answer it.
condition: When choosing surveys, observations, interviews, rating scales, or records.

statement: Anchor impact-study measures in the summative questions, learned skills, job requirements, work environment, and relevant learning or change theory.
Use direct descriptive analysis organized by study question unless the evaluation design genuinely requires more complex inference.
condition: When summarizing impact data for organizational decision makers.
exception: Longitudinal or otherwise sophisticated questions may justify advanced statistical analysis.

statement: Report each evaluation phase's purpose, questions, design, procedures, results, recommendations, and data-grounded rationale.
condition: When delivering summative findings.

statement: Lead a summative report with a concise executive summary of recommendations and rationale so readers can selectively inspect supporting technical details.
condition: When reporting to decision makers with limited time.

statement: If resources cannot support the ideal impact study, revise the design transparently and state what evidence and conclusions the reduced design can and cannot support.
condition: When negotiating an evaluation scope under budget or access constraints.

statement: Rate instructional content separately for accuracy, completeness, linkage to job requirements, and coverage by the posttest rather than collapsing these into one quality judgment.
condition: During expert content analysis.

statement: Evaluate content accuracy before other content criteria and stop the review if materially inaccurate instruction is not a viable candidate.
condition: When screening existing materials for adoption.
exception: A decision maker may retain the material only if correction is feasible and explicitly planned.

statement: Flag an assessment that omits one or more main goal steps because the evaluation cannot establish that learners acquired the complete target performance.
condition: When comparing posttest coverage with the goal-analysis framework.
exception: A posttest need not necessarily sample every subordinate skill if it validly assesses all main performances.

statement: Review whether instructional goals are clear, content is current and logically sequenced, materials fit learner prerequisites and characteristics, and assessments are congruent with objectives and learners.
condition: When synthesizing a systematic content analysis.

statement: Examine materials for cultural, racial, gender, contextual, and accessibility mismatches that could make them inappropriate for the intended learners.
condition: During learner-fit analysis.

statement: Evaluate motivation by asking whether instruction gains and sustains attention, is relevant to learner goals, supports realistic confidence, and produces valued satisfaction.
condition: When using the ARCS framework in design analysis.

statement: Judge confidence support by checking that purposes are clear, prerequisites are likely present, vocabulary and scope fit learners, progression is manageable, and challenges remain realistic.
condition: When evaluating the confidence component of learner motivation.

statement: Evaluate intellectual-skill instruction for explicit activation of prerequisites and clear links between prior capabilities and new skills.
condition: When reviewing instruction for intellectual skills.

statement: Require concept instruction to make defining physical, relational, and role characteristics visible through clear examples and nonexamples.
condition: When evaluating instruction for concepts.

statement: Require rule and procedure instruction to describe application steps and illustrate criteria for distinguishing adequate from inadequate results.
condition: When evaluating instruction for rules, principles, or procedures.

statement: Address common novice errors and salient but irrelevant characteristics so learners do not build incorrect concepts or procedures.
condition: When predictable misconceptions or misleading cues exist.

statement: Progress intellectual-skill examples and applications from familiar or simple cases toward unfamiliar, complex, or abstract cases.
condition: When the outcome requires transfer beyond familiar examples.

statement: Require intellectual-skill practice to exercise the actual application, not merely recall facts about how the skill is performed.
condition: When evaluating learner participation.

statement: Provide corrective feedback that explains errors and illustrates improvement rather than only revealing the correct answer.
condition: When learners are practicing intellectual skills or recalling verbal information.

statement: Present verbal information in a relevant context, connect it to existing knowledge, and organize it into meaningful subsets with explicit relationships.
condition: When designing or evaluating verbal-information instruction.

statement: Use logical mnemonics when new verbal information cannot be meaningfully linked to knowledge already in memory.
condition: When meaningful elaboration or organization cannot provide sufficient recall cues.

statement: Use verbal-information rehearsal to strengthen elaborations, organization, imagery, and other recall cues rather than relying only on rote repetition.
For attitude instruction, make desired and undesired behaviors and feelings explicit and connect them to consequences that target learners find truthful, credible, and important.
condition: When instruction is intended to influence a choice or disposition.

statement: Use vicarious attitude examples only when learners can relate to the context and are likely to experience the intended emotion toward the model and situation.
condition: When attitude instruction relies on observed models or stories.

statement: Ensure feedback delivers the promised consequences of attitudinal choices either directly or through a credible vicarious experience.
condition: When consequences are used to influence an attitude.

statement: Demonstrate a motor skill visually with its sequence and timing, then decompose complex performance into logical parts and reintegrate the parts into the complete skill.
condition: When designing or evaluating motor-skill instruction.

statement: Provide repeated motor practice with immediate corrective feedback so learners automate accurate execution rather than rehearse errors.
condition: When motor performance requires fluency or precision.

statement: Use current principles of motivation, learning-outcome type, and instructional strategy as explicit criteria in summative design analysis.
condition: When judging whether existing instruction is pedagogically sound.

statement: Record both strengths and problems for each instructional-strategy component so ratings can be translated into defensible final documentation.
condition: When using a structured rating form in expert judgment.

statement: Measure workplace use for each outcome with categories that distinguish nonuse, planned use, emerging use, routine use, and use that predated training.
condition: When surveying learners about post-training application.

statement: For each unused outcome, ask separately whether the barrier is relevance, insufficient learning, supervisor support, resources, or assistance, and allow respondents to identify additional causes.
condition: When investigating why learned skills are not used.

statement: Ask respondents to link observed changes in knowledge, skills, attitudes, work, or the organization to specific instructional outcomes rather than soliciting only global satisfaction.
condition: When collecting self-reported impact evidence.

statement: Measure the degree of transfer for each learned capability and record its frequency and context of use rather than asking only whether transfer occurred.
condition: During workplace impact evaluation.

statement: Investigate physical, social, and managerial factors that support or inhibit skill use in the performance setting.
condition: When explaining transfer outcomes.

statement: Ask whether performers are permitted and able to experiment with and adapt the new skills to their jobs.
condition: When target performance requires contextual adaptation rather than exact replication.

statement: Require concrete evidence that using the learned capability contributed to resolving the original organizational need.
condition: When assessing organizational impact.

statement: Assess users' perception of a new capability's relative advantage, job relevance, expectation fit, and ease of learning and use because these properties can influence adoption.
condition: When investigating sustained use after training.

statement: Investigate whether learners discuss the new capabilities with peers and supervisors because social exchange can reveal and influence implementation.
condition: During impact analysis.

statement: Collect objective or observable indicators such as time, cost, resource use, product quality, worker response, customer response, and supervisor ratings alongside perceptions of impact.
condition: When relevant organizational records or observations are available.

statement: Choose data sources and methods jointly: align each impact question with people or records that can answer it and with interviews, surveys, observations, ratings, or product evaluations that can capture the evidence.
condition: When constructing an impact-study matrix.

statement: Use remote surveys or interviews when resources are constrained, but prefer site visits, direct observation, personal interviews, and focus groups when the evaluation budget permits richer evidence.
condition: When selecting feasible impact-data methods.

statement: Do not compare a draft innovation with mature conventional instruction until the innovation has undergone formative evaluation and revision sufficient for routine use.
condition: When conducting comparative summative evaluation.

statement: Frame the ultimate summative question as whether the intervention solved the problem or met the goals that justified its development, not merely whether it outperformed another product.
Use external or third-party evaluators when an impartial judgment of an instructional product's value is important to the decision.
condition: When developers or advocates have a material stake in the outcome.

statement: Treat a case-study delivery format as an illustration of design products rather than as a universal prescription for how the underlying instruction should be delivered.
condition: When learning from abbreviated instructional-design artifacts.

statement: Use a common authentic performance task and a cross-role review team to identify recurring capability gaps across a learner population.
condition: When a needs assessment must compare performance across classes or groups.

statement: Trace every instructional goal to a specific pattern observed in needs-assessment evidence.
condition: When converting diagnosed performance gaps into instructional goals.

statement: Split a broad goal into coherent units when its subperformances rely on different organizing dimensions or prerequisite structures.
condition: When one broad performance contains separable learning progressions.

statement: Include prerequisite instruction when current performance evidence shows learners cannot apply a capability reliably, even if records indicate it was taught previously.
condition: When prior exposure and demonstrated entry skill conflict.

statement: Describe performance context, learning context, and required tools separately when they differ, including where and how learners can access the instruction.
condition: During front-end and context analysis.
exception: A single combined context analysis may suffice when learning and performance occur under the same conditions.

statement: Analyze entry skills, prior knowledge, ability levels, learning preferences, content attitudes, delivery attitudes, motivation, and attitudes toward the provider as distinct learner characteristics.
condition: When building a learner profile for instructional decisions.

statement: Triangulate learner characteristics through performance samples, records, teacher or supervisor interviews, and direct learner interviews rather than relying on one informant.
condition: When learner variation materially affects design.

statement: Do not assume an appealing delivery technology will motivate every learner; add a content-relevant motivational hook when attitudes and motivation vary widely.
condition: When learner analysis shows heterogeneous motivation.

statement: Shape practice duration and format around demonstrated learner preferences when doing so remains compatible with the target performance.
condition: When learners prefer short in-class practice over long independent assignments.

statement: Verify actual device reliability, network access, platform support, instructor readiness, and help availability rather than treating nominal technology ownership as sufficient implementation capacity.
condition: When instruction depends on a digital learning environment.

statement: Assess managerial support, physical infrastructure, social learning conditions, and available performance tools as separate dimensions of context readiness.
condition: When determining whether a context can support instruction and transfer.

statement: Use an authentic shared product or audience as a motivational vehicle when it gives learners a meaningful reason to apply the target capability.
condition: When the product does not distort the instructional goal or exclude intended learners.

statement: Maintain a design-evaluation matrix that connects each subordinate skill to its performance objective and one or more parallel assessment items.
condition: When checking internal alignment of a unit.

statement: State performance objectives with the prompt or condition, the observable response, and the criteria that define an acceptable response.
Use parallel assessment items that vary surface details while requiring the same capability and applying the same success criteria.
condition: When creating multiple measures of an objective.

statement: Assess a terminal capability through an authentic integrated product and a rubric that makes the component quality criteria explicit.
condition: When the goal is a complex productive performance.

statement: Assess both recognition and production when learners must first discriminate correct forms and then create them independently.
condition: When subordinate skills progress from classification to generation.

statement: Cluster objectives into lessons according to prerequisite relationships and a manageable learning progression, then verify the sequence within and across lessons.
condition: When planning an instructional strategy across multiple sessions.
