statement: Introduce the value of a target capability through an example that is relevant to learners and visibly demonstrates how the capability improves the product or performance.
condition: During preinstructional motivation.

statement: Assess every required entry skill before instruction and route learners who lack prerequisites to targeted preparatory instruction.
condition: When instructional analysis identifies entry skills that cannot safely be assumed.

statement: Keep an entry-skills assessment focused and short enough to support placement decisions without becoming an unnecessary barrier.
condition: When only a bounded prerequisite set must be checked.

statement: Combine an authentic pretest of the integrated performance with focused pretests for the subordinate skills of each lesson.
condition: When both whole-task readiness and lesson-level mastery affect instruction.

statement: Use lesson-level pretests as branching evidence so learners who already demonstrate mastery can bypass redundant instruction.
condition: When the delivery system can individualize paths and the pretest validly measures the objective.

statement: Place an embedded assessment immediately after a lesson to diagnose subordinate-skill problems and turn it into practice by supplying feedback.
condition: When rapid diagnosis can guide remediation or rehearsal.

statement: Pair an objective posttest of foundational skills with an authentic performance assessment of integrated application.
condition: When the goal requires both component mastery and whole-task performance.

statement: Have instructors, learners, and peers review authentic products using shared criteria, giving both validating praise and specific improvement guidance.
condition: When collaborative review is appropriate for the target performance.

statement: Collect authentic products and successive reviews in a portfolio to monitor progress across time and across related capabilities.
condition: When development unfolds through repeated performances.

statement: Give learners an initial evaluation checklist and have them adapt it for self-review and peer review as their understanding of quality develops.
condition: When learners can productively participate in defining and applying quality criteria.

statement: Promote transfer by applying a previously learned general strategy in a new context and by giving the target performance an authentic purpose beyond teacher assignment.
condition: When prior strategies and an authentic application are available.

statement: Use learner-relevant topics for examples while maintaining a coherent sequence that makes the target pattern easier to perceive.
condition: When examples can vary in subject matter without changing the target skill.

statement: Choose nonexamples that isolate the target distinction and explain why each fails without prematurely teaching unrelated categories.
condition: When teaching concept classification.

statement: Remove irrelevant surface cues from classification practice so learners must use the defining characteristic rather than guess from a shortcut.
condition: When a cue such as punctuation, formatting, or position could reveal the answer without the target judgment.

statement: Use feedback to restate the applicable rule and explain why each practice instance does or does not satisfy it.
condition: When practice involves classification or rule application.

statement: Treat independent production as a different and more demanding capability than recognizing or classifying a correct example.
Scaffold production by first transforming supplied examples and then creating a coherent set on a familiar self-selected topic.
condition: When learners are moving from recognition to generative performance.

statement: When a productive task admits multiple correct solutions, show representative solutions without implying that one wording or method is uniquely correct.
condition: When providing feedback on open production.

statement: Give learners a concise quality checklist during production so they can monitor essential criteria while performing.
condition: When working memory demands could otherwise obscure quality criteria.

statement: Plan time explicitly for motivation, prerequisite assessment, whole-task pretesting, subordinate-skill instruction, integrated review, and posttesting rather than budgeting only content presentation.
condition: When allocating instructional sessions.

statement: Combine individualized delivery with optional teacher or small-group support for questions, extra practice, and customized feedback.
condition: When learners vary in readiness and the setting can provide facilitation.

statement: Prepare instructors with additional examples, nonexamples, and practice even when web-based individualized instruction is the primary delivery mode.
condition: When instructors may need to remediate or extend the mediated instruction.

statement: Use an authentic project environment to integrate natural motivation, learner planning and management, application and assessment in context, prior problem-solving strategies, cooperation, and multiple perspectives on quality.
condition: When project-based learning fits the target outcomes and learners.

statement: Provide enough structure for learners to manage an authentic project, including task processes, example products, targeted instruction, policies, and job aids.
condition: When a constructivist environment delegates meaningful control to learners.

statement: Define publication or collaboration policies before project launch, including legal constraints, audience access, authoring and moderation roles, and acceptable content.
condition: When learners produce content for a shared or public digital space.

statement: Use job aids and age-appropriate example products to make project expectations and possible forms of quality concrete.
condition: When learners are new to the authentic product genre.

statement: Design project teams around distinct management and content functions, allow role choice or rotation, and monitor whether evolving tasks have adequate team coverage.
condition: When learners collaboratively manage an authentic project.

statement: Map the delivery ecosystem beyond the core instructor and platform, including research support, subject specialists, designers, technologists, administrators, and other contributors the project may require.
condition: When a project-based environment spans multiple content and production functions.

statement: Launch an authentic project by connecting it to a credible prior example, discussing its value, and giving learners meaningful participation in deciding whether and how to pursue it.
condition: When planning learner engagement in a constructivist environment.

statement: Let learners investigate audience interests, comparable products, required roles, product conventions, and possible content before fixing their project plan.
condition: When an authentic project admits multiple viable forms.

statement: Require work teams to articulate their task plans and product ideas to peers, teachers, advisors, and other relevant stakeholders.
condition: During collaborative project planning.

statement: Plan explicit opportunities for learners to apply project-acquired problem-solving, teamwork, and domain skills in other classes, home, community, or work settings.
condition: When transfer beyond the original project is an intended outcome.

statement: Provide adaptive guidance through worked models, teacher and specialist coaching, purposeful questioning, peer tutoring, and individualized instruction on diagnosed gaps.
condition: When learners undertake a complex authentic project with varied prior capability.

statement: Build authentic assessment across product development, prepublication peer review, natural postpublication audience feedback, and longitudinal portfolio review.
condition: When instruction produces a real artifact over an extended period.

statement: Invite learners to examine a teacher-proposed rubric and add defensible criteria before using it for self-critique and revision.
condition: When learners can contribute informed quality criteria for an authentic product.

statement: Use portfolios and periodic learner-teacher review to examine overall progress and progress on capabilities taught during each instructional period.
condition: When learner products accumulate over time.

statement: Motivate instruction by contrasting two versions of the same authentic product so learners can see how the target skill changes audience experience without changing core content.
condition: When the instructional value of a stylistic or quality skill can be demonstrated through comparison.

statement: State the component capabilities learners will practice and show how they combine into the authentic goal product.
condition: When introducing a unit built from several related subskills.

statement: Assess prerequisite concepts and discriminations before beginning new instruction, and link each item explicitly to the entry skill it measures.
condition: When later performance depends on identifiable entry skills.

statement: Choose an assessment format compatible with the delivery system and rapid feedback needs while preserving alignment to the targeted skill.
condition: When administering entry or embedded assessment in an online environment.

statement: Use an authentic pretest that asks learners to perform the complete goal under representative tools and constraints, accompanied by a goal-aligned scoring rubric.
condition: When the goal is an integrated product or performance.

statement: Omit rubric criteria for capabilities not taught in the unit so the assessment does not attribute unrelated performance to the instruction.
condition: When scoring a bounded instructional unit's pretest or posttest.

statement: Ask learners to self-review and revise an authentic draft before submission rather than treating first production as the final performance.
Use subordinate-skill pretest results to decide whether learners should bypass, receive, or be grouped differently for subsequent instruction.
condition: When learners may already have mastered some component skills.

statement: Teach a concept with clear definitions, varied examples, contrasting nonexamples, guided discrimination practice, and immediate explanatory feedback.
condition: When learners must distinguish a target category from similar alternatives.

statement: Use different examples on pretests, embedded tests, and posttests so repeated items do not substitute memory for demonstration of the intended capability.
condition: When parallel assessments measure the same objectives over time.

statement: Record assessment results in learner-by-item-by-objective arrays so designers can inspect individual mastery, objective-level patterns, and potentially faulty items.
condition: When revising instruction from group assessment data.

statement: Compare mastery of each objective across pretest, embedded rehearsal, and posttest rather than relying on a single total score.
condition: When diagnosing instructional effectiveness and retention.

statement: Analyze performance separately for learners who entered with and without required prerequisites because aggregate results can hide different learning and retention patterns.
condition: When entry-skill data are available.

statement: Temporary success on embedded practice does not establish durable mastery when learners lack prerequisites; verify retention on a later parallel assessment.
condition: When learners appear to master material during guided instruction despite entry-skill deficits.

statement: Collect learner reactions about motivation, objective clarity, entry content, assessments, instruction, examples, practice, feedback, pacing, and overall value—not only achievement data.
condition: During formative evaluation.

statement: Use follow-up comments or interviews to distinguish item ambiguity from learners simply not knowing the answer.
condition: When learners report that an assessment was unclear.

statement: Pair closed-response attitude ratings with open comments so learners can reveal missing context, prior exposure, or mismatches that fixed choices do not explain.
condition: When gathering formative learner reactions.

statement: Maintain a revision matrix that links each instructional component and diagnosed problem to a proposed change and the evidence sources supporting it.
condition: When converting formative findings into revision decisions.

statement: Develop prerequisite instruction for learners who need it rather than allowing them to begin a unit whose embedded support produces only short-lived success.
condition: When entry assessment and delayed performance show prerequisite deficits.

statement: Move already-mastered capabilities into the entry-skill check and remove redundant instruction and assessment from the unit.
condition: When most target learners demonstrate prior mastery.
exception: Learners needing review should still receive a suitable branch or refresher.

statement: Branch or individualize instruction from pretest results so learners receive only the teaching or review their profiles warrant.
condition: When prerequisite or objective mastery varies substantially across the group.

statement: Redundant instruction can frustrate high-performing learners even when it is clear and technically correct.
condition: When learners are required to complete content they have already mastered.

statement: Refocus practice items, examples, and nonexamples on the authentic project context when learners report that instruction feels disconnected from the stated goal.
condition: When formative feedback identifies a context or relevance gap.

statement: Do not use an untaught, hard-to-distinguish concept as an assessment distractor before learners have the knowledge needed to discriminate it fairly.
condition: When distractor difficulty reflects missing instruction rather than the target objective.
exception: The distractor may be reintroduced after instruction establishes the relevant distinction.

statement: Immediate, self-checkable feedback can make embedded assessment acceptable to learners and support correction during instruction.
condition: When online assessment lets learners inspect feedback after responding.

statement: Do not equate mastery of objective items with the ability to generate ideas and create an authentic product; provide and evaluate practice in the integrated performance.
condition: When the instructional goal requires original production.

statement: During collaborative production, monitor individual contribution so stronger peers do not conceal another learner's lack of performance.
condition: When teamwork is used to practice an individually expected skill.

statement: Use formative evaluation to find strengths and weaknesses in newly developed instruction for revision, and summative evaluation to decide whether completed instruction should be adopted, maintained, or adapted.
Prefer a summative evaluator without personal investment in the instruction when independence is needed to support objective reporting of both strengths and weaknesses.
condition: When selecting an evaluator for a high-stakes adoption or continuation decision.
exception: The original designer can serve if able to take an objective position and possesses the needed evaluation expertise.

statement: Distinguish learner assessment from instructional evaluation: assessments measure student achievement, while evaluations judge instructional materials and processes using assessment and other evidence.
Use formative assessment during instruction to guide and improve learning, and summative assessment after instruction to establish learner standing relative to a goal or standard.
Conduct formative evaluation through one-to-one, small-group, and field-trial stages with target learners, using observation and interviews to understand encountered problems.
condition: While instruction is still being developed.

statement: Structure summative evaluation as an expert-judgment phase followed, when warranted, by an impact-analysis phase in the performance setting.
condition: After instruction is complete and a decision about its value is required.

statement: In expert judgment, test congruence between organizational needs, target learners, resources, and instructional goals before examining content or design quality.
Evaluate content completeness and accuracy against a validated goal analysis and its required subordinate skills, using content experts to create or verify that standard.
condition: During expert judgment of existing instruction.

statement: Judge both the quality of the instructional strategy and its potential to support transfer from the learning setting to performance.
condition: During design and transfer-possibility analysis.

statement: In impact analysis, determine whether organizational needs were met, learners used the new capabilities on the job, and job performance or productivity improved.
condition: After learners have returned to the performance context.

statement: Collect impact evidence unobtrusively in the performance setting through observation, questionnaires, document analysis, and job-performance ratings.
condition: When evaluating workplace transfer and results.

statement: Use expert judgment to determine whether materials of uncertain development quality are sound enough to justify the cost of an impact study.
condition: When existing instruction may not have been systematically designed.
exception: A compelling decision need may still justify impact analysis despite design deficiencies.

statement: Report summative findings to decision makers as evidence about instructional soundness, transfer, and organizational impact rather than as a prescriptive revision plan.
exception: The findings may still motivate later revision.

statement: Evaluate workplace transfer as an interaction among instructional characteristics, learner characteristics, and the work environment.

When judging instructional support for transfer, examine motivation, goal clarity, difficulty, connection to prior knowledge and job needs, guidance, elaboration, authentic practice, targeted feedback, assessment, and explicit transfer strategies.
When judging learner readiness for transfer, examine ability, special needs, self-efficacy, motivation, perceived relevance, confidence, satisfaction, expectations, and organizational commitment.

When judging workplace support for transfer, examine supervisor involvement and feedback, consequences and remediation, accountability, peer discussion, opportunities and cues to use skills, implementation support, and social incentives.
Reuse front-end analysis, learner analysis, performance-context analysis, and instructional-strategy criteria when evaluating whether existing materials fit an organization and can transfer to work.
condition: When designing a summative evaluation.

statement: Begin congruence analysis by comparing the instruction's goals with the organization's strategic plans, current objectives, documented needs, and related job tasks.
condition: When evaluating whether existing instruction fits an organization.

statement: Closer alignment between training goals, organizational priorities, and actual job tasks is likely to increase managerial support and workplace transfer.
condition: When the selected employees and workplace can support the instruction.

statement: Compare the organization's learners with the materials' intended audience on experience, ability, motivation, attitudes, goals, and special needs.
condition: During congruence analysis.

statement: Compare available budget, facilities, equipment, staffing, and maintenance capacity with the full cost and implementation requirements of the instruction.
condition: During resource congruence analysis.

statement: Instruction that is effective but too costly to sustain may fail after initial implementation when maintenance exceeds organizational resources.
Share congruence findings with authorized decision makers and make clear who decides whether the summative evaluation continues.
condition: After comparing needs, learners, and resources.

statement: Ask whether materials and assessments are accurate and complete, whether the strategy fits the learning outcomes, and whether learning is likely to transfer before investing in an impact study.
condition: During expert judgment.

statement: Have content experts judge accuracy, currency, and completeness against organizational goals and preferably against the original design documents or a validated skill framework.
condition: When the evaluator lacks sufficient subject expertise.

statement: Convert the validated goal and subordinate-skill framework into a checklist or rating scale for reviewing both materials and accompanying tests.
condition: During content analysis.

statement: Review preinstruction, content presentation, learner participation, assessment, and follow-through as the stable components of an instructional strategy.
condition: During design analysis.

statement: Adapt design-analysis criteria to the outcome domain and learners' motivation and capability; advanced motivated learners may require less overt support than novices.
condition: When judging adequacy of instructional components.

statement: Examine logistics and management separately from learning design because implementation problems may arise from either layer.
condition: When design analysis uncovers poor instructional performance.

statement: Stop or explicitly reconsider summative evaluation when content or instructional strategy is fundamentally unsound, because later impact evidence may be uninformative or misleading.
condition: When expert judgment finds material deficiencies.
exception: Authorized decision makers may elect to continue for a clearly stated reason.

statement: Assess transfer support through portable materials, job aids, checklists, rapid help channels, performance-support systems, just-in-time resources, and platform compatibility.
condition: During transfer-possibility analysis.

statement: Check whether instruction adequately simulated critical job conditions and whether supervisors, equipment, and workplace conditions are compatible with the newly acquired skills.
condition: When estimating transfer feasibility.

statement: Verify that learners actually acquired the target capabilities before interpreting lack of workplace use as a transfer failure.
condition: When evaluating transfer potential or impact.

statement: Inspect posttest content and group achievement data rather than accepting attendance, certificates, or satisfaction surveys as evidence that skills were learned.
condition: When training culture may reward participation without mastery.

statement: Interview instructors and learners to supplement assessment records with evidence about what learning did or did not occur.
condition: When records alone cannot establish instructional attainment.

statement: Evaluate existing materials through sequential gates—congruence, content, design, and transfer feasibility—and continue only when each prior gate is adequate.
condition: When economizing expert judgment.

statement: Document expert-judgment design, procedures, findings, recommendations, and rationale before deciding whether to proceed to workplace impact analysis.
Focus an impact study on clearly stated questions about outcomes for learners, jobs, and the organization rather than on the instruction in isolation.
condition: When shifting from expert judgment to workplace study.

statement: Explain that the study evaluates specified training and materials rather than individual employees or the organization, and build trust before requesting access or data.
condition: When initiating an impact study in a workplace.

statement: Collect evidence about perceived transfer, progress on organizational needs, and observable physical or attitudinal impact using methods appropriate to the site and resources.
condition: During impact analysis.

statement: Include learners, peers or subordinates, supervisors, managers, customers, and study sponsors as respondents when their distinct perspectives can explain skill use, support, constraints, and organizational change.
condition: When selecting impact-study respondents.

statement: Choose impact-measurement timing from the nature of the skill, work opportunities, and organizational decisions, using repeated follow-up when transfer or routine use develops over time.
condition: When planning when to collect workplace evidence.

statement: Compare multiple worksites to identify transferable success practices, common implementation barriers, and whether failures arise from the instruction or local context.
condition: When the same training is implemented across sites.

statement: If the full trained population cannot be studied, sample across relevant variation in ability, posttest performance, job experience, goals, tenure, motivation, self-efficacy, and prior job ratings, then include associated supervisors and peers.
condition: When selecting a representative impact-study subgroup.

statement: Select each data-collection instrument from the study question and anchor it to the summative questions, learned skills, job performance, work environment, and relevant theory.
condition: When designing surveys, observations, interviews, ratings, or record reviews.

statement: Use straightforward descriptive analysis organized by study question unless the design genuinely requires more sophisticated statistics.
condition: When summarizing impact evidence for decision makers.
exception: Longitudinal or otherwise complex questions may require more advanced analysis.

statement: Report purpose, questions, design, procedures, results, recommendations, and data-grounded rationale, leading with an executive summary that lets decision makers inspect technical detail selectively.
condition: When producing a summative evaluation report.

statement: Estimate required people, sites, instruments, expertise, time, and analysis effort before negotiating the study budget; if the ideal design is infeasible, reduce scope transparently and state what conclusions remain supportable.
condition: When planning impact-study resources.

statement: Summarize congruence in a side-by-side form that compares organizational needs, learner entry skills and characteristics, performance context, and resources with corresponding properties of the instruction.
condition: When documenting expert judgment.

statement: Record both a standardized congruence rating and reviewer comments so decision makers can inspect the judgment and its rationale.
condition: When using an information-summary form.

statement: Rate every goal step and subordinate skill separately for content accuracy, completeness, job-analysis alignment, and posttest coverage.
condition: When evaluating content and test validity against a skill framework.

statement: Evaluate content criteria sequentially and stop if materials are inaccurate before spending effort on completeness, job alignment, or assessment coverage.
condition: During expert content analysis.

statement: Calculate coverage percentages for content, job alignment, and assessment to make systematic omissions visible while retaining item-level comments for interpretation.
condition: When summarizing a skill-by-skill content review.

statement: Flag missing assessment of main goal steps because it leaves no evidence that learners acquired essential performance components.
condition: When reviewing posttest coverage.
exception: Omitting some subordinate-skill items may be acceptable if the posttest validly measures integrated main-step performance.

statement: Review goal clarity, content accuracy and currency, sequence logic, learner appropriateness and bias, and assessment congruence as distinct design-quality questions.
condition: When interpreting content-analysis data from a systems perspective.

statement: Evaluate motivation by whether instruction gains and sustains attention, demonstrates personal relevance, supports realistic confidence, and produces worthwhile satisfaction.
condition: When applying the ARCS framework in design analysis.

statement: Judge learner confidence through purpose clarity, prerequisite readiness, progression from familiar to unfamiliar and concrete to abstract, appropriate language and context, and challenging but attainable tasks.
condition: When evaluating motivational design.

statement: Judge satisfaction using both credible external rewards and intrinsic outcomes such as accomplishment, curiosity, and intellectual enjoyment relative to learner effort.
condition: When evaluating the motivational payoff of instruction.

statement: For intellectual-skill instruction, check activation of prerequisites, links to prior knowledge, useful organization, explicit concept characteristics and rule procedures, quality criteria, and common-error treatment.
condition: During domain-specific design analysis.

statement: Use clear examples and nonexamples in familiar contexts, then progress toward more complex, unfamiliar, or abstract intellectual-skill applications.
condition: When evaluating or designing concept and procedure instruction.

statement: Require practice to apply the intellectual skill rather than merely recall facts about it, and require feedback to explain corrections rather than only reveal the answer.
condition: When evaluating learner participation and feedback.

statement: For verbal-information instruction, place new information in context, link it to prior knowledge, organize related subsets visibly, and use logical mnemonics only when meaningful links are unavailable.
condition: During domain-specific design analysis.

statement: Use verbal-information rehearsal to strengthen elaborations, organizational structure, imagery, and recall cues, with feedback explaining why responses are incorrect.
condition: When evaluating practice for recall outcomes.

statement: For attitudinal instruction, make desired and undesired feelings and behaviors explicit and connect each credibly to consequences the target learners consider important.
condition: During domain-specific design analysis.

statement: Use familiar, relevant models and situations for vicarious attitude learning, and ensure promised consequences are experienced directly or vicariously in feedback.
condition: When attitude change is taught through observation of others.

statement: For motor-skill instruction, activate related skills, visually model sequence and timing, decompose complex execution, reintegrate whole performance, address common errors, and provide repeated practice with immediate feedback.
condition: During domain-specific design analysis.

statement: Provide immediate motor-performance feedback to prevent learners from rehearsing and automating inaccurate execution.
condition: During repetitive motor-skill practice.

statement: Use established principles of motivation, learning domains, memory, practice, feedback, and transfer as explicit criteria for summative design analysis.
condition: When an independent evaluator reviews existing instructional materials.

statement: Rate preinstructional motivation, objectives, entry-skill preparation, organizational structures, elaborations, examples, practice, feedback, memory aids, and transfer strategy while recording specific strengths and problems.
condition: When producing a design-analysis summary.

statement: Use expert-review findings to focus the later impact study on the specific promises, risks, and transfer conditions identified in the materials.
condition: When expert judgment precedes workplace evaluation.

statement: Ask impact respondents to distinguish not using, planning to use, beginning to use, routine use, and use that predated training for each intended outcome.
condition: When surveying workplace skill use after training.

statement: For every unused skill, ask whether it is irrelevant, requires more training, lacks supervisor support, lacks resources, or requires additional assistance, while allowing other explanations.
condition: When diagnosing barriers to workplace use.

statement: Give respondents enough posttraining time to attempt transfer before asking them to reflect on skill use and observed personal or organizational changes.
condition: When scheduling an impact survey.

statement: Ask impact respondents to attribute posttraining changes separately to knowledge, skill, and attitudes for each intended outcome.
condition: When surveying perceived training impact.

statement: Collect outcome-specific strengths and improvement suggestions instead of only asking for a global course rating.
condition: When using learner reflections to interpret impact.

statement: Assess transfer at the level of all, some, or none of the learned capabilities and document how frequently and in what contexts each capability is used.
condition: During workplace impact evaluation.

statement: Investigate physical, social, and managerial factors that both support and inhibit workplace use of learned capabilities.
condition: When explaining observed transfer.

statement: Ask whether employees can experiment with and adapt learned capabilities to job conditions, not only whether they reproduce training procedures exactly.
condition: When the job requires contextual adaptation.

statement: Require evidence that skill use helps resolve the original need, including observable changes in time, cost, resource use, employee experience, customer satisfaction, supervisor satisfaction, or other relevant results.
condition: When judging organizational impact.

statement: Examine whether new capabilities improve on prior practice, fit job tasks and expectations, are usable, are discussed with relevant others, and support the learner's career path.
condition: When assessing the utility and diffusion of training outcomes.

statement: Triangulate impact using learners, supervisors, customers, peers, subordinates, trainers, and records through interviews, questionnaires, observations, product reviews, and job-performance ratings.
condition: When resources permit multiple evidence sources.

statement: Match impact data collection to available resources, using remote surveys and interviews under tight budgets and adding site visits, focus groups, and direct observation when resources permit.
Survey all relevant outcomes even when a published or illustrative form displays only a subset, so unmeasured capabilities are not silently excluded from impact conclusions.
condition: When adapting an impact-survey template.

statement: Allow a follow-up interval suited to the target skill before surveying transfer; an extended interval may be necessary for capabilities used intermittently in community or workplace roles.
condition: When skill-use opportunities arise gradually.

statement: Do not compare a draft innovation summatively with mature instruction until formative evaluation and revision have removed its major development problems.
condition: When comparing instructional alternatives.

statement: Evaluate a mature innovation on learner performance, attitudes, instructor reactions, costs, and durability rather than on novelty or advocacy claims.
condition: After the innovation is suitable for routine use.

statement: Use an external evaluator when a product advocate's involvement would undermine confidence in an impartial judgment of worth.
condition: When summative conclusions affect competitive selection or high-value decisions.

statement: Make the ultimate summative question whether the intervention solved the original problem and met the goals for which it was developed, not merely whether it outperformed another product.
Collect the design products from front-end analysis through assessment, strategy, materials, learner results, and revision so reviewers can trace decisions across the complete process.
condition: When documenting an instructional-design project.

statement: Novice designers can benefit from beginning with direct instruction because it forces them to take responsibility for every instructional component they create.
condition: When learning materials development before designing teacher-led or highly interactive formats.

statement: Use a common authentic performance task across the target population and have a cross-organizational evaluation team identify recurring patterns in the work.
condition: When conducting a curriculum needs assessment from learner products.

statement: Derive instructional goals directly from documented deficiencies in authentic learner work rather than from the content sequence of an existing course.
condition: When learner artifacts reveal a common performance gap.

statement: Split a broad performance need into coherent instructional units when its dimensions require distinct capability development.
condition: When a single need combines separable bases for performance such as purpose and structural complexity.

statement: Define the intended learner range explicitly and include both component-skill instruction and integrated application when the audience is heterogeneous in current performance.
condition: When learners share a goal but vary substantially in prior skill.

statement: Describe all expected performance settings, even outside the formal learning environment, so instruction can prepare learners for school, community, and job applications.
condition: When a general capability should transfer across subject or social settings.

statement: Verify that required learner devices, software, connectivity, delivery platforms, and access locations actually exist before basing the instructional plan on them.
condition: When technology mediates instruction or performance.

statement: Analyze entry skills, prior knowledge, ability, learning preferences, content attitudes, delivery attitudes, motivation, attitudes toward the organization, and overall group heterogeneity as distinct learner characteristics.
condition: When constructing a learner profile for design.

statement: Triangulate learner characteristics from performance samples, records, teachers, target learners, and tryout learners rather than relying on a single informant.
condition: When gathering learner-analysis evidence.

statement: Prior exposure to content does not demonstrate current mastery; compare curriculum history with authentic performance evidence.
condition: When learners have previously received related instruction.

statement: Do not assume an attractive delivery technology will motivate every learner; add a meaningful task or product that gives varied learners a reason to practice.
condition: When learner interest in the content and organization varies.

statement: For heterogeneous and variably motivated learners, use an authentic writing or production vehicle that permits frequent short practice rather than depending solely on long assignments.
condition: When extended tasks would reduce participation or obscure component practice.

statement: Do not duplicate performance- and learning-context analyses when the same site and conditions serve both; instead document why a combined analysis is sufficient.
condition: When learning and intended performance occur in the same context.

statement: Analyze context through managerial support, physical and technical conditions, social and learning arrangements, and available performance tools.
Account for actual equipment reliability and home-access variation, not only nominal device and network availability, when planning technology-mediated instruction.
condition: When learners depend on personal devices or connectivity.

statement: Specify the training and support responsibilities of instructors who must operate the delivery system, orient learners, manage progress, and provide elaboration beyond direct instruction.
condition: When a learning platform mediates individualized instruction.

statement: Use a design-evaluation chart to align each subordinate skill with its performance objective and parallel test items.
condition: When reviewing the internal consistency of an instructional design.

statement: Assess an integrated terminal performance with an authentic product and explicit quality criteria while also using focused items to diagnose subordinate capabilities.
condition: When the goal combines several subordinate skills into a product.

statement: Create parallel assessment items that vary surface content and response format while preserving the behavior, conditions, and success criteria in the objective.
condition: When developing multiple measures of the same subordinate skill.

statement: Assess concept definition, classification, error diagnosis, recognition, and production as distinct capabilities when the analysis treats them as separate subordinate skills.
condition: When a terminal performance depends on progressively different uses of knowledge.

statement: Cluster objectives into lessons by related skill type and sequence them within and across lessons according to their dependency structure.
condition: When converting an instructional analysis into a course sequence.

statement: Anchor motivation in a learner-managed authentic product and use a high-interest example to demonstrate the practical effect of the target skill.
condition: When introducing a unit whose component skills contribute to a larger project.

statement: Show the target features in an introductory example and state the unit purpose in terms of the integrated product learners will create.
condition: During preinstructional orientation.

statement: Keep an entry-skills test short, cover every identified prerequisite, and route learners who lack prerequisites to targeted preparatory instruction before the main unit.
condition: When a prerequisite set is known and individualized delivery is available.

statement: Combine an authentic whole-goal pretest scored with a rubric and lesson-level objective pretests that diagnose component mastery.
condition: When instruction targets both integrated performance and subordinate skills.

statement: Administer a lesson's component pretest immediately before that lesson and use its results as a future branching mechanism for learners with prior mastery.
condition: When the delivery system supports adaptive paths.

statement: Administer an embedded assessment immediately after each lesson to diagnose subordinate-skill problems and convert it into rehearsal with corrective feedback.
Use learner-facing labels such as review or recap when they accurately describe low-stakes diagnostic and rehearsal assessments and reduce unnecessary test anxiety.
condition: When the assessment supports learning rather than a high-stakes decision.

statement: Use both an objective posttest for component mastery and an authentic performance posttest for integrated application.
condition: When the goal combines basic knowledge with production.

statement: Review authentic work with both validating praise and specific improvement suggestions from the instructor, author, and peers.
condition: When a product can benefit from multiple relevant perspectives.

statement: Assess authentic products repeatedly over time and retain products with reviews in a portfolio to monitor growth across related capabilities.
condition: When the domain develops through sustained production.

statement: Have learners adapt a teacher-provided checklist for self- and peer-review and remind them to use it while drafting and editing.
condition: When quality criteria can serve as a reusable memory aid.

statement: Promote transfer by reusing a previously learned problem-solving process in a new context and by giving learners an authentic purpose beyond compliance with an assignment.
condition: When planning follow-through activities.

statement: Build examples and practice around topics learners have identified as interesting, while keeping each example set coherent enough to form a meaningful sequence.
condition: When contextualizing basic skill instruction.

statement: Use related nonexamples to clarify the target concept without diverting into full instruction on the nonexample categories.
condition: When nonexamples help establish a discrimination.
exception: Teach the contrasting category directly when it is itself an objective.

statement: Remove irrelevant clues from discrimination practice so learners must use the defining feature targeted by the objective.
condition: When superficial cues could make classification easier than the intended skill.

statement: Explain why each example or response is correct or incorrect rather than merely restating the rule or supplying the right answer.
condition: When feedback is intended to strengthen discrimination and transfer.

statement: Treat generating original content as a different capability from recognizing correct examples and provide dedicated production practice.
condition: When learners move from selected-response tasks to writing or creating.

statement: Begin original production with familiar topics so idea generation does not overwhelm initial practice of the target form.
condition: When content generation is not the primary new skill.

statement: In open-ended production feedback, show several valid solutions and state explicitly when multiple correct responses are possible.
condition: When a task admits different correct products.

statement: Give learners a short criteria list for evaluating their own products during creation rather than waiting for postsubmission scoring.
condition: When criteria can guide ongoing performance.

statement: Allocate sessions explicitly to motivation, entry assessment, whole-goal pretest, component instruction, integration review, higher-level selection, and posttest.
condition: When translating a strategy into an instructional schedule.

statement: Combine individualized primary delivery with teacher-led or small-group examples, nonexamples, practice, and customized feedback for learners who need additional support.
condition: When a web-based unit serves learners with varying needs.

statement: Plan a constructivist environment from a documented performance need, a clear goal and focal objective, an explicit learning rationale, a pedagogical model, and an authentic scenario.
condition: When choosing project-based learning for complex application.

statement: Use a project that gives learners a natural reason to practice, meaningful control over planning and production, and an audience for the resulting work.
condition: When designing a student-centered authentic environment.

statement: Embed component-skill practice and assessment within the authentic performance context rather than separating all formal instruction from project work.
condition: When direct instruction supports a larger constructivist project.

statement: Activate and apply previously learned problem-solving steps—clarify, seek alternatives, test, refine, and monitor—in the new project context.
condition: When prior problem-solving strategies are entry skills for the project.

statement: Have learners judge authentic work from multiple perspectives, including technical form, content, audience interest, aesthetics, appropriateness, values, policy, and legal constraints.
condition: When an authentic public product has multiple stakeholders and quality dimensions.

statement: Establish governance for a learner-published environment before launch, including legal obligations, audience access, authoring and moderation roles, deletion authority, and permissible content.
condition: When learner products are disseminated through an institutional platform.

statement: Seed the project with representative models and job aids while allowing participants to identify additional resources as new production needs emerge.
condition: When the full set of project needs cannot be known in advance.

statement: Separate project-management teams from creative content teams so operational roles and domain production both receive explicit ownership.
condition: When an authentic project requires both production management and individual creative work.

statement: Let learners select and rotate management roles for interest and breadth of experience while requiring every learner to perform the core target role.
condition: When optional project roles surround an individually required goal performance.

statement: Have learners monitor project progress and create or reassign teams as evolving work exposes uncovered tasks.
condition: When project requirements emerge through production.

statement: Map each project need to the appropriate delivery platform, research tool, content specialist, teacher, designer, technologist, or other organizational contributor.
condition: When planning resources for a cross-disciplinary project.

statement: Engage learners by examining a credible prior product, discussing benefits, inviting a decision to proceed, and connecting learners with authentic organizational stakeholders.
condition: When launching a school or workplace project.

statement: During exploration, have learners investigate required team structures, audience needs, comparable-product conventions, distribution choices, and possible content.
condition: Before learners settle a project design.

statement: Have teams explain planned tasks, collaboration choices, and product ideas to peers and relevant adults so assumptions become visible and reviewable.
condition: During project planning.

statement: Plan for project capabilities to be elaborated through use in other courses, home, community, and employment contexts.
condition: When broader transfer is intended.

statement: Combine scaffolding from models, coaching, questioning, peer tutoring, and individualized formal instruction rather than relying on unguided project work.
condition: When learners lack some skills needed for a complex project.

statement: Assess an authentic project at the individual draft, team prepublication, natural audience-response, and longitudinal portfolio levels.
condition: When both individual growth and collective product quality matter.

statement: Keep internal skill codes in design documents for traceability but omit them from learner-facing assessments when they add no instructional value.
condition: When assessment items are mapped to an instructional analysis.

statement: Select entry-assessment items from the design table in a format compatible with rapid administration and feedback, without weakening skill alignment.
condition: When deploying an entry test in a learning platform.

statement: Let learners choose an authentic pretest topic within the goal's domain, provide explicit performance criteria, and require self-review before submission.
condition: When measuring integrated production before instruction.

statement: Use a subordinate-skill pretest to decide whether to split or branch learners for subsequent instruction.
condition: When mastery scores show materially different learner needs.

statement: Use examples and nonexamples that jointly expose every defining feature of a target category rather than varying only one obvious surface cue.
condition: When teaching a concept defined by multiple attributes.

statement: Use closely matched examples and nonexamples in practice so learners must discriminate the relevant feature rather than topic or wording.
condition: When practicing concept classification.

statement: After embedded review, tell learners to inspect feedback, reason about errors, and revisit the relevant instruction when needed.
condition: When an online environment permits immediate review and navigation.

statement: Construct posttest items from the same strategy prescriptions and format as pretest and embedded items while using new examples.
condition: When parallel tests measure the same objectives.

statement: Summarize test data simultaneously by learner, item, and objective so individual deficits and shared design problems can be distinguished.
condition: When analyzing small-group formative results.

statement: Compare objective mastery at pretest, embedded rehearsal, and posttest to detect initial status, immediate learning, and retained performance.
Report mastery patterns for the whole group and separately for learners with and without prerequisites.
condition: When prerequisite status may moderate instructional effectiveness.

statement: Use attitude questions tied to motivation, objectives, entry behavior, tests, instruction, practice, feedback, and overall usefulness so dissatisfaction can be located within the strategy.
condition: During formative learner-reaction analysis.

statement: Include open-ended prompts with attitude scales because learner comments can reveal that an apparently clear lesson omitted the authentic product or repeated already-known content.
condition: When interpreting otherwise favorable ratings.

statement: Probe reports that a pretest is unclear because learners may be describing lack of knowledge rather than defective vocabulary or directions.
condition: When clarity ratings conflict with other evidence.

statement: Treat split learner opinions about the amount or usefulness of examples as evidence for adaptive support rather than assuming one fixed quantity fits everyone.
condition: When some learners report too many examples and others too few.

statement: Base each revision decision on converging evidence from appropriate tests, observation, questionnaires, and interviews, and record the sources in a revision matrix.
condition: When formative findings affect instruction.

statement: Add prerequisite instruction when learners without entry skills succeed during guided practice but fail to retain the capabilities at posttest.
condition: When embedded and delayed results diverge by entry-skill status.

statement: Remove objectives from required instruction and assessments when evidence shows broad prior mastery, while branching learners who need review.
condition: When pretest and learner-reaction evidence agree that content is redundant.

statement: Align practice and assessment contexts more closely with the promised authentic project when learners experience a mismatch between unit framing and actual tasks.
condition: When formative feedback identifies a relevance gap.

statement: Delay use of distractors that require an untaught discrimination, then reintroduce them after the contrast has been taught.
condition: When distractor difficulty is unrelated to the current objective.

statement: Supplement selected-response mastery with authentic idea generation and product-writing practice because objective posttest success may not transfer automatically to creation.
condition: When the terminal goal is generative.

statement: Provide research support and monitor individual authorship in writing teams so collaboration assists rather than replaces each learner's target performance.
condition: When learners collaborate on authentic production.

statement: Use formative evaluation to find strengths and weaknesses in newly developed instruction for revision, and summative evaluation to decide whether completed instruction should be adopted, maintained, or adapted.
Prefer a summative evaluator without personal investment in the instruction when independence is needed to support objective reporting of both strengths and weaknesses.
condition: When selecting an evaluator for a high-stakes adoption or continuation decision.
exception: The original designer can serve if able to take an objective position and possesses the needed evaluation expertise.

statement: Distinguish learner assessment from instructional evaluation: assessments measure student achievement, while evaluations judge instructional materials and processes using assessment and other evidence.
Use formative assessment during instruction to guide and improve learning, and summative assessment after instruction to establish learner standing relative to a goal or standard.
Conduct formative evaluation through one-to-one, small-group, and field-trial stages with target learners, using observation and interviews to understand encountered problems.
condition: While instruction is still being developed.

statement: Structure summative evaluation as an expert-judgment phase followed, when warranted, by an impact-analysis phase in the performance setting.
condition: After instruction is complete and a decision about its value is required.

statement: In expert judgment, test congruence between organizational needs, target learners, resources, and instructional goals before examining content or design quality.
Evaluate content completeness and accuracy against a validated goal analysis and its required subordinate skills, using content experts to create or verify that standard.
condition: During expert judgment of existing instruction.

statement: Judge both the quality of the instructional strategy and its potential to support transfer from the learning setting to performance.
condition: During design and transfer-possibility analysis.

statement: In impact analysis, determine whether organizational needs were met, learners used the new capabilities on the job, and job performance or productivity improved.
condition: After learners have returned to the performance context.

statement: Collect impact evidence unobtrusively in the performance setting through observation, questionnaires, document analysis, and job-performance ratings.
condition: When evaluating workplace transfer and results.

statement: Use expert judgment to determine whether materials of uncertain development quality are sound enough to justify the cost of an impact study.
condition: When existing instruction may not have been systematically designed.
exception: A compelling decision need may still justify impact analysis despite design deficiencies.

statement: Report summative findings to decision makers as evidence about instructional soundness, transfer, and organizational impact rather than as a prescriptive revision plan.
exception: The findings may still motivate later revision.

statement: Evaluate workplace transfer as an interaction among instructional characteristics, learner characteristics, and the work environment.

When judging instructional support for transfer, examine motivation, goal clarity, difficulty, connection to prior knowledge and job needs, guidance, elaboration, authentic practice, targeted feedback, assessment, and explicit transfer strategies.
When judging learner readiness for transfer, examine ability, special needs, self-efficacy, motivation, perceived relevance, confidence, satisfaction, expectations, and organizational commitment.

When judging workplace support for transfer, examine supervisor involvement and feedback, consequences and remediation, accountability, peer discussion, opportunities and cues to use skills, implementation support, and social incentives.
Reuse front-end analysis, learner analysis, performance-context analysis, and instructional-strategy criteria when evaluating whether existing materials fit an organization and can transfer to work.
condition: When designing a summative evaluation.

statement: Begin congruence analysis by comparing the instruction's goals with the organization's strategic plans, current objectives, documented needs, and related job tasks.
condition: When evaluating whether existing instruction fits an organization.

statement: Closer alignment between training goals, organizational priorities, and actual job tasks is likely to increase managerial support and workplace transfer.
condition: When the selected employees and workplace can support the instruction.

statement: Compare the organization's learners with the materials' intended audience on experience, ability, motivation, attitudes, goals, and special needs.
condition: During congruence analysis.

statement: Compare available budget, facilities, equipment, staffing, and maintenance capacity with the full cost and implementation requirements of the instruction.
condition: During resource congruence analysis.

statement: Instruction that is effective but too costly to sustain may fail after initial implementation when maintenance exceeds organizational resources.
Share congruence findings with authorized decision makers and make clear who decides whether the summative evaluation continues.
condition: After comparing needs, learners, and resources.

statement: Ask whether materials and assessments are accurate and complete, whether the strategy fits the learning outcomes, and whether learning is likely to transfer before investing in an impact study.
condition: During expert judgment.

statement: Have content experts judge accuracy, currency, and completeness against organizational goals and preferably against the original design documents or a validated skill framework.
condition: When the evaluator lacks sufficient subject expertise.

statement: Convert the validated goal and subordinate-skill framework into a checklist or rating scale for reviewing both materials and accompanying tests.
condition: During content analysis.

statement: Review preinstruction, content presentation, learner participation, assessment, and follow-through as the stable components of an instructional strategy.
condition: During design analysis.

statement: Adapt design-analysis criteria to the outcome domain and learners' motivation and capability; advanced motivated learners may require less overt support than novices.
condition: When judging adequacy of instructional components.

statement: Examine logistics and management separately from learning design because implementation problems may arise from either layer.
condition: When design analysis uncovers poor instructional performance.

statement: Stop or explicitly reconsider summative evaluation when content or instructional strategy is fundamentally unsound, because later impact evidence may be uninformative or misleading.
condition: When expert judgment finds material deficiencies.
exception: Authorized decision makers may elect to continue for a clearly stated reason.

statement: Assess transfer support through portable materials, job aids, checklists, rapid help channels, performance-support systems, just-in-time resources, and platform compatibility.
condition: During transfer-possibility analysis.

statement: Check whether instruction adequately simulated critical job conditions and whether supervisors, equipment, and workplace conditions are compatible with the newly acquired skills.
condition: When estimating transfer feasibility.

statement: Verify that learners actually acquired the target capabilities before interpreting lack of workplace use as a transfer failure.
condition: When evaluating transfer potential or impact.

statement: Inspect posttest content and group achievement data rather than accepting attendance, certificates, or satisfaction surveys as evidence that skills were learned.
condition: When training culture may reward participation without mastery.

statement: Interview instructors and learners to supplement assessment records with evidence about what learning did or did not occur.
condition: When records alone cannot establish instructional attainment.

statement: Evaluate existing materials through sequential gates—congruence, content, design, and transfer feasibility—and continue only when each prior gate is adequate.
condition: When economizing expert judgment.

statement: Document expert-judgment design, procedures, findings, recommendations, and rationale before deciding whether to proceed to workplace impact analysis.
Focus an impact study on clearly stated questions about outcomes for learners, jobs, and the organization rather than on the instruction in isolation.
condition: When shifting from expert judgment to workplace study.

statement: Explain that the study evaluates specified training and materials rather than individual employees or the organization, and build trust before requesting access or data.
condition: When initiating an impact study in a workplace.

statement: Collect evidence about perceived transfer, progress on organizational needs, and observable physical or attitudinal impact using methods appropriate to the site and resources.
condition: During impact analysis.

statement: Include learners, peers or subordinates, supervisors, managers, customers, and study sponsors as respondents when their distinct perspectives can explain skill use, support, constraints, and organizational change.
condition: When selecting impact-study respondents.

statement: Choose impact-measurement timing from the nature of the skill, work opportunities, and organizational decisions, using repeated follow-up when transfer or routine use develops over time.
condition: When planning when to collect workplace evidence.

statement: Compare multiple worksites to identify transferable success practices, common implementation barriers, and whether failures arise from the instruction or local context.
condition: When the same training is implemented across sites.

statement: If the full trained population cannot be studied, sample across relevant variation in ability, posttest performance, job experience, goals, tenure, motivation, self-efficacy, and prior job ratings, then include associated supervisors and peers.
condition: When selecting a representative impact-study subgroup.

statement: Select each data-collection instrument from the study question and anchor it to the summative questions, learned skills, job performance, work environment, and relevant theory.
condition: When designing surveys, observations, interviews, ratings, or record reviews.

statement: Use straightforward descriptive analysis organized by study question unless the design genuinely requires more sophisticated statistics.
condition: When summarizing impact evidence for decision makers.
exception: Longitudinal or otherwise complex questions may require more advanced analysis.

statement: Report purpose, questions, design, procedures, results, recommendations, and data-grounded rationale, leading with an executive summary that lets decision makers inspect technical detail selectively.
condition: When producing a summative evaluation report.

statement: Estimate required people, sites, instruments, expertise, time, and analysis effort before negotiating the study budget; if the ideal design is infeasible, reduce scope transparently and state what conclusions remain supportable.
condition: When planning impact-study resources.

statement: Summarize congruence in a side-by-side form that compares organizational needs, learner entry skills and characteristics, performance context, and resources with corresponding properties of the instruction.
condition: When documenting expert judgment.

statement: Record both a standardized congruence rating and reviewer comments so decision makers can inspect the judgment and its rationale.
condition: When using an information-summary form.

statement: Rate every goal step and subordinate skill separately for content accuracy, completeness, job-analysis alignment, and posttest coverage.
condition: When evaluating content and test validity against a skill framework.

statement: Evaluate content criteria sequentially and stop if materials are inaccurate before spending effort on completeness, job alignment, or assessment coverage.
condition: During expert content analysis.

statement: Calculate coverage percentages for content, job alignment, and assessment to make systematic omissions visible while retaining item-level comments for interpretation.
condition: When summarizing a skill-by-skill content review.

statement: Flag missing assessment of main goal steps because it leaves no evidence that learners acquired essential performance components.
condition: When reviewing posttest coverage.
exception: Omitting some subordinate-skill items may be acceptable if the posttest validly measures integrated main-step performance.

statement: Review goal clarity, content accuracy and currency, sequence logic, learner appropriateness and bias, and assessment congruence as distinct design-quality questions.
condition: When interpreting content-analysis data from a systems perspective.

statement: Evaluate motivation by whether instruction gains and sustains attention, demonstrates personal relevance, supports realistic confidence, and produces worthwhile satisfaction.
condition: When applying the ARCS framework in design analysis.

statement: Judge learner confidence through purpose clarity, prerequisite readiness, progression from familiar to unfamiliar and concrete to abstract, appropriate language and context, and challenging but attainable tasks.
condition: When evaluating motivational design.

statement: Judge satisfaction using both credible external rewards and intrinsic outcomes such as accomplishment, curiosity, and intellectual enjoyment relative to learner effort.
condition: When evaluating the motivational payoff of instruction.

statement: For intellectual-skill instruction, check activation of prerequisites, links to prior knowledge, useful organization, explicit concept characteristics and rule procedures, quality criteria, and common-error treatment.
condition: During domain-specific design analysis.

statement: Use clear examples and nonexamples in familiar contexts, then progress toward more complex, unfamiliar, or abstract intellectual-skill applications.
condition: When evaluating or designing concept and procedure instruction.

statement: Require practice to apply the intellectual skill rather than merely recall facts about it, and require feedback to explain corrections rather than only reveal the answer.
condition: When evaluating learner participation and feedback.

statement: For verbal-information instruction, place new information in context, link it to prior knowledge, organize related subsets visibly, and use logical mnemonics only when meaningful links are unavailable.
condition: During domain-specific design analysis.

statement: Use verbal-information rehearsal to strengthen elaborations, organizational structure, imagery, and recall cues, with feedback explaining why responses are incorrect.
condition: When evaluating practice for recall outcomes.

statement: For attitudinal instruction, make desired and undesired feelings and behaviors explicit and connect each credibly to consequences the target learners consider important.
condition: During domain-specific design analysis.

statement: Use familiar, relevant models and situations for vicarious attitude learning, and ensure promised consequences are experienced directly or vicariously in feedback.
condition: When attitude change is taught through observation of others.

statement: For motor-skill instruction, activate related skills, visually model sequence and timing, decompose complex execution, reintegrate whole performance, address common errors, and provide repeated practice with immediate feedback.
condition: During domain-specific design analysis.

statement: Provide immediate motor-performance feedback to prevent learners from rehearsing and automating inaccurate execution.
condition: During repetitive motor-skill practice.

statement: Use established principles of motivation, learning domains, memory, practice, feedback, and transfer as explicit criteria for summative design analysis.
condition: When an independent evaluator reviews existing instructional materials.

statement: Rate preinstructional motivation, objectives, entry-skill preparation, organizational structures, elaborations, examples, practice, feedback, memory aids, and transfer strategy while recording specific strengths and problems.
condition: When producing a design-analysis summary.

statement: Use expert-review findings to focus the later impact study on the specific promises, risks, and transfer conditions identified in the materials.
condition: When expert judgment precedes workplace evaluation.

statement: Ask impact respondents to distinguish not using, planning to use, beginning to use, routine use, and use that predated training for each intended outcome.
condition: When surveying workplace skill use after training.

statement: For every unused skill, ask whether it is irrelevant, requires more training, lacks supervisor support, lacks resources, or requires additional assistance, while allowing other explanations.
condition: When diagnosing barriers to workplace use.

statement: Give respondents enough posttraining time to attempt transfer before asking them to reflect on skill use and observed personal or organizational changes.
condition: When scheduling an impact survey.

statement: Ask impact respondents to attribute posttraining changes separately to knowledge, skill, and attitudes for each intended outcome.
condition: When surveying perceived training impact.

statement: Collect outcome-specific strengths and improvement suggestions instead of only asking for a global course rating.
condition: When using learner reflections to interpret impact.

statement: Assess transfer at the level of all, some, or none of the learned capabilities and document how frequently and in what contexts each capability is used.
condition: During workplace impact evaluation.

statement: Investigate physical, social, and managerial factors that both support and inhibit workplace use of learned capabilities.
condition: When explaining observed transfer.

statement: Ask whether employees can experiment with and adapt learned capabilities to job conditions, not only whether they reproduce training procedures exactly.
condition: When the job requires contextual adaptation.

statement: Require evidence that skill use helps resolve the original need, including observable changes in time, cost, resource use, employee experience, customer satisfaction, supervisor satisfaction, or other relevant results.
condition: When judging organizational impact.

statement: Examine whether new capabilities improve on prior practice, fit job tasks and expectations, are usable, are discussed with relevant others, and support the learner's career path.
condition: When assessing the utility and diffusion of training outcomes.

statement: Triangulate impact using learners, supervisors, customers, peers, subordinates, trainers, and records through interviews, questionnaires, observations, product reviews, and job-performance ratings.
condition: When resources permit multiple evidence sources.

statement: Match impact data collection to available resources, using remote surveys and interviews under tight budgets and adding site visits, focus groups, and direct observation when resources permit.
Survey all relevant outcomes even when a published or illustrative form displays only a subset, so unmeasured capabilities are not silently excluded from impact conclusions.
condition: When adapting an impact-survey template.

statement: Allow a follow-up interval suited to the target skill before surveying transfer; an extended interval may be necessary for capabilities used intermittently in community or workplace roles.
condition: When skill-use opportunities arise gradually.

statement: Do not compare a draft innovation summatively with mature instruction until formative evaluation and revision have removed its major development problems.
condition: When comparing instructional alternatives.

statement: Evaluate a mature innovation on learner performance, attitudes, instructor reactions, costs, and durability rather than on novelty or advocacy claims.
condition: After the innovation is suitable for routine use.

statement: Use an external evaluator when a product advocate's involvement would undermine confidence in an impartial judgment of worth.
condition: When summative conclusions affect competitive selection or high-value decisions.

statement: Make the ultimate summative question whether the intervention solved the original problem and met the goals for which it was developed, not merely whether it outperformed another product.
Collect the design products from front-end analysis through assessment, strategy, materials, learner results, and revision so reviewers can trace decisions across the complete process.
condition: When documenting an instructional-design project.

statement: Novice designers can benefit from beginning with direct instruction because it forces them to take responsibility for every instructional component they create.
condition: When learning materials development before designing teacher-led or highly interactive formats.

statement: Use a common authentic performance task across the target population and have a cross-organizational evaluation team identify recurring patterns in the work.
condition: When conducting a curriculum needs assessment from learner products.

statement: Derive instructional goals directly from documented deficiencies in authentic learner work rather than from the content sequence of an existing course.
condition: When learner artifacts reveal a common performance gap.

statement: Split a broad performance need into coherent instructional units when its dimensions require distinct capability development.
condition: When a single need combines separable bases for performance such as purpose and structural complexity.

statement: Define the intended learner range explicitly and include both component-skill instruction and integrated application when the audience is heterogeneous in current performance.
condition: When learners share a goal but vary substantially in prior skill.

statement: Describe all expected performance settings, even outside the formal learning environment, so instruction can prepare learners for school, community, and job applications.
condition: When a general capability should transfer across subject or social settings.

statement: Verify that required learner devices, software, connectivity, delivery platforms, and access locations actually exist before basing the instructional plan on them.
condition: When technology mediates instruction or performance.

statement: Analyze entry skills, prior knowledge, ability, learning preferences, content attitudes, delivery attitudes, motivation, attitudes toward the organization, and overall group heterogeneity as distinct learner characteristics.
condition: When constructing a learner profile for design.

statement: Triangulate learner characteristics from performance samples, records, teachers, target learners, and tryout learners rather than relying on a single informant.
condition: When gathering learner-analysis evidence.

statement: Prior exposure to content does not demonstrate current mastery; compare curriculum history with authentic performance evidence.
condition: When learners have previously received related instruction.

statement: Do not assume an attractive delivery technology will motivate every learner; add a meaningful task or product that gives varied learners a reason to practice.
condition: When learner interest in the content and organization varies.

statement: For heterogeneous and variably motivated learners, use an authentic writing or production vehicle that permits frequent short practice rather than depending solely on long assignments.
condition: When extended tasks would reduce participation or obscure component practice.

statement: Do not duplicate performance- and learning-context analyses when the same site and conditions serve both; instead document why a combined analysis is sufficient.
