condition: When learning and intended performance occur in the same context.

statement: Analyze context through managerial support, physical and technical conditions, social and learning arrangements, and available performance tools.
Account for actual equipment reliability and home-access variation, not only nominal device and network availability, when planning technology-mediated instruction.
condition: When learners depend on personal devices or connectivity.

statement: Specify the training and support responsibilities of instructors who must operate the delivery system, orient learners, manage progress, and provide elaboration beyond direct instruction.
condition: When a learning platform mediates individualized instruction.

statement: Use a design-evaluation chart to align each subordinate skill with its performance objective and parallel test items.
condition: When reviewing the internal consistency of an instructional design.

statement: Assess an integrated terminal performance with an authentic product and explicit quality criteria while also using focused items to diagnose subordinate capabilities.
condition: When the goal combines several subordinate skills into a product.

condition: When developing multiple measures of the same subordinate skill.

condition: When a terminal performance depends on progressively different uses of knowledge.

condition: When converting an instructional analysis into a course sequence.

statement: Anchor motivation in a learner-managed authentic product and use a high-interest example to demonstrate the practical effect of the target skill.
condition: When introducing a unit whose component skills contribute to a larger project.

condition: During preinstructional orientation.

statement: Keep an entry-skills test short, cover every identified prerequisite, and route learners who lack prerequisites to targeted preparatory instruction before the main unit.
condition: When a prerequisite set is known and individualized delivery is available.

statement: Combine an authentic whole-goal pretest scored with a rubric and lesson-level objective pretests that diagnose component mastery.
condition: When instruction targets both integrated performance and subordinate skills.

statement: Administer a lesson's component pretest immediately before that lesson and use its results as a future branching mechanism for learners with prior mastery.
condition: When the delivery system supports adaptive paths.

statement: Administer an embedded assessment immediately after each lesson to diagnose subordinate-skill problems and convert it into rehearsal with corrective feedback.
Use learner-facing labels such as review or recap when they accurately describe low-stakes diagnostic and rehearsal assessments and reduce unnecessary test anxiety.
condition: When the assessment supports learning rather than a high-stakes decision.

statement: Use both an objective posttest for component mastery and an authentic performance posttest for integrated application.
condition: When the goal combines basic knowledge with production.

statement: Review authentic work with both validating praise and specific improvement suggestions from the instructor, author, and peers.
condition: When a product can benefit from multiple relevant perspectives.

statement: Assess authentic products repeatedly over time and retain products with reviews in a portfolio to monitor growth across related capabilities.
condition: When the domain develops through sustained production.

statement: Have learners adapt a teacher-provided checklist for self- and peer-review and remind them to use it while drafting and editing.
condition: When quality criteria can serve as a reusable memory aid.

statement: Promote transfer by reusing a previously learned problem-solving process in a new context and by giving learners an authentic purpose beyond compliance with an assignment.
condition: When planning follow-through activities.

statement: Build examples and practice around topics learners have identified as interesting, while keeping each example set coherent enough to form a meaningful sequence.
condition: When contextualizing basic skill instruction.

statement: Use related nonexamples to clarify the target concept without diverting into full instruction on the nonexample categories.
condition: When nonexamples help establish a discrimination.
exception: Teach the contrasting category directly when it is itself an objective.

statement: Remove irrelevant clues from discrimination practice so learners must use the defining feature targeted by the objective.
condition: When superficial cues could make classification easier than the intended skill.

statement: Explain why each example or response is correct or incorrect rather than merely restating the rule or supplying the right answer.
condition: When feedback is intended to strengthen discrimination and transfer.

statement: Treat generating original content as a different capability from recognizing correct examples and provide dedicated production practice.
condition: When learners move from selected-response tasks to writing or creating.

statement: Begin original production with familiar topics so idea generation does not overwhelm initial practice of the target form.
condition: When content generation is not the primary new skill.

statement: In open-ended production feedback, show several valid solutions and state explicitly when multiple correct responses are possible.
condition: When a task admits different correct products.

statement: Give learners a short criteria list for evaluating their own products during creation rather than waiting for postsubmission scoring.
condition: When criteria can guide ongoing performance.

statement: Allocate sessions explicitly to motivation, entry assessment, whole-goal pretest, component instruction, integration review, higher-level selection, and posttest.
condition: When translating a strategy into an instructional schedule.

statement: Combine individualized primary delivery with teacher-led or small-group examples, nonexamples, practice, and customized feedback for learners who need additional support.
condition: When a web-based unit serves learners with varying needs.

statement: Plan a constructivist environment from a documented performance need, a clear goal and focal objective, an explicit learning rationale, a pedagogical model, and an authentic scenario.
condition: When choosing project-based learning for complex application.

statement: Use a project that gives learners a natural reason to practice, meaningful control over planning and production, and an audience for the resulting work.
condition: When designing a student-centered authentic environment.

statement: Embed component-skill practice and assessment within the authentic performance context rather than separating all formal instruction from project work.
condition: When direct instruction supports a larger constructivist project.

statement: Activate and apply previously learned problem-solving steps—clarify, seek alternatives, test, refine, and monitor—in the new project context.
condition: When prior problem-solving strategies are entry skills for the project.

statement: Have learners judge authentic work from multiple perspectives, including technical form, content, audience interest, aesthetics, appropriateness, values, policy, and legal constraints.
condition: When an authentic public product has multiple stakeholders and quality dimensions.

statement: Establish governance for a learner-published environment before launch, including legal obligations, audience access, authoring and moderation roles, deletion authority, and permissible content.
condition: When learner products are disseminated through an institutional platform.

statement: Seed the project with representative models and job aids while allowing participants to identify additional resources as new production needs emerge.
condition: When the full set of project needs cannot be known in advance.

statement: Separate project-management teams from creative content teams so operational roles and domain production both receive explicit ownership.
condition: When an authentic project requires both production management and individual creative work.

statement: Let learners select and rotate management roles for interest and breadth of experience while requiring every learner to perform the core target role.
condition: When optional project roles surround an individually required goal performance.

statement: Have learners monitor project progress and create or reassign teams as evolving work exposes uncovered tasks.
condition: When project requirements emerge through production.

statement: Map each project need to the appropriate delivery platform, research tool, content specialist, teacher, designer, technologist, or other organizational contributor.
condition: When planning resources for a cross-disciplinary project.

statement: Engage learners by examining a credible prior product, discussing benefits, inviting a decision to proceed, and connecting learners with authentic organizational stakeholders.
condition: When launching a school or workplace project.

statement: During exploration, have learners investigate required team structures, audience needs, comparable-product conventions, distribution choices, and possible content.
condition: Before learners settle a project design.

statement: Have teams explain planned tasks, collaboration choices, and product ideas to peers and relevant adults so assumptions become visible and reviewable.
condition: During project planning.

statement: Plan for project capabilities to be elaborated through use in other courses, home, community, and employment contexts.
condition: When broader transfer is intended.

statement: Combine scaffolding from models, coaching, questioning, peer tutoring, and individualized formal instruction rather than relying on unguided project work.
condition: When learners lack some skills needed for a complex project.

statement: Assess an authentic project at the individual draft, team prepublication, natural audience-response, and longitudinal portfolio levels.
condition: When both individual growth and collective product quality matter.

statement: Keep internal skill codes in design documents for traceability but omit them from learner-facing assessments when they add no instructional value.
condition: When assessment items are mapped to an instructional analysis.

statement: Select entry-assessment items from the design table in a format compatible with rapid administration and feedback, without weakening skill alignment.
condition: When deploying an entry test in a learning platform.

statement: Let learners choose an authentic pretest topic within the goal's domain, provide explicit performance criteria, and require self-review before submission.
condition: When measuring integrated production before instruction.

statement: Use a subordinate-skill pretest to decide whether to split or branch learners for subsequent instruction.
condition: When mastery scores show materially different learner needs.

statement: Use examples and nonexamples that jointly expose every defining feature of a target category rather than varying only one obvious surface cue.
condition: When teaching a concept defined by multiple attributes.

statement: Use closely matched examples and nonexamples in practice so learners must discriminate the relevant feature rather than topic or wording.
condition: When practicing concept classification.

statement: After embedded review, tell learners to inspect feedback, reason about errors, and revisit the relevant instruction when needed.
condition: When an online environment permits immediate review and navigation.

statement: Construct posttest items from the same strategy prescriptions and format as pretest and embedded items while using new examples.
condition: When parallel tests measure the same objectives.

statement: Summarize test data simultaneously by learner, item, and objective so individual deficits and shared design problems can be distinguished.
condition: When analyzing small-group formative results.

statement: Compare objective mastery at pretest, embedded rehearsal, and posttest to detect initial status, immediate learning, and retained performance.
Report mastery patterns for the whole group and separately for learners with and without prerequisites.
condition: When prerequisite status may moderate instructional effectiveness.

statement: Use attitude questions tied to motivation, objectives, entry behavior, tests, instruction, practice, feedback, and overall usefulness so dissatisfaction can be located within the strategy.
condition: During formative learner-reaction analysis.

statement: Include open-ended prompts with attitude scales because learner comments can reveal that an apparently clear lesson omitted the authentic product or repeated already-known content.
condition: When interpreting otherwise favorable ratings.

statement: Probe reports that a pretest is unclear because learners may be describing lack of knowledge rather than defective vocabulary or directions.
condition: When clarity ratings conflict with other evidence.

statement: Treat split learner opinions about the amount or usefulness of examples as evidence for adaptive support rather than assuming one fixed quantity fits everyone.
condition: When some learners report too many examples and others too few.

statement: Base each revision decision on converging evidence from appropriate tests, observation, questionnaires, and interviews, and record the sources in a revision matrix.
condition: When formative findings affect instruction.

statement: Add prerequisite instruction when learners without entry skills succeed during guided practice but fail to retain the capabilities at posttest.
condition: When embedded and delayed results diverge by entry-skill status.

statement: Remove objectives from required instruction and assessments when evidence shows broad prior mastery, while branching learners who need review.
condition: When pretest and learner-reaction evidence agree that content is redundant.

statement: Align practice and assessment contexts more closely with the promised authentic project when learners experience a mismatch between unit framing and actual tasks.
condition: When formative feedback identifies a relevance gap.

statement: Delay use of distractors that require an untaught discrimination, then reintroduce them after the contrast has been taught.
condition: When distractor difficulty is unrelated to the current objective.

statement: Supplement selected-response mastery with authentic idea generation and product-writing practice because objective posttest success may not transfer automatically to creation.
condition: When the terminal goal is generative.

statement: Provide research support and monitor individual authorship in writing teams so collaboration assists rather than replaces each learner's target performance.
condition: When learners collaborate on authentic production.

statement: An established design process is worth retaining when it reliably and efficiently produces the intended learning results.
condition: When the process demonstrably produces the intended results reliably and efficiently

statement: A process can be logical, comprehensive, manageable, and easy to report on without consistently producing strong learning products or productive teams.
condition: Across the instructional-development settings observed by the author

statement: Managerial visibility into phases and progress is not sufficient evidence that an instructional-development process is effective.
Evaluate an instructional-development process by learning-product quality and team effectiveness as well as by delivery and status-reporting performance.
Producing a deliverable does not establish project success when the deliverable requires major post-launch revision and the development effort exceeds schedule or budget.
condition: When judging the success of an instructional-development project

statement: Effective instruction should help learners become more capable, not merely expose them to facts.
An instructional-development process should support creativity, exploration, and revision of ideas as the work unfolds.
condition: When the desired learning product requires inventive design work

statement: Define the instructional product and outcomes sought before defining the process or tools intended to create them.
condition: Before selecting or formalizing an instructional-development process or tool

statement: Instructional experiences should be meaningful to learners, memorable after instruction, and motivating enough to sustain engagement and application.
Treat improved performance as the primary instructional goal and use knowledge acquisition as a means to that end.
condition: When designing instruction intended to improve workplace or academic capability

statement: Translate desired product characteristics into explicit criteria for selecting and tailoring the development process.
condition: Before selecting or tailoring an instructional-development process

statement: Self-directed e-learning requires especially careful design because the product must supply explanations, remediation, and motivation that an instructor might otherwise provide.
condition: When learners use an e-learning product without an available instructor
exception: When a capable instructor or facilitator is available to diagnose and fill product gaps

statement: Judge a development model successful only when it handles real constraints while also improving learner skill, behavior, program manageability, and sustained value.
condition: When evaluating an instructional-development model

statement: Instruction overloaded with text and content commonly leaves too little room for learning experiences and practice.
Design for learner attention because reduced attention weakens focus, willingness to practice, and the opportunity to learn.
condition: When learners must practice to acquire a new skill or behavior

statement: A poor learning experience can create aversion not only to the course format but also to its subject and to the learner's own perceived capability.
condition: When instruction is persistently boring or frustrating

statement: Mandatory low-quality instruction can signal that an organization does not value learners' time, undermining trust and participation.
condition: When learners are required to complete instruction they perceive as wasteful

statement: Allocate enough project effort to exploring alternative learning designs rather than concentrating most resources on upfront analysis.
condition: When analysis would otherwise consume resources needed for design and development

statement: Upfront analysis is inherently vulnerable to missing data, misleading evidence, and changing conditions, even when substantial resources are spent on it.
condition: When analysis precedes design and development by enough time for the situation to change

statement: Do not diagnose a delivery medium as ineffective from examples whose instructional design may be the actual cause of failure.
condition: When interpreting outcomes from existing learning programs

statement: Phase approvals based on specifications or storyboards do not guarantee a shared understanding of the eventual learning product.
condition: When approvers and developers must infer the experience from documents rather than experience a prototype

statement: Document-centered approval processes tend to suppress promising learning ideas that are difficult to describe or require exploration before evaluation.
condition: When approval is required before exploratory development can begin

statement: Use early experimentation and learner involvement to evaluate design ideas before committing to costly development.
condition: When alternative learning experiences can be represented and tried before full production

statement: Information presentation followed by retention testing does not establish that learners can perform better or apply knowledge appropriately.
condition: When assessment measures recall or comprehension without authentic performance

statement: A fixed amount and pace of content will predictably under-serve some learners and overload others because learning needs and rates vary.
condition: When all learners receive identical content on an identical schedule

statement: Consensus processes that resolve stakeholder concerns by adding every requested fact tend to produce excessive content rather than focused instruction.
condition: When each content item has an advocate and exclusion criteria are weak

statement: Select content according to the learning experience and required performance rather than treating coverage and completeness as the dominant goal.
condition: When deciding what information belongs in an instructional product

statement: Stakeholder assumptions about what learners know, need, prefer, and will do are often inaccurate.
condition: When assumptions have not been checked with representative learners

statement: Involve representative learners in shaping and testing a learning solution instead of relying solely on organizational beliefs about them.
condition: When representative learners can participate without compromising safety or validity

statement: Experience as a learner is not a substitute for professional instructional-design knowledge, skill, and practice.
Use contrasting examples of weak and excellent instruction to help project leaders recognize the value of professional design.
condition: When leaders or dominant stakeholders assume that content presentation alone will change performance

statement: A design process should make alternatives visible and balance stakeholder influence so reaching agreement does not displace the goal of effective learning.
condition: When team dynamics include dominant voices or conflict-avoidant participants

statement: Familiarity and apparent manageability can sustain confidence in an outdated process even when the process aggravates project problems.
condition: When organizations assess a process through tradition and comfort rather than outcomes

statement: Identify consequential project variables and obtain sufficiently accurate data about them before committing the design in a direction that is costly to reverse.
condition: Before high-cost instructional-development commitments are made

statement: A broad process label conveys little operational guidance when organizations apply materially different sequences, adaptations, and deviations under that label.
condition: When a named process has many incompatible implementations

statement: Define a process crisply enough that teams can understand, evaluate, select, and apply it consistently.
condition: When comparing or institutionalizing development processes

statement: Frequent informal iteration and deviation from a formally linear process indicate that iteration is a practical necessity rather than an optional variation.
condition: When practitioners repeatedly revise work across nominal phase boundaries

statement: Select a development process partly for the product characteristics it encourages, because process choices shape experimentation, learner involvement, practice, and content emphasis.
condition: When choosing among plausible instructional-development processes

statement: A simple process diagram can conceal major differences in step effort and the actual dependencies among tasks.
condition: When diagram elements use uniform visual weight and show only a nominal sequence

statement: Treat an initial instructional design as an informed approximation that must be tested rather than as a specification proven correct by analysis.
condition: When project-specific variation prevents design success from being predicted confidently

statement: Use short, low-cost design steps so evaluation can guide correction before one approach consumes the project's resources.
condition: When the design contains material uncertainty

statement: Continuous early evaluation reduces the risk and cost of discovering design mistakes near the end of development.
condition: When design decisions can be evaluated incrementally

statement: A list of generic activities does not define a useful process unless it also specifies sequences, criteria, and interdependencies.
condition: When materially different workflows contain the same named activities

statement: Choose the model that best enables the organization to meet project constraints and maximize desired performance outcomes.
condition: When selecting an instructional-development model for a specific organization

statement: Adapt a development model continuously as organizational needs evolve and credible better practices emerge.
condition: When changed needs or demonstrated practices make the current model less effective
exception: When the current process already meets requirements and produces the intended quality

statement: Process models trade applicability against operational clarity: narrower models fit fewer contexts, while highly general models provide less guidance.
Do not preserve familiar routines merely to make process administration predictable when those routines do not improve learning-product quality.
condition: When revising an established development process

statement: Define the desired learning product clearly before selecting and optimizing the process intended to create it.
condition: Before process selection and project-specific optimization

statement: E-learning is a demanding proving ground for design because its strategy is explicit in software and cannot rely on unplanned instructor adaptation.
condition: When evaluating whether a process can produce a self-contained learning product

statement: Evaluate learning events against four outcomes: meaningfulness, memorability, motivation, and measurable performance.
condition: When assessing an instructional product

statement: Make new learning meaningful by connecting it to learners' current knowledge, abilities, real situations, and recognizable performance gaps.
condition: When introducing new content or skills

statement: Unfamiliar terminology and unlearned prerequisite skills impede learners from making sense of instruction.
condition: When instruction assumes concepts or skills the learner does not yet possess

statement: Distribute practice over time rather than massing it when durable retention is important.
condition: When the learned performance must be recalled later

statement: Use appropriate mnemonic and novel elements to strengthen attention and memory rather than relying on repetition alone.
condition: When such elements reinforce rather than distract from the target performance

statement: Learning depends on what learners attend to, think about, and practice, all of which are influenced by motivation.
Design learning events to preserve and increase existing motivation because motivation can shift upward or downward during instruction.
condition: When learners must retain and apply the learning beyond course completion

statement: Do not infer skill acquisition from content exposure alone when the learner's performance has not been observed.
condition: When determining whether instruction produced the intended capability
exception: When direct observation is infeasible and a validated proxy is used

statement: Effective learning events emphasize observable behavior, sufficient practice, and performance feedback.
condition: When the objective is development of a performance skill

statement: Non-interactive instruction can be sufficient when material is mostly familiar, the task is simple and clearly demonstrated, success criteria are understandable, and failure is safe.
condition: When all of the stated familiarity, simplicity, clarity, and safety conditions hold
exception: When the task is complex, challenging, unfamiliar, or dangerous to practice incorrectly

statement: Use deliberately constructed learning events when many people must reach a defined proficiency in a complex or challenging task efficiently.
condition: When unguided observation, imitation, or trial and error would be too slow or inconsistent

statement: Interactive learning events are strongest when context, challenge, activity, and feedback are all present and mutually reinforcing.
condition: When designing interactive instruction
exception: A specific event may legitimately omit a component when its learning purpose does not require it

statement: Represent context as a vivid, explorable situation containing the conditions learners must interpret, rather than merely as a written condition statement.
condition: When situation recognition is part of successful performance

statement: Missing context weakens learners' ability to recognize when to act, transfer training, and see personal relevance.
condition: When correct performance depends on interpreting situational cues

statement: Use frequent, authentic challenges during learning rather than postponing challenge until a high-stakes end test.
condition: When learners can safely make choices and inspect results during instruction

statement: Adjust challenge difficulty to the learner's current progress and provide assistance when requested or evidently needed.
condition: When challenge difficulty can be adapted or support can be offered

statement: Give learners early opportunities to perform activities resembling the real post-training task instead of making reading or listening the dominant activity.
condition: When the instructional objective is real-world performance

statement: Conventional multiple-choice questions are weak substitutes for authentic performance because they present options the learner may not generate in practice and commonly emphasize facts.
condition: When the target performance requires producing, diagnosing, deciding, or acting without supplied options
exception: When recognizing among supplied alternatives is itself the target performance

statement: Prefer realistic consequences as feedback so learners can observe what their actions or inactions would produce.
condition: When consequences can be experienced or simulated safely
exception: When actual consequences would create unacceptable harm

statement: Delay evaluative judgments long enough for learners to inspect consequences and assess their own choices.
condition: When learners can productively interpret consequences without immediate correction
exception: When delay would reinforce a dangerous error or leave a beginning learner pointlessly stuck

statement: Provide more corrective support to beginners, then shift toward consequence-based feedback as proficiency grows.
condition: When learners progress from novice toward independent performance

statement: Make guidance and relevant information readily accessible during challenges without exposing the correct answer so easily that learners bypass engagement.
condition: When learners request or need help during a challenge
exception: When immediate disclosure is necessary to prevent harm

statement: Describe instructional designs in terms of context, challenge, activity, and feedback to make design assumptions comparable and communicable.
condition: When teams need to explain, compare, or review learning-event designs

statement: A development process is at risk when it formalizes process details without a functional language for defining and evaluating the instructional design being built.
condition: When teams cannot communicate the intended learning experience clearly

statement: Use an iterative process that exposes the emerging product early and continuously so evaluation and correction occur while changes are inexpensive.
condition: When design decisions contain uncertainty or stakeholder interpretation matters

statement: Keep early iterative steps small, experimental, and easy to reverse instead of perfecting work that depends on untested assumptions.
condition: During early design and development cycles

statement: Involve representative learners early and repeatedly because they can reveal needs and reactions that late-stage review cannot correct cheaply.
condition: When representative learners are available for safe participation

statement: Make collaboration operational by defining responsibilities, decision authority and timing, documentation, communication, and process flow.
condition: When multiple team members or stakeholders contribute to a project

statement: A team can perform worse than an individual when weak coordination, leadership, process clarity, or unresolved disagreement creates bureaucracy and indecision.
condition: When collaboration is poorly coordinated or managed

statement: Plan within known constraints while preserving capacity to address unexpected issues.
condition: When setting scope, schedule, staffing, and budget

statement: Do not pursue perfection as a project goal; direct limited resources toward improvements with the greatest expected learning impact.
condition: When possible refinements exceed available time or budget

statement: Produce a usable product early enough to leave time for late discoveries that materially improve impact.
condition: When development can be staged into increasingly complete versions

statement: A manageable process must support completion within expectations, prediction of change impacts, and attainment of quality criteria; task visibility alone is insufficient.
condition: When evaluating process manageability

statement: Select instructional-development models that are iterative, collaborative, efficient and effective, and manageable.
condition: When comparing candidate process models

statement: An integrated design-development cycle is best suited to a small, unified team that does not depend on separately scheduled specialist production.
condition: When selecting the simpler SAM1 form
exception: When scale, specialist production, programming, or contracted development prevents integration

statement: Begin and end each iteration with evaluation, including rechecking whether the original situation data remain accurate and sufficient.
condition: During successive design-development cycles

statement: Limit a first iteration to objectives, representative treatments, progress measures, and representative content rather than full breadth, depth, or polish.
condition: During the first cycle of an iterative instructional project

statement: Initial evaluation should establish the required performance change, current capability, existing-program problems, success measures, constraints, available resources, and decision authority.
condition: At the start of an instructional-development project

statement: A rough initial design should connect goals and behavioral objectives to performance appraisal, practical media, and several visualized treatment ideas.
condition: When preparing a design for early discussion and testing

statement: Build low-fidelity prototypes with just enough representative content and media to test learner activities and communicate the design idea.
condition: During early development iterations

statement: Test early designs with learners and, for instructor-led delivery, conduct a mock segment before the design appears finished.
condition: When learners or prospective instructors can participate

statement: Treat an iteration that clarifies needs or invalidates an initial idea as progress, and repeat the cycle when its evaluation requires it.
condition: When evaluation shows that the current direction should not advance

statement: Deliberately create a materially different alternative design to counter attachment to the first plausible idea.
condition: When the team has evaluated only one design direction

statement: Expand prototypes across representative content types before applying a favored treatment to the full body of content.
condition: When content varies in ways that may require different instructional treatments

statement: Test the intended delivery mechanism early, including instructor handoff, interface behavior, or communication-system compatibility as applicable.
condition: When delivery depends on instructors, software interfaces, or communications infrastructure

statement: As confidence accumulates, stop reopening issues that have been adequately resolved and shift later iterations toward development.
condition: When evidence from prior iterations supports the decision and no material new issue has appeared
exception: When development reveals evidence that invalidates a resolved design decision

statement: After representative coverage has been achieved through a few iterations, real use will often yield more valuable improvement evidence than another pre-release cycle.
condition: When all content areas and treatment types have been represented and the product is usable
exception: When unresolved high-risk issues make release unsafe or unfit for purpose

statement: Maintaining an early usable version reduces interruption risk because the project can still deliver something valuable if work stops unexpectedly.
condition: When each iteration leaves a coherent usable increment

statement: Prefer tangible prototypes over specification documents for review because stakeholders can inspect the same concrete design rather than divergent interpretations.
condition: When a learning experience can be represented functionally

statement: Invest only enough in early work to validate the direction and plan on some initial artifacts being discarded.
condition: During cycles intended to test assumptions and alternatives

statement: Excessive early refinement creates sunk-cost pressure that makes teams retain poor design choices.
condition: When substantial time and effort have been invested before the direction is validated

statement: Set a stopping discipline for iteration, release a sufficiently strong product, and reserve remaining resources for improvements informed by actual learner use.
condition: When further refinements threaten completion without resolving a critical defect
exception: When release would expose learners or the organization to unacceptable risk

statement: Separate iterative design from iterative development when scale, specialized production, programming, contracting, or organizational gates make a fully integrated cycle impractical.
condition: When design and final production cannot be performed by one integrated team and cycle
exception: When a small unified team can design and build the final product together

statement: Begin preparation with readily available information about prior efforts, current programs, content, constraints, key roles, the performance opportunity, and success criteria.
condition: Before the first collaborative design session

statement: Perform analysis in the context of candidate solutions rather than attempting exhaustive research before any design exists.
condition: When exhaustive backgrounding would be incomplete and consume resources before relevant questions are known
exception: When a known safety, legal, or feasibility issue must be resolved before any design activity

statement: Use prototype review to discover specific questions about why a proposed design may fail, then target further analysis to those questions.
condition: After an initial solution has made assumptions testable

statement: Bring the design team and key stakeholders together early to review background information, expose pre-existing solution ideas, and generate initial alternatives.
condition: At the start of iterative design for a multi-stakeholder project

statement: Use rapidly built disposable prototypes to stimulate brainstorming, clarify priorities, expose assumptions, and align team values.
condition: During an early collaborative design workshop

statement: Create detailed cost, schedule, staffing, scope, risk, and communication plans only after initial designs provide a concrete basis for estimating production.
condition: When initial prototype designs are available
exception: When a preliminary range is required earlier for authorization to explore

statement: Treat performance objectives without a prototyped solution as major planning risks because their production effort remains weakly understood.
condition: When estimating the remaining project after an initial design workshop

statement: Design for breadth before depth so the team understands the range of content and the distinct instructional treatments it may require.
condition: Before refining any one treatment to final detail
exception: When the project has a demonstrably narrow and homogeneous content set

statement: Prototype each materially different type of content or treatment rather than every individual objective or content instance.
condition: When project size makes a prototype for every objective impractical
exception: When an objective introduces a unique high-risk interaction or treatment

statement: Obtain key decision-maker review of evolved prototypes before committing to full development, especially when those people missed later design work.
condition: Before full production begins

statement: Build a design proof with representative polished components, final production tools, and the intended platform to test both design viability and the production system before alpha development.
condition: At the start of iterative development for a design with material production or platform risk

statement: Treat alpha as a complete implementation of approved designs, with all content and media present and every known unresolved issue explicitly listed.
condition: When entering full-product validation after design-proof approval

statement: Validate alpha against the approved design for style, graphics, text, sequence, completeness, clarity, and function.
condition: During alpha evaluation

statement: Schedule a distinct correction-and-validation cycle after alpha because even carefully produced complete versions almost always contain errors.
condition: For a production process using alpha and beta release candidates

statement: A beta candidate should incorporate alpha corrections and contain no known functional errors before it is considered for final release.
condition: When promoting an alpha build to beta

statement: Include representative target learners as well as subject experts in beta evaluation.
condition: When validating a release candidate for instructional use

statement: Do not designate a release as final until every identified release-blocking problem has been corrected and the candidate performs within approved parameters.
condition: Before rollout implementation

statement: After rollout, evaluate whether the targeted behaviors changed and whether those changes produced the intended performance result.
condition: Once learners have had a realistic opportunity to use the instruction

statement: Set and maintain explicit client expectations for timeline, budget, treatment alternatives, and review and approval obligations throughout the project.
condition: When leading an instructional project for a sponsor or internal client

statement: Project status reporting is insufficient leadership; the leader must identify alternatives, negotiate trade-offs, shape expectations, and coordinate the team.
condition: When the leader is accountable for the learning solution rather than only administrative tracking

statement: Adjust activities, designs, and project variables without allowing each adjustment to stall or reverse overall momentum.
condition: When new information or constraints require in-process changes
exception: When evaluation shows that continuing the current direction would compound a fundamental error

statement: A project leader should resist premature perfection, superfluous modifications, and indecision while maintaining focus on behavior change and learner needs.
condition: When change requests or discussion threaten delivery without a proportional learning benefit

statement: Build schedule contingencies for predictable availability, rework, and emergency risks rather than planning against uninterrupted execution.
condition: When establishing the project schedule

statement: Communicate schedule conflicts in terms of both resolution options and the client's expectations for how the situation will be handled.
condition: When an event threatens the agreed schedule

statement: Instructional negotiation should identify design alternatives and their project impacts, then secure informed agreement from sponsors, stakeholders, and team members.
condition: When an existing treatment is ineffective or a new opportunity emerges

statement: Challenge additions presented as simple improvements when they require unplanned time, budget, content, development, or media.
condition: When a proposed change exceeds the project's remaining resources
exception: When the change corrects a release-blocking defect or unacceptable risk

statement: Prefer releasing a sufficient product with resources reserved for rapid corrections over delaying for speculative perfection and exhausting the budget.
condition: When remaining changes are discretionary and the product is fit for responsible use
exception: When known defects make release unsafe or unable to achieve its core purpose

statement: Treat actual product use as an evaluation cycle that can generate better evidence for subsequent design and development than forecasts alone.
condition: After a fit-for-use release reaches representative learners

statement: Resolve newly discovered needs with the smallest effective intervention, including existing resources, scope separation, or a previously explored design alternative.
condition: When an unanticipated requirement arises during development
exception: When the new need is central to the agreed performance objective and requires a redesigned core treatment

statement: Require every design, media, budget, and schedule decision to remain traceable to the intended learner behavior change.
condition: Throughout instructional design and production

statement: Assign explicit responsibility for learner advocacy because budget, schedule, and production pressures otherwise tend to displace learner needs.
condition: When project pressures have stronger representation than learners do

statement: Use learner review and feedback to challenge the evolving design and recheck it against documented learner expectations.
condition: Throughout iterative design and validation

statement: Assess project leaders across instructional design, project management, consulting, and persuasion rather than assuming competence in one area covers all four.
condition: When selecting or preparing a leader for an iterative instructional project

statement: Limit initial backgrounding to a thorough review of information that already exists and is readily accessible, then gather harder evidence as specific design questions emerge.
condition: During preparation for an iterative project
exception: When a critical safety, legal, or feasibility fact must be established before design begins

statement: Document the project's starting direction and stakeholder expectations even though later evidence may justifiably change them.
condition: During initial backgrounding

statement: Initial project discovery should cover sponsorship, the performance change, audience, ongoing support, task frequency, delivery options, prior attempts, existing content, constraints, and available contributors.
condition: Before generating initial instructional approaches

statement: Supplement document review with brief interviews and direct observation of target performance when those methods can expose assumptions or constraints.
condition: When learners, supervisors, trainers, experts, or the work setting are accessible

statement: Early discovery may gain more value from identifying who holds needed knowledge than from trying to obtain every answer immediately.
condition: When time for initial backgrounding is limited

statement: Elicit the sponsor's view of the performance gap, desired involvement, treatment expectations, and definition of project success before collaborative design begins.
condition: During sponsor discovery

statement: Check whether performance could be improved through tools, communication, incentives, supervisor capability, or another non-course intervention before assuming training is the solution.
condition: When diagnosing an organizational performance need
exception: When the need has already been shown to arise from a learnable knowledge or skill gap

statement: Make budget and deadline constraints explicit before ideation so proposed approaches remain feasible.
condition: Before scoping and prototyping candidate solutions

statement: Do not commit to a ballpark cost or schedule before plausible approaches have been explored enough to estimate their resources responsibly.
condition: When project scope and treatment are still undefined
exception: When only a clearly qualified exploratory range is being requested

statement: Surface strongly held organizational values and preconceptions early so the team can address them at deliberate points rather than encounter them as late objections.
condition: Before the project commits to a treatment or medium

statement: Use a carefully prepared, concentrated collaborative workshop to align key players, expose decision authority, agree on success measures, and rapidly cycle through alternative prototypes.
condition: At the start of a substantial multi-stakeholder design effort
exception: When the project is small enough for the same alignment and rapid cycles to occur within a unified working team

statement: Select an early design team for complementary contributions to ideas, support, information, direction, creativity, and performance insight rather than for content expertise alone.
condition: When forming a collaborative instructional-design workshop

statement: A subject expert may lack learner perspective, work-context knowledge, or design creativity despite being essential for content accuracy.
condition: When the expert is close to the subject but not to current learners or target performance

statement: Choose the subject expert who can support both accurate content decisions and productive collaboration, rather than treating any available expert as interchangeable.
condition: When multiple experts could represent the content

statement: Represent budget authority, performance ownership, supervision, content, current and recent learners, project management, instructional design, and prototyping in early design decisions.
condition: For a substantial project where these perspectives materially differ
exception: When one participant credibly covers multiple roles or a role is irrelevant to the project

statement: Engage brand, legal, human-resources, delivery, and technology authorities early enough to prevent late blockers, but structure their participation so compliance review does not dominate creative design.
condition: When these functions can constrain the eventual product

statement: Keep the core brainstorming group small enough for every participant to speak, be heard, respond, and tell relevant stories.
condition: During a high-participation creative design session
exception: When facilitation is deliberately structured to support effective parallel participation in a larger group

statement: For a conventional Savvy Start, six or seven active participants is generally a practical upper range for preserving full participation.
condition: When discussion, storytelling, and whole-group response are the main collaboration methods
exception: When facilitation design enables equivalent participation at a larger scale

statement: After the initial workshop, distinguish a task-focused working team from a support, review, and approval team rather than carrying every stakeholder into daily design work.
condition: When the initial stakeholder group is larger than the group needed for ongoing production

statement: Define each working, support, review, and approval responsibility explicitly and secure the person's availability and commitment before relying on it in the plan.
condition: When forming post-workshop project and support teams

statement: Schedule milestone reviewers for specific dates because reviewer availability is a direct dependency of project schedule and budget.
condition: When approval gates or specialist reviews are required

statement: Require support-team members to respond promptly and consider perspectives outside their own role because unresponsiveness or role rigidity can cripple an iterative project.
condition: When cross-functional support is required throughout the project

statement: Use an agenda to keep a creative workshop moving toward decisions and artifacts without suppressing discussion and divergent ideas.
condition: When the session combines brainstorming with time-bound project outcomes

statement: Open the workshop by aligning on the process, desired outcomes, constraints, and relevant examples, and close it by agreeing how work will continue.
condition: When structuring an initial collaborative design workshop

statement: Adapt a workshop agenda to project conditions only after considering which prototypes, decisions, or risks the shortened activity will leave uncovered.
condition: When time or availability forces agenda changes

statement: Begin each work period with a process and progress review, end with a wrap-up, and include breaks that preserve cognitive energy and prototyping time.
condition: During a multi-day intensive design workshop

statement: Frame organizational goals in behavioral terms and connect them to learner success measures, constraints, prior efforts, and available delivery capabilities before prototyping.
condition: During the goals-and-constraints portion of early design

statement: Brainstorm learning events around what learners must do, what will motivate them, and what should happen before, during, and after the event.
condition: When generating candidate instructional treatments

statement: Repeat a rapid brainstorm-build-review cycle several times instead of ending the workshop after the first prototype.
condition: When workshop time permits evaluation of successive alternatives

statement: Plan representative-user testing while prototypes are still easy to change.
condition: During or immediately after the initial design workshop

statement: Map objectives to candidate treatments visibly, leave unresolved cells explicit, and assign ownership for analyzing the missing objectives.
condition: When the workshop cannot design every objective fully

statement: Decide early how performance will be assessed and tracked, including reporting, compliance, accessibility, access, and security requirements.
condition: Before the instructional architecture and production plan are finalized

statement: Compare alternative media approaches by their advantages, limitations, and fit to the desired experience before fixing look-and-feel preferences.
condition: When media choices materially shape the learning treatment

statement: Conclude early design by confirming the continuation process, feedback method, remaining cycles, responsibilities, and current project risks.
condition: At the end of an initial design workshop

statement: When removing or shortening workshop activities, make compensating substitutions that preserve the group's ability to make sound design decisions.
condition: When ideal workshop time, resources, or attendance are unavailable

statement: Retain a concise opening review of the iterative method, performance goals, and strong relevant learning examples even when the workshop is shortened.
condition: When customizing the initial design workshop

statement: Prepare the collaboration space, prototyping tools, display surfaces, technology, and background materials before the session so ideation can immediately become visible artifacts.
condition: Before an in-person rapid-prototyping workshop
exception: When equivalent remote collaboration tools and materials are prepared instead

statement: Focus the session on completing decisions and prototypes rather than giving every participant equal airtime on every topic.
condition: During a time-bounded collaborative design workshop

statement: Establish ground rules that require constructive, concise input, make timely dissent visible, permit changed minds, protect psychological safety, and authorize time control.
condition: At the start of a collaborative design session

statement: Teach participants that early work should advance in small steps, may be discarded productively, and must be checked with representative learners.
condition: When participants are unfamiliar with iterative prototyping

statement: Explain only the process detail participants need for their current role rather than burdening temporary workshop members with every later-phase task.
condition: When some attendees will not participate in later project phases

statement: Restate and validate the learning goal with the whole design group because initial discovery may reflect biased sources or invalid assumptions.
condition: At the beginning of collaborative design

statement: Continually test creative decisions against the agreed learning goal and success criteria so feasible embellishments do not displace useful outcomes.
condition: Throughout brainstorming and design
exception: When new evidence justifies revising the goal itself

statement: Allow the initial goal to be reconsidered during early iteration, but agree on a stable goal before advancing into detailed design.
condition: When prototyping reveals that the original goal may be wrong or incomplete

statement: Assess the organizational learning environment for motivation, prior reactions, equipment, work conditions, instructor capability, bandwidth, support, and policy constraints before finalizing delivery.
condition: When determining whether a proposed learning solution can succeed in its operating environment

statement: Review prior learning and performance-improvement efforts, including efforts on other topics, to reuse approaches that fit the organization and avoid repeating failures.
condition: During project backgrounding

statement: Evaluate previous efforts as systems that include instruction, incentives, mentoring, job aids, field experience, and other behavior supports rather than reviewing courseware alone.
condition: When investigating what previously changed or failed to change performance

statement: Use stories from recent learners, instructors, and supervisors to reveal situational detail that formal summaries omit.
condition: When examining past learning experiences and subsequent performance

statement: Ask recent learners what was easy, difficult, useful, unnecessary, engaging, and transferable to work, and make the setting safe enough for candid answers.
condition: When recent learners participate in discovery

statement: Convert divergent stakeholder views of good instruction into explicit, agreed acceptance criteria rather than designing from personal likes and dislikes.
condition: Before candidate treatments are judged
exception: When consensus is impossible, the authorized decision maker must state the required criterion

statement: Separate delivery criteria such as schedule, budget, coverage, rollout, and complaint volume from evidence that learner and organizational performance improved.
condition: When defining project success

statement: Define how instruction's effect on needed abilities and behaviors will be measured before designing the treatments.
condition: Before detailed instructional design begins

statement: Distinguish a skill gap, in which learners cannot perform, from a performance gap, in which they can perform but do not.
condition: When diagnosing the cause of insufficient performance

statement: Use instruction as a solution component when needed ability is missing; seek noninstructional causes and interventions when people already have the ability.
condition: After determining whether the gap is one of skill or performance
exception: When both ability and environmental or motivational barriers contribute and a combined intervention is needed

statement: Map current behavior to desired behavior and keep only gaps directly associated with the agreed project goal in scope.
condition: When translating a broad performance problem into instructional goals

statement: Investigate probable causes of problem behaviors before assuming that replacing those behaviors requires instruction alone.
condition: After target problem behaviors have been identified

statement: Create a skills hierarchy that links target complex behaviors to prerequisites down to abilities the audience already possesses.
condition: Before designing learning events for a complex performance

statement: Use a skills hierarchy to expose project magnitude, narrow scope, and identify prerequisite skills shared by multiple higher-order performances.
condition: When organizing the instructional target

statement: Do not automatically sequence instruction from the lowest prerequisite upward when doing so would begin with the least meaningful or interesting material.
condition: When sequencing content from a skills hierarchy
exception: When a prerequisite truly must be mastered before the learner can safely or meaningfully attempt the target task

statement: Cluster prerequisites that support several higher-order skills so instruction can be modular and avoid redundant treatment.
condition: When a skill hierarchy contains shared dependencies

statement: Use the initial design workshop to discover governance, decision authority, cost, constraint flexibility, information gaps, and team fit, not merely to create prototype ideas.
condition: When assessing whether the project is ready for iterative design

statement: Repeat or regroup the initial workshop when critical information, participants, or the proposed solution prove inadequate.
condition: When the first workshop exposes a faulty premise or cannot answer readiness questions

statement: Treat early abandonment or redirection as risk reduction rather than failure when it prevents investment in an unsuitable project or solution.
condition: When rapid discovery invalidates the original project framing or approach

statement: Do not present cost, resource, or duration estimates as accurate until discovery has established enough about the problem, constraints, team, and candidate approach.
condition: When stakeholders request estimates before solution discovery
exception: When the estimate is explicitly a preliminary range with stated assumptions and uncertainty

statement: End the initial workshop by documenting discoveries, recommendations, next actions, and the ongoing support expected from participants.
condition: Before handing work to the continuing project team

statement: Use tangible prototypes to align stakeholder expectations because small ambiguities in verbal or written descriptions can become major product discrepancies.
condition: When stakeholders must agree on an instructional design
exception: When the decision concerns an element that can be represented unambiguously without a prototype

statement: Use quick, inexpensive sketches for collaborative idea generation because their visible incompleteness invites contribution and reduces defensiveness.
condition: During divergent exploration of design possibilities

statement: Use sketches primarily to generate ideas and functional prototypes primarily to test the feasibility and experience of promising ideas.
condition: When choosing the fidelity of an iterative design artifact

statement: Do not move directly from sketches to production planning when timing, transitions, media, or interaction create design questions that words cannot resolve.
condition: For technology- or media-enhanced learning experiences

statement: Evaluate interactive learning by experiencing functional behavior because even expert designers can mispredict how an imagined interaction will work.
condition: When the quality of the design depends on interactivity, timing, or media integration

statement: Redraw rough sketches freely because visible revisions and restarts help the team distinguish ideas worth retaining from those worth abandoning.
condition: During early iterative ideation

statement: Prefer several fast prototypes over one refined prototype and implement only the key interactions needed for comparison.
condition: During early feasibility testing of alternative designs
exception: When a single high-risk concept must be isolated before alternatives are meaningful

statement: Preserve a visibly rough style in early artifacts so reviewers infer low investment, disposability, and openness to alternatives.
condition: When the artifact's purpose is collaborative exploration rather than specification

statement: Finding design problems and opportunities through prototypes before high-cost development can reduce total correction cycles, cost, and elapsed time.
condition: When prototype findings are acted on before full production

statement: Use repeated prototype review as part of analysis because it synthesizes content, instructional approach, stakeholder values, expectations, and technology into testable choices.
condition: When determining what learners need and how those needs might be met

statement: Alternate divergent idea generation with convergent combination and elimination until one or a few sufficiently tested concepts remain.
condition: During iterative concept selection

statement: Treat a quick prototype as an experiment on a serious design option, not as a draft that is presumed to advance into the final product.
condition: During early and intermediate design iterations

statement: Limit prototype content, art, prose, and functionality to what is needed to expose and discuss the target interaction.
condition: When an early prototype is intended to remain inexpensive and disposable
exception: When a specific fidelity dimension is itself the uncertainty being tested

statement: Avoid polishing early prototypes because visual refinement can attract admiration, hide instructional weakness, and increase reluctance to discard the concept.
condition: When appearance is not the design question being evaluated
exception: When stakeholders cannot assess a critical design issue without a targeted level of visual fidelity

statement: Address stakeholder concerns about future polish with existing finished examples rather than diverting early cycles into custom appearance prototypes.
condition: When superficial concerns prevent reviewers from focusing on core functionality
exception: When appearance is a genuine high-risk requirement that needs its own planned prototype

statement: Increase prototype fidelity by phase: use crude artifacts for ideation, functional artifacts for interaction testing, and integrated polished samples for design-proof validation.
condition: Across the lifecycle from brainstorming to production validation

statement: Simplify or modularize a simulation when environmental richness overwhelms the core decisions or actions learners need to practice.
condition: When prototype evaluation shows contextual complexity obscuring the target skill
exception: When managing the environmental complexity is itself part of the target performance

statement: Make prototype disposability explicit and minimize investment so attachment does not suppress exploration of stronger alternatives.
condition: During early design exploration
exception: When a later-stage prototype intentionally validates production-quality attributes

statement: Commit in advance to building several alternative prototypes even if the first receives an enthusiastic response.
condition: When the team has not yet compared materially different design concepts
exception: When a safety, legal, or feasibility constraint leaves only one viable concept and that constraint has been verified

statement: Force at least one prototype to avoid reusing the first design's central ideas to counter anchoring and expose alternatives that incremental revision would miss.
condition: When creating a second design alternative

statement: After genuinely distinct alternatives have been tested, a later prototype may synthesize their strongest elements or confirm that an earlier design was best.
condition: When multiple independent design directions have already been evaluated

statement: A prototyper must combine rapid technical construction with careful listening, synthesis of group criteria, instructional-design judgment, and willingness to discard work.
condition: When selecting or developing someone for the prototyper role
exception: When an instructional designer partners closely enough to supply the design judgment

statement: Do not automatically assign the strongest production developer to prototyping because habits that protect production quality may impede speed, roughness, and disposability.
condition: When selecting a rapid prototyper
exception: When the developer can deliberately switch from production discipline to exploratory shortcuts

statement: Permit implementation shortcuts in disposable prototypes that would be unacceptable in production code, provided they do not invalidate the design question being tested.
condition: When the artifact will not become production software and speed is essential
exception: When the shortcut changes the behavior, performance, accessibility, or feasibility under evaluation

statement: Choose prototyping tools for fast creation and revision of the intended experience, and ensure the prototyper is proficient before the collaborative cycle begins.
condition: Before an iterative design session

statement: Interactive e-learning prototypes need enough working timing, controls, animation, and input behavior to reveal whether the experience matches the design intent.
condition: When evaluating an interaction whose suitability cannot be inferred from static drawings

statement: Template-driven rapid-development tools can narrow the instructional paradigms a team considers even while increasing construction speed.
condition: When templates or presets embody a limited range of interaction patterns

statement: Evaluate whether a tool's affordances are silently choosing the instructional approach, because unrepresentable possibilities may go unconsidered.
condition: When selecting or using a prototyping tool

statement: Use linear presentation tools cautiously for prototyping individualized interactive experiences because their native structure can force the concept toward slides and transitions.
condition: When the intended learning experience depends on non-linear interaction
exception: When the tool can represent the key interaction faithfully and the prototyper can revise it rapidly

statement: Allow the prototyper to fill minor unspecified details needed to visualize a design while preserving the group's intended question and approach.
condition: When rapid construction encounters gaps in vague or conflicting directions
exception: When the missing decision is central enough that filling it would test a different concept

statement: A prototyper should implement the group's concept before advocating a personal alternative, then present the alternative separately for comparison.
condition: When the prototyper disagrees with the team's selected idea
exception: When implementing the idea would be unsafe, unlawful, or outside the agreed test scope

statement: Prototype a disputed idea fairly enough that its strengths and weaknesses become visible through evaluation rather than authority or argument.
condition: When the idea is plausible and inexpensive to test
exception: When testing it would create disproportionate cost or risk

statement: Alternate short periods of brainstorming and prototyping so dead-end ideas receive little investment and feedback remains concrete.
condition: During rapid collaborative design

statement: Prototype small representative content segments before trying to design the entire product, then consider how validated segments combine into larger events.
condition: When early alternatives are still being explored
exception: When system-level integration is itself the first critical uncertainty

statement: Favor active opportunities to learn and apply skills over adding content whose necessity has not been demonstrated.
condition: When content competes with time for meaningful learner activity
exception: When omitted content is required for safe, accurate, or successful performance

statement: Introduce additional content when activities and contexts show it is needed; otherwise eliminate it or make it available as reference support.
condition: When deciding the disposition of content not selected for core learning events

statement: Keep early design discussion centered on learning experiences and the learning they promote rather than on fine content nuances.
condition: During divergent, high-level design cycles
exception: When a content nuance materially changes safety, correctness, or the target performance

statement: Optimize early brainstorming for a quantity of distinct high-level paradigms rather than thorough refinement of one final design.
condition: Before the team has converged on a design direction

statement: Use prototypes as a safe sandbox for making and recognizing mistakes early, before those mistakes become expensive in development or harmful in use.
condition: When design mistakes can be represented without real-world harm

statement: Brainstorm only representative objectives, contexts, challenges, activities, and feedback opportunities during the initial session; expected omissions should be completed later.
condition: When available workshop time cannot cover full design breadth and detail

statement: Give the designer and prototyper a short, interruption-free construction interval, then reassemble the full group at a preset time for review.
condition: During a rapid in-session prototyping cycle
exception: When the group can construct the artifact collaboratively without slowing synthesis

statement: Experienced large teams may use parallel prototyping groups to keep ideation and construction moving concurrently.
condition: When the team is large, experienced, and capable of coordinating parallel alternatives
exception: When the group is new to the process or parallel work would fragment shared understanding

statement: Keep a rapid prototyping unit to one broadly skilled person or a small team with clear leadership, design, and construction responsibilities.
condition: When assembling a prototyping unit for a short cycle
exception: When the artifact requires a specialist whose contribution cannot be simulated

statement: Build enough of a classroom prototype to enact the activity and enough of an e-learning prototype to witness key learner inputs and system responses.
condition: When deciding the minimum functional scope of a prototype

statement: A rough incomplete prototype is sufficient when it enables the group to choose whether to continue, revise, or try another approach.
condition: When the current decision concerns design direction rather than final quality

statement: Respond to muted or indecisive prototype feedback by presenting a materially different alternative rather than forcing premature consensus.
condition: When review reactions do not provide a clear direction

statement: Keep initial-workshop prototype reviews brief and oriented toward alternatives and project discovery; allow deeper reviews as later prototypes address finer design decisions.
condition: When setting review depth across successive phases

statement: Walk reviewers through intentionally missing or nonfunctional prototype elements without defending the design or supplying commentary learners would not receive.
condition: When skeletal elements prevent reviewers from following the intended experience

statement: Capture all review reactions first, then evaluate them against learning objectives as design flaws, content errors, or prototype misunderstandings.
condition: During prototype evaluation

statement: Use prototype review to re-examine learner conditions, delivery assumptions, support availability, content volatility, and even target outcomes.
condition: When a concrete candidate solution makes background assumptions testable

statement: Step back during every prototype evaluation to decide whether the proposed solution remains appropriate, rather than blindly building successive versions.
condition: At each evaluation boundary

statement: Use recent and representative learners to challenge design assumptions because expert teams cannot reliably reproduce a novice's knowledge and reactions.
condition: When the prototype can be experienced by members of the target population

statement: During learner review, explain incompleteness only as needed and preferably after it causes a question so the learner experiences the prototype as authentically as possible.
condition: When an incomplete prototype is reviewed by representative learners
exception: When withholding an explanation would cause pointless floundering or invalidate the review

statement: Schedule learner checks throughout design and development: use early reviews for fundamental treatment decisions and later reviews for wording, instructions, media, interface, navigation, and feedback.
condition: Across an iterative project lifecycle

statement: Set project goals iteratively through several design-prototype-evaluation cycles, then stabilize clear outcome objectives before detailed design and major development.
condition: When early exploration may reveal a more valuable or feasible performance target
exception: When a fixed external mandate makes the target non-negotiable

statement: Write behavioral objectives with an observable performance, the conditions of performance, and a criterion for successful performance.
condition: When defining what instruction must enable and how success will be assessed

statement: Express cognitive or affective goals through observable manifestations rather than relying on verbs such as know, understand, think, or appreciate.
condition: When the goal must be measured or validated

statement: Use an objectives-by-treatments matrix to show which instructional designs address each objective and which design work remains unresolved.
condition: When planning treatment coverage across a multi-objective product

statement: Reuse an instructional treatment across objectives when it remains appropriate after adapting its context and content.
condition: When multiple objectives require the same kind of learner activity
exception: When objective-specific conditions or criteria require a materially different treatment

statement: Draft only enough objectives initially to select representative cases, prototype treatments, and demonstrate how the remaining matrix will be completed.
condition: During early iterative design
exception: When regulatory or contracting requirements demand a complete objective set before exploration

statement: Prototype each distinct objective-and-activity type rather than every instance that can reuse the same instructional model.
condition: When estimating the minimum set of prototypes needed for coverage
exception: When an instance carries a unique high-risk context, criterion, or interaction
