statement: Design backward from the final real-world performance learners must demonstrate in a context as close as practical to actual use.
condition: When sequencing objectives and learning events
exception: When the target performance cannot be simulated safely or ethically and a valid proxy is required

statement: From the terminal performance, work backward through prerequisite performances and remediation until reaching abilities the target audience already has.
condition: When constructing a learning sequence from performance objectives

statement: Let desired performance outcomes and selected treatments determine content requirements rather than beginning with a body of existing content to cover.
condition: When scoping instructional content

statement: Reuse existing content only when it supports the selected objectives and learning events; prior investment does not justify inclusion.
condition: When deciding whether to adapt pre-existing materials
exception: When content must be retained for legal, archival, or reference purposes outside the core instruction

statement: Clear content presentation alone is likely to be sufficient only when learners are highly motivated and performance requires little beyond knowing what to do.
condition: When the task is simple and knowledge directly enables performance
exception: When the task requires contextual judgment, complex execution, or practice

statement: Teach complex valuable tasks through meaningful context and practice rather than information presentation alone.
condition: When learners must apply information in variable real situations

statement: Concentrating instruction on a small set of key behaviors can produce greater impact than maximizing the volume of presented content.
condition: When content volume competes with contextual practice of priority behaviors

statement: Include content in core instruction only when it contributes to an objective, because extraneous presentation consumes time needed for learning and practice.
condition: When selecting content for the instructional flow
exception: When optional reference access is valuable without consuming required learning time

statement: Content created for one delivery mode is not automatically adequate for another because the new mode may require different explanations, demonstrations, learner support, and interaction.
condition: When adapting existing material to a different delivery mode
exception: When analysis shows the modes have equivalent content and support requirements

statement: More interactive and individualized products generally require more newly authored contextual, challenge, activity, and feedback content than passive products.
condition: When converting source materials into active or adaptive learning events

statement: Budget sufficient time and specialized talent to develop content in the form required by prototyped treatments, even when substantial source material already exists.
condition: When planning content development for active instructional events

statement: Interleave assessment with learning interactions so instruction can adapt, provide feedback, and reveal whether it is working.
condition: When the learning environment can observe learner responses during instruction

statement: A conventional immediate post-test may reward short-term test preparation without demonstrating durable behavior change.
condition: When post-test performance is used as the primary success measure
exception: When the test is an authentic criterion performance with demonstrated predictive validity

statement: Use delayed measures of real performance when possible because they provide more meaningful evidence of retention and application than immediate recall tests.
condition: When post-learning behavior can be observed after a suitable interval
exception: When delayed observation is infeasible and a validated authentic proxy is required

statement: Define criterion tasks from the objectives that demonstrate competency instead of constructing assessments around convenient question formats.
condition: When designing summative assessment

statement: Treat real-life behavioral change as the ultimate assessment of an instructional project's effectiveness.
condition: When the project exists to improve performance outside the course

statement: Prefer private assessment interactions when public response would add embarrassment that distorts performance or discourages practice.
condition: When individual evaluation can occur privately
exception: When public performance under social pressure is itself part of the target skill

statement: Design context, challenge, activity, and feedback so one interaction can both teach and provide evidence about learner capability.
condition: When in-line assessment can be embedded in an interactive learning event

statement: Use interaction evidence about learner strengths, weaknesses, and readiness to determine what the learner needs next.
condition: When instruction can adapt or an instructor can respond to individual evidence

statement: Meaningful individualization changes challenge, sequence, remediation, comparison, modality, or choice based on assessed needs and preferences; cosmetic personalization alone does not.
condition: When evaluating whether a learning product is genuinely adaptive

statement: Specify desired individualization early, then design the interactions and assessments needed to collect the data that adaptation requires.
condition: When an instructional product is expected to adapt to learners

statement: Use iterations to alternate between the whole solution and component detail, checking each component's contribution to the goal rather than repeating merely for polish.
condition: Throughout iterative design

statement: Cover the breadth of project content and treatment types before refining any one design deeply enough to create costly commitment.
condition: Before design fit across the complete solution is understood
exception: When an isolated high-risk element must be tested deeply to establish overall feasibility

statement: Premature depth can cause uneven refinement, inconsistent treatments, omitted essential content, overspending on minor topics, and inadequate attention to critical skills.
condition: When a team perfects one design before surveying the full problem

statement: Map how events in a blended solution synchronize and what reference, communication, and performance-support tools connect them.
condition: When the solution uses multiple delivery forms or learning events

statement: Do not expect one workshop or iteration to resolve the entire design; maintain whole-solution visibility while assigning unresolved segments to later cycles.
condition: When participants worry that early iterations leave gaps

statement: Schedule learner validation as a project dependency because skipping it for convenience often shifts rework until after introduction.
condition: When evolving designs can be tested with representative learners

statement: Define what learner interaction data, evidence of application, reports, privacy controls, and security protections the complete solution requires.
condition: Before finalizing assessment and tracking architecture

statement: Identify certification, liability, confidentiality, accessibility, interoperability, and technical-standard requirements early enough to shape the design.
condition: When the project operates in a regulated, high-risk, accessible, or integrated environment

statement: Verify that the required learning platform can collect, connect, protect, and report the specific assessment data the design needs.
condition: When an LMS or tracking system constrains implementation
exception: When an approved supplementary system can safely supply the missing capabilities

statement: Select media for its contribution to comprehension, emotion, motivation, retention, and the intended quality signal, not for appearance alone.
condition: When media choices shape the learner experience

statement: Check media choices against organizational culture, style requirements, cost, equipment, printing, bandwidth, and interaction constraints before setting stakeholder expectations.
condition: Before committing the project to a media treatment

statement: After initial design exploration reveals likely content, treatments, delivery, resources, cost, and duration, explicitly choose to fund the plan, resize its goals, or stop the project.
condition: At the post-workshop investment decision

statement: Formalize what will happen, when, by whom, and how only after exploratory design provides a credible basis for planning.
condition: When moving from initial exploration into planned iterative design and development
exception: When preliminary governance is needed to authorize the exploration itself

statement: Rank project priorities explicitly because schedule, budget, media, interactivity, content, design quality, collaboration, localization, and approval speed cannot usually all be maximized.
condition: When project constraints require trade-offs

statement: Use the ranked priorities to set shared expectations and resolve later trade-offs rather than renegotiating project values from scratch at each review.
condition: Throughout planning, design-proof review, and alpha review
exception: When material new evidence justifies changing the priorities explicitly

statement: Delay firm cost and duration estimates until backgrounding, representative prototypes, treatment coverage, and critical resource commitments have narrowed the solution range.
condition: When estimating a full instructional-development project
exception: When only a qualified preliminary range with explicit assumptions is needed to authorize discovery

statement: An objectives-by-treatments matrix improves estimation by revealing the number and depth of distinct treatments, content, and media required.
condition: When estimating production after initial design

statement: When the budget cannot support the intended solution, reduce scope to the smallest effective core or phase delivery by topic rather than spreading low quality across everything.
condition: When funding cannot be expanded to cover the full effective design
exception: When partial scope cannot produce a coherent or safe performance improvement

statement: Underestimating development cost can put the entire investment at risk by producing ineffective instruction, wasting learner time, and exhausting resources needed for correction.
condition: When the budget is fixed below what the selected effective treatment requires

statement: Do not assume learning solutions at opposite ends of a wide cost range offer equivalent effectiveness or return on investment.
condition: When stakeholders treat cost as independent of treatment capability and quality

statement: Define delivery-platform capabilities and constraints before further design commits to graphics, audio, video, animation, communication, or adaptive behavior.
condition: When remote or electronic delivery is under consideration

statement: Check hardware, network, browser, software-version, bandwidth, and continuity constraints because apparently minor platform limits can invalidate a design.
condition: When establishing technical feasibility for delivery

statement: Persistent adaptive instruction requires learner history to remain available across devices and sessions.
condition: When exercises depend on accumulated evidence of each learner's competencies
exception: When all adaptation can be completed within one self-contained session

statement: Treat access to subject experts and approvers as scheduled resource dependencies because delayed input and approvals commonly cause cost and schedule overruns.
condition: When expert content or formal approval is required for progress

statement: Do not estimate interactive content production from source material built for another delivery form because active practice and feedback require additional depth.
condition: When converting instructor-led or presentation content into interactive instruction
exception: When a content audit demonstrates that the source already contains the needed contexts, activities, responses, and feedback

statement: Plan the transition from the initial workshop group to the continuing project team, including how new contributors will learn prior reasoning and become productive.
condition: When workshop participation will differ from ongoing design and production staffing

statement: Assign authority to ensure scheduled reviews and approvals occur, rather than assuming an urgent delivery date will make reviewers timely.
condition: When reviews and approvals lie on the critical path

statement: Predefine who can approve scope and budget changes, obtain overdue decisions, or revise the schedule before problems occur.
condition: During project planning while stakeholder commitment is high

statement: Do not accept delegated decision making when an uninvolved superior retains an undocumented veto over the delegate's decisions.
condition: When an original decision maker steps back from the project
exception: When escalation and veto criteria are explicitly defined and compatible with the schedule

statement: A project plan should integrate the business need, performance gap, learner needs, instructional treatments, scope, quality, milestones, roles, decisions, communications, and issue resolution.

statement: Document both product-success criteria and process-success criteria so delivery quality and the quality of collaboration can be managed separately.
condition: When establishing acceptance criteria and project governance

statement: Product success criteria should include observable job application and the organizational support needed for learners to complete and use the instruction.
condition: When the project's purpose is workplace performance improvement

condition: When defining expectations for design and development collaboration

statement: Use the treatment matrix to show how objectives, sequence, instructional models, budget, and schedule fit together rather than documenting them in disconnected plans.
condition: When translating design discovery into a development plan

statement: Describe reusable instructional treatments functionally enough that developers understand learner inputs, system behavior, configurable elements, and available evidence or tools.

statement: Set localization as a design and resource requirement when learners differ materially in language or culture rather than treating it as a late content substitution.

statement: Let the cost of performance errors influence investment priority: high-consequence errors justify protecting instructional impact over cosmetic economy.
condition: When incorrect post-training performance carries substantial organizational or human cost

statement: A capable process can optimize within constraints but cannot make an internally inconsistent schedule, budget, scope, and quality target feasible.

statement: A classification exercise can introduce categories progressively as examples require them instead of presenting the complete taxonomy before practice.
condition: When learners can infer and apply category distinctions through examples

statement: Require learners who misclassify an item to revise the same decision until they identify the appropriate category, with feedback after each attempt.
condition: When classification accuracy is the target skill and repeated attempts do not expose harm

statement: Ask learners to justify a selected classification when the design needs evidence that the decision reflects sound reasoning rather than recognition or guessing.

statement: Before implementing a requested change, determine and approve its effects on completed work, design, content quantity, budget, and schedule.

condition: When a change does not alter budget or schedule

statement: Obtain approval for the cost of analyzing a substantial change before performing that analysis.

exception: When the analysis is already covered by an agreed change-management allowance

statement: Test with target users at the early-prototype, design-proof, alpha, and beta stages so both fundamental design and later implementation are challenged.

condition: When evaluating representative media in a design proof

condition: When reviewing representative content

condition: When evaluating feedback in a learning event

statement: Collect reviewer comments and ideas at each pause point and convert them into an explicit action plan for the next iteration.
condition: At the end of each structured or informal review

condition: When planning reviews across prototype, proof, alpha, and beta stages

statement: Evaluate appropriateness, correctness, functionality, usability, design consistency, and psychological impact as distinct quality dimensions.

statement: Review early text for scope and completeness, then defer detailed wording, terminology, grammar, tone, and cultural editing until design proof and alpha provide stable context.
condition: When scheduling text review across iterative stages

condition: Throughout design and development cycles

statement: After final acceptance, debrief the project, product, and process and preserve improvement notes for the next iteration or project.

statement: At alpha and beta, regression-check navigation, media, interaction, content, and feedback, including unusual inputs, repeat encounters, interrupted scoring, practice sufficiency, and every requested correction.

statement: Multimedia instruction is any communication that combines words and pictures with the intent of fostering learning; the term is defined by the words-plus-pictures combination, not by the delivery technology.
Multimedia instruction includes non-digital formats such as a printed textbook page carrying both prose and graphics, so a design principle for multimedia is not restricted to screen-based media.
People learn more deeply from words and pictures together than from words alone; this is the book's central thesis about multimedia learning.
Multimedia instructional design should be driven by experimental research evidence and grounded in a theory of how people learn, rather than by technology enthusiasm or educational fashion.
The third edition's design recommendations rest on 201 experimental comparisons using transfer-test performance, up from 45 in the first edition and 93 in the second.

The set of evidence-based multimedia design principles has grown from 7 (first edition) to 12 (second edition) to 15 (third edition), with embodiment, immersion, and generative activity added most recently.
The multimedia design principles are organised by the cognitive function they serve: reducing extraneous processing, managing essential processing, and fostering generative processing.

Cognitive load during multimedia learning is modelled triarchically as extraneous processing (does not serve the instructional goal), essential processing (needed to take in the essential material), and generative processing (aimed at making sense of the material).

A multimedia design principle must be applied in light of its boundary conditions — research-based constraints stating when the principle is likely or unlikely to apply — rather than as a universal rule.
Individual differences are treated as a boundary condition rather than a standalone principle: a design principle that helps beginners may not help more experienced learners.
condition: learners differ in prior knowledge of the material

statement: Boundary conditions are investigated as moderating variables spanning learner type (prior knowledge, age group), content type (subject area, level of objective), assessment type (immediate versus delayed, retention versus transfer), and media type (paper, desktop, tablet, immersive virtual reality).
Transfer-test performance is used as the primary outcome measure across the reported research because the target of instruction is meaningful learning rather than mere retention.

Scientific knowledge in education advances when findings are reproduced across a range of times and places and are integrated and synthesised, so replication is a core condition rather than an optional extra.
A growing empirical base has enabled meta-analyses of the popular multimedia design principles, which permits conclusions about what works to be drawn with higher certainty than single studies allow.

Most multimedia-learning research to date uses short-term studies with immediate tests in laboratory settings with college students, so conclusions about long-term learning in authentic training environments remain a continuing need rather than an established result.

Research emphasis has shifted from paper-based lessons toward computer-based media — narrated animation, narrated slideshows, instructional video, games and simulations, and virtual and augmented reality.

Explanations of multimedia learning are broadening beyond purely cognitive processes to include social, affective, motivational, and metacognitive processes, reflected in cognitive-affective, social-agency, and emotional-design theories.

Cognitive processing during learning can be measured with objective instruments — eye tracking, log-file data, and EEG — in addition to self-report questionnaires, and further use of physiological arousal measures is proposed as future work.
Educational practice built on a foundation of research evidence is preferable to cycles of educational fads that crest and recede.
The multimedia principle — people learn better from words and pictures than from words alone — is the guiding thesis under test, not an assumption to be taken for granted.

Multimedia learning is learning from words and pictures, while multimedia instruction is the presentation of material in both words and pictures with the intention of promoting learning; the design target is the instructional message, not the technology.

'Words' covers verbal presentation in printed or spoken form, and 'pictures' covers pictorial presentation including static graphics (illustrations, graphs, photos, maps) and dynamic graphics (animations, videos).

The definition of multimedia is deliberately restricted to two presentation formats — verbal and pictorial — because the cognitive-science research base is most relevant to that distinction; multimedia learning is more precisely dual-mode, dual-code, or dual-channel learning.
Instructional messages should be designed in light of how the human mind works, which is the underlying case for multimedia rather than any property of the delivery hardware.
Presenting material only verbally leaves the learner's capacity to process visual material unused, so purely verbal instruction under-uses the human information-processing system.

The quantitative rationale for two channels — that two channels carry more material than one, like two traffic lanes — is rejected as incomplete because it wrongly assumes the verbal and visual channels are equivalent.

The qualitative rationale is preferred: words and pictures are qualitatively different and complementary, and understanding arises when the learner mentally integrates corresponding pictorial and verbal representations.

Adding a picture is not a substitute for words; a graphic works by helping the learner understand the words, so graphics should be designed to be integrated with the verbal explanation rather than to replace it.
Deeper understanding comes from the learner's effort to build connections between corresponding words and pictures — for example, mapping a narrated step onto the matching motion in an animation.

Multimedia messages can be characterised in three ways: by delivery media (the devices used), by presentation mode (verbal versus pictorial representation), or by sensory modality (auditory versus visual reception).

The delivery-media view is rejected for instructional design because it centres the presentation devices rather than the learner; under its strictest reading a textbook or e-book would not count as multimedia at all.
The presentation-modes view is learner-centred and rests on dual-code theory (Paivio), which holds that verbal ways of representing knowledge are qualitatively different from pictorial ways.
The sensory-modality view is learner-centred and rests on the working-memory model (Baddeley), which holds that humans process sounds and visual images in qualitatively different ways.

Both the presentation-mode and sensory-modality views share the dual-channel assumption that humans process information in more than one channel, but they cut the channels differently (verbal/pictorial versus auditory/visual).

The cognitive theory of multimedia learning applies the sensory-modality view to early processing and the presentation-mode view to later processing, so which channel distinction applies depends on the stage of processing being analysed.
condition: analysing early (sensory intake) versus later (representational) processing

statement: Multimedia design can follow a technology-centred approach that starts from the capabilities of new technology, or a learner-centred approach that starts from the nature of the human cognitive system; the learner-centred approach is the one adopted.

Multimedia learning can be framed as response strengthening (drill and practice), information acquisition (delivering information), or knowledge construction (providing aids to sense-making); the knowledge-construction metaphor is the one that fits meaningful learning.

Three learning outcomes are distinguished by the retention-plus-transfer pattern: no learning (poor retention, poor transfer), rote learning (good retention, poor transfer), and meaningful learning (good retention and good transfer).

Meaningful learning outcomes depend on the learner's cognitive activity during learning, not on the learner's behavioural activity during learning, so hands-on or interactive activity is not by itself evidence of learning.

Basic research aims at a theory of learning and applied research aims at instructional-design principles; merging the two yields use-inspired basic research, in which design principles must be both theory-grounded and empirically supported.

Research on multimedia learning draws on and contributes to three distinct sciences: the science of learning (how people learn), the science of instruction (how to help people learn), and the science of assessment (how to determine what was learned).

Design principles are tested by experimental comparison: the test performance of a group learning from a lesson containing the to-be-tested feature is compared against a group learning from the same lesson without that feature.

The cognitive theory of multimedia learning is built on three cognitive-science ideas — dual channels, limited capacity, and active processing — and these are what let the theory both generate design principles and explain when they do and do not apply.

Multimedia instruction spans low-tech and high-tech alike: illustrated textbook pages, chalk-and-talk lectures, slideshow lectures, narrated animations and videos, online encyclopedia entries, digital games, simulations, and immersive virtual reality.
A technology-centred design approach starts from the functional capabilities of the technology and asks how to use them, with the goal of providing access to information.
A learner-centred design approach starts from an understanding of how the human mind works and asks how to adapt the technology to aid human cognition.

Design multimedia from the learner-centred starting point rather than the technology-centred one: adapt technology to fit the needs of human learners instead of forcing learners to adapt to the demands of the technology.
The premise of the learner-centred approach is that multimedia designs consistent with how the human mind works foster learning more effectively than designs that are not.

Media-comparison research — asking which delivery technology teaches better, such as online versus live lecture or virtual-reality game versus equivalent slideshow — is the characteristic research question of the technology-centred approach.

Twentieth-century educational technologies repeated one cycle: grand promises of revolutionising education, a rush to implement the cutting-edge technology in schools, and, decades later, largely unmet expectations.

Film, radio, educational television, and computer-assisted programmed instruction each followed the promise-implement-disappoint cycle; rigorous evaluation showed the two largest 1970s computer-based systems, PLATO and TICCIT, did not produce better learning than traditional teacher-led instruction.

The disappointing results of past educational technologies are attributed to the technology-centred approach of their promoters — the driving force was the power of the technology rather than an interest in promoting human cognition.
Strong claims that digital games and simulations will replace traditional education do not yet have strong research support, so such claims should be treated as unproven rather than established.
Asking 'what can we do with this technology?' or setting the goal as 'provide access to technology' reproduces an approach with a hundred-year record of failure in education.
Technology should complement human abilities — aiding the activities people are poorly suited to and enhancing those they are ideally suited to — rather than making people serve the machine.
Tools invented to improve thought or action are cognitive artifacts, and computer technology is a cognitive artifact with the potential to assist human cognition in previously impossible ways.

Computer use has an automation phase (replacing humans on tasks) and an augmentation phase (enhancing human performance on cognitively complex tasks); designing multimedia learning environments that promote meaningful learning belongs to the augmentation phase.
A designer's underlying conception of learning drives their multimedia design decisions, so the conception must be made explicit rather than left implicit.

Under the response-strengthening metaphor, learning is a change in stimulus-response association strength, the learner is a passive recipient of reward and punishment, and multimedia becomes a drill-and-practice reinforcement system.

The law of effect and the response-strengthening view are treated as limited rather than wrong: they can account for a contrived response in a laboratory task but not for complex conceptual learning by humans on realistic tasks.

Under the information-acquisition metaphor (also called the empty-vessel, transmission, or commodity view), information is an objective item moved from teacher to learner, the learner passively receives it, and the goal of multimedia is efficient delivery.

The information-acquisition view conflicts with the research base on how people learn complex material: learners are not tape recorders storing each word but focus on meaning and interpret material in light of prior knowledge.
The information-acquisition view is only defensible when the goal is learning isolated fragments of information; when the goal is understanding the presented material it is not helpful.
condition: the instructional goal is isolated factual fragments rather than understanding

statement: Under the knowledge-construction metaphor, multimedia learning is a sense-making activity in which the learner actively builds a coherent mental representation, the teacher acts as a cognitive guide, and multimedia acts as a sense-making aid.

Knowledge is personally constructed by the learner and cannot be delivered in exact form from one mind to another, which is why two learners given the same multimedia message can come away with different learning outcomes.
A multimedia presentation should not only present information but also guide how to process it — what to attend to, how to organise it mentally, and how to relate it to prior knowledge.
The knowledge-construction view is adopted over the other two because it fits the research base on how people learn and the goal of promoting understanding of the presented material.
Remembering is the ability to reproduce or recognise presented material and is measured by retention tests (recall or recognition), which index the quantity of learning.

Understanding is the ability to build a coherent mental representation and use the material in novel situations; it is measured by transfer tests requiring problems not explicitly covered in the lesson, which index the quality of learning.
Because retention and transfer measure different things, a design must be evaluated on transfer as well as retention; a treatment can produce good recall while leaving the knowledge inert.
Rote learning yields fragmented or inert knowledge — a collection of isolated factoids that can be remembered but not used in new situations — and shows up as good retention with poor transfer.

Meaningful learning yields integrated, transferable knowledge and shows up as good retention together with good transfer; educational experts hold that transferable knowledge is essential for success in the twenty-first century.

Conceptions of learning are shifting from memorising toward understanding, and assessment emphasis is shifting correspondingly from retention tests toward transfer tests, because easily accessible information has lowered the value of memorised facts.

Active learning must be distinguished into behavioural activity (what the learner's body does, such as hands-on interaction) and cognitive activity (what the learner's mind does, such as integrative processing).

Meaningful learning depends on the learner's cognitive activity during learning, not on the learner's behavioural activity, so multimedia should be designed to prime cognitive rather than merely behavioural engagement.

Behavioural activity by itself does not guarantee cognitively active learning: a learner can type answers into a fill-in-the-blank tutorial, or work through a highly interactive game or simulation, without being prompted to make sense of the material.

A learner who appears behaviourally passive can be cognitively active — for example by organising narrated steps into a cause-and-effect chain and generating self-explanations from prior knowledge where the presentation leaves a gap.

Well-designed multimedia instructional messages can promote active cognitive processing even when the learner is behaviourally inactive, so a 'passive' instructional method is not automatically an ineffective one.
Presenting material directly is not sufficient on its own: a long, incoherent, boring lecture or a disorganised textbook chapter is unlikely to foster meaningful learning.
condition: the presentation is incoherent or disorganised

statement: Active cognitive learning can be reached through passive instructional methods (well-designed multimedia messages) or through active instructional methods (interactive games and simulations, or prompts to use generative learning strategies such as building a knowledge map or writing a summary).
Pure applied research that identifies what works but not how or why is of limited value, because without a mechanism there is no basis for predicting the conditions under which the effect will hold.
Pure basic research that contributes to learning theory without testing predictions in realistic learning situations is likewise of limited value.

Use-inspired basic research — research designed to contribute to learning theory and instructional practice at once — is the target quadrant: it forces theory to explain learning on realistic academic tasks and tells practice under what conditions a principle can be expected to apply.

Treating basic and applied research as opposite ends of one pole is misleading; the two goals can overlap within a single study, and in the overlapping case successful basic and successful applied research are the same thing.
The science of learning asks how multimedia learning works, the science of instruction asks what works and when it works, and the science of assessment asks how to measure what someone knows.

Developing multimedia design principles is not a one-way application of psychological findings to lesson design; learning, instruction, and assessment stand in reciprocal relation and must be developed together.

The research programme deliberately narrows its scope to explanative material — instruction aimed at explaining how something works — presented in words and pictures, which bounds the domain over which the resulting principles were tested.
condition: the lesson explains how something works

statement: A multimedia design principle must satisfy two criteria: theory-grounded (derived from a cognitive theory of multimedia learning) and evidence-based (consistent with empirical research).
Theories of how people learn should be based on research evidence rather than on expert opinion, ideology, or fads.

Learning theory and research evidence stand in a reciprocal, self-correcting relation: theory generates hypotheses for experiments, incoming evidence adjusts and clarifies the theory, and accumulated evidence can force an entirely new theory.

Learning is a change in knowledge attributable to experience: the change is in the learner, it is a change in what the learner knows, and it is caused by the learner's experience in the learning environment.

The change in knowledge cannot be observed directly and must be inferred from a change in the learner's behaviour, such as test performance, so assessment design determines what learning can be detected.
Learning may involve reorganising and integrating existing knowledge rather than only adding new knowledge.

What is learned from a lesson may span five kinds of knowledge — facts and concepts (declarative), procedures and strategies (procedural), and beliefs (attitudinal) — and performance on most complex tasks requires a combination of them.

Theory-grounded practice means developing instructional methods that are consistent with how people learn; multimedia messages designed in light of how the human mind works are more likely to lead to meaningful learning than those that are not.

The cognitive theory of multimedia learning rests on three assumptions: dual channels for visual/pictorial and auditory/verbal processing, limited processing capacity in each channel, and active learning as the carrying out of appropriate cognitive processing during learning.

Meaningful multimedia learning involves five cognitive processes: selecting relevant words, selecting relevant images, organising selected words into a coherent verbal representation, organising selected images into a coherent visual representation, and integrating the visual and verbal representations with prior knowledge.

Pictures are processed mainly in the visual/pictorial channel and spoken words mainly in the auditory/verbal channel, but printed words enter through the visual/pictorial channel first and only then move to the auditory/verbal channel — so on-screen text loads the visual channel.

Extraneous cognitive processing does not serve the instructional goal and is caused by poor instructional design, so it is the designer's responsibility to remove rather than the learner's to overcome.

Essential cognitive processing is required to represent the material in working memory and is determined by the complexity of the material, so it is managed by restructuring the presentation rather than by deleting content.
Generative processing is deep processing — organising and integrating the material — and depends on the learner's motivation to exert effort, so it is fostered rather than merely permitted.
The three goals of multimedia instructional design are to reduce extraneous processing, manage essential processing, and foster generative processing; each design principle serves one of these goals.

Effective multimedia instructional messages guide appropriate cognitive processing during learning without overloading the learner's cognitive system — both halves of that constraint must hold simultaneously.
The cognitive theory of multimedia learning is being extended to include motivational processes during learning alongside cognitive processes.
The design of a multimedia environment should be compatible with how people learn, so design principles must be sensitive to what is known about human information processing during learning.

Every multimedia design decision reflects an underlying conception of how people learn, even when that theory is never stated — so an unstated theory is not an absent one and should be surfaced and checked.

A screen overflowing with multicoloured, flashing, moving words and images implicitly assumes a single-channel, unlimited-capacity, passive-processing learner, and that common-sense conception conflicts with cognitive-psychology research on how people learn.

The single-channel assumption holds that modality does not matter as long as information is presented; the unlimited-capacity assumption holds the designer's job is simply to present information; the passive-processing assumption holds learners need no guidance in organising and making sense of it. All three are rejected.

The dual-channels assumption holds that humans possess separate information-processing channels for visual/spatial and auditory/verbal material; material presented to the eyes begins in the visual channel and material presented to the ears begins in the auditory channel.

The two channels can be conceptualised by representation mode (verbal versus non-verbal, following dual-coding theory) or by sensory modality (visual versus auditory, following the visuo-spatial sketchpad and phonological loop); the two conceptualisations disagree specifically about onscreen text and background sounds.

The cognitive theory of multimedia learning adopts a compromise — the sensory-modality distinction for how material is initially taken in, and the representation-mode distinction for the pictorial and verbal models built in working memory — and further research is still needed to clarify the nature of the two channels.

Information entering through one channel may also be represented in the other — an experienced reader can convert onscreen text into sounds, and a narration can prompt a corresponding mental image — but only when the learner can devote adequate cognitive resources to the task.
condition: the learner has adequate spare cognitive resources

statement: Humans are limited in the amount of information that can be processed in each channel at one time, so a learner holds only a few images in the visual channel and a few words in the verbal channel of working memory at once.
What working memory holds is a selection of portions of the presented material, not an exact copy of an illustration or a verbatim recording of a narration.

Measured memory span averages roughly five to seven chunks with individual differences, and chunking increases the number of elements carried inside each chunk without increasing the number of chunks that capacity allows.

Because capacity is constrained, the learner must decide what incoming information to attend to, how far to build connections among selected pieces, and how far to connect them to existing knowledge — these allocation decisions are themselves part of learning.

Metacognitive strategies are the techniques for allocating, monitoring, coordinating, and adjusting limited cognitive resources, and correspond to the central-executive function in working-memory theory.

The active-processing assumption holds that humans actively engage in cognitive processing to construct a coherent mental representation: attending to relevant incoming information, organising it into a coherent structure, and integrating it with other knowledge.
Viewing learners as passive processors who file copies of experience in memory like tape recorders conflicts with the active-processing view and should not drive design.
Active learning can be understood as model building: the desired outcome is a mental model or knowledge structure representing the key parts of the presented material and their relations.

Five basic knowledge structures cover most instructional content — process (cause-and-effect chain, drawn as a flowchart), comparison (matrix), enumeration (list), classification (hierarchy), and generalization (branching tree) — and the target structure should be identified before designing the message.

Material that lacks an underlying coherent structure — a collection of isolated facts — makes the learner's model-building efforts fruitless, so structure the content before designing its presentation.
condition: the content is presented as isolated facts with no organising structure

statement: A message that presents structured material but gives no guidance on how to build that structure can overwhelm the learner's model-building effort, so coherent content and explicit structural guidance are both required.
Multimedia design is best conceptualised as assisting learners in their model-building efforts rather than as transmitting content.

Three cognitive processes are essential for active learning: selecting relevant material (attending and bringing it into working memory), organising selected material (building structural relations within working memory), and integrating it with prior knowledge activated from long-term memory.
The human mind is modelled as a dual-channel, limited-capacity, active-processing system, in direct contrast to the empty-vessel view in which learning is pouring information into an empty mind.

Three memory stores are involved: sensory memory (unlimited capacity, very brief duration, holding sensory copies), working memory (limited capacity, short duration, holding pictorial and verbal representations), and long-term memory (unlimited capacity, permanent, holding organised knowledge).
The central work of multimedia learning happens in working memory, which is where the capacity constraint binds and therefore where design decisions have their effect.
Knowledge in long-term memory must be brought into working memory to be actively used, so prior knowledge only helps when the lesson activates it.

In working memory, the incoming side is organised by sensory modality (visual images and sound images) while the constructed side is organised by representation mode (pictorial and verbal mental models plus links between them).

Meaningful multimedia learning requires five cognitive processes: selecting relevant words, selecting relevant images, organising selected words into a verbal model, organising selected images into a pictorial model, and integrating the verbal and pictorial models with prior knowledge.
The five cognitive processes do not necessarily occur in linear order; a learner may move among them in many different ways, so a design must not assume a fixed sequence.
Successful multimedia learning requires the learner to coordinate and monitor the five processes, and how that monitoring and coordination works is not yet clarified by research.
A multimedia instructional message is defined for research purposes as an instructional lesson in which material is presented in words and pictures.

Research attention has shifted from the architecture of the information-processing system (the boxes) to the learner's cognitive processing during learning (the arrows), which is where instructional design can intervene.

Selecting relevant words is the attentional process that carries some of the presented words through sensory memory into a word sound base in verbal working memory; only a subset of the message survives it.
Selection is forced by capacity limits, not by learner laziness: if channel capacity were unlimited there would be no need to focus attention on only part of the verbal message.
Selection is not arbitrary — the learner must judge which words and which images are most relevant for making sense of the presentation — so a design that obscures relevance degrades selection.
Spoken words begin in the auditory channel, whereas onscreen or printed words begin in the visual channel and may only later move to the auditory channel if the learner mentally articulates them.

It is not possible to process all parts of a complex illustration or animation, so learners compress what they take in and peripheral detail is lost — decorative elements such as background scenery, arrow styling, and texture are among the first casualties.

Organising selected words builds connections among the selected verbal pieces into a coherent verbal model; learners lack the capacity to build all possible connections and must focus on a simple structure.
Organising selected images builds connections among the selected pictorial pieces into a pictorial model in the visual channel, under the same capacity limits as selection.
The organising process reflects sense-making rather than arbitrary association — typically the construction of a simple structure such as a cause-and-effect chain that the learner finds meaningful.

Integrating word-based and image-based representations is the most crucial step of multimedia learning: corresponding elements and relations of the verbal and pictorial models are mapped onto each other and onto prior knowledge activated from long-term memory.

Integration is cognitively demanding and requires efficient use of cognitive capacity because it must coordinate visual and verbal working memory simultaneously, so a design that leaves no spare capacity blocks the step that matters most.

Prior knowledge can be used by the learner to coordinate the integration process — for instance supplying the unstated link between two presented steps — so activating relevant prior knowledge supports integration.

The five processes are applied segment by segment, repeatedly across a presentation, not once over the message as a whole: learners select, organise, and integrate the first sentence and first seconds of animation, then repeat for the next segment.

Because processing is segment-by-segment, incoming visual information can help represent the incoming words and incoming verbal information can help represent the incoming images within the same segment — the precise timing of this remains to be clarified by further theory development.

Multimedia messages should be designed to facilitate the selecting, organising, and integrating processes; messages designed in light of how the human mind works are more likely to lead to meaningful learning than messages that are not.
Presentation and sensory registration happen with little learner effort; conscious control — and therefore the designer's leverage — begins at the attentional selection step.
Sensory representations fade rapidly unless the learner pays attention to them, so material that is not attended in time is simply lost regardless of how well it was presented.

Printed text in a multimedia message creates a processing problem: the words must enter through the eyes, take a complex route through the visual channel before reaching the verbal channel, and initially compete for visual attention with the illustration being processed alongside them.

Five forms of representation mark the stages of processing: the presented words and pictures, acoustic and iconic sensory representations, selected sounds and images in working memory, organised verbal and pictorial models in working memory, and knowledge in long-term memory.
The pictorial model should be understood as a schematic spatial representation rather than as a sensory-like photographic image in the head.

Prior knowledge in long-term memory functions as schemas — structured knowledge that guides and aids the organising of incoming information — and newly constructed knowledge can be stored there to support later learning.
The central challenge for instructional design is to guide the learner's appropriate cognitive processing during learning without overloading working-memory capacity.
The triarchic model of cognitive load distinguishes three kinds of processing that all draw on the same limited cognitive capacity: extraneous, essential, and generative processing.

Extraneous processing is cognitive processing that does not serve the instructional goal and is caused by confusing or poor instructional design, so it is a defect of the material rather than of the learner.

Printing captions at the bottom of the screen while the animation runs above forces the learner to scan visually back and forth, wasting capacity; the repair is to place the words next to the portion of the graphic they describe.
If extraneous processing consumes all of the learner's available capacity, the learner cannot select, organise, or integrate at all, and the outcome is no learning — poor retention and poor transfer.
condition: extraneous processing consumes all available cognitive capacity

statement: Essential processing is the processing needed to mentally represent the presented material in working memory and is caused by the complexity of the material for that particular learner, so the same lesson imposes different essential load on different learners.
Essential processing consists of selecting relevant information and organising it as presented, producing verbal and pictorial representations that correspond to the material as given.

If learners engage mainly in essential processing and do not go further, the outcome is rote learning — good retention with poor transfer — so meeting the material is not the same as understanding it.
condition: the learner engages mainly in essential processing without generative processing

statement: Extraneous processing corresponds to extraneous cognitive load and essential processing to intrinsic cognitive load in cognitive load theory, from which the triarchic model was derived.
Generative processing is cognitive processing aimed at making sense of the presented material and is caused by the learner's motivation to learn, so it cannot be mandated by the material alone.

Generative processing consists of reorganising incoming information and integrating it with relevant prior knowledge, yielding an integrated mental model rather than a representation that merely mirrors the presentation.
Generative processing may be primed by an engaging learning environment — for example a narrator using conversational style and polite wording — rather than by adding more content.
Learners who engage in both essential and generative processing are more likely to reach a meaningful learning outcome with good retention and good transfer.
condition: the learner has capacity available for generative processing after essential processing

statement: Generative processing corresponds to germane cognitive load in cognitive load theory.

Each of the three capacity demands maps to a distinct design fault: extraneous processing to confusing physical layout, essential processing to the inherent complexity of the material, and generative processing to an unmotivating communication style — so diagnosis must identify which fault is present before a fix is chosen.

Cognitive capacity, extraneous processing, essential processing, and generative processing are all relative to the individual learner and that learner's interaction with the instructional situation, not fixed properties of the lesson.
Learners differ in working-memory capacity, in cognitive and metacognitive strategies, and in prior knowledge, so the identical multimedia lesson may overload one learner and not another.

Prior knowledge can help a learner absorb the extraneous processing caused by a poorly designed lesson and can guide essential and generative processing of familiar material, which is why individual differences in prior knowledge are a first-order design consideration.

The three demands are additive and bounded: extraneous plus essential plus generative processing cannot exceed the learner's cognitive capacity, so capacity spent on extraneous processing is unavailable for essential and generative processing.
Because the three demands are additive under a fixed ceiling, increasing one kind of processing necessarily decreases another — design is a reallocation problem, not an addition problem.

There have been calls to reduce cognitive load theory from three types of load to two; the triarchic model is nevertheless retained here for its usefulness in categorising instructional interventions and for preserving the meaningful-versus-rote learning distinction.

The three demands imply three corresponding design goals — reduce extraneous processing, manage essential processing, foster generative processing — and every design principle in the programme is classified by which goal it serves.

The extraneous overload scenario occurs when confusing instructional design drives extraneous processing that eats the capacity needed for essential and generative processing; the remedy is to reduce extraneous processing.
condition: confusing instructional design is driving extraneous processing

statement: The essential overload scenario occurs when essential processing consumes all or most of the learner's capacity, leaving too little for generative processing; the remedy is to manage essential processing.
condition: essential processing consumes all or most available capacity

statement: The generative underuse scenario occurs when capacity is available but the learner is not motivated to use it; the remedy is to foster generative processing rather than to simplify the lesson further.
condition: spare capacity exists but the learner is unmotivated to use it

statement: Five techniques target extraneous processing — the coherence, signaling, redundancy, spatial contiguity, and temporal contiguity principles.
Three techniques target essential processing — the segmenting, pre-training, and modality principles.
Techniques targeting generative processing include the personalization, voice, image, embodiment, immersion, and generative activity principles.
The multimedia principle itself can be read as fostering generative processing, because adding corresponding pictures prompts the learner to integrate words and pictures.

Across three decades of theory revision the three underlying elements — dual channels, limited capacity, active processing — have remained constant while components (sensory memory, long-term memory, additional processes) were added and clarified.
The triarchic model and the three learning scenarios exist to bridge the science of learning to the science of instruction, translating a processing model into design goals.

The theory is a useful framework for guiding instructional design, but many issues remain to be clarified through accumulating research evidence, so it should be applied as a working framework rather than as settled fact.

Research has progressed through three questions in order — what works (learning outcomes), when does it work (learner characteristics and boundary conditions), and how does it work (learning processes, including motivational, metacognitive, affective, and social processes).

A growing research base shows that some multimedia principles work best for low-knowledge learners rather than high-knowledge learners, so learner prior knowledge must be checked before applying a principle.
condition: the target audience's prior knowledge level is known

statement: Having to explain boundary conditions is what drives refinement of the theory, so an unexplained boundary condition is a theory gap rather than a nuisance.

Process measures — eye tracking, log-file analysis, and some initial brain-activity work — are used to test the proposed causal chain from the multimedia lesson to learning processes to learning outcomes to test performance.

Academic motivation is an internal learner state that initiates and maintains goal-directed behaviour; it is personal, activating, energizing, and directed, and shows up as willingness to exert effort on the selecting, organising, and integrating needed for meaningful learning.

The learner's willingness to exert effort on a multimedia lesson can be shaped by affect, beliefs, interest, and feelings of social connection, so motivational design is part of instructional design rather than separate from it.

Emotional design — such as onscreen characters who are likable and easy to identify with — is one route to incorporating affect into multimedia lessons, and this work is presented as a step rather than an established principle.
Self-efficacy beliefs — the learner's assessment of their own capability to perform the learning task — are a target of techniques tested in online multimedia lessons.

Social agency theory proposes that positive social cues, such as conversational or polite language, prime a social stance in the learner that motivates active cognitive processing aimed at understanding the lesson.

Incorporating motivational processes (affect, beliefs, interest, social connection) alongside cognitive processes is described as initial and preliminary work that modifies the basic model, not as a completed theory.
e-Learning design guidelines should be derived from empirical research rather than from opinion, fads, or folk wisdom.
Cost and time savings from e-learning are illusory unless the training quality actually improves job performance.
e-Courseware should be designed to match human psychological learning requirements, not merely to deliver content.
The multimedia design guidelines summarized in this book rest on more than twenty-five years of experimental research by Mayer's group on how words, graphics, and audio should be combined.
The same evidence-based instructional guidelines apply to both asynchronous (self-study) and synchronous (virtual classroom) e-learning.
The guidelines are stated as applying primarily to workforce learning, though the authors believe they extend to educational and academic settings.
condition: when transferring guidelines from workforce training to academic settings

statement: Evidence-based e-learning guidelines should be applied in concert as a checklist across a whole course rather than adopted individually in isolation.
Instructional methods, not the delivery medium, are what cause learning: when methods are held constant, learning outcomes are equivalent across media.

Hundreds of media comparison studies over sixty years, including a meta-analysis of distance versus classroom instruction, found effect sizes clustered near zero, failing to show any single delivery medium superior.
exception: a few studies at the tails showed large advantages in either direction, attributable to instructional quality

statement: Do not justify an e-learning investment by the medium; justify it by the instructional methods embedded in the course.

Media are not fully interchangeable in practice: each delivery environment carries tradeoffs in cost, pacing, social presence, media elements supported, and adaptivity, which should drive medium selection instead of learning-effectiveness claims.
Learning styles are a myth: they remain popular among practitioners despite a lack of supporting evidence, so instruction should not be customized to a learner's claimed style.
Useful customization means tailoring content and instructional method to the learner's work role and prior knowledge, particularly prior knowledge.

Engagement has two independent dimensions: behavioral activity (overt learner action) and psychological activity (cognitive processing that builds knowledge); only the psychological dimension produces learning.
High behavioral activity such as clicking through screens or playing an arcade-style game does not imply the psychological processing that supports learning.
Meaningful learning can occur with little or no overt behavioral response, for example when a learner attentively watches a narrated animation.
Select media elements and instructional methods that produce high psychological activity, regardless of how much behavioral activity they generate.
Activities that prime psychological engagement include self-explaining a complex visual, summarizing a lesson segment, generating an outline or drawing, and taking a practice test.

Because the human cognitive system is limited, adding an eye-catching mix of animation, sound, audio, and text to convey content typically hurts rather than helps learning: less is almost always more.

Minimalist e-learning is also a failure mode: wall-of-words screens that ignore relevant visuals, and page-turners whose only interactivity is forward and back, omit features proven to promote learning.

Any training development process must first identify the key skills that promote organizational goals and build the training around the tasks constituting those skills, rather than around an appealing technology.
Over fifty years of research indicates that unguided discovery learning rarely works; a structured lesson that provides guidance is the recommended alternative.

e-Learning goals divide into inform goals (transmit information, no specific new skill expected) and perform goals (build specific job skills), and the applicable design guidelines differ by goal type.
Perform goals split into procedural tasks done the same way each time (near transfer) and strategic tasks with no single correct approach requiring judgment and adaptation (far transfer).

Three e-learning architectures map to distinct learning views and goals: receptive (information acquisition, low interactivity, inform goals), directive (response strengthening, medium interactivity, near-transfer procedures), and guided discovery (knowledge construction, high interactivity, far-transfer strategic tasks).

Guided discovery architectures impose more mental load because learners must solve a problem and learn from the solution, making them generally more appropriate for more experienced learners and far-transfer skills.
condition: when learners already have relevant prior experience and the goal is far transfer

statement: The high structure and guidance of a directive explanation-example-question-feedback sequence makes it suitable for learners new to the content and skills.
condition: when learners are novices in the content domain

statement: A receptive lesson can only teach if it includes techniques that prompt high psychological engagement in the absence of behavioral activity.
condition: when the architecture offers no overt learner response

statement: Which design guidelines apply must be adapted to three considerations: the training goal, the learners' prior knowledge, and the development and deployment environment including technological, cultural, and pragmatic constraints.

Simulated job-realistic scenarios can accelerate expertise by compressing rare or slow real-world situations into minutes, addressing the roughly ten years of experience otherwise needed to reach high proficiency.
condition: when the required situations occur rarely or take long to resolve on the job

statement: Benefits from new instructional technologies depend on whether they are used compatibly with human cognitive learning processes; ignoring mental limitations forfeits the technology's advantage.
Online learning can be as effective as traditional classroom learning, but online learners' outcomes are affected by the quality of the instructional design and delivery.

Of the individual learner differences studied, prior knowledge of the course content exerts the most influence on learning, so instructional method should be selected against prior knowledge rather than against learning style.

The guidelines in this book were derived mostly from research with adult learners new to the course content, so some of them are less applicable when the target audience already has strong background knowledge.
condition: when the audience has substantial prior knowledge of the content

statement: For experienced learners overload is less likely, so they will probably learn effectively from either text or audio explanations of visuals, weakening load-reduction guidelines such as the modality principle for that audience.
condition: when learners are experienced in the skills being taught

statement: Psychologically optimal guidelines must still be adapted to environmental constraints: delivery platform, network and software limits, institutional technology culture, and budget, time, and management expectations.
Technology can deliver more sensory data than the human nervous system can process, and to the extent that audio and visual elements interfere with cognition, learning is depressed.
A technology-centered approach, which designs instruction around the capabilities of new technology, has repeatedly failed since the 1920s across film, radio, television, and programmed instruction.
Adopt a learner-centered approach in which the technology is adapted to how people learn; this does not rule out new technology but requires adapting it to support human learning processes.
e-Learning design should rest on two foundations together: a cognitive theory of how people learn, and scientifically valid experimental research on which features promote learning.
Learning is defined as a change in the learner's knowledge caused by experience; because knowledge change cannot be observed directly it must be inferred from a change in behavior.

Three metaphors of learning drive different designs: response strengthening (passive recipient of reward and punishment), information acquisition (empty vessel filled by a dispenser of information), and knowledge construction (active sense maker guided cognitively).
The response-strengthening view is criticized as incomplete rather than incorrect, because it does not explain meaningful learning.
The information-acquisition (empty vessel) view conflicts with evidence about how people learn because it ignores the requirement for psychological engagement.
The goal of effective instruction is not only to present information but to encourage the learner to engage in appropriate cognitive processing during learning.

Three cognitive-science principles underpin the design guidance: dual channels (separate visual/pictorial and auditory/verbal processing), limited capacity (only a few items processed per channel at once), and active processing (learning requires selecting, organizing, and integrating).

Meaningful learning occurs only when the learner engages in all three processes: selecting relevant words and images, organizing them into coherent verbal and pictorial models, and integrating them with each other and with prior knowledge from long-term memory.

Cognitive processing demand splits into three kinds: extraneous processing caused by poor instructional layout, essential processing caused by the inherent complexity of the material, and generative processing driven by the learner's motivation to make sense of it.

Diagnose an overload problem into one of three scenarios and apply the matching fix: extraneous overload calls for reducing extraneous processing, essential overload calls for managing complexity such as chunking or pretraining, and generative underutilization calls for adding engagement techniques such as practice.
Cognitive load is the burden on working memory from information that must be held plus information that must be processed; methods that reduce load foster learning by freeing capacity for rehearsal.

Instruction must support four processes in sequence: selection of important information, management of limited working-memory capacity, integration of new material with long-term knowledge, and later retrieval of that knowledge.
Use visual signalling such as a circle or colour to direct the learner's attention to the important text or graphic elements, because too many information sources compete for limited capacity.

Presenting verbal and visual information together rather than separated makes integration easier; an integrated text-and-graphic screen produced better learning than a version with text at the bottom of the screen.
Practice exercises and worked examples stimulate integration by forcing active processing that links new material to the learner's prior knowledge.

Knowledge must be encoded with job-context retrieval hooks: embed the job context in examples and practice, because knowledge stored without contextual cues often fails to transfer even when it is retained.

A trivia-recall exercise such as a Jeopardy-style fact game is a weaker design than a job-realistic scenario exercise that requires applying the same facts to a work decision, because the game risks storing facts without a job context.
Apply cognitive-load reduction techniques especially when learners are novices to the knowledge and skills being taught.
condition: when learners are novices in the target knowledge and skills

statement: e-Learning designs fail at both extremes: glitz-heavy lessons overload working memory, while text-only lessons forfeit the proven learning gain from relevant graphics.

The productive question about a technology feature such as a game or simulation is not whether it is good or bad, but whether it can be used in a way that supports selection, rehearsal, load management, and retrieval.
Most historical learning research used contrived laboratory tasks; more methodologically rigorous, theoretically grounded research situated in realistic e-learning settings is still needed.
Base design decisions on research findings and research-based theory rather than on fads, expert opinion, organizational politics, or ideology.
Reading individual research studies will not tell a designer exactly what to do; the useful input is what the preponderance of evidence says about a particular instructional feature.

Three research questions require three different methods: 'what works' calls for an experimental comparison, 'when does it work' calls for a factorial experimental comparison, and 'how does it work' calls for observation, interview, or questionnaire.
There is no single best research method; a method is useful when it fits the question asked, and the same criterion governs the choice of measure.

There is consensus among educational researchers that the correctly implemented randomized controlled experiment is the most powerful design for detecting whether an instructional method causes learning.
condition: when the goal is to determine causal treatment effects

statement: Select research whose learners, materials, and learning environments resemble your own situation before weighing its conclusions.

Three criteria mark a sound experimental comparison: experimental control (groups identical except for the one instructional feature), random assignment to conditions, and appropriate measures reporting mean, standard deviation, and sample size on a relevant learning outcome.

A comparison in which versions differ on many features at once, such as a virtual-world lesson versus a textbook differing in visuals, interaction, and novelty, cannot attribute the outcome to any one feature.

When learners self-select into conditions, as in comparisons of problem-based versus traditional medical curricula, population differences cannot be ruled out and the comparison is not sound evidence.
A study that measures only learner satisfaction ratings or discussion behaviour, without a direct learning measure, cannot support a conclusion about learning effectiveness.

A null result does not establish that a treatment is ineffective; six alternative explanations must first be ruled out: inadequate sample size, insensitive measure, inadequate treatment implementation, insensitivity of the learners, and confounding variables.
Studies with fewer than about twenty-five learners per group are suspect for detecting an instructional effect, especially when the effect is not strong.

A null result can arise from a treatment that was not implemented strongly enough, for example background music played too quietly to be heard, so check treatment strength before concluding no effect.
A treatment can show no effect because the material was already easy enough for all learners that the added feature was unnecessary.
condition: when the content is easy relative to learner ability

statement: Powerful instructional methods should yield both high mean scores and low standard deviations, indicating consistent outcomes across learners.
Treat a difference as statistically significant when the reported probability is less than .05, meaning under a 5 percent chance the observed difference does not reflect a real one.

Effect size is the mean difference divided by the standard deviation and measures practical significance: below .2 the practical impact is too small to act on, .5 is moderate, and .8 or above is large.
Adopt instructional methods whose evidence shows both statistical significance at p below .05 and an effect size of .5 or greater.

With a large sample size even a trivially small learning difference can reach statistical significance without justifying the cost of implementing the method, so practical significance must be assessed separately.
condition: when sample sizes are large

statement: Research that measures outcomes only by recall tests may not apply to workforce learning goals, where the required outcome is application of new knowledge and skills.
condition: when the training goal is job application rather than recall

statement: Prefer conclusions drawn from replicated results across multiple studies, such as those synthesized in review journals and research handbooks, over a single study.
Research conducted on children may have limited applicability to adult workforce populations; studies using college-age or older subjects are more relevant.
condition: when the target audience is adult learners

statement: Meta-analysis averages effect sizes across many experiments of the same instructional method and can additionally pinpoint the conditions under which strong effects occur, such as graphics benefiting low-knowledge learners more than high-knowledge learners.
Multimedia principle: include both words and graphics rather than words alone, converting a words-only instructional message into a coordinated words-plus-pictures presentation.

Across eleven experimental comparisons of words-plus-pictures against words alone, the multimedia group produced 55 to 121 percent more correct transfer solutions, with a median gain of 89 percent and a median effect size of 1.50, which counts as a large effect.
The evidence for the multimedia effect is stated as holding at least for some simple instructional situations, chiefly lessons explaining scientific and mechanical processes.
condition: for relatively simple explanatory content such as how a system works

statement: The multimedia principle is among the most well-established principles of learning, independently endorsed by an Association of Psychological Science review of twenty-five learning principles and by an Institute of Education Sciences practice guide.
Plan visuals together with words during job analysis and course design; do not select pictures after the text is already written.
Words alone can push learners, especially less experienced ones, into shallow processing in which they fail to connect the words to other knowledge.
condition: particularly for learners with less experience or expertise

statement: Graphics fall into six functional types: decorative, representational, relational, organizational, transformational, and interpretive.
