Not all graphics are equally helpful: minimize decorative graphics that merely adorn the page and representational graphics that only show a single object, and use organizational, transformational, and interpretive graphics that help the learner understand or organize the material.
Match graphic type to what the text is doing: use a relational graphic when the text describes a quantitative relationship and a transformational graphic when the text describes change over time.

Match graphic type to content type: facts suit representational and organizational graphics, concepts suit representational, organizational and interpretive, processes suit transformational, interpretive and relational, procedures suit transformational, and principles suit transformational and interpretive.
A graphic that decorates the screen without supporting the text, such as a photo of a general beside scrolling text on ammunition, does nothing to improve learning.
The instructional professional's job is not merely to present information but to leverage both the verbal and pictorial processing channels so learners can make sense of the material.
Relevant visuals are a powerful way to support psychological engagement in the absence of behavioral activity, and so are appropriate for receptive lessons.

The information-acquisition view, on which format does not matter as long as information is delivered, is judged an inadequate conception of learning and is the reason words-only design seems defensible.
Adding graphic organizers such as hierarchies, matrices, causal diagrams, or flow charts alongside text improves test performance.
The multimedia principle extends to interactive multimedia: learners in a signed-number math game learned better when feedback included a graphic number-line representation than from symbols alone.
The multimedia principle extends to examples: learners did better reading a lesson followed by video examples than the same lesson followed by text descriptions of the examples.

The multimedia principle works best for novices: in experiments on brakes, pumps, and generators, low-knowledge learners learned better from text plus illustrations than from text alone while high-knowledge learners performed equally well in both conditions.
condition: when learners have low prior knowledge of the domain

statement: Experienced learners appear able to generate their own mental images from text, which is the proposed reason they gain less from supplied graphics.
Expertise reversal effect: instructional supports that help low-knowledge learners may not help and may even hurt high-knowledge learners.
condition: when learners already have high domain knowledge

statement: Be especially careful to supplement text-based instruction with coordinated graphics for beginning trainees; more advanced learners such as experienced engineers or medical residents may learn well mainly from text or mainly from graphics.
condition: gauge the audience's prior knowledge before deciding how much graphical support to add

statement: Graphics can serve as topic organizers by mapping the relationships among lesson topics, and as lesson interfaces that provide a case-study backdrop in guided discovery designs.

Dynamic and static graphs can make invisible phenomena visible and expose relationships, for example an interactive line graph letting a learner vary cooking temperature and observe the effect on bacterial growth.
Multiple studies have failed to find animations more effective than a series of static frames depicting the same material.

In four comparisons covering lightning, ocean waves, hydraulic brakes, and toilet tanks, the static-illustrations-and-text group always outperformed the narrated-animation group, with a median effect size of .57.

Static frames plausibly beat animation because learners must mentally animate the transitions and can control the order and pace of processing, whereas animation is transient, rich in detail, and learner-paced control is lost.
Animation or video may be particularly helpful for tasks requiring complicated manual or motor skills, such as paper folding, tying knots, or completing puzzle rings.
condition: when the content is a hands-on manual procedure

statement: Static visuals appear most effective for promoting understanding of how a complex system or process works, while animated visuals appear more effective for teaching hands-on procedures.
Use static illustrations as the default graphic and adopt animation only when there is a compelling instructional rationale, since animations cost more to develop.
exception: hands-on procedural or motor-skill content, and special-effect displays that reveal otherwise invisible relationships

statement: For an explanative illustration, present a series of static frames depicting the successive states of the system rather than a lock-step animation.
condition: when the graphic explains how a system works

statement: Animation can serve an interpretive function when special effects distort reality usefully: slowing or speeding processes, changing viewpoint, cueing attention to relevant parts, or leaving motion traces.
condition: when the phenomenon is otherwise invisible at natural speed or scale

statement: Open questions about visuals remain: when animation beats a static graphic, the long-term rather than immediate effects of graphics, and the return on investment for custom-produced explanatory visuals.
Most graphics research measures learning immediately after the lesson, so evidence about the durability of visual gains is limited.
Contiguity principle 1: place printed words near the corresponding part of the on-screen graphic they describe, using a pointing line, rather than in a caption, legend, or separate text block.
Integrating text and graphics helps because it removes the visual search for which words match which parts of the graphic, freeing limited cognitive resources for understanding.
When text does not fit beside the graphic, a mouse-over or rollover text box anchored to the relevant region is an acceptable integration technique.
condition: when screen space cannot hold both the graphic and the full text
exception: not when the learner must see several text blocks at once or act on the text, because rollovers are transient

statement: On a scrolling screen, do not stack text above and graphic below so that scrolling hides one from the other; integrate them, use pop-up text over the graphic, or use a fixed display with text embedded near the element described.
Do not place feedback on a separate screen from the question and the learner's answers; carry the learner's responses forward next to the correct answers so comparison needs no paging back.
A linked reference window that covers the content it describes violates contiguity; make the linked window small, movable, or printable instead.
Do not present exercise directions on a screen separate from the screen where the actions are performed; put step-by-step directions in a movable or minimizable box on the application screen.
Do not standardize on a caption box at the bottom of the screen; relocate the text next to the visual with connecting lines, or split it into segments each placed beside the part it describes.

Do not run an animation while related printed text is displayed simultaneously, since the learner can only attend to one; present the text first and let the learner start the animation with a play button while the text stays available.

Do not number graphic elements and explain them in a legend below; place each name and description in a box near the corresponding part, using a fixed display rather than a rollover when several parts must be seen at once.
Contiguity principle 2: present spoken words and the corresponding graphic at the same time, so narration of a step plays while that step is shown.

Splitting narration and animation behind separate speaker and movie icons forces the learner to hold the words in working memory and match them to the graphic later, creating extraneous processing that crowds out deep learning.
Even a continuous presentation that narrates an orientation first and shows the graphic afterwards creates extraneous load; present the narration simultaneously with the static frames instead.
Decorative clip art added for interest is unlikely to contribute to learning and may actively detract from it under the coherence principle.
Do not separate corresponding words and pictures on the rationale that duplicate placement lets learners choose a preferred format; that reasoning rests on an inaccurate model of learning.
Bandwidth or traffic constraints do not justify separating words from pictures; the separation still costs the learner scarce cognitive capacity.

Split attention occurs when corresponding words and pictures are far apart in space or time, forcing the learner to spend limited working memory coordinating two disparate information sources; avoid designs that cause it.

Across five studies on lightning formation and car braking systems, learners with text integrated into the illustration produced 43 to 89 percent more transfer solutions than learners with the same text as a caption, a median gain of 68 percent and an effect size of 1.12.
A systematic review of thirty-seven studies found strong support for spatial contiguity with an average effect size of .72.

Spatial contiguity gains replicate beyond laboratory science lessons: in technical task training, physical-therapy practical training, single-illustration screens, and pop-up text placed beside the described part of an online heart lesson.

Eye-tracking shows successful learners alternate between reading a text portion and searching the diagram for the object described, and readers look back and forth more when words sit next to their corresponding graphic; breaking text into chunks placed beside the matching graphic part simplifies this for all learners.
Spatial contiguity may apply most strongly for low-knowledge learners and when the graphic and words are complex.
condition: when learners have low prior knowledge or the material is complex

statement: Across eight experimental comparisons involving pumps, brakes, lightning, and lungs, learners receiving temporally integrated narration and graphics generated 60 percent more transfer solutions with a median effect size of 1.30.

A systematic review of thirteen studies found strong evidence for temporal contiguity with an average effect size of .87, and learners have difficulty even when words and graphics are separated by only a few seconds.
Temporal contiguity applies most strongly when the narration and animation segments are long and when learners cannot control the order and pace of the presentation.
condition: when segments are long and learner pacing control is absent

statement: Prefer a permanent integrated text-and-graphic display over a transient rollover when the text will be referred to over time, such as exercise directions.
condition: when the learner must revisit the text while acting

statement: Modality principle: present words as audio narration rather than on-screen text whenever a graphic is the focus of those words and both are presented simultaneously.
condition: when words and the graphic they explain are presented at the same time

statement: The modality principle has the most research support of any principle in this book, and it holds especially when the presentation is complex or fast-paced and the verbal material is familiar or short.
condition: strongest when the graphic is complex, the pace is fast, and the words are familiar or brief

statement: Audio narrations must be brief and clear to be effective.

The psychological basis of the modality principle is dual-channel offloading: concurrent graphics and on-screen text both enter the visual channel and compete for the same limited visual attention, whereas speech enters the separate auditory channel so neither channel is overloaded.
The modality principle does not apply when words are presented without a concurrent graphic requiring simultaneous visual attention, because in that case the visual channel is not in competition.
exception: when there is no concurrent visual input competing for attention

statement: Keep words as on-screen text when they must remain available for memory support: technical or unfamiliar terms, words not in the learner's native language, formulas, step keywords used as organizers, and directions needed for future reference.
exception: this overrides the default preference for audio narration

statement: Implementing the modality principle may be impractical when bandwidth, sound cards, headsets, ambient noise, cost, or the need to update rapidly changing content make audio infeasible.
condition: when the delivery environment cannot support audio

statement: In a virtual classroom, suspend instructor narration at a practice screen and leave the practice directions on screen as text for reference while learners work.
condition: during learner practice in a synchronous session

statement: Virtual classroom facilitators should place text on slides for practice directions, memory support, and technical terms even while explaining graphics by voice.

Unresolved contiguity questions include how much detail belongs in graphics versus words, when printed rather than spoken words are better, and how conversational style and voice characteristics affect learning.

Modality effect: learners perform better on transfer problems when words explaining a concurrent graphic are spoken rather than shown as on-screen text; in a lightning-formation study the narration group produced more than twice as many solutions, an effect size greater than 1.

A review of twenty-one published experimental comparisons found a modality effect in every one, with a median effect size of .97, across topics from mathematics and electrical engineering to aircraft maintenance.

A broader review including unpublished sources found forty-three tests of the modality principle with an average effect size of .72, stronger for more complex material and for computer-controlled rather than learner-controlled pacing.
condition: strongest with complex material under system-controlled pacing

statement: The modality effect replicated in a naturalistic high school biology setting, which raises confidence that laboratory-derived guidelines transfer to real-world learning environments.
Eye-tracking shows learners given narration spend more time looking at the graphic, whereas on-screen text captures gaze and processing of the graphic suffers.
The modality effect is stronger for less-skilled learners than for more-skilled learners.
condition: when learners are less skilled

statement: Treat these design principles as guidance applied consistently with how the mind works, not as unbending rules to be rigidly applied in all situations.
The modality principle becomes less important when the material is easy for the learner or when the learner controls the pacing.
exception: when the content is easy or learner-paced

statement: Present words in writing when they are technical, unfamiliar, lengthy, not in the learner's native language, or needed for future reference, such as technical terms, key procedural steps, and practice directions.

Open modality questions remain: when printed words alongside a graphic help, whether concise on-screen summaries or component labels help, how to mitigate on-screen text when audio is infeasible, and whether the penalty for on-screen text fades over long-term training.
Redundancy principle 1: do not add on-screen text that duplicates the narration explaining a graphic; present the words in audio or in text, not both.
Redundant on-screen text hurts for two reasons: the eyes cannot read printed words and inspect the graphic at once, and learners spend capacity trying to reconcile the printed and spoken versions.

Across four comparisons on lightning formation, the non-redundant narration-only group produced 43 to 69 percent more transfer solutions than the group given identical redundant on-screen text, with a median effect size greater than 1.

The redundancy effect replicates in technical skills training: soldering and power-machinery control trainees given diagrams plus speech outperformed those also given duplicate printed text, with effect sizes of .8 or greater.

When duplicate text cannot be avoided, presenting it sequentially after the narration produced better test performance than presenting text and narration at the same time, with a median effect size of .8.
condition: when both text and narration must be delivered

statement: Redundancy hurt whether the duplicate text appeared sentence-by-sentence with the narration or all at once on the slide, with effect sizes of .72 and .63 in a fast-paced system-controlled online lesson.

In an educational game and its virtual-reality version the redundancy penalty was much smaller, about .2, suggesting learners could partly ignore the on-screen text although it still mildly hurt learning.
condition: in game-like environments

statement: The redundancy penalty is most evident when the program is system-controlled and fast-paced, the words are familiar to the audience, and a lot of on-screen text is displayed.
condition: fast pace, system control, familiar words, high text volume

statement: Redundancy principle 2: redundant on-screen text is acceptable when there is no pictorial presentation, when there is ample time to process the pictures, when learners would struggle more with spoken than printed words, or when only a few key words are placed beside the graphic element they label.
exception: these four boundary conditions override the default omit-redundant-text rule

statement: Presenting a few key words next to the corresponding part of a graphic is signalling, which aids processing by directing the learner's attention.
Printing unfamiliar technical terms on screen can reduce processing demand because the learner no longer has to decode the spoken form.
condition: when terms are unfamiliar or technical

statement: The learning-styles hypothesis — that words should be given in both spoken and printed form so visual and auditory learners can each pick their format — rests on the information acquisition theory and lacks empirical support.

A review of research on adapting instruction to learning styles found no evidence that visualizers learn better from visual instruction or verbalizers from verbal instruction, and called the gap between the approach's popularity and its evidence striking and disturbing.
Accessibility compliance is not a valid reason to duplicate all narration as on-screen text in the same screen; meet accessibility needs without defaulting to full redundant text over graphics.
When there are no graphics on the screen, presentations with concurrent spoken and printed text produced roughly three times as many correct transfer answers as spoken text alone.
condition: when the screen carries no competing graphic

statement: Redundant text helped by 79 percent when each sentence was seen and heard before its ten-second animation clip, but this choppy sequential design is unusual and unlikely to apply to most e-learning.
condition: when text and animation are strictly alternated rather than concurrent

statement: Adding a few printed words next to the corresponding part of an illustration alongside narration significantly improved retention and did not hurt transfer, prompting a published revision of the redundancy principle to permit short adjacent text.
condition: when the printed text is short and placed beside the graphic element it labels

statement: Redundancy principle stated fully: when the message includes graphics, explain them with narration alone and omit redundant on-screen text, except where graphic information on screen is limited, the words are technical, the audience has language difficulties, or the printed words are unobtrusive.
exception: limited on-screen graphics, technical vocabulary, language difficulty, or unobtrusive printed words

statement: To meet accessibility needs without violating redundancy, default to audio describing visuals and provide an audio-off control that replaces narration with on-screen text, never offering both simultaneously.
condition: when accessibility requires a text alternative to narration

statement: Coherence principle: avoid adding any material that does not support the instructional goal, weeding out words, graphics, and sounds that are not central to it.
The coherence principle is called perhaps the single most important recommendation in the book because it is commonly violated, straightforward to apply, and has a strong impact on learning.
Seductive details are interesting but irrelevant sounds, pictures, or words added to spice up a presentation; adding them to counter boredom or dropout harms learning.
Coherence principle 1: avoid extraneous sounds in the form of background music or environmental sounds.

Background music and sounds are most dangerous when the material is unfamiliar, presented at a rapid rate, or not under learner pacing control, because those conditions already impose heavy cognitive load.
condition: when material is unfamiliar, fast-paced, or system-paced

statement: Adding an unobtrusive low-volume instrumental music loop that did not mask the narration still reduced retention and transfer by 20 to 67 percent across lightning and brakes lessons.

Combining background music with environmental sounds produced the worst outcome, with learners performing 61 to 149 percent better without them, an average gain of 105 percent and an effect size of 1.66.

Environmental sounds synchronized to the animation events showed a mixed result: no difference on the lightning lesson but a loss on the brakes lesson, so they are not a safe substitute for music-free narration.

Arousal theory — that emotion-grabbing embedded effects raise engagement and therefore learning — predicts the opposite of what the evidence shows and should not justify adding entertaining sounds or pictures.
Interest cannot be added to an otherwise boring lesson like seasoning; the argument that material must be made interesting is itself evidence that intrinsic interest is missing.

Reported uses of sound to direct attention or of music to promote deeper processing in award-winning instructional software came with no evidence of effectiveness, as did sound effects used for game feedback.
Irrelevant background speech reduced recall of read text compared with a silent environment, and both vocal and instrumental music slowed writing production without improving quality.
Coherence principle 2: avoid adding extraneous pictures and video clips, which are harmful to the extent that they interfere with the learner's sense-making.

Extraneous pictures and their captions damage learning three ways: distraction that pulls attention to irrelevant material, disruption that blocks building links among relevant pieces, and seduction that primes inappropriate prior knowledge for organizing the content.

Inserting six ten-second entertaining but topic-related video clips into a narrated lightning animation cut transfer solutions by about 30 percent, an effect size of .86 — a case where presenting more material produced less understanding.

Adding interesting captioned colour photos to an illustrated lightning passage cost about 52 percent of transfer solutions with an effect size above 1, and four follow-up experiments reproduced the loss.

The claim that a younger generation raised on high-intensity media is immune to these overload effects is rejected: the seductive-details experiments used eighteen-to-twenty-two-year-old college students.
Extraneous illustrations hurt lower-capacity learners most, who also spent more gaze time on the irrelevant images, so coherence matters most for the learners most at risk.
condition: when learners have low working-memory capacity

statement: Content that is related to the lesson topic but not to the learning objective, such as background facts about a disease in a product sales lesson, should be excluded.
Reviews of science and mathematics books found most illustrations irrelevant to the main theme of the lesson they accompanied, and purely decorative pictures are unlikely to improve learning.
Use simpler visuals with fewer details presented at one time, especially when the goal is understanding a process or principle.
condition: when the instructional goal is conceptual understanding of a process or principle

statement: Visual simplicity is ordered: a two-dimensional line drawing is simpler than a three-dimensional drawing or photo, a reviewable series of line drawings is simpler than a transient animation, and a computer-generated animation without background clutter is simpler than a full video recording.
Learners studying a heart lesson with text and simple drawings understood the system better and made more integration inferences than those given text and detailed drawings.

Schematic animations beat video-recorded animations on a cell-replication lesson, and the schematic group even identified realistic images accurately without having seen any; the video group appeared overwhelmed by realistic detail.
The simpler-visuals evidence sounds a cautionary note for highly realistic learning or simulation interfaces, though some learning goals may still benefit from realistic visuals.
Coherence principle 3: avoid adding extraneous words, whether added for interest, to elaborate key ideas, or to supply technical depth.
Concise narration also serves the modality principle in practice: short audio segments per screen keep learners from waiting through lengthy playback and fit limited screen space and bandwidth.
Inserting six short interesting narration segments into an otherwise silent part of a three-minute lightning animation cut transfer solutions by about 34 percent, an effect size of .66.

Seductive details made learners spend less time reading the relevant text, recall less of it, and process it more shallowly, confirming that they harm by distracting attention and disrupting lesson coherence.
Making seductive details more interesting made learning worse: students learned less from lessons with highly interesting embedded sentences than from lessons with less interesting ones.

In three experiments, learners given only a summary of five captioned illustrations using about eighty words outperformed learners given the full six-hundred-word passage, in some cases producing twice as many causal steps and twice as many transfer solutions.
Adding complementary lessons on related systems hurt learning of the target system: learners taught only about hydraulic brakes outperformed those also given lessons on caliper and air brakes.
Providing a concise summary of what learners should learn produces better learning than providing the same material plus additional complementary material.

Adding quantitative and computational technical detail to an ocean-waves lesson depressed conceptual transfer, with effect sizes of .69 computer-based and .97 paper-based, replicated with Dutch students; the detail apparently distracted from building a qualitative model.
condition: when the objective is conceptual understanding

statement: Subject-matter experts tend to push technical elaboration beyond the basics; when tempted to add words, test whether the extra verbiage is required to meet the instructional objective and weed it out if not.
The latest review found positive results for eliminating extraneous material in thirteen of fourteen experiments with a median effect size near 1.

Most coherence research used short lessons in controlled lab settings with novice learners, so whether the effect holds for longer authentic training programs and for high-knowledge learners is unresolved.

Signalling — headings, bold, italics, underlining, capitals, larger font, colour, white space, and arrows that draw attention to specific parts of the display — shows preliminary evidence of improving multimedia learning but needs more research.
There is insufficient evidence to guide the use of sound effects and music in educational games and simulations, where they may play a useful role under some circumstances.
condition: in game and simulation contexts

statement: The coherence principle does not mean lessons should be boring; learners do learn better when interested, so the task is to stimulate interest without adding material that distracts from the cognitive objective.

Distinguish emotional interest, evoked by dramatic adjuncts with little evidence of promoting deep learning, from cognitive interest, which arises when the learner successfully constructs a model that makes sense: understanding leads to enjoyment, not the reverse.
Make a lesson engaging through job-relevant examples and practice exercises and by making the benefits of the content explicit, rather than through decorative visuals, music, or interesting asides.
Before adding any sound, picture, or word, ask whether it could distract, disrupt, or seduce the learner's knowledge construction.
Personalization principle 1: use conversational rather than formal style in spoken or printed text, including first- and second-person language and active voice.
Conversational style works through social presence: social cues make the learner feel in conversation with the author, which drives deeper cognitive processing and better learning outcomes.
Do not over-use conversational style to the point that it distracts the learner; personalization works best when the amount is modest enough not to detract from the lesson.
exception: excessive personalization becomes a distraction

statement: The argument that formal style preserves seriousness rests on the information delivery view and is inconsistent with evidence that people work harder to understand material when they feel they are in a conversation with a partner.

In five out of five experiments with a botany learning game, learners given personalized conversational wording produced 20 to 46 percent more transfer solutions than those given formal wording, with all effect sizes above 1.

Very small wording changes carry the personalization effect: replacing 'the' with 'your' in eleven places in a lungs lesson produced transfer gains with a median effect size of .79 across three experiments.
Personalization gains replicate across content: a stellar-evolution multimedia lesson with added personalized comments beat the formal version on problem solving with an effect size of .71.

Implementing personalization should be a subtle change: a few first- and second-person pronouns or a friendly comment accomplishes a lot, while excessive slang or hype offsets the benefit by distracting the learner and setting an inappropriate tone.
exception: personalization can be overdone and then becomes counterproductive

statement: Consider the audience and the cognitive consequences of the script: write informally enough that learners feel they have a conversational partner, but not so informally that they are distracted or the material is undermined.
Voice principle: people learn better from narration in a human voice than in a machine-simulated voice, with effect sizes of .69 to .79 across lightning and mathematics agent studies.
Preliminary evidence favours a standard over a foreign accent, but the work is limited to one accent over a short presentation.

Evidence on narrator gender is conflicting: one line of work reports listeners prefer gender-stereotype-matched voices, while a probability-lesson study found better learning from female narrators regardless of stated preference, leading its authors to recommend female narrators at least for mathematical subjects.
How narrator gender and ethnicity affect learning across domains and learner backgrounds is not yet established and needs more work.
Phrase on-screen agent feedback politely — as a suggestion or a shared action rather than a command — since politeness preserves the learner's face and freedom of action.

Learners given a polite agent in an engineering game outperformed those given a direct agent on transfer with an effect size of .73, and the effect was significant only for students without an engineering background.
condition: when learners lack domain background

statement: In a chemistry intelligent tutor, low-knowledge learners did better with polite language while high-knowledge learners showed the reverse trend, so the politeness benefit is strongest for learners with little domain knowledge.
condition: when learners have low prior domain knowledge
exception: high-knowledge learners trended the opposite way

statement: Learners with less computer experience were most sensitive to the politeness tone of agent feedback, being more offended by direct statements and more impressed by polite ones.
condition: when learners have limited computer experience

statement: Virtual classroom instructors, whose voice is often the only channel transmitted, can apply polite conversational language as a tool to maximize the learning benefit of social presence.
condition: in synchronous instructor-led sessions

statement: Pedagogical agents are on-screen characters that guide the learning process; they may be cartoon, talking-head video, or avatar, and may speak with machine voice, recorded human voice, or printed text.

Adding a pedagogical agent improved transfer: the agent group produced 24 to 48 percent more solutions in a botany game and 30 percent more correct solutions on proportionality word problems than matched no-agent groups.

On-screen pedagogical agents do not need a realistic human-like appearance: a cartoon character performed as well as a talking-head video of a real person, and learning held with the image absent as long as the voice was heard.

Agents do need realistic human-like behaviour: a fully embodied agent using human-like locomotion, gesture, and eye-gaze produced better learning than a minimally embodied one, and learners gaze at gesturing agents as at conversational partners.

Deliver agent words as speech rather than on-screen text, in conversational rather than formal style, and with human-like rather than machine articulation — the modality, personalization, and voice effects all apply to agents.
Letting learners select an agent matching their own gender or ethnicity produced worse transfer performance than not offering the choice.

Use agents for instruction — hints, worked examples, demonstrations, explanations, and feedback — never for entertainment; a character with no instructional role, such as an inserted theme character from a popular game or movie, is not an agent and is likely to depress learning.

Recommendations on pedagogical agents are offered as suggestions from an early field rather than firm rules, since the educational value of lifelike gesture and expression is only beginning to be demonstrated.

Personalization principle 3: make the author visible by revealing personal perspective or experience, which primes social presence and deeper processing, in both synchronous and asynchronous e-learning.
Over-emphasized author self-revelation becomes a seductive detail that distracts the learner and violates the coherence principle; add just enough social cues to prime social presence and no more.

Visible-author evidence is preliminary: readers of a visible-author history lesson wrote longer more audience-sensitive essays, and non-native speakers benefited more than native speakers, but the database does not yet support widespread use.
condition: possibly strongest for learners who would otherwise lose interest

statement: Unresolved personalization questions include when personalization turns distracting or condescending, which agent features actually drive learning, whether learner type moderates the effect, and whether the benefit of conversational style or politeness fades over a long course.
Segmenting and pretraining are the techniques for managing essential processing, distinct from the coherence, contiguity, and redundancy techniques that reduce extraneous processing.
Gauge lesson complexity by tallying the number of elements or concepts and the number of interactions among them.

Complexity is relative to the audience: a linear four-step text-editing procedure with familiar icon metaphors is simple, while constructing an Excel formula is complex for someone new to spreadsheets.
condition: complexity must be judged against the target learners' prior knowledge

statement: Do not simplify complex material by omitting elements or steps, because that destroys the accuracy of the lesson; manage the complexity by segmenting instead.
Segmenting principle: break a complex lesson into smaller parts presented one at a time, each conveying only one to three steps or relations.
condition: when the material is complex for the target learners

statement: A continuous fast-paced presentation of many interrelated concepts overloads an unfamiliar learner, and missing one link breaks the whole causal chain; segmentation gives time to consolidate each link before continuing.
condition: when learners are unfamiliar with the content

statement: Implement segmenting with a short clip of roughly ten seconds and one descriptive sentence per segment, ending in a Continue button the learner presses when ready.

In three of three studies — lightning formation, a teaching-techniques video, and an electric-motor animation — segmented presentations beat continuous ones on transfer with identical content, a median effect size near 1.
The segmenting evidence is described as tantalizing preliminary evidence that still needs additional research.
Offering a pause button is not equivalent to segmenting: a study found no learning difference because most learners never pressed pause and let the animation play through.

The designer, not the learner, should determine the optimal segment boundaries: build animations that stop at a logical segment with a continue or replay button rather than relying on learner-initiated pausing.
condition: especially for novice learners, who may not make good instructional decisions

statement: Pretraining principle: provide pretraining in the names and characteristics of the key concepts before the lesson that shows how the process or procedure works.
condition: when the main lesson is complex for the audience

statement: Pretraining works by redistributing essential processing to an earlier stage: knowing component names and characteristics in advance frees capacity for building the cause-and-effect model during the main lesson.
Learners already familiar with the content area may not need pretraining because they already know the names and characteristics of the key concepts.
exception: when learners already know the key concepts

statement: To implement pretraining, evaluate whether the target material is complex for the audience, identify the key concepts, and teach them first in a short section that may include its own practice exercise.
Show pretraining parts in the context of the whole interface, equipment, or process rather than in isolation, so the individual components keep their relation to the whole environment.
In three studies on how brakes work, learners given a clickable labelled-diagram pretraining before the narrated animation outperformed those without it on transfer, with a median effect size of .9.

Pretraining generalizes to technical training: electronics troubleshooting learners did better receiving factual information before rather than within training, and electrical-safety trainees shown each component individually first beat the whole-system group with effect sizes above 1.
The pretraining effect may be strongest for low-knowledge learners, an important possible boundary condition on the encouraging but preliminary evidence.
condition: when learners have low prior knowledge

statement: Apply pretraining to the learning environment itself: start a virtual classroom session with a short orientation showing the parts of the interface followed by exercises in which each learner uses those facilities.
condition: when learners or instructors are new to the delivery platform

statement: Research on segmenting and pretraining is less developed than the other principles: how big a segment should be, where to place breaks, how to choose pretraining concepts, and how extensive pretraining must be are all unresolved.

There may be situations where learning is better when key concepts are presented inside an authentic whole task rather than as separate pretraining, so the segmenting-and-pretraining answer depends partly on learner prior knowledge.
exception: whole-task learning designs may embed key concepts in an authentic task instead

statement: Teach supporting concepts in job context: present pretraining concepts within the context of a simple instance of the real task rather than abstractly.
The multimedia principles of Chapters 4 through 10 apply to all forms of e-learning, both inform and perform goals.
Learners prefer examples over verbal descriptions: when text deliberately contradicted the accompanying examples, learners' solutions showed they relied on the examples rather than the text.
A worked example is a step-by-step demonstration of how to perform a task or solve a problem, and can target either procedural or strategic skills.

Worked examples now have evidence for strategic tasks such as constructing an argument, devising a proof, identifying design styles, electrical troubleshooting, and applying teaching principles, not only for well-structured mathematical problems.

A modeling example is a worked example in which a person demonstrates the task with commentary; cognitive models show an expert resolving a problem while interpersonal skills models show expert performance of a social task.
The borrowing and reorganizing principle holds that the main path to building knowledge in long-term memory is imitating others, which is what makes worked examples an efficient learning mechanism.
Rely more heavily on worked examples in place of some practice exercises early in learning, then transition into practice to consolidate and automate the new skills.
condition: during the initial stages of learning

statement: Studying an example leaves working memory relatively free to borrow and reorganize knowledge, whereas solving a problem consumes that capacity, which is why example-first sequencing reduces extraneous load.
Learners given four example-practice pairs instead of eight practice problems finished training almost six times faster and made fewer errors both during training and on the subsequent test.
Worked example principle 1 — fading: start with a fully worked example, then progressively remove worked steps so the learner completes more of them, ending with a full practice problem solved alone.

Worked examples can impede learning as expertise grows — an expertise reversal effect — because once the knowledge is stored an example adds no value and may conflict with the learner's own approach; experienced learners need practice to automate instead.
exception: when learners already have the relevant knowledge stored

statement: Many learners ignore worked examples or review them shallowly, so successful learning from an example requires psychological engagement, not mere exposure.
Better learners self-explain worked examples by stating the underlying principle a step illustrates, whereas shallow processors merely restate what the example did.

Worked example principle 2 — add self-explanation questions that require the learner to identify the principle or rationale behind each worked step; this both blocks bypassing the example and forces meaningful processing.
Faded worked examples with self-explanation questions produced greater learning than the same faded examples without questions, justifying the extra development and learner time.
Active observing — pairs of learners solving a problem while watching a video of a tutor helping a student solve the same problem — produced learning equal to being tutored directly.
Three conditions maximize active observing: learners solve problems as they watch, they work in pairs rather than alone, and the video model features a high-ability tutee who asks deeper questions.
Active-observing research is in its early stages, demonstrated in physics, and its transfer to other problem-solving domains and to online collaboration is not yet established.

Worked example principle 3 — instructional explanations of a worked example help only in specific conditions and can otherwise depress learning; the earlier blanket recommendation to add them was withdrawn.

Instructional explanations help in three boundary conditions: when conceptual understanding rather than problem-solving performance is the goal, when no self-explanation question demands a learner response, and with mathematical content.
condition: conceptual-understanding goal, no self-explanation question present, mathematical content

statement: Learners may invest less effort in a self-explanation question when an instructional explanation is available, so do not supply both for the same step.

Worked example principle 4 — apply the multimedia principles to examples; early research found worked examples failed to help when those principles were violated, for instance when split attention from separated text and visuals negated the benefit.

Visualized modeled examples in video or animation produced better learning of teaching principles than narrative-text examples or no examples, and the text and no-example conditions did not differ significantly.
For complex worked examples where cognitive load is highest, explaining the graphic with audio alone produced better learning than text or text plus audio.
condition: when the problem is complex

statement: Applying the modality principle can cost more load than it saves: use text, not audio, when learners must re-read steps at their own pace, such as alongside a self-explanation question or a faded example.
condition: when learners need to review the words at their own pace
exception: this overrides the audio-default for worked-example steps

statement: Make audio the default modality for steps tied to a visual, but present steps in text for learners with hearing impairments, non-native speakers, or environments without sound — placing that text close to the relevant visual.

Group worked-example steps into conceptually meaningful chunks and signal them by visual isolation, overlays, or boxes, since learners otherwise follow steps individually and miss the rationale; presenting each step on a new screen in building fashion beat showing all steps at once.
Pause a complex animated demonstration after a few steps and let the learner click continue when ready, rather than playing it as non-stop video.
condition: when the worked example is complex

statement: Knowledge of the example's cover content correlated significantly with acquiring the intended skill, so either pretrain the example context or choose illustrative content already familiar to the learners.
condition: when the example content may be unfamiliar to learners

statement: Near transfer applies steps learned in training to similar work situations, while far transfer requires adapting strategies to situations that vary each time, as in management, customer service, consultative selling, and non-routine troubleshooting.
Do not teach strategic skills as an invariant set of steps, because each work situation requires adaptation; teach a set of strategies instead.
condition: when the task has no single correct approach

statement: Far transfer guideline 1 — build at least two worked examples that vary the context while illustrating the same guidelines, since learners abstract a general principle better when they meet it in several different contexts.
condition: when the goal is far transfer of strategic skills

statement: In the classic tumor-problem experiment, only learners who had read two analogous stories from different contexts reliably reached the convergence solution; one analogue was not enough.
Examples that varied context across statistical test types produced significantly better discrimination among those test types than example sets that held context constant.
Far transfer guideline 2 — worked examples built argumentation skills only when learners had to answer self-explanation questions focused on the argumentation principles.
condition: when teaching strategic skills from modeled examples

statement: Far transfer guideline 3 — when presenting varied-context worked examples, display them contiguously such as on the same page and ask questions that force an active comparison between them.
condition: when teaching far-transfer strategic skills from multiple examples

statement: In a negotiation lesson tested by role-played performance, the version requiring active comparison of two differently-contexted examples beat both separate-example and same-page-without-comparison versions.

Combining fading with self-explanation questions is not automatically better: some studies found self-explanation questions alone produced the best learning, possibly because the combination added too much load in complex skill domains.

Whether the traditional worked-example guidelines — fading, self-explanation questions, comparison — carry over to modeling examples, and how to minimize extraneous load from their video visuals, is unresolved.

Worked examples accelerate learning only when paired with an engagement technique — fading, self-explanation questions, or active observation; which technique suits which learner and goal is not yet determined.
Practice interactions must produce both behavioral and psychological activity: a response format alone is not enough, since a mindless response supports no learning-relevant processing.
Regurgitative questions that only require recognizing facts stated in the lesson promote shallow processing; they are common because they are quick to develop, but they should generally be avoided.
The psychological effectiveness of a practice exercise matters more than its format, whether multiple choice, true-false, short answer, drag-and-drop, or simulation.
Practice time alone does not build expertise: studies of expert performers conclude practice is a necessary but not sufficient condition for high competence.

Deliberate practice has five elements: effortful exertion to improve, intrinsic motivation, tasks tailored to areas of weakness, feedback giving knowledge of results, and repetition sustained over years.
Deliberate practice targets tasks just outside the performer's current reliable range that can be mastered by concentrating on critical aspects and refining through repetition after feedback.

Expert-level performance follows targeted practice on payoff skills, not general activity: elite Scrabble players out-practised average players on Scrabble-specific study but not on unrelated word games.
Practice principle 1 — add enough practice interactions to achieve the learning objective; adding learner interactivity to a game lesson improved learning with a moderate effect size of .63.

One form of interaction is probably enough: asking learners to explain answers helped only when the agent rather than the learner made the selection, and explanations paid off only for correct answers, so strike a balance that requires processing without overloading.
The power law of practice: proficiency keeps improving with practice indefinitely but at a diminishing rate, with the greatest gains on early trials.
Most jobs do not require elite performance, so weigh the return on investment of each additional practice interaction against the proficiency actually needed.
A lesson with sixty-six practice questions produced higher test scores than the same content with twenty-two questions, an effect size of .45, for both higher- and lower-ability learners.
When uncertain how much practice to include, designers should favour more practice over less if higher achievement is an important goal.
condition: when higher achievement is an important goal

statement: Extra practice costs learner time disproportionately for lower-ability learners, who needed 75 percent longer for a roughly four-point gain, so whether that time is warranted depends on the consequences of error on the task.
Adjust the amount of practice by task criticality: include more practice for highly critical skills where the consequence of error is severe.

Over-learning showed no benefit at one week or four weeks: nine practice permutation problems produced no better retention than three, and beyond three or four problems per new concept additional same-type problems were called a very inefficient use of study time.
condition: for mathematical procedure learning measured after a delay

statement: Most over-learning experiments measured learning within an hour of practice, which is why their reported benefits do not settle the question of durable retention.

Practice principle 2 — mirror the job: begin with a job and task analysis to define the cognitive and physical processing the work demands, then build transfer-appropriate interactions that require the same responses as the work environment.
The more features of the job environment are built into an interaction, the more likely the right retrieval cues are encoded into long-term memory for later transfer.

A quiz-show style recall game reflects neither the psychological nor the physical context of the work environment and will not promote transfer, unlike a question requiring the learner to apply content to a realistic job case.

Feedback ranked tenth in influence among 138 factors affecting learning in a synthesis of meta-analyses, yet hundreds of experiments show both positive and negative effects with few consistent patterns.
Feedback effectiveness depends on the objective and task, on learner features including prior knowledge and self-confidence, and on how and when the feedback is formulated and presented.

Practice principle 3 — give explanatory feedback that says whether the answer is right or wrong and adds a succinct explanation, rather than corrective feedback alone; a missed question is a teachable moment.
Explanatory feedback beat corrective feedback in a botany game with effect sizes of 1.16 and 1.87 in two studies, and learners also rated the explanatory version as more helpful.
Crafting explanatory feedback is far more labour-intensive than corrective feedback, which authoring tools automate, so the investment must be justified by the measured learning return.
Focus feedback on the task or the task process and minimize anything the learner reads as feedback about themselves.

Praise and normative feedback such as grades direct attention to the ego and diminish the effect; praise carries little task information and rarely converts into engagement, commitment, self-efficacy, or task understanding.
For problem solving, process feedback should address the strategy the learner used rather than only the answer.

Provide step-by-step feedback when solution steps are interdependent: learners given feedback on all algebra solution steps were more motivated and learned more than those given feedback only on the final answer.
condition: when an early wrong step can derail the remaining steps, as in highly structured subjects

statement: There is some evidence that delayed feedback is more effective for conceptual or strategic skills and for simpler tasks, but firm timing recommendations await more research.
condition: for conceptual or strategic skills, and for simpler tasks

statement: Position feedback so the learner sees the question, their own response, and the feedback together to minimize split attention, and for multiple-answer items show the correct answers beside the learner's with an explanation.
Emphasize progress feedback that focuses attention on the learner's improvement over time rather than comparison with others.

Practice principle 4 — distribute practice across the learning environment; the spacing effect is described as one of the most reliable phenomena in human experimental psychology, robust across verbal materials and motor skills.
Spaced practice does not improve immediate learning and its benefit shows only after a delay, so training programs that never measure delayed learning systematically miss it.
Spacing gains persisted as long as eight years after the original training, and phonics practice split into three two-minute daily sessions improved six times more than one six-minute daily session.

Massed and spaced practice dissociate by test timing: rereading a text twice in a row helped the immediate test while rereading a week apart helped the delayed test, and math practice split across sessions matched massed practice at one week but far exceeded it at four weeks.

Apply spacing operationally by distributing practice within a lesson, across lessons, and across separate learning events using different delivery media, for example an asynchronous class before a synchronous session followed by a supervised workplace assignment.

Mixed practice beats blocked practice on delayed tests even though it produces poorer scores during practice itself: interleaving four geometry problem types lowered practice scores but yielded much better next-day test results.
Mix problem types during practice when the goal is discriminating among them, because mixing supplies discrimination practice; where types are easy to tell apart, mixing may have less benefit.
condition: when learners must learn to discriminate among problem categories
exception: less benefit when the problem types are easy to discriminate

statement: Set practice quantity from a task analysis: ask whether automatic performance is required and when, and whether the task needs conceptual understanding and reflection; assign more exercises where automaticity is needed and avoid over-learning where it is not.
For tasks requiring automatic responses, measure both response accuracy and response time, since automated responses are both accurate and fast.
condition: when automaticity is the performance requirement

statement: In synchronous e-learning, extend learning by scheduling several short one-to-two-hour sessions with asynchronous practice assigned between them.
The modality principle inverts for practice: audio is too transient, so directions, questions, and any information needed to answer must remain on screen as text while the learner responds.
condition: during practice interactions
exception: this overrides the general audio-for-visuals default

statement: Present feedback in text so learners can review explanations at their own pace, and do not narrate on-screen text directions, practice questions, or feedback.

Lay out practice for contiguity: distinguish response areas by placement, colour, or font next to the question, reserve open screen space for feedback near the response, and mark correct options with colour or bold in the feedback.

Contiguity extends to the response mode: adjusting simulation parameters via scroll bars or drag-and-drop produced greater transfer than text input, because splitting attention between keyboard and screen depressed learning.
Keep practice free of extraneous visual or audio elements such as gratuitous animations or applause, bells, and whistles tied to correct or incorrect responses.
Study time does not predict university grade point average but deliberate practice does, and distraction-free study alone in a quiet room outperforms studying with a radio or in a team.
During virtual classroom practice events the instructor should maintain a period of silence.
condition: during synchronous practice

statement: Practice principle 6 — transition from examples to practice gradually via faded worked examples, since completing practice imposes heavy mental load and fading raises it in step with growing expertise.

Practice does not necessarily make perfect, but deliberate practice with effective feedback does; open questions remain about feedback detail, timing, and whether guided peer feedback can supplement instructor feedback.
Despite sixty years of face-to-face research and the arrival of social media, experimental evidence on computer-supported collaborative learning remains insufficient for firm guidelines.

Cooperative learning substantially improves achievement under well-specified conditions and ranked twenty-fourth of 138 influences on learning with an effect size of .59, yet not all comparisons favour learning together over learning alone.
condition: under well-specified conditions

statement: Three criteria govern collaboration success: social interdependence, clearly defined outcome goals, and dialog quality in which all parties contribute substantively and no one is ignored.

Group rewards must reflect individual learning: of sixty-four studies with rewards summed from all members' learning, 78 percent showed positive achievement effects with a median effect size of .32, whereas rewards based on a single group product not reflecting individual learning gave a negligible .07.
Build individual incentives into team work, for example by requiring each member to meet a minimum criterion on an individual assignment or test for the team to receive project credit.
Decide before designing collaboration whether the goal is individual learning or project quality, because the two outcomes require different structuring.

Group performance is not predictive of individual performance: a meta-analysis separating individual-achievement from group-product outcomes, plus two later studies, found no relationship between team project quality and individual learning.
Effective collaborative learning requires dialog in which each partner builds on others' contributions, clarifies or challenges assertions, and asks and answers mutual questions.

Where collaboration underperformed individual work, 72 percent of the verbal interaction was knowledge-telling in which a partner merely restated what they already knew rather than extending knowledge.

Merely telling pairs or teams to work together or discuss the project does not produce the rich exchange that drives deeper learning; shallow or non-participation is common when one or two members do most of the work or the assignment is too easy or too unstructured.

The benefits of social media, like any technology, depend on how instructional professionals exploit its features to fit human cognitive learning needs, so adapt lessons from in-person and prior online collaboration rather than assuming novelty helps.
CSCL research is highly heterogeneous in what it measures and how, which is why it yields few universal guidelines despite the volume of work.

In face-to-face settings, working together yields greater individual learning than studying alone when there is an incentive for mutual support and goal achievement and a structured assignment ensures on-task dialog.
condition: when both mutual incentive and assignment structure are present

statement: For creative products or ill-defined problems, a team produces a better quality product than an individual, with a reported effect size of 2 or more, because the group compares alternative interpretations, corrects misconceptions, and forms a more holistic picture.
condition: when the goal is a creative product or an ill-defined problem solution

statement: For creative products or ill-defined problems a virtual collaboration environment has the potential to beat face-to-face collaboration on output quality, because it can produce more reflection and idea sharing.
condition: when the outcome measured is product quality on an ill-defined task

statement: Avoid teams composed entirely of low prior knowledge learners; heterogeneous teams mixing high and low prior knowledge, or homogeneous high prior knowledge teams, work best.
Size teams to the goal: use pairs when the aim is individual learning, and three to five members when the aim is creative problem solving that needs more expertise.
Social presence raises class satisfaction ratings when participants feel they connected with the instructor and other participants, and collaborative learning is one way to increase it.

Match the collaboration tool to the outcome goal: asynchronous tools suit reflection over longer periods while synchronous tools give higher social presence, and many common tools cannot capture or display group thinking.
CSCL suits ill-structured far-transfer problem solving with groups of three to five, and shows mixed results with near-transfer and well-structured far-transfer assignments.
condition: when the task is complex, ill-defined, and has no single correct solution

statement: Greater structure and more specific instructions in a collaborative assignment generally lead to better outcomes than low structure and general instructions.
CSCL takes longer than individual work and can exceed individual outcomes only when ample processing time is allowed.
condition: when sufficient working time is provided

statement: Teamwork skills training improves collaborative outcomes as long as the trained group stays intact.
condition: when the trained team remains together

statement: Award points or grades on a synthesis of individual outcomes rather than on a group product alone or on individual products alone.
Student moderators may work better than instructor moderators for advanced learners when argumentation structures are used.
condition: with advanced learners and an argumentation structure

statement: Pairs solving an ill-structured practice problem via synchronous chat scored higher on a later individual essay test than solo practisers, but the effect size of .11 is negligible despite statistical significance.

Virtual and face-to-face collaboration trade off by outcome: chat pairs produced better team spreadsheet projects and asked more questions, while face-to-face pairs scored better on the individual post-test and shared information more easily.
Teams containing one or two higher prior knowledge members outperformed pairs of two low-knowledge learners on both the team project and the individual post-test.

On a hidden-profile decision task, synchronous-chat trios reached 63 percent correct versus under 20 percent face-to-face, but only when given unrestricted discussion time; time-restricted chat groups were far less accurate.
condition: provided the virtual group has sufficient working time

statement: Proposed reasons chat outperforms face-to-face on shared-information decisions are parallel communication, a persistent text record of the discussion to reference, and the anonymity of contributions.

Chronologically ordered discussion boards make it hard to infer shared agreement, make gained knowledge explicit, find relevant contributions, or determine outcomes, which motivates graphical knowledge-map representations of collaborative work.
A graphical knowledge-map collaboration interface produced greater convergence of ideas in individual essays than a threaded discussion, but no difference in solution quality or post-test scores.

Assigning a student the moderator role produced higher-level contributions from that student, and deeper knowledge construction appeared in student-moderated groups only when another member was assigned to generate alternative solutions.
condition: when a distinct alternatives-generator role is also assigned

statement: The role study measured discussion quality ratings rather than learning and used high-prior-knowledge medical interns, so it assumes deeper discussion means better learning and may not generalize to novices.
Collaborative assignments that are too simple will not motivate meaningful dialog and assignments that are too general or vague give too little structure for effective collaboration.

Structured controversy is a three-phase argumentation method: teams of four split into pro and con pairs to build evidence-backed positions, each pair presents and the other must restate the argument to demonstrate understanding, then the full team synthesizes a unified reasoned position.
Structured controversy outperformed traditional debate, individual learning, and concurrence-seeking groups with effect sizes from .42 to .77.

Successful constructive controversy needs a cooperative context aimed at understanding opposing views then synthesizing them, mixed-ability groups, rich relevant information, adequate social skills to manage conflict, and interactions focused on rational argument.

Do not assume learners can argue effectively: quality argumentation is a skill that must be trained and guided, using video-modeled worked examples with stage-identification questions or synchronous argumentation templates.

Structured controversy adapts to CSCL by combining asynchronous research and position development with synchronous breakout discussion, posted arguments and opposing-argument summaries, and a shared integrating artifact.

Four enablers for online collaborative learning: ensure social interdependence through sufficiently complex assignments, right-sized teams, and incentives rewarding all members' learning; assign ill-structured case problems to heterogeneous groups of three to five; use guided assignments such as structured controversy; and provide clear guidance, roles, and objectives.
More is unknown than known about CSCL practice; what works for one combination of learners, outcomes, and technology features is likely different for another.

Whether deeper CSCL discussions actually translate into more learning is an open question, as is which computer representations aid which group tasks and what combination of synchronous and asynchronous processes fits which outcome.

A knowledge-sharing wiki may extend learning beyond a formal event, but the incentives and resources for contributing to and maintaining it afterwards must be planned, and the evidence does not yet warrant a conclusion.
For far-transfer classes, favour group projects or case assignments that include asynchronous work so learners have time for reflection and individual research.
condition: when the course targets far-transfer outcomes

statement: Evaluate student work in a way that reflects each team member's accomplishment, to encourage interdependence.

Learner control means the course offers choices over content, pace, and instructional elements; program control means the instruction supplies a single path, which is how most synchronous e-learning and classroom teaching operates.

Learner control has three distinct domains — content sequencing, pacing, and access to learning support such as examples and practice — so two courses both labelled learner-controlled may differ substantially.

Adjust the amount of learner control primarily by learner prior knowledge: higher prior knowledge learners typically choose well under high control, while most novices do not know enough about the domain to benefit from it.
condition: gauge prior knowledge before granting content control

statement: Always allow learners to control pacing in asynchronous e-learning so they can proceed at their own rate, following from the segmenting principle.
condition: in asynchronous e-learning

statement: Learners like learner control and will expect Internet-like freedom, so it satisfies student appeal even where it does not serve learning.
Two lines of evidence — calibration accuracy and student lesson ratings — show most learners are not good at self-assessment, which undermines the premise that they can choose what to study.
Calibration is the correlation between a learner's confidence in their knowledge and their actual performance; it measures the accuracy of what people think they know, not what they know.
Calibration accuracy is generally poor: measured correlations were close to zero, and poor calibration of comprehension is described as the rule rather than the exception.
Self-assessment does not improve with seniority: medical students' knowledge estimates correlated poorly with test scores and showed no improvement from year one to year three.

Among 305 medical specialists, physicians with poor peer ratings rated themselves 30 to 40 percentage points above their peers' rating while high performers underestimated themselves, giving strong evidence that many practising experts self-assess badly.

Calibration improves after answering test questions, so including questions in training leads to more accurate learner self-assessment; calibration was best for learners who studied text with both examples and questions.

End-of-course learner ratings correlated only .12 with post-training knowledge and .15 with procedural skill across roughly eleven thousand ratings, so reactions must not be used as an indicator of learning.

Matching instruction to a learner's stated preference does not improve outcomes: regardless of whether they preferred high or low practice, learners assigned the high-practice version scored significantly higher.
Liking is not the same as learning: there is little correspondence between learner perceptions of a lesson's effectiveness and its actual instructional value.

Metacognition is the learner's awareness and control of their own learning; high-metacognition learners set realistic goals, self-assess accurately, and pick appropriate study strategies, while low-metacognition learners make flawed decisions under high learner control.

High prior knowledge learners used more planning and monitoring in a hypermedia environment while low prior knowledge learners just took notes, likely because planning and monitoring consume working memory they did not have to spare.
Add guidance to hypermedia environments used by novices — for example frequent questions with detailed feedback — so learners need not spend working memory monitoring their own progress.
condition: when the audience is novice to the domain

statement: Learner control principle 1 — give experienced learners control; learners with little prior knowledge and poor metacognitive skills do better under program control, especially in high-complexity courses.

Learner control is more likely to succeed when learners already know the content, the lesson or course is at an advanced point in the curriculum, learners have good metacognitive skills, and the course is of low complexity.
condition: all four conditions favour granting control

statement: Low prior knowledge learners under learner control practised too little and dwelt on material they already knew, showing they did not use good learning strategies or sequencing decisions; high prior knowledge learners did well under either control mode.
Learners under learner control viewed under 50 percent of the available screens, and low-metacognitive learners scored 20 percent under learner control versus 79 percent under program control.

Program control gave better results during initial learning while learner control was more effective at later stages, so favour greater program control at least in the beginning lessons of a course for novices.
condition: shift control to the learner as their knowledge base grows

statement: Learner control principle 2 — make important instructional events the default: set the continue button to lead into practice and examples so the learner must deliberately choose to bypass them.
condition: when the design grants high learner control

statement: Making practice the default route rather than the bypass route led learners to view nearly twice as many screens and to score higher on the final test.

One research team argued program control should be preferred because learner-controlled programs show no instructional advantage, disadvantage low-ability learners, and cost more — but their subjects took a required university course, so voluntary-audience settings cannot discount learner preference so far.
condition: when learners are free to abandon the course, preference carries more weight

statement: Learner control principle 3 — adaptive control dynamically adjusts lesson difficulty and instructional support based on the program's evaluation of learner responses.

Expertise reversal implies a general trajectory: increase the difficulty of assignments and decrease instructional support as learning progresses; because learners advance at different rates, when to make that transition is the design problem adaptive control solves.
In an air traffic control simulation, adaptive control matched program control on learning while requiring an average of ten tasks instead of twenty, an efficiency rather than achievement gain.

An adaptive dietetics course selecting each next task from the learner's competence score and effort rating produced mean competence of 73 against 48 for the non-adaptive version, with lower rated mental load but more time spent in training.

Rapid verification assesses competence quickly by showing a problem then a series of intermediate solution steps the learner judges right or wrong; it correlated .71 to .75 with a traditional test at over three times the speed, making it valid for real-time adaptation.

To build a rapid verification item, define the main intermediate stages of the solution procedure, write one correct and two or three incorrect steps per stage, show the problem briefly, then present the steps one at a time for quick verification and use the score to adjust difficulty or guidance.

Accuracy of self-explanation selections can drive adaptive fading of worked examples without extra test items, and this adaptive fading beat both a standard tutor and fixed fading on immediate and delayed post-tests.

Adaptive learning requires extra investment in assessment design, decision logic, and alternative instructional paths, so justify it by a large heterogeneous audience whose time savings outweigh development cost, or by a requirement that every participant reach a minimum competence.
condition: when the audience is large, heterogeneous, or highly paid, or universal competence is mandatory

statement: Learner control principle 4 — give pacing control: a learner-controlled lightning lesson with stop, replay, and slide-selection produced better transfer than the automatically advancing version, at the cost of nearly three times the time spent.

Learner control principle 5 — provide navigational support in hypermedia: use screen headings combining lesson title and topic, and brief descriptive labels on text segments and visuals, since headings act as signalling and improve memory and comprehension.
Use links sparingly for novices and never for essential instructional elements such as worked examples or practice, because a link signals the content is peripheral and many learners will bypass it.
condition: particularly with novice audiences

statement: Contrary to expectation, extensive use of cross-lesson comparison links was negatively related to learning, attributed to the cognitive load of hypertext navigation; about half of learners abandoned the links for linear reading.
If links must be included, annotate them so novices get a short preview of what lies behind, or highlight the few links especially relevant to the learning goal.

Research on course maps' contribution to learning is mixed: learners frequently opened a topic map to orient themselves but rarely navigated with it, and its correlation with learning was only slight.

Low knowledge learners comprehended most from a hierarchical map while map type made no difference to high prior knowledge learners, suggesting maps matter less for navigation than for orienting novices to the content structure.
