statement: Displaying steps in lined rows cues learner recognition of the serial nature of the information being provided.
Include a labelled picture of the equipment as part of the how-to treatment, because it cues recognition of exactly the parts that will be manipulated.

A single lesson event can serve two treatment roles at once — observing the magnified specimen both confirms correct operation as routine reinforcement and supplies concrete experience of a concept as a nonroutine treatment.
Fading can be implemented as a learner choice — offering the opportunity to perform with less help available — rather than as a designer-imposed removal.
Practice on different instances of the equipment is intended specifically to facilitate transfer of the skill to any instance that might have to be used.
The final stage of practice must match what the objectives call for — if the objective says unaided performance, the last practice has no cues available.

Count the stimulus characteristics a concept's definition depends on: when their number is judged likely to make one overall definition too hard for the audience, treat the characteristics individually as a shaping treatment.
condition: when the number of criterial attributes is large for the audience

statement: Reducing the unit of behaviour means presenting and practising each stimulus characteristic separately instead of going directly to practice recognizing whole instances.
Defer practice at recognizing the whole concept to the last stage of practice, after the per-characteristic practice.
Splitting a four-part definition across four display rows cues learners to recognize that there are four separate considerations in the definition.

Use annotational cues on examples in two distinct ways: identify differences among lens types to facilitate discrimination, and identify similarities among varied instances of one class to facilitate generalization.
Multiple-choice recognition practice is an altered, easier practice mode than requiring the learner to identify individual instances as belonging to the class or not.
Schedule full-blown practice last, after the easier shaping practice, because the routine element is what the objective actually requires.
When examples and nonexamples differ by minute features, feedback should include annotation cuing recognition of the defining characteristics rather than merely marking the answer right or wrong.
condition: when instances and noninstances differ only in fine detail

statement: When the ultimate skill is judged too large a chunk of behaviour to learn at once because it has too many elements, teach each constituent set of skills separately as part of an overall shaping approach.
condition: when the target performance has too many elements to learn at once

statement: Itemize individual facts as separate points on the page rather than running them together, to make learning multiple facts easier.
Visual examples make information concrete enough that learners can respond correctly to individual features of the examples.
Practising only a portion of the total performance — describing one aspect rather than the whole relationship — is practice at a smaller unit of behaviour.
Having learners draw a result rather than state it is practice in an alternative concrete mode designed to make learning easier.
Recognize when a practice problem's visual support almost completely gives away the answer: that is heavy cuing, appropriate early in a shaping sequence but not as the terminal practice.
Practising facts individually rather than in combination is one of the levers that makes practice easier.
Review prerequisite concepts that were only minimally practised earlier, because weakly to moderately learned prerequisites need the extra cuing before dependent material.
condition: when prerequisites were practised only minimally

statement: Defer practice of the ultimate performance — stating a complete explanation or making the target prediction — until the end, which is the customary end point of a shaping approach.
Sequence a practice problem that exercises parts of the performance immediately before the problem that requires the whole performance, so the first prepares for the second.

A routine presentation for an explanation objective consists of stating the relationship and supplying examples to which the explanation applies; presenting the statement's constituent parts individually is the nonroutine addition.
When an objective requires associating pairs of concepts that were themselves only newly and minimally learned, review those concepts inside the presentation before introducing the association.
condition: when the concepts being associated are newly learned

statement: For pure fact recall, the routine treatment is to present the facts in a table and have the learner practise stating them, with the association pairs — inventor to invention, invention to date — made explicit.
condition: when the objective is recalling facts

statement: Pair each recall exercise with its cued and uncued version — one problem allowing reference to the fact table and the next forbidding it — so fading happens within the same skill.
Frame learning hints as the specific questions the upcoming material answers, so the learner's search is directed at the associations that will be tested.
When no learning difficulty is anticipated for a small set of factual associations, a routine treatment alone suffices: state the facts and have learners practise recalling them.
condition: when the number of facts is small and no difficulty is anticipated

statement: Design the visual form of a fact display so its look alone cues how many separate facts there are and what types of information are being presented.
Even a small fact set can be judged too hard to recall on one read-through for a given audience, which justifies a first cued practice before the uncued one.
condition: when one read-through is judged insufficient for the audience

statement: Landa's central content-selection prescription is that for complex tasks you should teach the actual thought processes an expert uses while performing the task, not merely the task's outputs.

Expert thought processes are hard to identify because experts are usually not consciously aware of them, so objective methods are needed to penetrate expert minds rather than relying on expert self-report.
Landa's snowball approach teaches an algorithmic or heuristic process step by step, and after each step is mastered that step is practised together with all the preceding steps.

Students who possess a body of knowledge are often unable to apply it — to think, reason, solve problems and make decisions — so instruction must target the process of applying knowledge, not only the knowledge.
To teach knowledge application effectively one must know the composition and structure of the cognitive operations involved — the internal mechanisms of thought — and how to develop them in students.
An algorithm is a precise, unambiguous and sufficiently general prescription of what one should do manually or cognitively to solve any problem in a given class.

A heuristic prescription indicates what a problem solver should do to find a solution more easily but not exactly how; its directions carry some uncertainty and do not determine the solution process completely.
Problems, processes and prescriptions also occur in semialgorithmic and semiheuristic forms between the fully algorithmic and fully heuristic poles.

Because experts and teachers are often unaware of the processes they actually perform, students are left to discover those processes independently; since discovery is complex and is not itself taught, only some students succeed and the rest become underachievers.

Landamatics is a system of techniques that penetrates unobservable expert processes, breaks them into relatively elementary component operations, describes those operations explicitly as descriptive models, composes algorithmic or heuristic prescriptions from them, and builds instruction from those prescriptions.

Distinguish descriptive models of a cognitive process from prescriptive models: the first describes what the expert does, the second states what a nonexpert should do in their mind to learn and perform at expert level.

Knowledge and mental operations are interdependent, so instruction must be designed both to teach knowledge in a way that develops mental operations and to teach operations in a way that develops high-quality, applicable knowledge.
Before choosing a teaching method, define which type of knowledge is at stake — an image, a concept, or a proposition — because each requires different instruction.
To teach a concept, first identify every attribute of the object deemed essential for students to know in order to use the concept for theoretical and practical purposes.

Split a concept's essential attributes into two groups: those the student uses to identify the object, and those used to solve other kinds of problems such as drawing inferences, building hypotheses, or deciding whether the object serves a practical purpose.
Select indicative features for instruction on psychological criteria: they should be comprehensible, sufficiently elementary, unambiguous, workable, economical, and convenient to use.

Analyse each indicative feature for its logical properties — necessary and sufficient, necessary but not sufficient, or not necessary but sufficient — because each type must be acted upon differently during identification.
When several sufficient indicative features exist, determine all of them so students can be given more than one method of identifying the object.
condition: when more than one sufficient feature set exists

statement: Determine the logical structure connecting a concept's indicative features — conjunctive, disjunctive, or a mixed conjunctive-disjunctive structure — before designing instruction on it.
Express the logical structure of indicative features as an implicational if-then proposition, with the features on the left and the inference to be drawn from their presence or absence on the right.

The implicational proposition models the conceptual component of instruction but not the operational component; only an algorithm or system of algorithms models the operational process of identification.
Once the logical structure of a concept's indicative features is explicit, develop an algorithm directing what the student should do mentally to determine whether an object belongs to the class.

Algorithms are not only a means of teaching how to apply a concept but also a means of developing the concept itself, because performing the operations on the indicative features teaches those features more quickly and better.

Several identification algorithms can be built from one logical structure; being logically equivalent does not make them psychologically equivalent, since some require more operations or are less comfortable to execute.
The designer's task is to develop the most efficient algorithm among the logically equivalent alternatives, not merely a correct one.

Identify by psychological analysis and diagnosis of the target population which mental operations are elementary for them, and build the algorithm out of those operations, because elementariness is relative to the audience.
Make every instruction in an algorithm comprehensible and unambiguous for the given student population.
Make the instruction set complete so that the algorithm provides guidance under every logically possible condition.
Make each instruction as general as possible within the limits of elementariness and comprehensibility, so the algorithm covers as wide a class of problems as it can.

Order an algorithm's instructions in a logically reasonable and natural sequence — testing the partitioning attribute before the finer ones — since a reverse order may still be logically correct but is not natural.
Among the logically reasonable and natural algorithms, choose the one that solves the problem in the minimum number of mental operations.
The algorithm produced by this design process is itself the program of processes to be formed in students' minds during instruction.

Develop algorithms down to the level of elementary operations, which corresponds to the entry level of behaviour in a learning hierarchy, and teach them with prescriptions (generalities) and demonstrations (examples).

Sequence a purely factual, historical section after the practical and explanatory sections, so that learners can recognize the relevance of the facts from concrete and abstract experience already gained.
Most rules for teaching mental operations are conditional rather than absolute: a method that produces positive results under one set of conditions may not do so under another.
The purpose of algorithm-based instruction is to teach algorithmic processes, not algorithmic prescriptions; the prescription is only one means of teaching the process.
Algorithmic prescriptions make students more aware of the algorithmic operations and lead to easier and faster generalization and transfer of them.

Use explicit algorithmic prescriptions when the objective is to develop awareness of the algorithmic process and faster generalization; omit them when the objective is only to develop a particular cognitive or manual skill.
condition: depending on whether awareness and generalization or bare skill is the objective

statement: Knowledge of the prescription is unnecessary for solving problems oneself but becomes critical for communicating a method of solving problems to others.
Teach the prescription explicitly when the target audience will have to communicate the learned skill to others, as teachers, supervisors or managers must.
condition: when learners must later teach or explain the skill

statement: Independent discovery of an algorithm is educationally much more valuable than receiving it ready-made, but it requires much more time.

Lead students through guided independent discovery of the prescription when sufficient time is available; present it ready-made when it is not, and mixing the two — some operations given, others discovered — is legitimate.
condition: depending on available instructional time

statement: The sequential step-by-step method makes an algorithmic process easier to learn and speeds internalization and automatization, but demands more direct teacher involvement; the integral whole-presentation method needs less teacher time and lacks those benefits.
Choose the sequential method when the teacher has sufficient time for direct interaction with students, and the integral method when self-learning must carry part of the instruction.
condition: depending on available direct teacher interaction time

statement: Under the sequential approach, use the snowball principle: join each new operation to the block of operations already formed, and likewise join new subalgorithms to those already acquired to build more branched and comprehensive algorithms.
Whichever presentation method is used, treat internalization and automatization of the learned operations as a specific educational objective and instructional task in its own right.
The techniques of internalization and automatization depend on whether the sequential or the integral method was used to introduce the algorithm.

Join each subsequent concept's algorithm to the previous ones so that a comprehensive system of algorithms covering the whole subject-matter area is gradually built, each successive system being of a higher order and more general.
Form interdisciplinary connections between the systems of knowledge and operations developed in related disciplines, producing systems of still higher order.
Building systematism and generality across subject matters is what allows teachers to produce general intellectual abilities in students purposefully and reliably rather than incidentally.
Developing the most general, content-independent cognitive abilities is a task of instruction distinct from — and no less important than — developing specific problem-solving skills.

A learning objective stated too narrowly can be the wrong unit for a general-ability approach; broadening it to the whole class of related discriminations may be necessary to make the method's value visible.
condition: when the design method targets general abilities

statement: State explicitly which aspects of a theory a demonstration cannot show — for instance an identification topic that contains no heuristic problems can only exercise the algorithmic aspect.
To make an indicative feature workable, find the operations that let students identify that feature; only after those methods are mastered can the feature be used in an algorithm without difficulty.
Textbooks usually give students knowledge of an object's properties without teaching them what to do cognitively with that knowledge — how to think and reason in applying it.

The properties a textbook uses to characterize a class can themselves create difficulties both in understanding the class and in applying those properties to classify instances; analyse the source material for this before adopting its features.
Design the algorithm to overcome the specific difficulties learners have with the existing account, aiming at a general and easy-to-follow method that classifies any instance accurately and quickly.
Lesson content depends not only on the objectives, the terminal algorithm and the theory's requirements, but also on the initial psychological state — the entry level — of the students.
State the assumed entry level explicitly when presenting a designed lesson, and expect a teacher implementing it to adapt it to each specific instructional condition.
Motivate a classification topic by showing that class membership predicts the consequence the learner cares about, so knowing the type immediately tells them what behaviour to expect.
Lead learners to the criterial dimension by presenting two instances that differ on it and asking what makes the difference, rather than by asserting the dimension.

Present a contrasting pair whose parts are identical on the obvious attribute but differ on the intended one, so learners are forced to discover that the distinction lies in the relationship between parts rather than in the parts themselves.
Have the learner summarize the factors just discovered in their own words before moving on, so the generalization is produced rather than received.
Refresh and give additional practice on prerequisite discriminations at the point of use, even when learners are assumed to already possess them.

Teach a relational concept by having learners mentally perform the transformation that produces it — imagining themselves at a reference position and acting on the target — so the concept is defined by an operation rather than by appearance.
Have learners construct the algorithm themselves by asking how they would explain the procedure to someone who does not know it, and requiring the answer as a numbered step-by-step prescription.

Introduce the term algorithm only after learners have produced one, defining it as a prescription that states precisely what to do and in what sequence to achieve a result, solve a problem or make a decision.
Derive the identification algorithm from the formation algorithm: once learners can state what to do to produce an instance, ask them what to do to decide whether a given case is one.

The three stages of practice that internalize and automatize an operation are executing the algorithm from the written text, then self-instructing aloud with the text removed, then self-instructing silently and reporting only the answer.
Vary the instances used for algorithmic practice deliberately across the range of cases the algorithm must cover, and continue until the task is mastered.
Have learners walk the algorithm step by step aloud with the teacher prompting only what comes next, so every operation of the process is externalized before it is internalized.

Automatization has a fourth stage beyond silent self-instruction: drilling until the learner can execute the operations with no self-instruction at all, and then until recognition is instantaneous within about a second on sight.

Time the terminal recognition drill explicitly against a stopwatch-level criterion, and continue until learners meet it, because speed is the observable evidence that the operation has been automatized.

After an identification algorithm for a designated element is mastered, pose the harder search problem — the element is not designated and the learner must find which ones qualify — and have learners expand the algorithm to cover it.
A search algorithm built on top of an identification algorithm has the form: select a candidate, apply the identification test, move to the next candidate, and continue until all have been examined.

Teach each parallel concept in a contrasting pair through the identical stage sequence — enhance the concept, design a formation algorithm, design an identification algorithm, practise it, internalize and automatize it, then formulate the search algorithm.

Lead learners to a classification by presenting instances grouped into the target classes and asking what is common within each group and what distinguishes the groups, before supplying the class names.
Introduce the class names only after learners have established the distinguishing features themselves, so the term labels a distinction they already hold.
Ask explicitly whether all the indicative features must be used to classify an instance or whether one suffices, because that question is what turns a list of attributes into a usable decision rule.
Have learners state each candidate definition in an explicit if-then form with the indicative feature in the antecedent and the class conclusion in the consequent.
Two definitions of the same class are not necessarily equally good; test them by asking whether each applies to all possible objects of the type and leads to the correct conclusion.
A definition is better when it is more general — when it applies to a larger variety of instances and yields a correct conclusion in a greater number of cases.
Probe a candidate definition with a constructed edge case that has one indicative feature but not the other, so learners discover for themselves which feature is the more general criterion.
Represent a completed algorithmic prescription in diagrammatic form as a branching decision structure, so the sequence of tests and their conclusions are visible at once.

Extend an algorithm branch by branch: establish the superordinate class first, then ask which additional question separates one subtype from the rest, and add that question and its conclusions to the diagram.
Have learners propose the names for newly distinguished subtypes and then correct the guess to the conventional term, because a near-correct guess shows the naming convention is itself learnable.
Make the naming convention explicit as a rule — the distinguishing feature is named by the word preceding the class word — so learners can generate and interpret unfamiliar compound terms by analogy.
Build the comprehensive algorithm by putting the already-mastered subalgorithms together, and note that synthesis presents no difficulty once the components have been internalized and automatized.
condition: when the component subalgorithms are already automatized

statement: Material that is boring in itself requires learners to first understand its practical use and why the skill matters, otherwise motivation for it will not exist.
condition: when the content is intrinsically unengaging

statement: A theory need not prescribe every step: where the AHT has no prescription for how to run an explanation and demonstration, the step is carried out in a conventional manner and this gap is stated rather than hidden.

Where possible, present or have students identify the basic concept-forming phenomena — the components and attributes whose combinations generate the object types — rather than presenting the finished types.
Teach students the generating operations by which different types of objects are produced, so they can actively and independently generate the types and their concepts.
The active generative approach to concept formation is preferred over the passive receptive approach.
Methods of independent or guided discovery are educationally superior for transfer learning and should be used when time permits.
condition: when instructional time permits

statement: Showing students two or several objects and having them compare to identify common and distinctive features is a good and effective method for discovering criterial attributes, even where a theory offers no specific prescription for it.
Students often recognize objects only in a standard position or typical form, and a nonstandard position or atypical form frequently prevents recognition.
Vary the position and form of the objects being studied to prevent narrow concepts from forming and to overcome narrow concepts already formed.

Use a review of prerequisite knowledge to do double duty: confront learners with familiar objects in positions and forms that are new to them, so the review broadens the concept as well as refreshing it.
Convex and concave are relational concepts, and the best way to form relational concepts and the ability to identify relations is to teach the cognitive operations of relating explicitly.

People who identify relations are always performing operations of relating without being aware of them, and learners' difficulty with relational classification is frequently caused by never having been taught those operations explicitly.
Every process of relating includes three operations: isolating the object that serves as the reference point, isolating the object to be related to it, and performing the relating operation itself.
Getting the reference-point and to-be-related roles the wrong way round immediately produces the inverse relation and a wrong conclusion, so role assignment must be taught as an explicit step.
The best way to know something deeply enough to identify it easily and reliably is to generate it, whenever that is possible and time-efficient.

Transformational operations are one of the operation types by which relationships between objects are established and identified, and they can be used to generate the very classes learners must recognize.

An operational-generative approach to concept formation yields much more general concepts and a much more general identification method than conventional instruction, because learners acquire one cognitive procedure whose particular cases cover the whole family of types.

Once learners have mastered the generating operations they have effectively acquired the concepts without knowing the names or formal definitions, which is exactly when the terms and definitions should be introduced.
Introduce paired contrasting concepts simultaneously and against each other rather than one at a time.
Definitions grounded in the operations that generate the class are operational and therefore easy to apply to identification tasks.

However skilfully a concept is introduced, it must be associated with a variety of objects whose irrelevant attributes are varied, or the concept and its term become tied to irrelevant features that narrow its generality.
Providing a large and varying empirical basis for a concept also leads to faster generalization of it.

Students must be taught not only the algorithmic and heuristic operations for solving a class of problems but also the ways of becoming aware of those operations and of formulating explicit prescriptions from them.

The operations involved in generating an object and forming its concept are not necessarily the same as those involved in identifying an object and assigning it to a class, so both a generative and an identification algorithm must be taught.

An identification algorithm can be given ready-made, discovered by students, or designed by students becoming aware of identification operations they already perform; the last two are educationally more valuable.

Providing a ready-made technique is preferable to leaving learners to discover it when discovery time is unavailable — as it is better to teach someone a swimming technique than to throw them into water hoping they discover it before drowning.
condition: when the time for independent or guided discovery is not available

statement: Knowing which cognitive operations to perform is a necessary but not sufficient condition for mastering a cognitive skill; internalization of those operations, including their automatization, is the other necessary condition.

Experts do not execute cognitive operations sequentially or continually self-instruct; their operations run simultaneously or nearly so and are actuated by the external objects and conditions of the problem and by other operations rather than by instructions.

There is a distinctive difference between the format and the psychological regulation mechanism of the cognitive operations of experts and of novices, so teaching the operations does not by itself produce the expert format.
In conventional instruction the expert format of cognitive operations develops only spontaneously through lengthy experience, if it develops at all.

The expert-level format of cognitive operations can and should be created purposefully and controllably by gradually transforming sequential conscious algorithmic operations into simultaneous postconscious ones.
The terminal aim of automatizing an identification procedure is to convert sequential algorithmic operations into a pattern-recognition mechanism that solves the identification problem on sight.

Searching operations are specific and are not formed automatically as a by-product of identification skill; they consist of sequentially isolating candidates in order to apply the identification algorithm to each.

Someone may recognize a sought object instantly when it is pointed out yet be unable to find it, which shows identification is working while systematic search is absent — the two skills must be trained separately.
Search skill is a prerequisite for classifying a composite object, because without the ability to isolate and check every component a learner may overlook one and misclassify the whole.
Uncover all the small and unnoticeable operations involved in the terminal mechanism of a skill and train them specifically, rather than assuming they come along with the visible ones.
Students should be taught general methods of constructing theories and definitions, which includes knowing how to decide which of several possible definitions is best and why.

Knowing something and being able to apply it to solving problems are two different psychological phenomena with different underlying mechanisms, and this holds for definitions as well as for other knowledge.

Applying any definition or theoretical proposition to identify instances requires converting it into an algorithm; learners do this spontaneously for simple definitions but often cannot for complex ones.

Students make identification errors on definitions they know and can accurately reproduce, because they cannot derive the algorithm for applying them — accurate recall is therefore no evidence of applicability.

Explicit algorithm instruction is unnecessary when a definition is simple enough that students classify correctly from it directly; it becomes worthwhile when the objective extends to finer varieties whose identification builds on that first test as a subalgorithm.
condition: when the objective extends beyond a single simple distinction

statement: Teach students how to represent an algorithm in flowchart or diagram form as an objective in its own right.

Once subskills have been automatized separately, an explicit synthesis objective is still required: practise the comprehensive algorithm to internalize and automatize the whole identification process.
The most important focus for an instructional theory can be deciding what to teach rather than how to teach it.
Structural Learning Theory prescribes that all content be taught in the form of rules, and that higher-order rules be used in place of lower-order rules whenever possible.

A structural-learning rule has three components — domain, range, and operation: the content operated on, the results the rule is expected to produce, and the sum of decisions and actions that produce a specific result.
Require mastery of each equivalence class — each homogeneous problem type — for each rule, and in individualized instruction teach only the paths for the classes a learner has not yet mastered.
Equivalence classes give an operational way to identify the categories across which examples and practice should diverge, rather than leaving divergence to intuition.
Teach the simplest unmastered path through a rule first and proceed to progressively more complex unmastered paths until the entire rule is mastered.

The primary requisite for designing a lesson under Structural Learning Theory is a structural analysis of the content that defines the cognitive rules a learner must acquire to master the objectives; those rules then become the content to be taught.
A rule component is atomic when it is a single unit of behaviour or an individual decision whose further refinement has no distinct behavioural consequences for learners.

A path is the sequence of atomic rules whose performance satisfies an objective at a specific level of difficulty, and each path of a solution rule defines an equivalence class of problems within that objective.

Different paths through the same rule represent different levels of complexity implied by the objective's conditions or by the domain elements provided; a less complex path is subordinate to the more complex ones.
Develop a test for all paths through a solution rule, since precise diagnosis of learner competence comes from the atomic decomposition plus accurate identification of every subordinate path.

Test selectively rather than exhaustively: sequence test items by the hierarchical structure of the paths and probe until the learner fails, then begin instruction at the most subordinate path they cannot perform.

All examples within one equivalence class test the same learner ability and are therefore interchangeable for testing and instruction, so success on one item implies success on the others in that class.
condition: assuming the prior structural analysis is adequate for the target population

statement: The interchangeability assumption does not generalize beyond an equivalence class, so repetition within a class is unnecessary but coverage across classes is not optional.
Automation of a rule is its redefinition to incorporate several atomic rules into a single cognitive step, and automated rules then serve as the basis for more complex training in the subject.

The distinguishing value of a structurally analysed lesson is the precision of content selection and sequencing, its match to learner needs, and the validity of the supporting test items — the analytic work happens long before the lesson begins.
Medium and delivery-strategy decisions depend on secondary objectives and require analysis of learner traits and logistic variables, which content-and-behaviour analysis does not supply.
Structural analysis of an objective establishes whether it requires a single rule or higher-order rules that act on other rules; only objectives of the latter kind need higher-order-rule instruction.

Rules for separate objectives may share component decisions and operations; those relationships can be captured by building a single rule hierarchy across all objectives rather than analysing each in isolation.

When several objectives specify similar decision-operation combinations, base the detailed lesson design on the objective with the greatest number of paths, since the others are covered by the same analysis.
The domain of a solution rule is the full set of situations the rule must handle, and which domain items are used to test a given path depends on the path selected.
Paths through a solution rule are conveniently represented as subgraphs of the full solution flowchart, one per equivalence class.

Two paths are hierarchically related when the longer one contains all the steps of the shorter plus additional operations or decisions; that containment is what licenses inferring inability on the superordinate path from failure on the subordinate.

The solution rule is the final report of structural analysis and is simultaneously a cognitive and a behavioural task analysis, containing every operation and decision needed to produce the specified outcomes on the domain.
Atomicity assumes each cognitive component is either fully available to a learner or completely unavailable, since partial knowledge cannot be represented without refining the component further.
The output of structural analysis specifies all critical domain attributes — the equivalence classes — and those attributes become the learning environment for the lesson.
No single instance of the domain need exercise all the variations the analysis identifies, so not every decision or operation in the rule is required to succeed on any given instance.

What counts as atomic is of necessity somewhat arbitrary and depends on the ability level of the population, so a designer may legitimately collapse several steps into one when the audience is known to possess them.
condition: depending on the target population's existing ability

statement: Collapsing atomic steps carries the risk of assuming more about learner ability than is justified; set atomicity as the least common denominator across the target population.
When learners already perform all paths and complete mastery is desired, further practice can be expected to yield a more efficient automated version of the rule with far fewer components.
condition: when the learner already performs every path

statement: Teach and practise the automated, collapsed rule at its own level of specificity until the behaviour is mastered across the range of outputs.
Practising the collapsed rule maximizes path completion with the association of fewer steps, which improves long-term retention of the rule.
Derive the test directly from the equivalence classes: one item per path, each requiring the learner to complete every step in the path corresponding to that class.
A test that covers four paths need contain only four items, because items within one equivalence class are interchangeable.

A recall objective can have two paths — verbatim recall and paraphrase — whose equivalence classes differ: one contains essentially the given wording, the other any reply containing the critical elements.
When a rule has only one step, the test must vary instances across the range for each learner rather than relying on a single item, because there is no path structure to exploit.
condition: when the solution rule has a single step

statement: Cause-and-effect principles can be expressed as chained if-then decisions and taught with the same procedure form used for concept classification.

When one objective's solution path is the first step of another's, teach the shorter objective first and use correct performance on its test as the input to testing the remaining steps of the longer one.

The first contact a learner has with a structurally designed lesson is an individualized test of key paths, so two learners starting from the same item do not take the same test once their performances diverge.
Begin testing at a level of skill complexity greater than the most subordinate path in a group, then test more subordinate levels until the existing competence level is determined.
Two adaptive-test assumptions license skipping items: competence on a path implies competence on all its subordinate paths, and failure on a path implies failure on all its superordinate paths.
When a rule contains independent groups of paths, assumptions established on one group cannot be generalized to the other without testing that group separately.
condition: when path groups are independent rather than hierarchically related

statement: Each path at which the learner is not competent becomes an element selected for instruction, and instruction begins at the most atomic path where competence fails.
Instruction on a path the diagnostic test shows the learner already performs is unnecessary and should be omitted.
If the learner fails even the simplest path, test the component behaviours within that path to locate the learning need.
condition: when the learner fails the most subordinate path

statement: Sequence instruction simple-to-complex, teaching subordinate paths before the superordinate paths that contain them.
Where two path hierarchies are independent, the order between them is not prescribed and several instructional sequences are equally acceptable; only order within a hierarchy is fixed.
Skills learned in one independent path sequence can be deliberately generalized to another to improve learning efficiency, by taking shared components into account when prescribing instruction.
Between paths, briefly describe the similarities and differences of the path just taught and highlight them by comparing one concrete instance from each path's equivalence class.
Intermingle testing with instruction so the learner advances to the next path only after the prerequisites for it have been mastered.

When a learner still fails after instruction, repeat the lesson at a higher level of detail by redefining the level of atomicity and giving feedback at the level of individual steps, restarting from the last path performed successfully.
condition: when path performance remains incorrect after instruction

statement: Structural Learning Theory does not specify how the selected content is to be taught, so a lesson plan derived from it prescribes content and sequence but not method.

Once structural analysis is complete, the designer knows what the student must be able to do, what they must learn to do it, and the most effective presentation sequence — but all of this is only as complete and useful as the analysis it derives from.

Instructional content for a path is stated as the discriminations and manipulations underlying each step — telling parts from one another, reading a scale from a physical cue, and operating each control — not merely as the step's imperative.

An instructional theory can be built purely inductively — by observing expert teachers, cataloguing the strategies they use, and formulating prescriptions for when to use each — without deriving it from any learning theory.

Inquiry teaching requires learners to formulate hypotheses — to discover the generalities themselves — from observation of varied cases, which is intended to force greater depth of processing of the new knowledge.
In an inquiry approach, questions provide the focus and direction of the instruction, which is intended to improve motivation.
Many inquiry strategies aim at developing higher thought processes rather than content-specific knowledge, and inquiry teaching is distinctive in prescribing how to teach independence of thought.

Inquiry teachers hold two goals at once: teaching deep enough understanding of a domain that students can make novel predictions in it, and teaching students to be good scientists who construct and test general rules and theories on their own.
Inquiry teachers do not teach facts and concepts for their own sake, but only insofar as they fit into a general framework or theory of the domain.
Select paradigm cases in which the values of all relevant factors are consistent with one value of the dependent variable, using a clear positive exemplar and a clear negative exemplar.
Vary cases systematically: choose each comparison case so it differs from the previous one along one factor, so the learner can observe how the outcome changes with that factor.
When a student forms a hypothesis that is not completely true, select a counterexample that satisfies the student's hypothesis but violates its predicted outcome.
condition: when the learner's hypothesis is partially but not wholly correct

statement: Generate hypothetical cases to force reasoning about situations that are hard to reproduce naturally.
Continually ask learners to predict how a dependent variable varies with one or more independent factors — naming both what the outcome depends on and in which direction.
Once a learner has formed a hypothesis, have them work out how to test it rather than confirming or refuting it yourself.
Encourage learners to consider whether a prediction different from the one they hold might be correct, in order to foster differential diagnosis as a habitual strategy.
Entrap learners by deliberately suggesting an incorrect hypothesis, in order to get them to reveal the misconceptions underlying their reasoning.
Trace the implications of a learner's answer until it contradicts another belief they hold, which forces them to build consistent theories.
Tracing a learner's answer to a contradiction is a form of feedback that requires deeper thought about the error than typical correct-answer or process feedback does.
When learners ask for the right answer or defer to a textbook, decline to supply it and push them to run their own experiment and reach their own conclusion.

An inquiry teacher maintains a continuously updated agenda of goals and subgoals: high-level goals spawn the choice of problems and opening questions, and learners' answers reveal misconceptions and knowledge gaps that generate new diagnostic subgoals.
The teacher's agenda of goals and subgoals functions as a macro-level sequencing strategy driven by diagnosis rather than by a pre-fixed order.
Inquiry teaching can be applied to procedures by getting learners to invent the correct procedure through considering everything that could go wrong at each step.
Inquiry teaching can be applied to history only if the teacher knows how events led to other events, so learners can be asked to predict how history unfolded.
condition: when the causal links between events are known

statement: Content supplied as a bare series of steps with no reasons given, or as a set of unrelated facts, cannot be turned into an inquiry dialogue without substantial additional work.
An instructional method that does not fit the material as supplied should be declined for that material with the reason stated, rather than applied superficially.
Inquiry dialogue works with groups as well as individuals, and fostering multiple competing hypotheses and argumentation among a group can make the method more effective.
Every inquiry strategy must be paired with an explicit account of when and why it is used, otherwise the catalogue of strategies gives no guidance on which to apply.
An instructional approach should be interrogated for the situations in which it is not advisable and for its cost-effectiveness, not only for the situations it fits.
Systematic case variation in inquiry teaching applies to the examples presented rather than to the practice items, which distinguishes it from prescriptions for variety of practice.

Open a dialogue by finding out what the learner already knows in order to build on that knowledge, and settle the basic terminology the rest of the dialogue will depend on before pursuing the substantive goals.
Teach a distinction by presenting different cases of each class and testing whether the learner can classify them, rather than by asserting the criterion.
Ground a new term in an experience the learner has already had, by asking what they observed and letting the term name that observation.
Restating a learner's vague suggestion as an explicit but incorrect hypothesis to which they will assent is a form of entrapment that surfaces the misconception for testing.
Follow an entrapment immediately with a mini-experiment the learner performs, so the incorrect hypothesis is refuted by observation rather than by the teacher's authority.

Systematic case variation for a continuous variable should span the qualitatively distinct regions — below the critical value, at it, and above it — so the learner sees that the outcome is not monotonic.
When a learner's answer reveals a misconception mid-goal, suspend the current goal, pursue the correcting subgoal, and return to the original goal once the misconception is repaired.

Correct a misconception by asking the learner to consider the alternative predictions explicitly — naming the two or three possible outcomes and asking which will occur — rather than by stating the right one.
A learner's non sequitur is a common occurrence in dialogue and can be taken up productively — used to review earlier terminology or to open the next topic — rather than being suppressed.
A hypothetical case combined with a counterexample lets the teacher probe a prediction the learner cannot reach by direct observation, then show the case where the prediction fails.
Reintroduce a systematically varied case immediately after a learner gets one right, phrasing the question so it slightly entraps, in order to test whether the understanding is general or case-bound.
Push a learner's newly formed rule beyond the class it was induced from by asking whether it also applies to the contrasting class, which is hypothesis testing rather than confirmation.
When a learner lacks the concept needed to extend a rule to a new class, supply it by analogy to a case they can reason about, then let them make the generalization themselves.
Pause an experiment midway and ask the learner to revise their hypothesis in light of what has happened so far, rather than waiting for the final result.
Praise a well-reasoned conjecture warmly even when it turns out to be incorrect, and say explicitly that it was a good hypothesis; inquiry teachers use this frequently to foster hypothesis formation.
When a learner appeals to the teacher's authority for the answer, question your own authority — say you may be wrong — and turn the question into a measurement the learner performs.
Get the learner to invent the measurement procedure themselves — deciding what to measure before measuring it — which gradually turns the thinking over to them.
Have learners draw representations of each varied case, so they can see how the representation changes from case to case and acquire the rules for representing new configurations.

When a learner's drawing embodies an error, pick as counterexample a representation they produced earlier and ask a series of questions tracing the consequences until they see the contradiction between the two.
Consequence-tracing to a contradiction may be particularly useful for getting learners to give up wrong hypotheses, because the learner rather than the teacher discovers the inconsistency.

Introduce a representational device — such as dotted construction lines showing how something appears as opposed to how it is — as the vehicle for a new concept, and let the learner read the concept off the drawing.
Have the learner explain an earlier empirical finding in terms of the representation just built, which tests whether the model and the observation have been connected.
When a learner offers a plausible mechanism, do not confirm or deny it — tell them to draw it and see whether it is true.
An inquiry dialogue with a naive but cooperative learner is idealized; real learners are likelier to lead the dialogue astray, so the strategy set must handle detours rather than assume a clean path.
The aim of inquiry teaching is to get learners to analyse problems like scientists — systematically considering different cases, forming and testing hypotheses, and looking for counterexamples.
Inquiry teaching is a time-consuming way to teach, but where the goal is to teach learners to solve problems or invent theories creatively it may be the only method available.

Each move in an inquiry dialogue should be traceable both to the strategy it instantiates and to the objective it serves, so the dialogue can be audited rather than treated as unstructured conversation.
A single dialogue goal may remain open across many exchanges and be completed only much later, so the teacher must track open goals rather than expecting each to close before the next begins.
A prescriptive theory can be built inductively from a literature review of empirical research findings, drawing prescriptions from behavioral, cognitive and humanistic perspectives at once.
Narrowness buys guidance: a theory limited to microlevel strategies within the cognitive domain can give designers considerably more detailed direction than a broad theory covering all domains.

Component Display Theory is a theory about the components comprising every instructional presentation rather than a method, so a designer must still select a method that carries the prescribed components.
Classify every instructional outcome, whether stated as an objective or as a test item, on two dimensions: the student performance required and the type of subject-matter content.
The four performance levels are Remember Instance, Remember Generality, Use, and Find, where Use means applying a generality to specific cases and Find means finding a new generality.

The four content types are fact (an association between two particulars), concept (a set of objects, events or symbols sharing common characteristics), procedure (a set of steps for carrying out an activity), and principle (the cause-and-effect relationships in a process).
A generality is a statement of a definition, principle, or the steps of a procedure; an instance is a specific illustration of an object, symbol, event, process or procedure.
Every instructional presentation is a sequence of discrete displays plus the interrelationships among them, so any presentation can be described and audited in those terms.

The four primary presentation forms come from crossing content mode (generality or instance) with presentation mode (expository — present, tell or show; inquisitory — question, ask or require practice).

Each performance level requires its own combination of primary presentation forms; when the necessary forms are present, achievement and learning efficiency increase, and when they are absent or inappropriate both decrease.
Practice and test instances must be new — different from those used in earlier parts of the instruction — or the item tests recall rather than the intended performance.
When practice requires the learner to state a generality, require a paraphrase rather than a verbatim restatement.

Content consistency requires that each presentation form actually contain the information the content type needs; the same form must be filled differently for a fact, a concept, a procedure and a principle.

An adequate concept definition names the concept, identifies the superordinate concept, states the attributes distinguishing instances of one coordinate concept from another, and states the relationships among those attributes.

An adequate classify-practice item for a concept presents a new instance with all relevant attributes present, uses a form of representation that shows all the relevant attributes, and asks the learner to supply the name or judge class membership.

An adequate procedure presentation states the goal or name, the steps, their order, the decisions and branches, and the response mode; procedure practice supplies new materials and requires execution.
An adequate principle presentation names the principle, identifies the concepts it relates, and states the relationship; principle practice presents a new problem and requires a prediction.
Secondary presentation forms are information added to a primary form to enhance learning, and an enhanced presentation produces an increment in achievement and learning efficiency.
The main secondary presentation forms are attention-focusing help, repeated prerequisite information, alternate representation, mnemonics, and feedback.
Repeat prerequisite information the learner should already have acquired earlier in the instruction, because repeating it facilitates recall of what the current display depends on.
An alternate representation can be a restatement of a generality, an instance shown in a different context, or the same information delivered in another medium.

Feedback comes in distinct kinds: correct-answer feedback, helped feedback that adds attention-focusing information or works the problem to show how it should have been done, and feedback intrinsic to using the new generality.
For a find-level objective the best feedback is intrinsic — seeing whether the newly invented generality actually works.
condition: when the performance level is find

statement: The relationships between displays affect learning independently of the displays themselves, so interdisplay relationships must be designed rather than left to arise.
Divergence means successive instances differ in their variable attributes, so that irrelevant features do not become part of the learned concept.
Range means the set of instances spans a range of difficulty rather than clustering at one level.

Matching means pairing each example with a nonexample that shares the superordinate attributes but differs on the relevant ones; for procedures and principles it means showing inappropriate applications matched against the correct execution.
Fading means the help supplied by secondary presentation forms is gradually eliminated across displays.

For fact learning, present the set in a different random order each time, chunk it so no more than five to seven new items are required at once, require immediate recall with no delay, and require that all the facts be learned.
condition: when the objective is remember-instance for facts

statement: Isolation means the primary presentation forms are clearly identified for the learner, so they can tell a generality from an example from a practice item.
Learner control means the student decides how many instances to study, when to receive help, and other strategy choices — control exercised at the level of microstrategy components.
Test items are governed by their own adequacy rules: they keep divergence and range but drop matching, fading, and help, since the item must measure rather than teach.

For a remember-instance fact objective, drill with paired-associate cards, recalling the reverse side before turning the card for correct-answer feedback, and repeating until the criterion of no errors and immediate recall is met.
Shuffle a fact set between drill passes so the association is to the cue rather than to the position in the sequence.

A use-concept segment can be built expositorily as reference example, then definition, then elaboration, then matched example-nonexample pairs each with attention-focusing help, then classification practice, then helped feedback.

State at the start of a segment what the learner should do with each part of it — study the reference example and key idea, then the examples, then the practice problems — so the display types are explicitly isolated.
Distinguish a new term from the term it is most often confused with at the point of introduction, and illustrate both contrasts side by side.
Annotate each matched example-nonexample pair with the specific features that decide the case, listing the attributes present and absent rather than only labelling the pair.
Tell learners explicitly that peeking at an answer before writing their own may leave them unable to recall the information during the actual test, and that practice items resemble the test items.
Vary practice instances across representational modes — drawings, a recalled instance from an earlier segment, and an imagined real-world object — so classification is not tied to one depiction.

Helped feedback explains for each item why it is or is not an instance, naming which criterial attribute the incorrect options fail, and directs the learner to review the key ideas and examples if any item was missed.
An integrated lesson would not use a wide variety of methods and delivery systems; varying method per segment is a demonstration device, not a design recommendation.

Given only objectives, test items, generalities and text, a designer would normally perform task analysis first and would expect it to yield additional objectives and modifications to the ones supplied.
A remember-generality objective would not normally stand as its own lesson segment but would be integrated with the segment teaching the corresponding concept or principle.
Define a composite term by first defining each component term it depends on, so the target definition is assembled from already-defined parts rather than introducing several unknowns at once.
Supply a mnemonic as a secondary presentation form when the objective is to remember a generality, tying the term's meaning to an image the learner can reconstruct.
Practise a remembered generality by having the learner label a diagram from memory and then check it against the labelled version, so recall is produced before it is confirmed.
Cloze items that require supplying the correct term in a described situation test the generality in use rather than as verbatim recall.
Two objectives that rest on understanding the same principles can be combined into a single presentation rather than taught as separate segments.
condition: when the objectives depend on the same underlying principles

statement: A manipulable simulation in which the learner varies one factor and observes the corresponding change serves as a set of reference examples that later tutorial displays refer back to.

Follow a simulation with a conversational tutorial whose questions direct the learner to think about what they just observed, leading them to state the principle themselves before it is formally stated.
When a learner's stated observation is incorrect, advise them to return to the simulation rather than correcting them, and leave the choice to return or continue under learner control.
Accompany formal statements of a generality with questions that direct the learner's attention and force them to process the information rather than read past it.
Confirm a prediction with a simulation that draws the actual outcome after the learner has answered, so right-or-wrong feedback is followed by the mechanism that produced it.
Escalate successive simulations to slightly more complex arrangements of the same components, so the same principle is exercised against progressively harder configurations.
Before a learner can transfer a principle to a system containing a new component type, they must first be led to see that the new component behaves like one they already understand.
A demonstration of a procedure should let the learner repeat any step or substep as many times as necessary and view them in any order.

Structure a procedural demonstration as an overview menu of the major steps with a drill-down to substep details, and advise learners it is usually wise to view the overview before the details for a step.
Illustrate the major steps of a process first to give the big picture, then explain each step with its own pictures and captions.
State the number of major steps before naming them, and name each step in imperative form while a still picture representing it is highlighted.
Synchronize the narration with the demonstrated action and pause after each action so the learner can complete watching it before the next statement.
Say why a step matters, not only what to do — for instance that light adjustment is critical because without it the specimen cannot be seen at all.
Explain the failure mode a substep prevents — what contamination, damage or wrong reading would result if it were skipped — because that is what makes the step's constraints memorable.
Show the wider professional practice a simplified classroom procedure abstracts from, and state explicitly which parts are unnecessary for present purposes.
Adequate practice for a procedural skill is not possible from demonstration alone; subsequent practice must occur where the learner has access to equipment of the type demonstrated.

Sequence laboratory practice by backward chaining: the learner first performs only the last step with the earlier steps already completed, and each successive exercise adds the preceding step until they perform the whole procedure.

Interleave demonstration and practice rather than completing all demonstration first: view the overview, then the detail for the step to be practised, then do that lab exercise, then return for the next step's detail.
The ideal interleaving of demonstration and hands-on practice is often difficult or impossible to arrange in most school situations, so the design must acknowledge that constraint.
After initial practice, integrate the learned tool into the wider curriculum as a working instrument, which supplies the variety and additional practice a dedicated exercise cannot.

When practising a preparatory step, give learners the opportunity to work with different kinds of material rather than a single specimen type, and integrate that variety into the surrounding curriculum.
For a remember-instance fact objective the required presentation is an expository instance followed by a practice instance that is the same instance, since there is nothing to generalize.
condition: when the objective is remember-instance for facts

statement: A fact is an arbitrary association between two particulars — symbol to symbol, object to symbol, event to symbol — arbitrary in the sense that no generality can be used to derive it.
Feedback for fact practice should consist of correct-answer information alone, since there is no reasoning to help with.
condition: when the content type is fact

statement: A mastery criterion of less than 100% is not meaningful for fact learning: either a particular association is needed or it is not, and accepting partial mastery raises the question of why any of the facts were taught.
Fact recall must be immediate: although problem solving takes time, an association should require minimal processing time, so response latency is part of the criterion.

Every prescription used in preparing a lesson segment should be listed alongside a comment on how it applies to that segment, so the design can be checked against the theory prescription by prescription.
A use-concept presentation consists of the definition, then several different examples, then previously unencountered practice instances that differ from the examples used for teaching.
condition: when the objective is use-concept

statement: Elaborate a definition with attention-focusing information that helps the learner identify the relevant attributes and recall the prerequisites, and restate it in a different mode such as a graphic, chart or diagram.
Every teaching and practice instance must be a specific member of the class or a representation that includes all the relevant attributes as the definition states them.
Diagrams exclude the irrelevant characteristics real objects carry, so classifying diagrams may be easier than classifying real instances and a diagram-only design overstates what learners can do.
Isolate each primary presentation from surrounding text with explicit section labels and visual separation, so learners can tell the main idea from its illustration and from practice.
Prompt examples with attention-focusing information that links the specific attributes of each example to the labels for those attributes used in the definition.

Fade prompting during the later stages of the presentation, because when attention-focusing information is always available learners rely on it before studying an example long enough and get the illusion of understanding.
Fading attention-focusing information is what promotes the increased mental effort that produces real understanding.
Match each teaching example to a potentially confusing nonexample drawn from a coordinate concept under the same superordinate, which helps the learner discriminate members from nonmembers.

Use matched pairs early in the presentation and fade them later; do not use matching during practice, where instances and noninstances are presented one by one in random order to avoid unintentional prompts.
Successive instances in both examples and practice must be divergent from one another, so the learner sees the variety the class contains and can generalize to all its members.
Feedback on a practice classification should give attention-focusing information showing why the instance does or does not belong, and must not be available before the learner responds.
When help in feedback is not faded, learners become help-dependent and try less hard before responding because they know an explanation will follow regardless.

Instances in both the example and practice stages should span a range of difficulty, so learners meet the variety of cases they will encounter after instruction; more complex concepts require an even greater range.
For a remember-generality objective, present the generality, a single reference example, and practice in paraphrasing the generality — recognizing it stated in two or more different ways.
condition: when the objective is remember-generality

statement: Learners tend to remember examples more easily than verbal statements and will probably use the reference example to reconstruct the definition, so the reference example must clearly indicate every critical attribute.
Feedback for a remember-generality practice item should indicate the synonyms involved, since the performance is recognizing the same generality in different words.
A use-principle presentation states the proposition, gives several different explanations of specific applications, then requires practice explaining or predicting in additional instances.
condition: when the objective is use-principle

statement: Asking a question does not make a display practice: rhetorical questions on an expository generality or example display are attention-focusing devices, and it is legitimate to ask them there.
A manipulable simulation supplies matched examples automatically, because only the relevant attribute changes from one state to the next while everything else is held constant.

Requiring the learner to predict before manipulating a simulation increases the mental effort they must put forth, and the design is stronger if the system prevents access to the simulation until the prediction is made.
A statement of a principle must name the component concepts it relates and the causal or correlational relationship between them.
Instances used for a principle must adequately represent every component concept the principle involves, not only the outcome.

Situations chosen to illustrate and practise a principle should span a wide range of difficulty — some where the principle's application is obvious and others where it is subtle — which increases the learner's ability to apply it later.
Illustrative explanations of a principle should include common misconceptions and show where the principle does not work or does not apply, so learners become discriminating in applying it.
Practice that asks the learner to predict a given situation is better than practice that asks them to choose between an appropriate and an inappropriate application.

A use-procedure presentation gives a general description of the process, then demonstrations with specific objects, then opportunities for the learner to perform the procedure with a similar but different object or materials.
condition: when the objective is use-procedure

statement: A process description must identify the outcome that following the procedure produces, every step and its order of execution, and every decision with the branches following each alternative.
A represented rather than hands-on demonstration must clearly illustrate each step, the proper execution sequence, and the expected consequence of each step.
condition: when the demonstration is a representation rather than hands-on

statement: Where the procedure will be used with a variety of objects and materials, the learner must practise with that variety rather than with a single case.

Elaborate a process description with aids that help the learner remember the individual steps and their order, review the prerequisite concepts any decision depends on, and present the process in at least two alternative representations.
Give each step a single-word label so the learner can hold the most important aspect of the step in memory.

Identify each step of a demonstration as it is executed and focus attention on the decisions required and their consequences; a second demonstration should fade that attention-focusing information so the learner must attend more closely.
A process description must be concise, with critical steps and actions clearly separated from elaborative information.
Where the real world uses different types of equipment, demonstrate a variety of equipment and let learners practise on a variety; where that is impossible, vary the materials instead.
condition: when the target environment contains varied equipment

statement: Show common incorrect ways of performing steps or making decisions during a demonstration, label those incorrect paths clearly, and warn the learner, because identifying them helps avoid the mistakes during their own practice.

When a process has both simple and more complex means of execution, illustrate the range during demonstration and let learners practise both, even showing advanced variants they will not be required to perform, so they see the range of possibilities.

During early practice tries, feedback should be immediate and precise, naming steps omitted, steps performed correctly, and decisions omitted or incorrect; later practice should let the consequences of the learner's own actions supply the feedback.
Presenting the major steps first and then elaborating their detail is an application of elaboration theory within a procedural demonstration.

A design should be audited against each prescription and its shortfalls named — where fading is insufficient, where divergence of representation is too narrow, where misconception coverage is missing — rather than presented as fully conforming.
Divergence in principle instruction comes from using systems that each require some modification in how the principle is applied, not merely from changing surface details.
Making the learner's prediction a precondition for checking it with the simulation is itself a form of isolation, since it separates the practice display from the example display.
A macro-level theory of instruction supplies prescriptions for selecting, sequencing, synthesizing and summarizing content, which micro-level presentation theories do not address.

A theory can be built by analysing the differences among existing strategies, identifying the situations each fits best, and then extending and operationalizing the optimal strategy for each situation.
Explicitly teaching the interrelationships within the content — synthesis — is a distinct strategy component, not a by-product of teaching the parts.
Most of the Elaboration Theory's prescriptions lack empirical research support, so confidence in their validity is correspondingly limited.

Elaboration sequencing works like a camera zoom lens: start with a wide-angle view showing the major parts and their relationships without detail, zoom in on one part, then zoom back out to review the whole and the part's context before zooming in again.
Begin instruction with an epitome — a special overview containing the simplest and most fundamental ideas — and then add complexity or detail to one part in layers called elaborations.
To epitomize is to present a few of the most fundamental and representative ideas at a concrete application or skill level, which is different from summarizing them.

Each elaboration lesson also reviews earlier content and teaches the relationships between the newest ideas and those presented before, and this elaborate-summarize-synthesize pattern repeats until the desired complexity is reached.
An elaborative sequence rests on a single content orientation: whether the instruction is primarily about what (concepts), how (procedures), or why (principles).

Virtually every course holds one of concepts, procedures or principles to be more important than the other two, so the kind of simple-to-complex sequence must differ with the content type central to the goals.
Elaborations based on concepts, principles and procedures are the only three kinds found in the sequencing literature, matching the three content types identified for generalizable knowledge.

For a conceptual course, analyse and organize the concepts into conceptual structures showing superordinate, coordinate and subordinate relationships, then sequence the most important structure from the top down, from the most general and inclusive concepts to progressively more detailed ones.
condition: when the course goals are primarily conceptual

statement: For a procedural course, identify the simplest possible version of the task and the simplifying assumptions that define it, then relax those assumptions in order of importance so progressively more complex paths are taught.
condition: when the course goals are primarily procedural

statement: For a theoretical course, order principles from the most basic and observable to the most detailed, complex and restricted, an order that usually resembles the historical order in which the knowledge was discovered.
condition: when the course goals are primarily theoretical

statement: Build a theoretical sequence by repeatedly asking what principle you would teach if you had the learners for only one hour, then for one more hour, until every principle is placed.
To find the elaborations of a principle already placed, interrogate it with why, which way, how much, and what else.

Whatever the organizing content type, other content types and learning prerequisites are fleshed onto the sequence skeleton at the point where each is most relevant, rather than forming the skeleton themselves.
The product of macro-level sequencing is a course blueprint showing, per lesson, the organizing content, its elaborations, and the supporting content and prerequisites attached to it.
A top-down conceptual sequence and a bottom-up learning-prerequisite hierarchy both run simple to complex, and the elaboration sequence does not violate the hierarchical sequence's principles.

Within a lesson, present the easiest and most familiar organizing concepts first for a conceptual organization, the steps in performance order for a procedural one, and the simplest organizing content first for a theoretical one.
Place supporting content immediately after the organizing content it is most closely related to.
Place each learning prerequisite immediately before the content for which it is prerequisite, applying the prerequisite rule at the scale of an hour-long unit rather than across the course.
Group coordinate concepts together within a lesson.
Teach a principle — the meaningful understanding of the process — before teaching the related procedure.
A summarizer provides a concise statement of each idea or fact taught, a typical easy-to-remember example, and diagnostic self-test practice items for each idea.

Distinguish lesson summarizers, which close a single lesson, from set summarizers, which cover everything taught so far in a whole unit — a set being all the lessons that elaborate directly on a single lesson.
