A synthesizer interrelates and integrates ideas in order to give the learner a valuable kind of knowledge, deepen understanding of the individual ideas, increase meaningfulness and motivational appeal, and increase retention.
There are three types of synthesizer — conceptual, procedural and theoretical — each interrelating ideas of a single content type.
Synthesis can be placed contextually at the start of a lesson to situate what follows, or as post-synthesis at the end of a lesson or unit.

An analogy relates new information to a more familiar and meaningful body of organized knowledge the learner already possesses, reminding them of something concrete in their experience to prepare them for a more abstract idea.

A cognitive-strategy activator prompts the learner's use of a generic skill and can be embedded, as when a mnemonic or analogy is supplied, or detached, as when the learner is merely told to think up an analogy or a mnemonic.
Elaboration sequencing is designed to build stable cognitive structures by assimilating new content to existing ones, which is the rationale that unifies its otherwise borrowed strategies.
An elaborative sequence can allow the learner considerable freedom to choose which part to zoom in on next and how far to zoom in on each.
Learner control at the macro level covers selection and sequencing of content, which is a different thing from learner control over microstrategy components.
Presenting procedural steps in the order of their performance is a forward-chaining sequence, distinct from the backward-chaining used for some procedural practice.
A procedural blueprint records, per lesson, which simplifying condition is relaxed and which specific steps that relaxation adds, so the growth of the task version is auditable.
Learner control of content means the learner may select any lesson whose prerequisites they have already acquired, which is a different offering from learner control of instructional strategies.
condition: only for lessons whose prerequisites the learner has acquired

statement: Learner control of strategies covers the type, order and number of microstrategy components such as examples, practice items and alternative representations, and the type and timing of macrostrategy components such as summarizers, synthesizers and analogies.

A complete elaboration design comprises an elaborative sequence of lessons, a within-lesson sequence including any prerequisite sequences, a summarizer and a synthesizer for each lesson, analogies and cognitive-strategy activators as needed, and learner control to the extent appropriate.

A macro-level sequencing theory gives no guidance for teaching the individual skills and pieces of knowledge that make up a course; that guidance must come from a micro-level presentation theory, and the two are complementary rather than competing.
To illustrate a purely macro-level theory, present course and lesson outlines rather than a finished lesson, since lesson detail lies outside what the theory prescribes.

The first design decision is whether the simple-to-complex sequence will be based on conceptual knowledge (what classes of things exist), procedural knowledge (how a person accomplishes things), or theoretical knowledge (why certain processes occur).

Choose the organizing content type from what the objectives emphasize: an emphasis on understanding a dynamic natural process indicates a theoretical organization rather than a conceptual or procedural one.

Simple-to-complex sequencing operates at five nested levels — ideas within a lesson, lessons within a unit, units within a module, modules within a course, and courses within a curriculum — spanning roughly one hour to a full year of instructional time.

It is common for different content types to organize the sequence at different levels: modules sequenced by concepts, their units by the principles relating to each concept, and those units' lessons by the procedures relating to each principle.

Build a theoretical sequence by brainstorming all the principles first, listing the most obvious ones from the objectives, and then epitomizing — looking for the simplest principles that are the most basic, observable, and representative of the whole set.
Two heuristics elicit the epitome from a subject-matter expert: ask which principle they would teach if only one were possible, and ask which principles were discovered earliest.
A simpler principle is one in which fewer things happen, but where the things that do happen are the essence — the most important and observable aspects — of the larger set.

Simplification proceeds along identifiable dimensions of the phenomenon, and each dimension should be named with the reason a case is simpler — fewer interfaces, fewer interacting variables, or a more precise and intuitive relationship.
A case is simpler when the governing relationship is precise and intuitive rather than dependent on several factors at once.
After simplifying down to the level of student entering knowledge, check the opposite direction: confirm that every more complex principle the course should cover has been identified.
Two heuristics surface more complex principles: asking what else happens, and asking why, which way, and how much about a principle already placed.
After the organizing sequence is fixed, allocate supporting content to each elaboration, assign all content to individual lessons, and sequence the content within each lesson.

Designing a curriculum blueprint without a subject-matter expert violates the procedure and yields a product with more shortcomings; state that the design should not be implemented without further consultation and revision.

Where no elaborative relationship exists between two bodies of content — neither being a more complex iteration of the other — their order is arbitrary with respect to sequencing criteria and should be settled on other grounds.
condition: when the content areas have no elaborative relationship

statement: Grade-level and module divisions in a blueprint are often arbitrary organizational choices driven by how the content interleaves with the rest of a curriculum, not consequences of the sequencing theory.
The same content can be re-sequenced for a different audience: what is spread across three courses for a school timetable might be studied in order within a single year by an interested adult.

Teach the target phenomenon's behaviour first through simpler physical analogues that share its behaviours, so learners meet each behaviour in the medium where it is easiest to observe before meeting it in the target medium.
Use the same behaviour categories across each successive analogue — linear movement, reflection, refraction, absorption — so the parallel structure itself carries the transfer.
Teach the simplest case of each behaviour in a way that lets students predict what will happen in that case, before adding the cases where the behaviour interacts with others.
Where an analogue breaks down — a behaviour the target has that the analogue does not, or vice versa — state that difference explicitly rather than leaving the analogy to over-extend.
A later elaboration lesson explicitly carries forward the principles established earlier and adds only the new ones, so the accumulating principle set is visible in each lesson outline.

Two structurally adjacent cases can be distinguished by a single stated condition — whether the entering and exiting surfaces are parallel — so that a family of cases is derived from one principle plus one varying condition.
Organize the elaborations of a principle by the question each answers — what else happens, why, which way, how much — so the lesson outline shows which kind of complexity each addition supplies.
Course outlines show only the organizing content and its sequence; a course blueprint adds the supporting content, prerequisites and objectives attached to each lesson.
Supporting content should ordinarily be worked out for every lesson of a blueprint, not only for an illustrative one.
Marking which prerequisites are unmastered — rather than listing all prerequisites — keeps a blueprint focused on what actually has to be taught.
An elaborative sequence within one lesson can be built by naming the simplifying and elaborating conditions that generate each successive case of the organizing content.

Open a lesson with an initial synthesizer that states the context — naming where this lesson's topic sits among the sibling topics, briefly reviewing each, and stating which one the lesson will explore.
Follow the context statement with demonstrations of the most important causes and effects the lesson will explain, posed as questions about each case to be covered.

Tag every content element in a lesson outline with both its type — prerequisite concept, principle, supporting concept, supporting information, supporting procedure — and the performance level at which it is to be taught.
Teach a prerequisite concept immediately before the principle that uses it, and name in the outline exactly which later items that prerequisite serves.
Some prerequisites need only be taught at remember level while others must be taught at application level; the required level depends on what the dependent principle does with them.
Teach principles at the application or skill level rather than the remember level, since the point of a principle is prediction and explanation in new cases.
State each principle in the outline as a complete conditional sentence naming the situation and the outcome, not as a topic label.
Pair each case with two complementary principles — what happens to the observed outcome and what happens to the underlying mechanism — so learners connect appearance to cause.
Order the cases within a lesson from the one with the fewest interacting effects to the one with the most, so each case adds a single new behaviour to the previous.
Place a conceptual synthesizer-summarizer immediately after a group of coordinate concepts has been taught, rather than deferring all synthesis to the end of the lesson.
Attach supporting information about real-world uses, history and manufacture at remember level to the lesson whose principles they depend on, rather than teaching them as separate topics.
Close a lesson with a summarizer that includes the appropriate synthesizer for the lesson's organizing content type.
A concept summarizer lists each term against its concise definition and instructs the learner to cover the definition column, attempt each definition, and reveal the answer one line at a time.
A principle summarizer is a table whose rows are the situations and whose columns are the distinct outcomes, so the parallel structure across cases is visible at a glance.
Include a prototypical illustration alongside each summarized principle, since the summarizer is meant to supply an easy-to-remember example as well as a statement.
Summarize a procedure as a labelled diagram with numbered steps and arrows pointing to the parts each step acts on.
Self-test a procedure by having the learner mentally rehearse every step with eyes closed, picturing exactly what they would do, then check the written version for missed steps and wrong order.
Self-test paired facts in both directions — cover one column and recall the other, then swap columns — so the association is not learned in one direction only.

A summarizer should give each content type its own review form: definitions for concepts, a situation-outcome table for principles, a labelled step diagram for procedures, and a two-column drill for facts.
In an elaborative curriculum, what was taught as a single lesson at one level receives a whole unit at the next level of elaboration, and each module elaborates a unit of the module before it.
Some lessons at any level of elaboration may have no lessons elaborating further on them, so an elaboration tree need not be uniform in depth.
An epitome version is chosen for concreteness as well as simplicity: the case that can be seen and touched and that has the fewest behaviours comes first.
A later lesson can elaborate on more than one earlier lesson at once, when its subject combines the behaviours of two simpler subjects taught before it.
When several dimensions of simplification are available, expand on the most important and most representative dimension first, and defer any dimension that presupposes elaboration of another.

When one dimension is deferred, tell learners from the beginning that the deferred contrast exists and that they will learn more about it later, so the simplification is not mistaken for the whole story.
Cycling back to substantially the same principles in a new and more complex application builds systematic review into the sequence itself rather than adding review as a separate activity.

A spiral sequence leads learners through the same process of discovering similarities that characterized the historical development of the discipline, which matters for anyone who treats process as part of the curriculum.
An expository mode can still give learners some of the excitement of and feel for the process of discovery; the spiral sequence is not exclusive to discovery instruction.
Each principle in an elaboration lesson is often the same principle applied to a special case, with each case producing different effects within the same behaviour category.
Elaborate an already-taught principle by stating explicitly what learners may already have realized but that was never stated or demonstrated as such.
Order sibling topics by how many factors govern the outcome: a topic where the relationship is single-surface, precise and intuitive precedes one where it depends on several interacting factors.

Pair each principle about an observable outcome with a principle about the underlying mechanism, and teach the observable one first, because the observation-to-deduction order is also a concrete-to-abstract order.

The mechanism principle is a more complex elaboration of the outcome principle because it explains why the outcome occurs, involves many simultaneous elements that are hard to show at once, and is less concrete since the outcome can be seen and the mechanism cannot.

After all organizing content is listed for every lesson, identify the supporting content for each lesson; completing that step means all content has been selected, allocated to lessons, and sequenced.

Breaking supporting content into concepts, procedures, learning prerequisites and information is not strictly necessary but reduces the chance of the designer overlooking important supporting content.
List learning prerequisites as their own category to remind the designer to identify prerequisites not only for the organizing content but also for the supporting concepts and procedures.

An elaborative sequence communicates that the more one learns the more one realizes how little one knows: it raises questions, broadens horizons and creates realizations that might not otherwise surface.

When many lessons elaborate on two earlier lessons at once, the available learner control over content selection is more limited than usual, but options should still be offered wherever prerequisites allow.
condition: when lessons have multiple elaboration parents

statement: A learner need not complete every lesson at one level before selecting a lesson at the next: a deeper lesson can be taken as soon as the specific lesson it elaborates has been mastered.

Assign each supporting concept the performance level its use actually requires: classification tasks are at the use level, while a concept needed only for meaningful understanding is listed as information at the remember level.
A procedure the learner need only understand rather than execute is listed as information, not as a supporting procedure.
Design within-lesson sequencing after all lessons in a course have been sequenced, because working on the later parts of the overall sequence often forces revisions to the earlier parts.

A sequencing theory makes no prescriptions about discovery versus expository, inquiry versus non-inquiry, game versus non-game, medium selection, example and practice-item sequencing, or management strategy — all of which a truly comprehensive theory of instruction would need.
Inquiry, as distinct from discovery, begins instruction with a major question and directs the following instruction — expository or discovery — toward answering it.
For a school audience where motivation is a major concern, some form of inquiry is likely beneficial, with discovery used occasionally but not too often because of time limitations.
An initial synthesizer supplies external synthesis by relating the lesson to the larger picture and some internal synthesis by previewing how this lesson's ideas relate to each other.
Analysis must precede synthesis, so explicit internal synthesis has to wait until the learner has analysed and understood each individual element.

For principles and procedures, demonstrations are generally the most effective way to show interrelationships at the start of a lesson; for concepts, a combined summarizer-synthesizer is generally better.
Research has shown that stated objectives are often of little value to learners, probably because objectives are usually too abstract to communicate meaningfully.

Replace an abstract objective statement with a concrete demonstration of the terminal capability the learner will acquire, which serves the objective's purpose while also previewing, motivating and synthesizing.
Identify a principle's unmastered prerequisites by performing a standard hierarchical analysis on it, and teach those prerequisites immediately before the principle.
Non-prerequisite supporting content is taught immediately after the organizing content it relates to, with one exception: highly related coordinate concepts should always be taught together.

Teach a concept's sole coordinate concept alongside it even when the coordinate is not a prerequisite, because learning one exhaustive alternative entails learning the other and its label may as well be attached.
condition: when the two concepts exhaust the superordinate class

statement: Place a summarizer-synthesizer at the point where all the content it covers has already been taught, rather than automatically at the end of a lesson.
A summarizer must present a concise generality for each idea containing just enough critical words to stimulate recall, not a full restatement that tries to create new understanding.
A summarizer should provide a prototypical example, preferably visual; line drawings are ideal for concepts and all critical attributes must be visible.
A synthesizer should show the major relationships among the ideas simply and with a minimum of words — for concepts, which are kinds of which.

A summarizer-synthesizer should encourage active processing of the relationships and offer a low-risk self-test with immediate feedback available; computer-based delivery is ideal because it can prevent premature peeking and ensure a response.
Arrange a summarizer's generalities so they can be used expositorily as a summary and inquisitorily as a self-test, and preferably use them both ways.
Review prerequisite concepts before the principles that depend on them within a summarizer, and review the remember-level information last.
In a learner-controlled system the summarizer-synthesizer should be accessible on demand at any time during the lesson and perhaps before or after it.
Concept review should include practice on instances — classifying new examples and nonexamples — not only recall of definitions.

A theoretical synthesizer can explicitly integrate only principles that are parts of the same causal chain; principles that are merely parallel cases can be compared and contrasted but not synthesized.
A dynamic demonstration on computer or video is better than a static diagram for a theoretical synthesizer, because what is being illustrated is a cause-and-effect process.
A slower learner may need extra explanation to benefit from a synthesizer that a brighter learner does not need at all, so its inclusion is a coverage decision rather than a universal requirement.
A procedural synthesizer shows the order of the steps making up the complete performance; for more complicated procedures a flow diagram is preferable to a numbered list.
Always relate the steps of a procedure to a picture or drawing of the object being operated, so the generality is paired with a prototypical example.
A self-test that requires effort learners can skip will usually be skipped, so a delivery system that enforces the response is preferable when active cognitive processing is required.

A unit or set summarizer-synthesizer — sometimes called an expanded epitome — contains the same elements as a lesson one and differs only in scope, covering all lessons that elaborate directly on a single lesson.
A motivational design model is not an instructional-design model and is not intended to stand alone: its prescriptions supplement other instructional theories.
Motivational strategies are prescribed in a smorgasbord fashion rather than as a fixed model, because any module of instruction could require anywhere from none to all of the strategy kinds.
The ARCS model organizes motivational variables into four categories — Attention, Relevance, Confidence and Satisfaction — each with three subcategories of strategies.

Gaining and sustaining the learner's attention is the first step in motivation, and the motivational concern for getting attention is distinct from the information-processing concern for directing it to what is to be learned.
Gain and maintain attention through perceptual arousal — novel, surprising, incongruous or uncertain events in the instruction.
Stimulate information-seeking behaviour by posing a question or problem to solve, or by having the learner generate one.
Maintain interest by varying the elements of the instruction rather than holding its form constant.
After curiosity is stimulated, learners question the relevance of the situation before becoming highly motivated, asking what importance the instruction has for their lives.

Establishing the relevance of instruction is generally harder than generating attention, and unless relevance is established externally by job or admission requirements the instructor must connect the objectives to the learners' own interests and motives.
Build relevance through familiarity: use concrete language and choose examples and concepts related to the learner's own experience and values.
Build relevance through goal orientation: present the objectives and the utility of the instruction, and either supply goals for accomplishment or have learners define them.
Build relevance through motive matching: use teaching strategies that fit the motive profiles of the students.
People avoid pursuing an interesting and desired goal when they believe the likelihood of achieving it is too low, so a positive expectancy for success is the third requirement for motivation.

Adjust the risk level to the confidence of the learners and the type of objective: learners acquiring a new skill need low psychological risk with no fear of losing face, while a degree of challenge is needed to stimulate peak performance once they have begun to master it.
Build confidence by making learners aware of the performance requirements and the evaluative criteria.
Build confidence through challenge setting: provide multiple achievement levels so learners can set personal standards, and performance opportunities where they can experience success.
Build confidence through attribution molding: give feedback that supports the learner's ability and effort as the determinants of their success.

Learners become unmotivated quickly when outcomes are inconsistent with their expectations — when grading seems subjective and arbitrary, when an intrinsically motivated person is locked into an externally controlled contingency system, or when the experience simply is not what was expected.
The designer must manage the delicate balance between fostering intrinsic motivation and the appropriate, sometimes unavoidable, use of extrinsic reinforcement.
Create satisfaction through natural consequences: give learners opportunities to use newly acquired knowledge or skill in a real or simulated setting.
Create satisfaction through positive consequences: supply feedback and reinforcement that will sustain the desired behaviour.
Create satisfaction through equity: maintain consistent standards and consequences for task accomplishment.

Motivational design has four critical events — audience analysis, motivational objectives, strategy selection, and evaluation — which are development procedures for the designer rather than specifications of what the instruction will be like.
Analyse the audience to determine which motivational category actually needs emphasis, because adding motivational strategies increases the length or expense of development and implementation.

An audience may be interested and already aware of the relevance yet lack confidence in their ability, and may be driven by extrinsic reward rather than intrinsic enjoyment; the diagnosis determines which strategies are needed.

Write motivational objectives specifying the student behaviours to be observed, which may be cognitive (a higher expectancy for success midway through), affective (rating the instruction as at least moderately interesting), or psychomotor (duration of attention, time on task, or duration of participation).

Motivational strategies should not take up too much time, should not detract from the learning objectives, should fall within development and implementation budgets, should be acceptable to the audience, and should be compatible with the delivery system including the instructor's personal style.
Where attention and relevance are already present, the goal is only to avoid boredom and maintain the sense of relevance the learners arrived with, rather than to add further strategies.
condition: when the audience already has attention and perceives relevance

statement: For extrinsically motivated learners, produce the expected rewards for success or evidence that the immediate achievement is a step toward that reward.
condition: when learners are extrinsically motivated

statement: Achievement is not a valid measure of motivational success: achievement can vary independently of motivation because of other psychological and environmental factors.

A global measure of affect shows whether learners basically liked the instruction but is usually too general to be useful in motivational design; measures should be tied specifically to the motivational objectives, as they are for learning objectives.

A demonstration lesson may deliberately include more motivational strategies than an actual application would need; final decisions on which to use require placing the lesson in its broader course and unit context.
Illustrating a supplementary model by annotating and modifying another designer's lesson implies no criticism of that lesson; the modifications reflect stated assumptions about the audience.
Applying a supplementary model to segments originating from different theoretical viewpoints shows that its prescriptions are not tied to one instructional approach.

Motivational design requires explicit assumptions about the audience: their responsiveness to curiosity arousal, their sense of the subject's relevance, their confidence from prior experience in the domain, and their responsiveness to feedback.
Learners with little prior success in a subject area tend to be low to moderate in confidence for it, which is a diagnosis about the audience rather than about the content.
Learners low in perceived relevance will still respond if they see some immediate utility or are stimulated by the instructional methods themselves.

Wherever the original design already contains motivational elements, build on them rather than replacing them, and add strategies judiciously so the original structure and purpose are enhanced rather than altered.
Do not overload instruction with motivational strategies for their own sake: motivational strategies must not overshadow the primary instructional objectives.
Games, simulations and extensive motivational illustrations are expensive to create and are not warranted when the scope of the learning objectives is simple and limited.
condition: when the instructional scope is small

statement: Open a lesson with a concrete scenario in which the learner must make a consequential decision that the skill being taught would settle, so the need for the skill is felt before it is taught.
Frame the opening scenario as an explicit challenge to the learner's capability, naming the desirable and undesirable outcomes.
Acknowledge that a dramatized scenario is unlikely, then name the real occupations that face the same discrimination daily, so the artificial hook is anchored to genuine utility.
State in the introduction what the learner will be able to do, how often the skill will recur in the course, and where it generalizes beyond the immediate topic.
Pose an intriguing everyday question the lesson will answer and promise that the learner will know the answer by the end, so curiosity persists across the lesson.
Show the lesson's parts as a labelled diagram of the target object, so the structure of the instruction maps visibly onto the structure of the thing being learned.
A memorable rhyme or verbal formula encoding the criterial attributes gives learners a retrievable form of the definition, and learners should be told to rehearse it until it comes easily.
Explain how a confusable term differs by tying each to a concrete image whose name contains the cue, so the contrast is self-checking.
Let learners self-test on annotated examples by covering the notes and attempting the classification and the reason before revealing them.
Require learners to explain why each example is or is not an instance, not merely to classify it, before moving to the practice problems.
Tell learners that effort applied to the examples predicts success on the problems, linking their outcome to controllable effort rather than to ability alone.
Ask learners to predict how many problems they expect to get right before attempting them, which makes the performance standard personal and self-set.
Tell learners the typical success rate of students who complete the segment, so their expectation of success is calibrated by a realistic norm rather than by fear.
Direct learners who struggle to complete as many items as they can unaided first, then review the specific sections, rather than abandoning the attempt.
Give learners a scorecard to fill in per item so they see their own progress against the stated criterion.
Offer an optional further-challenge problem for learners who want one, so multiple achievement levels exist within the same lesson.
State the scoring criterion for an exercise before the learner attempts it, and instruct them to take the exercise as if it were the quiz.
After scoring, instruct learners who succeeded to work out why any missed item was wrong, and learners who did not to restudy and seek help from a teacher or another student.
Attribute the learner's success explicitly to their ability and their effort — stating there is no luck or magic involved — immediately before the graded assessment.
Embed a short, true anecdote about someone the learner's age using the skill for a purpose they care about, to answer the unspoken question of why anyone would do this.
Reframe abstract example content in terms the learner already values — naming the ordinary object being examined and why someone would examine it — instead of using a neutral placeholder.
Supply a concrete analogy for a quantitative relationship, mapping the varying attribute onto a familiar human contrast, as a memory aid for the direction of the relationship.
Weight exercise items by the number of points they carry, so a multi-part explanation is scored as more than a single-choice recall item.
Close a segment by connecting what was just learned to the terminal task the learner will perform, stating what they will now understand while doing it.
Note explicitly when a demonstration design has not been taught and formatively evaluated, and give the reasons, rather than presenting it as validated.
Titles occupy a visually and conceptually strategic position in a lesson, so a title can be revised to add novelty while also carrying learning cues about the content.
Using a specific person's name, personal pronouns and a visualizable example helps learners relate to instruction as a relevant human experience.
Providing a normative standard helps a learner set a reasonable level of challenge for themselves.
An illustration that would improve a point only marginally is not worth the space and expense when the point is simple; motivational enhancements are subject to cost-benefit judgement.
Posing even a low-level problem before a presentation stimulates information-seeking and can simultaneously clarify a critical viewing convention the learner needs.
A mnemonic serves motivationally as well as cognitively: novel word sounds, visual language and the surprise of rhyme give the learner an interesting as well as memorable tool.
Varying format — margin width, text versus illustration, white space, type style — across pages contributes to sustaining learner attention.
Simple early exercises give an immediate sense of accomplishment and build confidence; moderately challenging exercises with immediate feedback contribute the same way.
Helping learners recognize and avoid obstacles to success increases their confidence, independently of the content taught.
An unexpected everyday object used as an example both captures attention and supplies another familiar association for the concept being taught.
Varying the response format across exercises helps maintain the stimulation level of a lesson.

Knowledge of results serves two functions at once: it promotes learning by confirming correct responses and correcting wrong ones, and it lets the achievement-motivated learner obtain a measure of success.
Never insert esteem-building attributional comments unless you know the learners have the ability to succeed — that is, that they will succeed if they exert effort in the lesson.
condition: only when learners who exert effort will in fact succeed

statement: State a caution positively rather than negatively — that a current success predicts future success because the required performance is the same — instead of warning that shortcuts will cause later failure.
Make goal-setting optional so it remains nonthreatening for learners who do not wish to exercise an achievement motive, while giving a salient feedback and scoring system to those who do.

An optional problem-solving task with high inherent interest lets intrinsically motivated learners use newly acquired knowledge, and their willingness to re-engage in similar activities is one of the best indicators of motivation.
A teacher can gauge a lesson's motivational level by informally polling students on their reaction to an optional exercise.

Immediately available answers reward successful responses and support the expectation that effort leads to success, but only if the items are moderately challenging and if learners who exert effort answer most of them correctly.
condition: only when items are moderately challenging and effort reliably yields correct answers

statement: When the answers are self-evident, the feedback is largely redundant and the motivational benefit is lost.
Restarting the motivation process from scratch at each lesson wastes design and learning time; a closing passage that ties the present lesson to the next provides a motivational bridge.
A how-to segment title both stimulates an information-seeking attitude and creates the prospect of a useful, relevant payoff.
Keep segment titles consistent with the lesson's promised scope, since a title that shifts scope makes the learner expect something other than what follows and erodes expectancy for success.
Keep terminology consistent across a lesson, replacing a synonym introduced later with the earlier term, because terms that confuse learners undermine motivation even in highly motivated students.
Give parallel objectives parallel length and phrasing, so none appears less important than the others.
Do not claim that effort leads to success unless the instructional materials have been validated; better still, cite an approximate measured figure from your own tests.
condition: only when the materials have been formatively validated

statement: Choose example objects that are concrete, familiar and let the learner verify the result from the diagram, because clear confirmation keeps learners from running aground on incidental impediments.
Avoid introducing an unexplained technical term in a caption or diagram when a plain word suffices, since the extra term adds confusion without serving the objective.
Motivational and learning strategies interact closely: the same edit that makes an example clearer also sustains the learner's expectancy for success.
Drawing an answer is an effective form of active responding that also provides variation in response mode.
Competition against a fixed criterion score during a learning exercise should be avoided when some learners would be discouraged rather than challenged by failing it the first time.
condition: when learners would be discouraged rather than challenged by an initial failure

statement: Telling learners explicitly that it is acceptable to get help bolsters confidence and keeps expectancy for success alive.
When most learners are already highly confident, leave attributional feedback out of the printed material and let the teacher present it selectively to the students who need it.
condition: when most learners are already confident of success

statement: Tying each lesson to the greater unit keeps learners in contact with the larger mission of their learning and supplies more payoff than merely finishing the lesson.

A designer's approach depends on the subject matter as well as on the theory being applied, so a reader must compare the subject matter, instructional objectives, processes and learning tasks of a demonstrated application against their own.
Each demonstrated application is only one of many ways the theory could be used with that subject matter; another designer, or the same designer at another time, might apply it differently.
Demonstrated lesson plans are tentative rather than final: they precede the customary formative evaluation and revision, so some of the needed modifications should be assumed still to come.
Instructional-design literature has four overlapping audiences — researchers, theorists, designers, and practitioners — each with different expectations of a theory.
Researchers and theorists care about the underlying rationale, the main variables, and how effects are measured, and treat implementation detail and contextual coverage as low-priority concerns.

Designers and practitioners want a sound basis for practice but care primarily about the practical roles and activities for instructors and students, and expect every major facet of their setting to be addressed whether or not the theory covers it.
Whether to rely on one theory or draw from several depends on the reader's purpose, and the answer differs for researchers and theorists as against designers and practitioners.

Researchers and theorists are more likely to obtain coherent results when their efforts are organized around one specified conceptual system, so focusing on a single theory is generally best for research and principle derivation.

Advising practitioners to rely exclusively on one preferred approach — even when that theory does not address all the important variables — has produced theories stretched to cover practical matters never within their scope.
Systematic eclecticism — selecting theories and techniques that fit particular practical situations — has been gaining support as an alternative to exclusive reliance on one approach.

Practitioners tend to use the approach they are familiar with rather than to consider carefully whether it fits the problem at hand — the trap of treating everything as a nail because one has only a hammer.
Practitioners are consistently far more eclectic than researchers and theorists in the same field, even where each new system has claimed superiority over its predecessors.
Guidance on which theory to select for which situation under what conditions is scarce, which is itself the gap that integrative movements exist to fill.
Novices may sensibly rely mainly on one theory because considering several at once can be overwhelming, while more experienced designers can comfortably derive ideas from several.

Selecting a theoretical model is in the last analysis a decision having no truth character: it involves personal and professional judgement, so appropriateness lies partly — but not entirely — in the eye of the beholder.

Clarify carefully what you expect a theory to provide, because education and training have tended to adopt allegedly good innovations without evaluating what they contribute to teaching and learning processes and outcomes.
Several prominent instructional innovations, including individually prescribed instruction, new math, computer-assisted instruction and programmed instruction, failed to persist in education.
Reforms most likely to persist are those that involve constituencies and that are easy to monitor while staying within cost constraints.

Theories have historically been chosen for reasons other than fit: the philosophical views associated with the theorist, ease of analysing locally relevant components, presumed compatibility with certain goals, and the instructor's preference for particular kinds of classroom activity.
Problems in selecting a theory more often come from considering too few features than too many, because most practical situations involve a wider range of variables than any single theory addresses.

Before selecting a theory, explore in depth the purpose and global goals of the instruction, its specific objectives, and the conditions under which it will be available; clarifying those gives the basis for recognizing which theories match the situation.

When some aspect of the practical situation is not addressed by any available theory, a researcher may simply delimit the inquiry and say so, but the designer and practitioner must decide how — not whether — that aspect will be handled.
A gap that no theory addresses is an opportunity for researchers to identify new variables to study and for practitioners to draw on prior experience to fill it.
When comparing theories, attend to their common characteristics as well as their unique features, because recognizing commonalities is what makes integrating ideas from different theories possible.
Note which aspects of instruction are central to a given theory and which are peripheral to it, since that tells you where the theory has important contributions to make.

Theories are usable as analytic instruments as well as design guides: they supply a systematic means of conceptualizing a practical situation and identifying the conditions and variables most pertinent to effective, efficient and enticing instruction.
Theories can reveal that quite different instructional problems share common features and possibly common solutions.

Similar practical approaches can be derived from several different theories even where the rationales differ, and the same theories can dictate quite different approaches in other cases — so practice does not map one-to-one onto theory.

A modern behavioral approach to instruction is broader than 1960s programmed instruction in both the topics it addresses and the resources it draws on, covering attention and conceptual understanding rather than overt behaviour alone.

A behavioral design is recognizable by objectives specified in measurable terms for each component and by instructional techniques and evaluation procedures tied to each objective, with emphasis on evaluation including learner self-evaluation.

Cognitively based instructional theories share the assumption that cognitive operations provide the necessary and sufficient conditions for appropriate behaviour to occur, which reverses the direction assumed by behavioral theories.

An inquiry-teaching approach supplies theory-based techniques for a dialogue between instructor and student, starting with the terminology needed before higher levels of understanding can be attained.

A structural approach analyses the structure of the subject matter to identify the rules students must learn and the rules that guide such learning; its technical sense of rule differs from the casual sense used elsewhere and must not be conflated.

An algo-heuristic approach emphasizes interaction with the subject matter over the subject matter itself, focusing on the procedural cognitive operations of learning and using knowledge rather than on the content's hierarchical structure.
Expert practice is taught as a combination of algorithms — dependable step-by-step procedures — and heuristics, the rules of thumb used where no set procedure applies.

A motivational model requires the designer and practitioner to continually take the student's perspective and ask why the student might be motivated to learn this content, whereas other theories consider how students interact with the subject matter.

A theory is eclectic in two senses: it addresses a wide range of issues about the subject matter rather than a narrow band of objectives, and it draws on diverse resources rather than deriving everything from one approach.
A micro theory that focuses on the details of presentation and a macro theory that addresses the broader design of a course should be treated as complementary rather than competing.
A component-classification theory is especially useful for ensuring consistency across the designation of objectives, the presentation of instruction, and the evaluation of outcomes.

Even a theory that specifies instructional events in considerable detail leaves many ways to implement its prescriptions: it supplies the context within which specific procedures are planned, not the procedures themselves.

A macro theory intentionally does not specify how the instruction is to be presented; it supplies a means of examining how instructional activities relate to each other and to plans reflecting the purposes of the instruction.
The sequence a macro theory produces depends on the subject matter: a different content area would yield a different organization from the same theory.
The subject matter addressed partly delimits and shapes how any theory's topics are handled, so a single demonstrated application does not exhaust what the theory can do.
Selecting an instructional theory is a decision closely parallel to selecting a therapeutic approach, and work on treatment-selection guidelines in that field is transferable to instructional design.

What distinguished instructional theory when it emerged at midcentury was the combination of systematically clarifying objectives, describing in detail the techniques and conditions that facilitate them, and using empirical methods to assess merit and plan revisions.
Progress in developing instructional theory has not been consistently positive: support and reception have fluctuated, and much of the work was done during periods when the enterprise was unpopular.
An educational innovation is likelier to persist when it has an identifiable support group and constituency and offers means for monitoring cost-effective application.
Producing technology-assisted instruction that is relevant, effective and within reasonable cost is much harder than most instructors and administrators realize.

Technology-assisted learning can leave audit trails of the steps taken and progress attained by individuals and groups, which conventional classroom instruction cannot, and those trails can guide improvement of both the instructional plans and the theories.

Instructional theory contributes to technology-assisted instruction by identifying both the characteristics needed to facilitate learning and the design-development steps required to produce the resources and systems.

Using computers does not make analysis and planning unnecessary: computer-based instruction requires at least as much careful planning as any other instructional resource, and someone must still decide on the instructional relevance of each use.
Instructional theory is one means of deciding why and how to use a given instructional resource, rather than adopting the resource and inferring its value afterwards.
No theory can address all aspects of a given instructional setting, so every theory must set priorities about which topics it will cover.
A theory's omissions are informative: what a treatment ignores or treats as peripheral, whether stated explicitly or shown by mere omission, tells you where it will not help.
Studying a set of worked theory applications should yield transferable procedures and decision rules for evaluating the potential value of other instructional theories encountered later.
Any collection of demonstrated theories is a representative sample rather than a comprehensive or exhaustive listing of what is available.
Many instructional-design efforts stop at clarifying objectives and evaluating student progress, leaving the design of techniques, procedures and resources to intuition.
A developed instructional theory goes beyond curriculum design and evaluation to make systematic, detailed provisions for planning, presenting and evaluating instruction.

Teacher-effectiveness studies conducted in classrooms and instructional-design projects conducted in training contexts have identified many of the same issues, problems and solutions, so instructional theory is not confined to military or industrial training.

Despite differences stemming from local situations, communication across instructional contexts — industry, higher education, early childhood, military — helps clarify issues and find means of improving instruction.
Researchers and theorists should treat every point where an application failed to address a relevant aspect as an opportunity to expand the range of variables their theories cover.
Designers and practitioners must never overlook the limitations of the theory they are using, however useful its guidelines.
Proceed with caution and evaluate relatively modest implementations of a plan before embarking on more ambitious applications.
Whether relying on one theory or several, exercise discretion in selecting which ideas to implement and in evaluating the results of doing so.
Instructional theories and the designer's work built on them are only as good as they prove to be in facilitating learning for actual students, whatever rationale guides them.

Pressure to improve instructional quality has brought instructional theory and design into discussions where they were previously absent, including textbook selection and the future of educational psychology.
